INCLYTIS ET GENEROSIS COMITIBUS, D. IOHANNI, & D. NICOLAO, COMITIBUS AB OSTROROG, Virtute & Stemmatis Illustribus, S. D.
units.tr: TO THE RENOWNED AND NOBLE COUNTS, LORD JOHN AND LORD NICHOLAS, COUNTS OF OSTRORÓG, ILLUSTRIOUS FOR THEIR VIRTUE AND THEIR LINEAGE: GREETINGS.

units.la: CUm in theatro urbis Attica olim recitarentur isti versus Aeschyli, de laudibus Amphiarai: Οὐ γὰρ δοκεῖν ἄρι-στος[?], ἀλλ' εἶναι θέλει, βαθεῖαν ἄλοκα διὰ φρενὸς καρπιμένος[?], ἀφ' ἧς τὰ κεδνὰ βλαστάει[?] βυλεύματα[?]: Spectatores quotquot aderant, oculos coniecerunt in Aristidem, cognomento Iustum: quem noverant nequaquam simulare amore studiumq; honesti, iusti & boni: sed ipsis factis declarare, totaq; vita testari.
units.tr: When those verses of Aeschylus in praise of Amphiaraus were once recited in the theatre of the Attic city, "For he wishes not to seem best, but to be so, from a deep furrow of the mind, from which his sound counsels spring," all the spectators who were present turned their eyes upon Aristides, surnamed the Just. They knew that he did not feign love of study and of what is honourable, just and good, but showed it by his very deeds and bore witness to it through his whole life.

units.la: Existimo sanè, Generosi & Inclyti Do-mini mini Comites, idem plane & vobis, & aliis illustris vestri ordinis hominibus, nunquam non evenire. Quo enim flemmatis & generis nobilissimi splendore, Maiorum virtutibus, & gloria rerum praeclarè bello paceq; ab ipsis gestarum, & dotibus corporis, multisq; aliis praesidiis, Deus vos praemultis aliis excellere voluit: tantò magis o-culis iudiciisq; multorum hominum expo-siti, spem praeclaram fovetis, pietatis erga Deum aeternum, iudice universorum, & eius uberrimorum fructuum, qui ad Ecclesiam & Rempub. Deo benedicente vestris studiis & consiliis, redituri sunt. Quanto enim maiores habentur ij, qui in familiis Heroi-cis nati sunt: tantò eorum virtutes sunt cō-spectiores, cum in generis humani theatro praecipuo versentur loco, & omnium spectatorum non oculis solum, sed etiam iudiciis sint expositi.
units.tr: I am sure, noble and renowned Lords, Counts, that the same thing happens, without fail, to you and to other men of your illustrious order. For God has willed that you excel many others in the splendour of your noble race, in the virtues of your ancestors, in the glory of the deeds they performed in war and peace, in the gifts of body and in many other advantages. The more exposed you are to the eyes and judgments of many people, the more you foster a brilliant hope of piety towards the eternal God, the judge of all, and of those most abundant fruits which, by God's blessing, are to come to the Church and the Commonwealth from your efforts and counsels. For the more those are esteemed who are born into heroic families, the more conspicuous their virtues are, since they stand in the chief place in the theatre of mankind and are exposed not only to the eyes but also to the judgments of all spectators.

units.la: Erit autem eximia vestra virtutis humanitatisq; optimam in partem accipere, quòd ea quae mihi, posteaquam vos & nos-se, & egregias animi corporisq; dotes in u-troq; vestrum admirari coepi, de vobis, Illustres Domini Comites, saepenumero cogitanti, in mentem venire solent, hoc tempore publice exponenda censui. Quod enim mihi propemodum fatale esse videam, a flore Nobilitatis & ingeniosa Iuventutis, huc ad nos accedente, officijs humanitatis exhilarari: mei muneris esse reor, non solum amabilem suavissimorum colloquiorum & beneficiorum usumfructum (quem ad mitigandos leniendosq; dolores meos, quos multis jam annis sustinui, non parum esse efficacem, reipsa expertus sum) magnifa-cere: sed etiam Reipub. gratulari messem copiosam vera Nobilitatis: cui hoc studio est, cum externis illis praesidijs & ornamē-tis veras animi dotes, Timorem Dei, Veritatem, Iusticiam, Temperantiam, Fortitudi-nem, Modestiam, & alias eximias virtutes, prudenter & constanter adiungere. Donec enim iuvenes eiusmodi ingenys & donis praestantes, divinitus excitari, & in theatrum Reipub. Christiana a Deo Opt. Max. produci videro: Catone nostri seculi contentus, bene sperabo de Repub. ut qui non sine propicia Dei providetia hac exi-mia mia dñna & præsidia cuiquam uestrûm cõ ferri,persuasum habeam:eaq; non uobis so lum, sed generis humani societati, ex toto corde meo gratuler.
units.tr: It will be a mark of your outstanding virtue and courtesy to take in the best part what has come into my mind, Illustrious Counts, when I have often thought about you since I began to know you both and to admire your distinguished gifts of mind and body. I have judged that it should now be set out publicly. For I consider it my duty, since I see that it is almost my destiny to be cheered by the courtesies of the flower of nobility and of talented youth who come to us here, to value not only the pleasant enjoyment of delightful conversations and kindnesses (which I have myself found, in fact, to be no small help in easing and soothing the pains I have endured for many years now), but also to congratulate the Commonwealth on the abundant harvest of true nobility. Those who pursue this aim add to those outward supports and ornaments the true gifts of the mind: the fear of God, truth, justice, temperance, fortitude, modesty and other outstanding virtues, joined prudently and steadily. For until I see young men of such talents and gifts raised up by God and brought forth by the Best and Greatest God into the Christian theatre of the Commonwealth, I shall be content with Cato of our age, and I shall hope well for the Commonwealth. I am persuaded that these outstanding gifts and endowments have been conferred on each of you, not without the favourable providence of God, and I congratulate them with all my heart, not only on your behalf but on behalf of human society.

units.la: Verumenimuero, ut ad uos ueniam, si magna est eorû Germania nostra Rerum-pub. & Principum laus, qui initio renascentis Euangelij,non sine magno suo labo-re & periculo aperuerunt portas Iehoua exercituum, ac non ipsi solùm sunt amplexi incorruptam & salutarẽ Euangelij doctrinam, sed etiam subditos suos ad eiusdẽ studium inuitârunt: magna sanè laus est etiam laudatissimorum uestrorum Maio-rum,quos omnium primos, abiecta Ponti-ficiorum τὴν ἑτεροδοξαν καὶ ματαιο-λογίαν & tetra idolomania, Euangelion Christi amplexos fuisse, ac ueritatis uexil-lum in fortissima Polonorum gente (quæ professo populos Scythicos longo iam tem-pore repressit, & nunc uictricib.armis im-manè Moscorum rabiem contundit)erexis-se: ac uirtute in fide, ueramq; perseueran-tiam & constantiâ in religiosissimo hoc in-stituto,haftenus probatisse,uidemus. Det Dominus ille dominatium & Regum Rex, pro immensa sua bonitate, ut hoc opus bo-num, quod ad suā gloriam, & Ecclesiæ in-staurationem, ac Reipub. utilitatem, in in-clytis uestris maioribus cœpit, in uobis con-tinuet, ac in posteritate uestra perficiat: ne unquam fraude & dolis Satanæ & eius satellitum sacrum & salutare hoc institutū interrumpatur.
units.tr: But, to come to you: if our Germany's commonwealths and princes deserve great praise, those who at the beginning of the renewed Gospel, not without great labour and danger of their own, opened the gates to the Lord of hosts, and who embraced not only the uncorrupted and saving doctrine of the Gospel but also invited their subjects to take up its study, then indeed great praise is due also to your most praiseworthy ancestors. We see that they were the first of all to cast off the other-teaching and vain-speaking of the Papists and their foul idolatry, to embrace the Gospel of Christ, and to raise the banner of truth among the most valiant Polish nation, which for a long time has held down the Scythian peoples and now with victorious arms crushes the monstrous rage of the Muscovites. We see that they have proved their courage in the faith and their true perseverance and constancy in this most religious institution up to the present. May that Lord of lords and King of kings, in his immense goodness, grant that the good work which your illustrious ancestors began, for his glory, for the restoration of the Church and for the good of the Commonwealth, he may continue in you and bring to completion in your posterity, so that this holy and salutary institution may never be interrupted by the fraud and deceits of Satan and his minions.

units.la: Credo autem magno uobis usui fore, si accurate perpendatis, quorū exemplis De-us, pietatis & uirtutum heroicarum, eru-ditaq; doctrinæ studium, uobis magnopere commendet. Habetis sane ξυμπαραςάτας [?] multos, illustres, & laude maxima dignos: inter quos, ut de cæteris iam nihil dicam, mihi nunquam non cordi est illustris Do-minus Carolus, Baro à Zerotin, qui dum nobiscum Basileæ uixit, non minorem sui amorem & desiderium in animis optimorum doctissimorumq; uirorū, quam spem maximam præclaræ Σερ-γείας [?] in Ecclesi-am & Rempub. excitauit. Intelligit enim, ἀ πρὸς ὕβριν [?], ἀλλὰ πρὸς Σεργείαν [?], diuinitus conferri nobilitatis ἀξιώματα [?], eoq; no-mine mine religiosè illo utedum,ad Deigloriam, & subiectorum emendationem & incolumitatem. Deus Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi,& ipsum & uos perpetuo sanctifi-cet per ueritatem suam: nec unquam uersutia Satanæ circumueniri,aut a laudabi-li uera tum pietatis, tum uirtutis studio abduci,patiatur.
units.tr: I believe, however, that it will be of great use to you if you weigh carefully the examples by which God greatly commends to you the study of piety, of heroic virtues and of learned doctrine. You indeed have many companions, illustrious and worthy of the highest praise. Among them, to say nothing now of the rest, Lord Charles, Baron of Žerotín, is always dear to my heart. While he lived with us at Basel, he aroused in the minds of the best and most learned men no less love and longing for himself than the greatest hope of an excellent seriousness for the Church and the Commonwealth. For he understands that the dignities of nobility are conferred by God not for arrogance but for seriousness, and he uses that name in a religious way, for the glory of God, and for the correction and safety of his subjects. May God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ sanctify both him and you for ever through his truth, and never allow you to be circumvented by the cunning of Satan or drawn away from the praiseworthy pursuit of true piety and virtue.

units.la: Mirifice delector Anacharsis Philosophi Epistola ad Lydorum Rege Croesum, in qua, cur Aulica uita,ad quà humanissimè inuitabatur, Academicum puluere sibi præferre dum iudicârit,rationes his uerbis exponit: Ego, Lydorum Rex, in Graciam profectus sum, Graecorum mores, studia atq; instituta percepturus. Auro autem non egeo:satisq; mihi est, si ad meos Scythas redeam MELIOR & DOCTIOR. Veniam tamen ad te Sardis, plurimi faciens tibi familiarem & amicum fieri.
units.tr: I am greatly delighted by the letter of the philosopher Anacharsis to Croesus, king of the Lydians, in which he sets out, in these words, his reasons for preferring the academic dust to the courtly life to which he was most courteously invited: "I, king of the Lydians, have gone to Greece, to learn the customs, studies and institutions of the Greeks. I have no need of gold, and it is enough for me if I return to my Scythians BETTER AND MORE LEARNED. Yet I shall come to you at Sardis, very keen to become your familiar friend and companion."

units.la: Si homo Ethnicus,nõ solum ut DOCTI-OR.sed etiâ ut MELIOR fieret,sibi & peregrinandū in Gracia,& summo studio elaborandū censuit: quàto magis nos omnes, qui in Christū Iesum nos credere ꝓfitemur, totis viribus eò eniti decet, ut indies nobis ipsis meliores & doctiores evadamus? Ut autem in studio boni, sinceritatem καὶ ἐπιγνώσεως[?] sic in doctrina veritatem, in utriusque exercitio & professione constantiam & perseverantiam, Deo hominibusq; pro-bemus. Dici autem non potest, quantopere ad religiosum hoc institutum & incoandum & prosequendum faciant, ordinis viri[?] hominum egregia exempla. Etenim vel unus vir Heroicus totam illustrat gentem, ut Demosthenes olim dixit. ac verum est illud Ciceronis: Omnes boni semper Nobilitati favemus: & quia Reipub. utile est nobiles esse homines, dignos maioribus suis: & quia valere debet apud nos senex clarorum hominum de Repub. meritorum memoria, etiam mortuorum. Vestrum itaq; fuerit, fidei erga Christum, caritatis erga proximos, perseverantia in vera pietatis professione & exercitio, & multarum pulcerrimarum virtutum lampadem, & ijs quos nobis regendos commisit Deus, & multis aliis praeferre.
units.tr: If a heathen man thought it right to travel in Greece and to labour with the greatest zeal, not only to become more learned but also to become better, how much more should all of us who profess that we believe in Christ Jesus strive with all our strength to become daily better and more learned than we were? We must prove to God and men our sincerity in study and our truth in doctrine, and our constancy and perseverance in the exercise and profession of both. It cannot be said how greatly the outstanding examples of men of rank help both to begin and to pursue this religious institution. For indeed one heroic man alone brightens a whole nation, as Demosthenes once said, and that saying of Cicero is true: "We good men always favour nobility, both because it is useful to the Commonwealth that men be noble and worthy of their ancestors, and because the memory of those who have deserved well of the Commonwealth, even when dead, ought to have weight among us." It will therefore be your task to set before those whom God has committed to your rule, and before many others, the lamp of faith in Christ, of love towards neighbours, of perseverance in the true profession and practice of piety, and of many most beautiful virtues.

units.la: Cedrenus in suis Annalibus auctor est,
units.tr: Cedrenus, in his Annals, is the authority for the following.

units.la: Placillam Augustam marito suo Theodo-sio, Imperatori laudatissimo, identidem inculcasse sententiam hanc: Ἀεί σε, ὦ ἄνερ, ὡς [?]ὀφείλει λογίζεσθαι, τῆς μὲν ἡδονῆς, τῆς δὲ [?]γένους [?]γυνῶ[?]. κυβέρνησον ἐν τῷ βασιλείῳ πώτῳ εὐνόμως, καὶ ὅταν [?]Ἱεραπτόλης [?]τὸν δεδωκότα.
units.tr: Placilla Augusta repeatedly impressed on her husband, the most praiseworthy emperor Theodosius, this maxim: "Always, O man, you ought to reckon what you owe to the one who gave you your office, and to your own origin. Govern the empire in the palace lawfully, and you will honour him who gave it." [Ἀεί σε, ὦ ἄνερ, ὡς ὀφείλει λογίζεσθαι, τῆς μὲν ἡδονῆς, τῆς δὲ γένους γυνῶ. κυβέρνησον ἐν τῷ βασιλείῳ πρῶτον εὐνόμως, καὶ ὅταν ... τὸν δεδωκότα.]

units.la: Semper te, mi nir, reputare conuenit, Quis fueris, & Quis factus sis. Guberna ergo Imperium hoc legitime: sic honorabis eum qui dedit. Neque vero iis solum, qui, Theo-dosij exemplo, ex humili loco evecti sunt in summum dignitatis humanae & civilis fastigium: sed etiam iis, qui illustribus Pa-rentibus nati, non multo post ad Rempub. gubernandam accessuri sunt: & omnibus in universum piis, de origine sua & de donorum incrementis cogitandum, & ut Paulus Apostolus loquitur, pie, iuste & sobrie vivendum est.
units.tr: Always, my husband, it is fitting that you consider who you were and who you have been made. Govern this empire lawfully: so you will honour him who gave it. And this applies not only to those who, like Theodosius, have been raised from a humble place to the highest summit of human and civil dignity, but also to those who, born of illustrious parents, are soon to come to the government of the Commonwealth, and to all pious people in general: we must think about our origin and about the increase of our gifts, and, as the Apostle Paul says, live soberly, righteously and godly.

units.la: Cogitemus itaq; diligenter, Qui fuerimus, Qui sumus, & Qui futuri sumus: eoq; nomine ad severiores calculos revocemus cōsilia, cogitationes, dicta & facta nostra: nec unquam nobis blandiamur. Non enim nos fugit, Deum esse universorum [?]ἐπόπτην & iudi iudicem, eiusq; iudicium ineuitabile & in stissimū esse. Videmus quàm multi, hoc exulceratissimo rerum humanarum statu, dū φιλήδονοι esse malunt quàm φιλόθεοι, seipsos eant perditum. Nos contrà studeamus esse φιλόθεοι: nec amplius cupiditatibus hominum, sed uoluntati Dei, quod reliquum est temporis in carne uiuamus: ut monet iubetq; Spiritus sanctus, 1. Pet. 4. 2.
units.tr: Let us therefore consider carefully who we have been, who we are, and who we are going to be, and on that account let us bring our plans, thoughts, words and deeds before a stricter reckoning, and never flatter ourselves. For it does not escape us that God is the overseer [ἐπόπτης] and judge of all, and that his judgment is inescapable and most severe. We see how many, in this most ulcerated condition of human affairs, prefer to be lovers of pleasure [φιλήδονοι] rather than lovers of God [φιλόθεοι], and so ruin themselves. Let us instead strive to be lovers of God, and no longer live the rest of our time in the flesh according to the desires of men, but according to the will of God, as the Holy Spirit admonishes and commands, 1 Pet. 4:2.

units.la: Celebratur à Dione Seuerus Imperator, quòd fuerit [?]ἀτιμελὴς τῶν τραχέων, καὶ ἀ-μελὴς τῶν περὶ αὐτὰ λογομαχιῶν. Si laus di ducitur uiro Principi, diligentia in omni officio, & contemtus fabellarum, quæ ab imperita multitudine etiā de optimis Principibus spargi & circumferri solent: multò magis laudi uertendum erit omnium ordinum hominibus, pietatis, uirtutum & erudita doctrina studium. Huius uero studiï (quod à Paulo Apostolo, Dei nomine requiritur illustri hac sententia: τῇ σπουδῇ μὴ ὀκνηροὶ, Studio minimè pigri: Rom. 12. 11.) si Principes, si Comites, si tota Nobilitas ἐργο-διδάσκης sit, & exemplo suo præeat inferioribus, nihil sanè dubium est, magna ex parte hos quoq̃ promtè & libêter secuturos, meliusq̃ res humanas esse habituras. Noti sunt elegantes hi uersus Claudiani, de institutione Principis: Tu ciuem patremq̃ geras, tu consule cunctis. In commune iubes si quid, censesq̃ tenendum, Primus iussa subi: tunc obseruantior æqui Fit populus, nec ferre uetat, cum uiderit ipsum Auctorem parere sibi. componitur orbis Regis ad exemplum: nec sic inflectere sensus Humanos edicta ualent, quàm uita regentis. Mobile mutatur semper cum Principe uulgus.
units.tr: Dio records of the Emperor Severus that he was indifferent to harsh matters [ἀτιμελὴς τῶν τραχέων] and careless of the verbal disputes that surrounded them [ἀμελὴς τῶν περὶ αὐτὰ λογομαχιῶν]. If praise is given to a prince for diligence in every duty, and for scorning the idle tales that the uneducated crowd is accustomed to spread and pass around even about the best princes, then far more praise ought to be given by people of every rank to zeal for piety, virtue and sound learning. If princes, counts and the whole nobility were teachers of this zeal (which the Apostle Paul demands in God's name with that famous saying, "not slothful in business" [τῇ σπουδῇ μὴ ὀκνηροί], Rom. 12:11), and went before their inferiors by example, there is no doubt that to a great extent these too would follow promptly and willingly, and that human affairs would be in a better state. Those elegant verses of Claudian on the instruction of a prince are well known: "Be the citizen and father of your people; take thought for all. If you command anything for the common good and judge it to be kept, be the first to submit to your own orders. Then the people will become more observant of what is just, and will not refuse to obey when they see the author himself obeying. The world is shaped after the example of its king; and edicts cannot bend men's minds as much as the life of the ruler does. The fickle crowd always changes with the prince."

units.la: Idem Historicus laudans Antoninum Philosophum Imperatorem, hac de eo memoria mandauit: Ὅτι μὲν ἐκ πάντων ... bi demandatam constanter tueretur: dum sibi ab Antichristianis fucum fieri patitur, & frustra captat terrenum quoddam regnum, non solum miserè interiisse: sed etiam nimia indulgentia sua constabilita γυναικοκρατεία, immo tyrannide plusquam Neroniana, Regno pulcerrimo & posteris magnarum calamitatum fuisse auctorem.
units.tr: The same historian, praising the emperor Antoninus the philosopher, left this memorial of him: "That from all ..." [Ὅτι μὲν ἐκ πάντων ...] ... he steadfastly guarded the charge entrusted to him; but while he allowed himself to be deceived by the Antichristians and vainly sought a certain earthly kingdom, he not only perished miserably, but also, through his excessive indulgence, established the rule of women, or rather a tyranny more than Neronian, and became the author of great calamities for a most splendid kingdom and for posterity.

units.la: Cum familiares quidam Vespasianum Augustum, podagra laborantem, à labore cognoscendi controversas causas dehortarentur, & Principi valetudinis rationem habendam dicerent: heroicè profectò respondit: Imperatorem stantem mori oportet. Utinam hoc persuasum habeant omnes Gubernatores Regnorum & Rerumpub. aliarum, sic ut per omnem vitam cōsilio Dei servire, stantes, vigilantes & morientes, parati sint: nec se adversorum casuum μοχθο[?] [illegible, ~9 letters]λογίας abste-rreri à laudabili proposito: nec etiam rerum secundarum illecebris, adulatorum [?] vanis spebus[?], (quibus potissimum nugis Idololatræ & Antichristiani heroicis & generosis Iuve-nibus, de quibus multis de causis præcipua spes est, imponere conantur) laborum & periculorum, quae pietatis studium & Reipub.gubernationem comitari solent, declinandi & defugiendi vana persuasione, abduci patiantur. Vtinam in verae Religionis agnitione & professione ac propagatione, & in civili sua statione, ad extremum usque spiritum fortiter perseverantes, retineant propositum pietatis, constantiae, gravitatis, & aliarum pulcerrimarum virtutum.
units.tr: When some friends urged the Emperor Vespasian, who was suffering from gout, to abstain from the labour of hearing disputed cases, and told him that he must have regard to his health, he answered most heroically: "An emperor ought to die standing." Would that all governors of kingdoms and of other commonwealths were persuaded of this, so as to be ready to serve the counsel of God throughout their whole life, standing, watchful and dying; and that they would not be turned aside from their praiseworthy purpose by the adversities of fortune, nor allow themselves to be led away by the vain persuasion of avoiding and shunning the toils and dangers that usually accompany the pursuit of piety and the governance of the commonwealth. Such vain persuasion the idolaters and Antichristians try to impose, with their flatteries and empty hopes, on heroic and noble young men, concerning whom there are many reasons for especially great hope, and by the enticements of prosperity. Would that they, persevering bravely to the last breath in the knowledge, profession and propagation of the true religion, and in their civil station, keep their purpose of piety, constancy, gravity and the other most excellent virtues.

units.la: Sed de his & aliis ordinis vestri hominum ornamentis καὶ σωφρονισμοῖς, paucis καὶ ἀμαθέστερον [?] agere placuit, ut videretis me συμφωνεῖν viro virtute & doctrina praestanti, D. Ioanni Iona, Morauo, quae propitia Dei providentia, vitae & studiorum vestrorum gubernatorem fidum & cordatum esse voluit: qui etiam institutionis fidelis fructus coepit percipere, cum videat doctrinam virtutesque vestras eximias, quarum ille ἐργοδιώκτης [?] fuit, non minus quam vestri generis & stemmatu decora, viris intelligentib. et bonis mirifice probari, spemque ut maximam, sic indubitatam facere fructuum, qui ad inclyti Regni Polonici Rempub.& ad Ecclesiam non multo post reditu ri sunt. Hunc insignem virum non minoris uobis (qui quid inter Philosophiam & Theologiam interfit, recte intelligitis) faciendum iudicabitis, quam Philippus Macedonum Rex Aristotelem, Peripateticorum philosophorum facile principem, olim fecit. Ei enim cum Alexandrum quasi in manus traderet, filio dixisse fertur: Philosophiae operam dato: ne multa committas, quae me fecisse nunc paenitet. ἐκέλευε αὐτὸν Ἀριστοτέλει προσέχειν καὶ φιλοσοφεῖν, Ὅπως, ἔφη, μὴ πολλὰ τοιαῦτα πράξῃς, ἐφ' οἷς ἐγὼ πεπραγμένοις μεταμέλομαι. Si magni nobis faciendi sunt verae philosophiae doctores: multo certe maioris nobis sunt faciendi caelestis sapientiae fideles promi & condi, qui, cum sint Θεοῦ συνεργοί, inspergunt tenueris mentibus pietatis semina, & ea herbescentia fideliter colunt, lolio pravarum opinionum & epicureismi exstirpato, ut matu rescere possint, & suo tempore uberrimos fructus ferant.
units.tr: But I have thought fit to speak briefly about these and other ornaments and admonitions of your order of men, and [to show] that I agree with the man distinguished for virtue and learning, Master John Iona of Moravia, whom by God's gracious providence you have wished to be the faithful and wise guide of your life and studies. He has also begun to reap the faithful fruit of his instruction, since he sees that your outstanding learning and virtues, of which he was the spur, are no less admired by intelligent and good men than the distinction of your family and lineage, and he makes the highest and undoubted promise of fruits which will soon return to the Commonwealth of the renowned Kingdom of Poland and to the Church. You, who understand rightly what lies between philosophy and theology, will judge this distinguished man to be no less worth your esteem than Philip, King of the Macedonians, once esteemed Aristotle, the easy prince of the Peripatetic philosophers. For when he was handing Alexander over to him, as it were into his hands, he is said to have said to his son: "Apply yourself to philosophy, so that you do not commit many such things as I now regret having done." He ordered him to attend to Aristotle and to philosophize [ἐκέλευε αὐτὸν Ἀριστοτέλει προσέχειν καὶ φιλοσοφεῖν], "so that," he said, "you may not do many such things [μὴ πολλὰ τοιαῦτα πράξῃς] for which I now regret what I have done [ἐφ' οἷς ἐγὼ πεπραγμένοις μεταμέλομαι]." If we must hold the teachers of true philosophy in high regard, we must surely hold in far higher regard the faithful dispensers and storers of heavenly wisdom, who, being fellow-workers of God [Θεοῦ συνεργοί], sow the seeds of piety in tender minds and faithfully tend them as they sprout, with the darnel of wicked opinions and Epicureanism rooted out, so that they can ripen and bear the most abundant fruit in due time.

units.la: Verum enimuero, ut quibus rationibus ad pietatem & resipiscentiam Auditores meos, quorum uirtus, φιλομαθία καὶ φιλαληθία[?] mihi magno est solatio, hortari consueuerim, uideretis: & ut exstaret publicum aliquod testimonium meae erga uos, & inclytam familiam Comitum ab Ostro-rog, obseruantiae ac studij: laudatissimo uestro nomini, Generosi Domini Comites, Praelectionum mearum in IONAM, poe-nitentiae praeconem, κεφάλαια[?], mediocri diligentia collecta & edita, nominatim in-scribere uisum est. Id officium, si pro excel-lete uestra uirtute & humanitate, optimā in partem acceperitis: exoptatū laboris mei fructum ad me reddisse iudicabo. Quodsu-perest, precor toto pectore Filium Dei, Do-minum nostrum Iesum Christum, ut uobis, Inclyti Domini Comites, ubertim bene-dicat, & uos ab omni malo clementer custo-diat, ad gloriam suam, & uestram ac sub-ditorum incolumitatem. Amen.
units.tr: But in truth, so that you may see by what reasons I have been accustomed to exhort my hearers to piety and repentance, whose virtue, love of learning and love of truth [φιλομαθία καὶ φιλαληθία] are a great comfort to me, and so that there may stand some public testimony of my respect and devotion towards you and the illustrious family of the Counts of Ostrorog, I have thought fit to inscribe by name to your most praiseworthy name, Noble Lord Counts, my Lectures on Jonah, the herald of repentance, with the headings [κεφάλαια] collected and published with moderate care. If you receive this service in the best part, according to your outstanding virtue and courtesy, I shall judge that the longed-for fruit of my labour has come back to me. For the rest, I pray with my whole heart that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, may richly bless you, Renowned Lord Counts, and graciously keep you from all evil, to his glory and to your and your subjects' welfare. Amen.

units.tr: PREFACE TO THE LITTLE BOOK OF THE PROPHET JONAH.

units.la: VM omnia quęcũq; agimus sermone aut facto,in nomine Iesu faciēda, & gratiæ agendę nobis sint Deo & Patri per eũ,Col.3.17. primùm quidem ago gratias quas possum maximas, æterno Patri Domini nostri Iesu Christi,quòd annis iam aliquot dedit, ut in hac Academia incorrupta vox cœlestis doctrinæ sonaret,nec traditos in reprobā mentē passus est in tetros & Epicureos su tores & errores incidere:deinde eundem toto pectore oro,ut sancti Spiritus sui unctione, nos de omnibus ad salutē nostrā scitu necessarijs erudire dignetur, ut per nos nomē illius sanctificetur,& sic luceat lux nostra,ut alij videat nostra bona opera, ac Patrem cœlestē glorificent.Amen.
units.tr: Whatever we do or say, all of it is to be done in the name of Jesus, and thanks are to be given to God the Father through him (Col. 3.17). First of all I give the greatest thanks I can to the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who for some years now has allowed the uncorrupted voice of heavenly doctrine to sound in this Academy, and has not suffered those given over to a reprobate mind to fall into the foul errors and slanders of the Epicureans. Then I pray with my whole heart that by the anointing of his Holy Spirit he may deign to teach us all things necessary for our salvation, so that through us his name may be sanctified, our light may so shine that others may see our good works, and they may glorify the heavenly Father. Amen.

units.la: Antequam verò, carissimi fratres & ornatissimi auditores, ad Ionæ Prophetæ, cuius libellum enarrare constitui, προσωπο-γραφίαν accedam, ut in meo & vestris cordibus ardens studium legendi & expendendi Oracula Prophetarum accen-datur, recitabo præclara quædá Spiritus sancti apophthegmata, quæ in Nouo Testamento & Patrum quorundam orthodoxorum libris, uelut radiantes quędam stellæ, emicant: & Prophetarum τῷ ἀξιώ-ματί fidem nostram fulciunt & confirmat.
units.tr: But before I come, dearest brothers and most distinguished hearers, to the prosopography of the Prophet Jonah, whose little book I have decided to expound, I will recite some excellent sayings of the Holy Spirit, so that an ardent zeal for reading and weighing the oracles of the Prophets may be kindled in my heart and yours. These sayings shine forth in the New Testament and in the books of certain orthodox Fathers like radiant stars, and they support and confirm our faith by their authority [τῷ ἀξιώματι].

units.la: Act.10.43. Huic Iesu Christo omnes Prophetæ testimonium ferunt, quòd remissionem peccatorū accepturus sit per nomen eius, omnis qui crediderit in e-um. Ex hoc dicto κεφαλαιωδῶς colligimus, 1. Suauissimam esse Veteris & Noui Testamenti ministrorum συμφωνίαν. 2. Cum utriq; Christo testimonium perhibeant, quòd sit Saluator mundi. 3. Ac doceat, nullo alio quàm fidei instrumento Christum à nobis apprehendi ad salutem nostram. Certò itaq; nobis persuasum esse debet, in Ionæ prophetæ historia & cōcionibus nihil esse magis spectandum, quàm μαρτύριον περὶ τῆς χάριτος, quod studiosi & religiosi iuuenes nō tantùm in signo Ionæ, sed etiā in exèplo pœnitetiæ Ninivitarum, & remissionis peccatorū, quæ illis fide in Mesfia benedictū ad iusticiā imputata, concessa fuit, spectare debent.
units.tr: Acts 10.43. To this Jesus Christ all the Prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him will receive forgiveness of sins through his name. From this saying we gather, in summary: (1) that the agreement of the ministers of the Old and New Testaments is most sweet; (2) that since both bear witness to Christ, he is the Saviour of the world; (3) and that it teaches that Christ is apprehended by us for our salvation by no instrument other than faith. Surely we ought to be persuaded that in the history and preaching of the prophet Jonah nothing is to be looked at more than the testimony concerning grace [μαρτύριον περὶ τῆς χάριτος]. Studious and religious young people should look to this not only in the sign of Jonah, but also in the example of the repentance of the Ninevites and the remission of sins which was granted to them, imputed to them for righteousness, through faith in the blessed Messiah.

units.la: 2. Pet.i.19.20.21. Habemus firmissimū sermonem propheticum: cui recte facitis quòd attendatis, uelut lucernæ splenden ti in obscuro loco, ufq; dum dies illuce-scat, & lucifer exoriatur in cordibus ue-stris: si illud primum noueritis, quòd nul la Prophetia Scripturæ, sit proprij impul-sus, τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως [?]. Non enim uoluntate hominis allata est olim Prophetia, sed acti à Spiritu sancto locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Vt nihil aliud de hoc dicto dicam, erit uestræ pietatis, precari, ut quo acti Spiritu, locuti sunt Prophetæ, eodem nos quoq; ducamur, & in eorum interpretatione uersemur.
units.tr: 2 Pet. 1.19-21. We have a most sure prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. Know this first: no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation [ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως]. For prophecy was never brought forth by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. To say nothing more about this saying, it will be the task of your piety to pray that we too may be led by the same Spirit by which the Prophets spoke, and that we may be engaged in their interpretation.

units.la: Cæterum quæ'nam & quanta sit Prophetarum auctoritas, & qua religione in eorum monumentis, Spiritus sancti Commentariis de fide, caritate & spe, uersandum nobis sit, diuus Chrysost. Homilia 2. in caput 6. Iesaiae, hisce uerbis mihi uidetur exposuisse: Prophetarum ora, Dei sunt os. Tale uero os nihil dixerit obiter extraq; rem. Ne igitur nos obiter & aliud agentes audiamus. Addit idem Chrysostomus elegas simile. Etenim si hi qui fodiunt metalla, ne minima quidè frustula praetereunt, verum ubi nacti fuerint aliquam venam auri,meatus omnes exacte circūspiciūt: multò magis nos hoc facere oportet in Scripturis. Et tamen in metallis difficile est invenire quod venantur. Etenim cum & metalla sint terra, & aurū nihil aliud fit quàm terra, ipsa quoq; naturæ communio similitudoq; celat aspectum eorum quæ quæruntur. Attamen ne sic quidem desistunt illi, sed omnem adhibent diligentiam, etiamsi posteaquā inspexerint sciat, quid verè fit terra, quid verè fit aurum. In Scripturis autè non est eadem ratio. Neq; enim proponitur aurū terræ commistum, sed purum est aurum. Eloquia, inquit, Dei pura, argentum igni exploratum, probatum terræ. Siquidem Scripturæ non sunt metalla quæ indigeant operarijs, sed thesaurum præbent paratum ijs qui quærunt opes in ipsis recōditas. Satis est enim introspexisse, ut omni expleti fructu, discedatis: satis est tantùm aperuisse, ut ilicò videas gemmarū splendorem.
units.tr: Moreover, what and how great the authority of the Prophets is, and with what reverence we must handle their writings, the Spirit's own commentaries on faith, love and hope, the divine Chrysostom seems to me to have set out in these words, in his second homily on Isaiah 6: The mouths of the prophets are the mouth of God. Such a mouth would say nothing in passing and beside the point. Let us not, then, listen to them carelessly and while we are doing something else. The same Chrysostom adds a similar comparison. For if those who dig for metals do not pass over even the smallest crumbs, but when they have found some vein of gold they carefully examine every passage, much more ought we to do this in the Scriptures. And yet in metals it is hard to find what they hunt for. For since metals are earth, and gold is nothing but earth, the very commonness and likeness of nature hides the appearance of what is sought. Yet even so they do not give up, but apply every diligence, even after they have learned what is truly earth and what is truly gold. In the Scriptures, however, the case is not the same. For gold is not presented mixed with earth, but the gold is pure. "The words of the Lord," it says, "are pure, silver tried in the fire, proved in the earth." For the Scriptures are not metals that need workers; they offer a treasure ready to hand to those who seek the riches hidden in them. It is enough to have looked into them, so that you depart full of every fruit; it is enough merely to have opened them, so that you may at once see the splendour of the gems.

units.la: Gregorij nobile dictum est: In Prophetis verbis res, & verba rebus exponūtur. Hom.2.in Cantica.
units.tr: A noble saying of Gregory: In the Prophets, words are explained by things, and things by words. Hom. 2 on the Canticles.

units.la: Augustinus de Consensu Euang.lib.3. Prophetae omnes uno prophetarunt Spi-ritu. Idem de Ciuitate Dei lib.18.Prophe-tica auctoritas omnibus caeteris Scriptis antiquior est.
units.tr: Augustine, On the Harmony of the Evangelists, book 3: All the Prophets prophesied by one Spirit. The same, On the City of God, book 18: The prophetic authority is older than all other writings.

units.la: His sententijs in praesentia contenti accedamus ad Ionae Profopographia, in qua haec decem capita breuiter tractabimus: Aetatem qua uixit & docuit, Nomen, Parentem, Patriam, Gentem, Religionem, Adiunctum seu officium propheticum, Auditores, Doctrinae genus quod ille professus est, & denique Signum, quod ipsemet Filius Dei celebrauit, Matt.12.39.40.
units.tr: Content with these sayings for the present, let us come to the prosopography of Jonah, in which we will briefly treat these ten heads: the age in which he lived and taught; his name; his parent; his country; his nation; his religion; his attendant or prophetic office; his hearers; the kind of teaching he professed; and finally the sign which the Son of God himself celebrated (Matt. 12.39-40).

units.la: 1. Aetas. Certum est Ionam paulo post Elisaeum uixisse, & docuisse sub Amasia Rege Iudae, & Iarobeamo Rege Israelis. Hi duo reges regnare coeperunt, ille quidem anno mundi conditi 3105, ante Christum natum 866. hic uero an. mundi 3119, ante Christum natum in carne 852. Qualis tum fuerit Ecclesiae & Reipub.Israeliticae κατάγραφις[?], ex hoc loco sacrae Veteris Testamenti historiae liquet, 2.Reg.14.23. Anno xv Amafiahu filij Ioas Regis Iehu-dah, regnauit Iarobeam filius Ioas Regis Israel in Someron 41 annis. 24. Et fecit malũ in oculis Iehoue,non declinauit ab ullis peccatis Iarobeā filij Nobat,qui pecc are fecit Israelem.25.Is restituit terminũ Israelis ab introitu Hemath, usq; ad mare solitudinis: iuxta uerbum Iehouæ Dei Israelis, quod locutus fuerat per manum Ionah filij Amithai, Prophetę,qui erat de Gath-hahepher. 26.Vidit enim Iehouah afflictionem Israelis mutabilem ualde:& nõ erat clausus neq; derelictus, neq; qui auxiliaretur Israeli. 27.Neq; locutus fuerat Iehouah, quod deleret nomen Israelis sub cœlo:ideo seruauit eos per manũ Iarobeam filij Ioas. Habuit Ionas, ueluti successuriatos[?] & successores, Amos & Hosea,qui prophetarę cœperūt paulò quàm ipse serius,uideliçet circa annum ab orbe creato 3150,ante Christũ natum 821. Innarrabili enim Dei clementissimi,Eccle-siæ suæ reliquijs benedicentis, beneficio sit,ut docentium series dulcissima imagine Citreæ seu Medicæ arboris repræsentari uideatur. Vt enim tanta huius fœcunditas est,ut fructus tum maturos, tum immaturos,& flores omni tempore habeat, iucundum sane & utile spectaculum aspi-çientibus;[?] cientibus:sic Elia & Elisæo in cœlestè patriam uocatis, docuit Ionas:& hociam se ne,Amos & Hosæas:qui quos habuerint εὐγχόνυς[?] Prophetas,no est obscurum mediocriter in sacra historia uersatis.
units.tr: 1. Age. It is certain that Jonah lived and taught shortly after Elisha, under Amaziah king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. These two kings began to reign, the one in the year of the world 3105, before the birth of Christ 866, the other in the year of the world 3119, before Christ was born in the flesh, 852. What the state of the Church and the Israelite commonwealth was then is clear from this passage of the sacred history of the Old Testament (2 Kings 14.23-27): "In the fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel reigned in Samaria forty-one years. And he did evil in the eyes of Jehovah; he did not turn from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin. He restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of Jehovah, the God of Israel, which he had spoken through his servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher. For Jehovah saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter, and there was none shut up or left, nor any to help Israel. Nor had Jehovah said that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven; therefore he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Joash." Jonah had, as it were, successors and followers, Amos and Hosea, who began to prophesy a little later than he, namely about the year 3150 from the creation of the world, before the birth of Christ 821. For by the unspeakable kindness of the most merciful God, who blesses the remnants of his Church, the succession of teachers is pictured in a most pleasant image, that of the citron or Median tree. For as this tree is so fruitful that it bears ripe and unripe fruit and flowers at all times, a pleasant and useful sight to onlookers, so Jonah taught after Elijah and Elisha had been called to the heavenly fatherland, and Amos and Hosea likewise. It is no secret to those who are moderately well versed in sacred history what prophets they had.

units.la: 2. Ionæ nomen Hebræis columbam significat,ut est uidere Gen.8.v.8.&10. Piè & ἀντρόχως[?] Hieronymus in Præfatione: Si enim,inquit, Ionas interpretatur columba,columba autem refertur ad Spiritum sanctum,nos quoq; columbam & aduenum ad nos interpretemur columbæ.
units.tr: 2. The name Jonah means "dove" to the Hebrews, as can be seen in Gen. 8.8 and 10. Jerome piously says in his preface: "For if Jonah is interpreted as dove, and the dove is referred to the Holy Spirit, let us also interpret the dove as the one who comes to us."

units.la: Celebratur autem in Scripturis columbina simplicitas & innocentia (Matt.10.16.) Ionæ nomine designata, cuius utinam non minus quàm serpentinæ prudentiæ simus studiosi, secundum illud Apostoli dictum: Volo uos sapientes quidé esse in rebus bonis, innocentes uerò in malis. Rom.16.19.
units.tr: Columbine simplicity and innocence are praised in Scripture (Matt. 10.16), signified by the name of Jonah. Would that we were no less zealous for this than for serpentine prudence, according to the saying of the Apostle: "I want you to be wise in what is good, but innocent in what is evil" (Rom. 16.19).

units.la: Non est autem nobis illud prætereundum, quod Hieronymus ad Chromatiū de Hebræorū quadam παραδόσει[?], de persona Ionæ scripsit: Tradunt Hebrei, hunc esse filium uiduæ Sareptanæ, quem Helias propheta mortuum suscitauit: matre postea dicente ad eum: Nunc cognoui, quia uir Dei es tu; & uerbum Dei in ore tuo est veritas.
units.tr: Nor must we pass over what Jerome wrote to Chromatius about a certain tradition of the Hebrews concerning the person of Jonah: "The Hebrews relate that this is the son of the widow of Sarepta whom the prophet Elijah raised from the dead; the mother afterwards said to him: 'Now I know that you are a man of God, and the word of God in your mouth is truth.'"

units.la: Si ita res habet, Hebraeos quoq; in Sarepta Sidoniae habitasse oportuit. Nam Ionas, cap.1.v.9. & Hebraeum se esse fatetur. Atqui illa Christi oratio, Luc.4.25.26. non admodum ei opinioni respondet: Sed in veritate dico vobis, multae viduae erant diebus Eliae in Israel, quando clausum est coelum ad annos tres & sex menses, adeo ut fuerit fames magna per totam regionem: sed ad nullam illarum missus est Elias, nisi Sareptam urbem Sidoniae, ad mulierem viduam. Cum & Sarepta opponat urbibus Israeliticis, & viduis Israeliticis Sareptanam, initio Ethnicam hanc fuisse, non Hebraeam, quae tamen conversa sit & vocata ad agnitionem & cultum veri Dei, consentaneum est. Ex his autē colligi posse videtur, traditionem Hebraeorum non esse certam.
units.tr: If that were so, the Hebrews too would have had to live in Sarepta of Sidon, for Jonah at chapter 1, verse 9, also confesses that he is a Hebrew. Yet Christ's saying in Luke 4:25-26 does not fit that opinion very well: "But I tell you truly, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut up for three years and six months, so that there was a great famine throughout all the land; but Elijah was sent to none of them, except to Sarepta, a city of Sidon, to a widow woman." Since Sarepta is set over against the Israelite cities and the Israelite widows, it is consistent that it was at first a Gentile town, not a Hebrew one, though it was later converted and called to the knowledge and worship of the true God. From these things it seems possible to conclude that the tradition of the Hebrews is not certain.

units.la: 3. Parens Ionae vocatur Amithai, quod eodem Hieronymo interprete veritatē aut veracem significat. De eius vitae circumstantijs non liquet. Nominis etymologia vel propter φιλαλήθειαν[?], virtutem omnium pulcerrimam, nobis grata esse debet, bet. Studiosi in transcursu hæc D.Augustini apophthegmata obseruent. 1. Veritas cum inquiritur, arrogatia deponatur. Recte sane Augustinus: nam arrogantia ὑ φιλαυτία[?] indociles reddit, ἀδοξομανίᾳ[?] confirmat, ἰδιογνωμοσύνῃ[?] suadet, pia docentiū & uerae doctrinae contemtrix est. 2. Veritas & dulcis & amara est. Hoc intelligatur respectu noui hominis, cui suauis est veritas: & ueteris, cui amara & ingrata est, quia odium parit, & persecutioni ansam (per accidēs) præbet. Addamus unicum Bernardi dictum, quod eximiæ consolationis fructū veritatis studiosis subministrat: Veritas magis elucet impugnata. Est enim ei fatale ἐν τῷ ἥττασθαι νικᾶν[?].
units.tr: 3. Jonah's father is called Amittai, which, according to the same Jerome as interpreter, means truth or truthful. Nothing certain is known of the circumstances of his life. The etymology of the name, because of the love of truth, the most beautiful of all virtues, ought to be pleasing to us. Students should note these sayings of St Augustine in passing. (1) When truth is sought, arrogance must be laid aside. Augustine speaks rightly, for arrogance ὑ φιλαυτία [self-love] makes men unteachable, ἀδοξομανίᾳ [vainglory] strengthens them, ἰδιογνωμοσύνῃ [self-opinion] persuades them, and it despises the pious teachers and true doctrine. (2) Truth is both sweet and bitter. This is to be understood with respect to the new man, to whom truth is sweet, and the old man, to whom it is bitter and unwelcome, because it breeds hatred and provides, by accident, an occasion for persecution. Let us add one saying of Bernard, which supplies the fruit of a remarkable consolation to those who study the truth: truth shines more brightly when it is attacked. For it is its destiny ἐν τῷ ἥττασθαι νικᾶν [to conquer by being defeated].

units.la: 4. Patria Ionæ uocatur Gath-hahepher, 2.Reg.14.25. Hanc à Græcis Γίθ[?] uocari, & uicum exiguum, ortu & sepultura Ionæ Prophetæ nobilem, iuxta Sephorim situ, auctor est Vvolfgangus Vvissembur-gius in descriptione Terræ sanctæ. Libet hoc loco D.Hieronymi (qui in illis locis uersatus, quæ αὐτόπτης didicit, bona quoque fide exposuit) uerba recitare: Porrò Geth in secundo Sephorim miliario, quæ hodie appellatur Diocæsaria euntibus diosi hæc apophthegmata Chrysostomi[?]. 1.Oculis metis futura prophetæ viderut: Hom.12.in Genes.Interest itaq; inter Prophetas qui sunt ἐξωτικῶν[?], de quibus loquitur Paulus,1.Cor.14.& 1.Thes.5. & inter eos qui etiam quædam futura prænunciant. 2. Prophetarum silentium, signum est iræ diuinæ. Huc facit testimonium Psalmi 74.9. Signa nostra non uidemus, non est ultrà Propheta, nec est nobiscum qui cognoscat, usquequò? 3. Prophetæ aliqua Euangelistis dicenda seruauerunt. Hom.12.sup.Matth. Hæc res dispensationi oraculorum Dei, mundi ætatibus responedti[?], seruivit: de qua dicitur Luc.10.24. Dico enim vobis, quòd multi Prophetæ & Reges cupierunt videre quæ videtis, & non viderunt: & audire quæ auditis, & non audierunt.
units.tr: 4. Jonah's homeland is called Gath-hepher, 2 Kings 14:25. Wolfgang Wissenburg, in his description of the Holy Land, states that this place is called Geth by the Greeks, a small village, noted for the birth and burial of the prophet Jonah, and situated near Sepphoris. It is worth quoting here the words of St Jerome, who lived in those regions and, having learned by αὐτόπτης [autopsy], set them out in good faith: "Moreover, Geth, at the second mile from Sepphoris, which today is called Diocaesarea..." Those who go there... Likewise, these sayings of Chrysostom are worth noting. (1) The prophets saw the future with their eyes: Homily 12 on Genesis. There is therefore a difference between the prophets who are ἐξωτικῶν [outsiders], of whom Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians 14 and 1 Thessalonians 5, and those who also foretell certain future things. (2) The silence of the prophets is a sign of divine wrath. Psalm 74:9 supports this: "We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet, nor is there anyone among us who knows, how long?" (3) The prophets reserved some things to be told by the Evangelists: Homily 12 on Matthew. This served the arrangement of God's oracles, which was fitted to the ages of the world, of which Luke 10:24 speaks: "For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it."

units.la: 7. Religio. De sua religione Ionas ipse paucis, sed admodum significanter pronunciauit,cap.1.9. Iehouam Deum cœli ti meo, qui fecit mare & aridam. Huius disti explicationem suo tempore institue mus: nunc autè piarum de religione sententiarum condimeto, προσωπογραφίαν[?] pijs dulcem reddemus. Ne quidem Ethni-ca hæc ea hæc dicta nobis aspernanda sunt, etsi auctoribus τὸ ὅτι, non autem τὸ τί ἐστι, nec[?] διότι uerae religionis, notum fuit.
units.tr: 7. Religion. Jonah himself spoke briefly but very significantly about his religion, in chapter 1, verse 9: "I fear Jehovah, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land." We shall set out the explanation of this statement at its proper place; now, by way of seasoning with pious sentiments about religion, we shall make the portrait pleasing to the godly. Nor are these sayings of the Gentiles to be despised by us, although those authors knew τὸ ὅτι [the that], but not τὸ τί ἐστι [the what it is], nor διότι [the why] of true religion.

units.la: 1. Cum in amicitia, quae honesta non sunt, postulantur, religio & fides anteponantur amicitiae. Cic. 3. Officiorum. Vere pronunciat, cultum Deo debitum maioris nobis faciendum, quàm obligationem amicitiae.
units.tr: 1. When things that are not honourable are demanded in friendship, religion and faith are to be preferred to friendship. Cicero, On Duties, book 3. Truly he says that the worship owed to God must be valued more highly than the obligation of friendship.

units.la: 2. Religione uita constat. Plinius lib. 14. c. 19. Etsi autem superstitiosa sunt & idololatrica, quae ibi scribit auctor de uinis, quibus fas non est ad sacra uti: hoc tamen recte dicitur, sic religione uita constare, ut huius & illius diuortiū, nefas sit statuere.
units.tr: 2. Life consists of religion. Pliny, book 14, chapter 19. Although the things the author writes there about wines, which it is not lawful to use in sacred rites, are superstitious and idolatrous, this is nonetheless rightly said: life so consists in religion that it is wrong to decide on a separation of this from that.

units.la: 3. Religiones pie magis, quàm magnifice, coli debent, ut ait Liuius. Pura enim mente Deum qui spiritus est, colendum esse, Ethnici saniores recte statuerūt. Sed ab Ethnicis ad nostros iam transeamus, qui luce fidei instructi rectius de religione pronunciauerunt.
units.tr: 3. Religions ought to be practised with piety rather than with show, as Livy says. For the Gentiles of sounder judgement rightly determined that God, who is spirit, must be worshipped with a pure mind. But let us now pass from the Gentiles to our own people, who, instructed by the light of faith, have spoken more rightly about religion.

units.la: 1. Religio, pietas est erga Deum. Augustinus de Ciuitate Dei lib. 4. c. 23. Pietas enim uera est, uerax ueri Dei cultus, non cultus falsorum tot deorum, quot dæmoniorū. Vbi non est religio uera, ibi nec uerae uirtutes.De Ciuit.Dei 15.l.25.c.
units.tr: 1. Religion is piety towards God. Augustine, The City of God, book 4, chapter 23. For piety is true, the true worship of the true God, not the worship of as many false gods as there are demons. Where there is no true religion, there are no true virtues either. The City of God, book 15, chapter 25.

units.la: 2. Augetur religio, quanto magis premitur: ut ait Lactantius. Eadem est religionis, quae iustorum, coditio. Iustus ut palma florebit, ita religio oppressa emergit.
units.tr: 2. Religion grows the more it is pressed down, as Lactantius says. The condition of religion is the same as that of the righteous: "The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree"; so religion, when oppressed, rises up again.

units.la: 3. Superstitione, ut ait Cyprianus, religio peruertitur. Nam illa corporali exercitationi, quae parum habet utilitatis, pietatem, quae ad omnia utilis promissiones habet huius & aeternae uitae, postponit.
units.tr: 3. Religion, as Cyprian says, is perverted by superstition. For superstition prefers bodily exercise, which has little use, to piety, which has promises useful for all things, of this life and of the life to come.

units.la: 4. Piae religionis & ueritatis ratio cognitioq; non tam indiget humana institutione, quam ipsa se suis notis indicijsq; prodit: cum prope quotidie ipsis id operibus clamitet, & per Christi doctrinam Sole clarius sese demonstret. Athanasius in Orat.contra Idola. Ex hoc Athanasij dicto colligimus, 1. Religionem, lucidissima Christi doctrina, aeftimadam.2.Eandem operibus Dei nobis commendari. 3. Institutione fidelium hominum inseruire doctrinae Christi, & operibus Dei.
units.tr: 4. The reason and knowledge of pious religion and truth does not so much need human instruction as it reveals itself by its own marks and signs, since it proclaims this almost daily by its works, and shows itself more clearly than the sun through the teaching of Christ. Athanasius, in the oration Against the Idols. From this saying of Athanasius we gather: (1) religion is to be esteemed through the most lucid teaching of Christ; (2) the same religion is commended to us by the works of God; (3) by the instruction of faithful men it serves the teaching of Christ and the works of God.

units.la: 8. Auditores Ionae. Docuit Ionas non tantum apud Israelitas, sed etiam ad Niniuitas ad poenitentiam uocandos ablegatus est a Domino.Matth.12.41. Viri Niniuitae resurgentin iudicio cum natione hac,& condemnabunt eam,quòd ipsi re-sipuerint ad prædicationem Jonæ:& ecce plus quàm Jonas est in hoc loco. Fuit itaque eius apud Ninivitas præconiū, typus quidam ablegationi Apostolorum in orbem terrarū ad prædicandum omni creaturæ Euangeliū:ut suo loco dicendū erit.
units.tr: 8. Hearers of Jonah. Jonah taught not only among the Israelites but was also sent by the Lord to call the Ninevites to repentance. Matthew 12:41: "The men of Nineveh shall rise up in judgement with this generation and shall condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, a greater than Jonah is here." Therefore his proclamation among the Ninevites was a certain type of the sending of the Apostles into the world to preach the gospel to every creature, as will have to be said in its place.

units.la: 9. Doctrinæ genus. Certum est,Jonam prophetam non aliud genus doctrinę tradidisse,quàm cæteri Prophetæ. At hi Legem & Promisionem de Mesia dictis, factis,exemplis & symbolis illustraverūt. Itaq; non aliam doctrinam in hoc Scripto traditam esse statuamus.
units.tr: 9. Kind of teaching. It is certain that the prophet Jonah delivered no other kind of teaching than the other prophets. But these prophets illustrated the Law and the promise about the Messiah by words, deeds, examples and symbols. Therefore let us establish that no other doctrine is delivered in this writing.

units.la: 10. De Signo Jonę inquit Salvator: Natio mala & adultera signum requirit: sed signum non dabitur ei, nisi signum illud Jonæ Prophetæ. Sicut enim fuit Jonas in ventre ceti tres dies, & tres noctes: ita erit & Filius hominis in corde terræ tres dies & tres noctes. Matth.12.39.40. Signū vocat,rem stupendā & prodigiosam, qua Christi Jesu Domini nostri mors, sepultura & resurrectio fuit adumbrata.
units.tr: 10. Concerning the sign of Jonah the Saviour says: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so the Son of man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights." Matthew 12:39-40. He calls it a sign, a wonderful and prodigious thing, in which the death, burial and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ were foreshadowed.

units.la: DE CANONICA LIBRI huius auctoritate.
units.tr: ON THE CANONICAL AUTHORITY OF THIS BOOK.

units.la: Optimo consilio tradita est jam olim BibliBiblicorum librorum distinctio in Canonicos & Apocryphos, ut est videre apud Eusebiū Ecclesiasticæ historiæ lib.6. cap. 18. & in Hieronymi Prologo galeato, eiusdem q; præclara ad Paulinum epistola de omnibus libris Biblicis. Neq; uero animus est, elenchum librorum texere, cum is omnibus pijs sit notissimus. Satis fuerit, si initio uerbis Augustini, sententiam meam declarauero. Exstant autem illa in epistola ad Hieronymum, quæ est numero 19. Ego enim fateor charitati tuae, solis eis Scripturarum libris, qui iam Canonici appellantur, didici hunc timorem honoremq; deferre, ut nullum eorum austo rem scribedo aliquid errasse firmissime credam. Ac si aliquid in eis offendero literis, quod videatur contrarium veritati, nihil aliud quàm vel mendosum esse Codicem, vel interpretem non assecutum esse quod dictum est, vel me minimè assecutum esse, minimè ambigam.
units.tr: Long ago, and with the best judgment, the distinction of the biblical books into canonical and apocryphal was handed down, as may be seen in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History book 6, chapter 18, and in Jerome's galeated Prologue, and in his excellent letter to Paulinus on all the biblical books. Nor is it my intention to draw up a list of the books, since that is very well known to all the godly. It will be enough, at the outset, to set out my view in the words of Augustine. They are found in his letter to Jerome, which is number 19. "For I confess to your charity that I have learned to pay this reverence and honour only to those books of Scripture which are now called canonical, so that I firmly believe none of their authors has erred in writing. And if I meet in them something that seems contrary to the truth, I have no doubt that either the copy is faulty, or the translator has not grasped what was said, or I myself have not understood it at all."

units.la: Ionæ librum Canonicum esse, non autem Apocryphum, sic probo.
units.tr: That the book of Jonah is canonical and not apocryphal, I prove as follows.

units.la: 1. Certissimum est, Christum Iesum ad fidei mysteria demonstranda nō nisi Canonicorum librorum testimonia adhibuisse.
units.tr: 1. It is most certain that Christ Jesus, in setting out the mysteries of the faith, used only the testimonies of the canonical books.

units.la: Vsus est autem testimonijs libri Ionæ, Matt.12.v.39.40.41. item cap.16.v.4. Qua re nihil dubium est, Canonicam esse libri Ionæ auctoritatem.
units.tr: Now Christ used the testimony of the book of Jonah, at Matthew 12:39, 40, 41, and likewise at chapter 16:4. Therefore there is no doubt that the authority of the book of Jonah is canonical.

units.la: 2. Canonici libri doctrinæ integritate, grauitateq;, & sermone sano, sibi inuicē exactissimè respondent. Liber Ionæ his duobus χαρακτῆρσιν, doctrinæ uidelicet τῆς ἀληθοφόρίας, & sermonis sanitate egregiè respondet omnibus aliis Propheticis & Apostolicis libris. Itaq; ē Canonicorum librorum albo neutiquam expungendus est.
units.tr: 2. Canonical books correspond most exactly to one another in the integrity and weight of their teaching and in their sound style. The book of Jonah corresponds admirably to all the other prophetic and apostolic books in these two marks: the truthfulness of its teaching and the soundness of its style. Therefore it must by no means be struck from the roll of the canonical books.

units.la: 3. De quorum Prophetarum diuina uo-catione, ministerio & doctrina probè con-stat, eorum scripta nō sunt explodenda, aut pro apocryphis habenda. Constat au-tem, diuinitus uocatum esse Ionam ad Propheticum munus: constat non modò de doctrinæ, quam ille tradidit, sinceritate, sed & de eiusdem fructu: deniq; certū est, Ionę typo adumbratam esse mortem, sepulturam & resurrectione Christi. Non itaq; est, cur eius scripta in dubium uoceamus, tanquam ἀντιβολὰς.
units.tr: 3. The writings of those prophets whose divine calling, ministry and teaching are sufficiently established must not be rejected or regarded as apocryphal. Now it is established that Jonah was called by God to the prophetic office; it is established not only that the teaching he delivered was sound, but also that it bore fruit. Finally, it is certain that the death, burial and resurrection of Christ were foreshadowed by the type of Jonah. There is therefore no reason why we should call his writings into doubt, as though they were disputed.

units.la: 4. Nunquam etiam inter pios, de auctoritate canonica libri Ionę, dubium fuit. Itaq; it. Itaq; nobis quoque religio esse debet de eadem ἐπιχαρ[?].
units.tr: 4. Nor has there ever been any doubt among the godly about the canonical authority of the book of Jonah. Therefore it ought to be a matter of conscience for us too to hold the same view of it.

units.la: ΑΝΑΚΕΦΑΛΑΙΩΣΕΙΣ.
units.tr: SUMMARIES.

units.la: Capitis primi ὑπόθεσις est: Jonam, dum subterfugit munus prædicandi pœnitentiâ apud Ninivitas, incidisse in offensam Domini, & summum vitæ discrimen. Eiusdem thesis: Divinam vocatione stu-diosissimè nobis sequedam[?], ne eam defugientes incidamus in mala inextricabilia humanis viribus.
units.tr: The subject of the first chapter is this: Jonah, when he shrank from the duty of preaching repentance to the Ninevites, fell into the displeasure of the Lord and into mortal danger. The thesis of this is: that we should follow with the greatest diligence the calling of God, lest by fleeing from it we fall into evils from which no human strength can extricate us.

units.la: Secundi capitis ὑπόθεσις est: Jonam in ventre ceti tribus diebus & totidem noctibus egisse, Deumq; exorasse, ut vivus è tanta morte prodiret. Thesis: Deum servos suos vocationem detrectâtes mortificare, ut eosdem postea vivificet. Μυστήριον: Filius hominis tribus diebus & totidem noctibus erit in corde terræ. Matt.12.40.
units.tr: The subject of the second chapter is this: Jonah spent three days and as many nights in the belly of the whale, and prayed to God that he might come forth alive from so great a death. The thesis: God mortifies his servants who refuse their calling, so that afterwards he may make them alive again. Mystery [μυστήριον]: the Son of man will be three days and as many nights in the heart of the earth. Matthew 12:40.

units.la: Tertij capitis ὑπόθεσις: Viri Ninivitæ resurgent in judicio cum natione hac, & condemnabunt eam, quòd ipsi resipuerint ad prædicationem Jonæ. Seu, Jona ad pœnitentiam hortante, resipuerunt Ninivitæ. Thesis: Deus non delectatur morte impij: sed resipiscentis miseretur. Ezech. 18.23. Nunquid seriò desidero ut moriatur impius: dixit Dominus Iehouah? An non,si auersus fuerit a uijs suis,uiuet?
units.tr: The subject of the third chapter is this: The men of Nineveh will rise up in judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah. Or: at Jonah's call to repentance, the Ninevites repented. The thesis: God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but has mercy on the one who repents. Ezekiel 18:23: "Do I at all desire that the wicked should die, says the Lord God? Is it not rather that he should turn from his ways and live?"

units.la: Vltimi capitis ὑπόθεσις hæc est: Peccauit Ionas,dum vanitatis fuga ductus,Dei misericordiam erga Niniuitas reprehendit. Thesis: Non est nostrum, misericordiæ & iusticiæ Dei declarationem in contro-uersiam vocare: cum iudicium de vasis non luti,sed figuli sit.
units.tr: The subject of the last chapter is this: Jonah sinned, when, driven by the flight from vanity, he found fault with God's mercy towards the Ninevites. The thesis: It is not for us to call into controversy the declaration of God's mercy and justice, since judgment over the vessels belongs to the potter, not to the clay.

units.la: REDVCTIO CAPITIS PRIMI, QVOD EST ἱστορικὸν[?], ad suas Theses.
units.tr: THE REDUCTION OF THE FIRST CHAPTER, WHICH IS HISTORICAL, TO ITS THESES.

units.la: IAm vero,quo res tota iunioribus dilucidior fiat, historicas de Iona ὑπόθεσιν[?] reuocabimus ad suas theses,ut officiorum & actionum fontes aspici possint, & ut hæc omnia nostræ institutioni seruiant. Dominus Iesus mentes nostras luce sua collustret, & linguas regat, ut sint ad beneplacitum eloquia oris nostri, & meditationes cordis nostri. Psal.19.verf. vltimo. Vt autem hoc non præteream[?], poterunt Studiosi theses distinguere secundum hæc capita: 1.Officium. 2.Eius seu neglectionem,seu fugam. 3.Poenam, quæ culpam sequitur. 4.Præsidia aduersus mala pœnarum. 5. Inuestigationem culpæ. 6.Confessione culpæ. 7.Expiationem ciuilem. 8.Correctionem aliorû: quæ approbatione iudicij diuini, gratiarum actione, couerfione ad Deû constat.
units.tr: Now, so that the whole matter may become clearer to younger readers, we shall reduce the historical subject of Jonah to its theses, so that the sources of duties and actions can be seen, and so that all these things may serve our instruction. May the Lord Jesus enlighten our minds with his light and govern our tongues, so that the words of our mouth and the meditations of our heart may be acceptable. Psalm 19, last verse. But so that I do not pass this over, students may distinguish the theses according to these headings: (1) the duty; (2) its neglect or flight; (3) the punishment which follows the fault; (4) the safeguards against the evils of punishments; (5) the inquiry into the fault; (6) the confession of the fault; (7) the civil expiation; (8) the correction of others. These things consist in acknowledging the judgment of God, in giving thanks, and in turning to God.

units.la: THESES.
units.tr: THESES.

units.la: 1. Cum & creationis & redemtionis no strę ratio ea sit, ut opifici & liberatori nostro optimo & sapientisimo quenquam nostrum, præcipuo suo bono, parére con ueniat: cuiq; nostrum, in quo uocatus su-it, in hoc manedum est apud Dominum. 1.Cor.7.24.Ion.1.v.1.&2.
units.tr: 1. Since the reason both of our creation and of our redemption is that it becomes each of us to obey our Maker and Deliverer, who is most good and most wise, above all for his own good, each of us must remain in that calling in which he was called before the Lord. 1 Corinthians 7:24; Jonah 1:1, 2.

units.la: 2. Pessimè itaque faciunt, qui uel inertia, uel metu difficultatum & periculorum fracti & debilitati, de λεπτοταξία cogitant. uers.3.
units.tr: 2. Therefore those do very badly who, broken and weakened either by sloth or by fear of difficulties and dangers, think about desertion [λειποταξία]. Verse 3.

units.la: 3. Ad uindicandam neglestionem ossi cij nõ solùm priuatas ɛrumnas, sed etiam mala publica & cõmunia Dominus zelotes adhibere solet.uers.4.
units.tr: 3. To avenge the neglect of duty, the Lord, as a jealous God, is wont to use not only private calamities but also public and common evils. Verse 4.

units.la: 4. Cum pœnæ communes grassantur, confugiunt homines, malis suis nonnihil dosti, ad præsidia caussarum tum secundarum, tum primæ. uers.5.
units.tr: 4. When common punishments are raging, men, somewhat conscious of their own evils, take refuge in the safeguards of causes, both secondary and primary. Verse 5.

units.la: 5. Veternum, quo malè sibi conscij cæco & occulto conscientiæ vulneri mederi conantur, sensu rerum adversarum, & reprehensionis acrimonia, Dominus excutit. verf.6.
units.tr: 5. The Lord shakes off the lethargy by which those who are conscious of their guilt try to heal a hidden and secret wound of conscience, through a sense of adverse things and the sharpness of reproof. Verse 6.

units.la: 6. Inquisitio fontium fervit providentiæ, cui omnia manifesta sunt, etiam occulta hominum. verf.7.
units.tr: 6. The inquiry into the sources belongs to providence, to which all things are manifest, even the hidden things of men. Verse 7.

units.la: 7. Etsi peccata publicè grassantia accer sunt fatales & publicas pœnas, tamè sunt quidam προπαραπτωτικοί[?] & irritatrices sanctorum lapsus, quos Deus mirabiliter retegit.v.8. Ut hoc loco, tempestate excitata, ad inquisitionem fontis excitat navigantes: & forte Ionam reum esse oftedit.
units.tr: 7. Although sins that spread publicly are the cause of deadly and public punishments, there are nevertheless certain occasions of sin [προπαραπτωτικοί] and provokers of the falls of the saints, which God wonderfully brings to light. Verse 8. Thus in this place, the storm having been raised, it stirs up the sailors to inquire into the cause, and perhaps shows Jonah to be the guilty one.

units.la: 8. Nec raro fit, ut ministerio peccatorum Deus utatur ad fervorum suorum culpam specialem explorandam & retegedam. v.9. 1.Pet.4.17. Nam tempus est, quo iudicium incipiat à domo Dei. quod si primùm incipit à nobis, quis finis erit eorum qui non parent Dei Euangelio?
units.tr: 8. It not infrequently happens that God uses the ministry of sinners to search out and bring to light the particular fault of his servants. Verse 9; 1 Peter 4:17. For the time has come when judgment begins at the house of God; but if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not obey the gospel of God?

units.la: 9. Iusti, præoccupati in aliqua offensa, sic fidem suam profitentur, ut & peccatum suum notum faciant, seq; ipsos accusent. verf.9.
units.tr: 9. The righteous, when they have been overtaken by some offence, so confess their faith that they both make their sin known and accuse themselves. Verse 9.

units.la: 10. Sensum irae Dei adversus peccatū, ingens in alijs quoq; consternatio sequitur,cum saepe unius ob noxam multi malis publicis inuoluantur.uerf.10.
units.tr: 10. Great dismay among others also follows the sense of God's wrath against sin, since often, on account of one man's offence, many are involved in public evils. Verse 10.

units.la: 11. Appellatione conscientiae elicienda est sententia abipfis reis. v.11. Sic Nathan propheta, parabola Dauidi proposita,fecit ut aduersus seipsum iustam proferret sententiam.
units.tr: 11. The sentence must be drawn out of the guilty by appeal to their own conscience. Verse 11. Thus the prophet Nathan, having set before David a parable, caused him to pronounce a just sentence against himself.

units.la: 12. Vt iustus, cum peccauit, accusator fui ipsius,& αὐτοκατάκριτος est: ficnon uult offensae suae caussa alios,quam seipsum,periclitari. v.12.
units.tr: 12. The righteous man, when he has sinned, is his own accuser and self-condemned; so he is unwilling to endanger others on account of his offence, rather than himself. Verse 12.

units.la: 13. Praepostera est clementia,quae iudicijs Dei aduersatur: ac nulla hominum consilia,nullę uires executionem iudiciorum Dei remorari possunt. v.13.
units.tr: 13. That clemency is perverse which opposes the judgments of God; and no counsels of men and no powers can delay the execution of God's judgments. Verse 13.

units.la: 14. Nemefis,peccata uindicans,Dei ui luntati, non hominum crudelitati, seruire debet.v.14.
units.tr: 14. Nemesis, avenging sins, ought to serve the will of God, not the cruelty of men. Verse 14.

units.la: 15. Etsi fontium afflictiones, non sunt κῦτρα,sed τιμωρίαι: tamen publica mala mitigantur,aut etiam tolluntur,cum ęae seruiunt gloriae & iufticiae Dei. v.15.
units.tr: 15. Although the afflictions of the sources are not chastisements but punishments, public evils are nevertheless softened, or even removed, when they serve the glory and justice of God. Verse 15.

units.la: 16. Poenas publicas & priuatas, earuq; mitigationem, conuersio ad Deum, gratiarum folennis actio, & alij pietatis fructus,sequi debent. v.16.
units.tr: 16. Public and private punishments, and their mitigation, ought to be followed by conversion to God, the solemn giving of thanks, and other fruits of piety. Verse 16.

units.la: 17. Etiam bestiae Dei iudicijs exequen-dis dis seruire coguntur. uers.17.
units.tr: 17. Even beasts are compelled to serve the carrying out of God's judgments. Verse 17.

units.la: 18. Certa temporum spacia afflictionibus seruorum Dei praestituta sunt.v.18.
units.tr: 18. Fixed spans of time have been appointed for the afflictions of the servants of God. Verse 18.

units.la: VERSVS I. CAP. I.
units.tr: VERSE 1, CHAPTER 1.

units.la: Et fuit uerbum Iehouæ ad Ionam filium Amithai dicendo.
units.tr: And the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying.

units.la: Quia ὑποθέσεως[?] manifesta est, ad thesin de oraculorum propheticorum fonte & æstimatione digrediemur: ac de efficiente principali, de causa organica, deq; forma oraculorum, ea quæ Dominus suggeret, dicemus. De omnibus istis causis aguntur hæc & similia dicta.
units.tr: Since the subject [ὑποθέσεως] is clear, we shall turn aside to the thesis concerning the source and worth of prophetic oracles. We will speak of the principal efficient cause, the organic cause, and the form of the oracles, namely, the things which the Lord suggests. These matters, and others like them, are treated in what follows.

units.la: Amos 3.7. Quia non facit Dominus Iehouah quicquam, nisi revelauerit secretum suum seruis suis Prophetis. 2. Petr.1.21.[?] Non enim hominum voluntate allata est olim prophetia, sed acti a Spiritu sancto locuti sunt sancti Dei homines.
units.tr: Amos 3.7: "Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets." 2 Pet. 1.21: "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost."

units.la: EFFICIENS PRINCEPS CAUSA oraculorum istorum.
units.tr: THE PRINCIPAL EFFICIENT CAUSE of these oracles.

units.la: Syllogismi instrumento adhibito, a forma, efficacia, usu, oracula θεόπνευστα[?] esse ostendemus. Argumentum enim hoc est ἐπιχειρηματικόν[?].
units.tr: By means of a syllogistic instrument, we will show from their form, their power, and their use that the oracles are divinely inspired [θεόπνευστα]. For this is an argument drawn from its effects.

units.la: Quæcunque oracula, perfecta sunt, animam conuertunt: fidelia sunt, & sapi-entes efficiunt paruulos: recta sunt, & cor-da laetificant: pura sunt, & oculos illumi-nant: ea e diuinae sapientiae perenni & in-exhausto fonte promanant: nec humanae intelligentiae accepta ferri possunt, nisi per nefarium sacrilegium, quo sapientiae donum non Patri luminum, sed creatu-ris rationalibus tribuitur. Atqui eiusmo-di sunt oracula prophetica & apostolica, qualia Psaltes describit: nihil est in eis mutilum, nihil [illegible, ~12 letters], nihil dubiū aut stultum: omnia sunt in eis rectissima, & ad exhilarandos pios accommoda: syn-cera & lucidissima sunt omnia. Rectè sanè Hugo lib.3. de Anima, de istorum oraculorum Commentariis loquens: In sacra Scriptura, inquit, quicquid docetur, veritas; quicquid praecipitur, bonitas; quicquid promittitur, felicitas est. Nam Deus veritas est, sine fallacia: bonitas, sine malitia: felicitas, sine miseria. Quare firmiter statuendum, haec oracula esse θεό-πνευστα, id est diuinitus inspirata, &c.
units.tr: Whatever oracles are perfect convert the soul; they are faithful and make the simple wise; they are right and gladden the heart; they are pure and enlighten the eyes. They flow from the perennial and inexhaustible fountain of divine wisdom, and they cannot be ascribed to human understanding, except by the wicked sacrilege which gives the gift of wisdom not to the Father of lights but to rational creatures. Yet such are the prophetic and apostolic oracles, as the Psalmist describes them: nothing in them is maimed, nothing is doubtful or foolish; all of them are most upright and suited to cheering the godly; all of them are pure and most clear. Hugo rightly says in the third book of On the Soul, speaking of commentaries on these oracles: "In Holy Scripture, whatever is taught is truth; whatever is commanded is goodness; whatever is promised is happiness. For God is truth without deceit, goodness without malice, happiness without misery." Therefore we must firmly hold that these oracles are divinely inspired [θεόπνευστα], that is, breathed into by God, and so on.

units.la: Sed quis eorum promus & cōdus[?] est? Filius Dei, λόγος & Sapientia æterni Patris, qui eo nomine Propheta, Deut.18.v.18.19; & Apostos & Apostolus nostræ confessionis, Heb. 1.1.dicitur. Nam Deum quidem nemo unquam uidit: unigenitus ille Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ille nobis exposuit. Ioan.1.18. Ideo etiam λόγος ἐξαγγελτικὸς uocatur. Rectè Basilius in secunda ad diuites oratione, Christum uocat τὸν ἀληθῶς διδα-σκαλον, & μόνον ἀληθινὸν καὶ ἀγαθὸν διδάσκα-λον: hauddubiè alludens ad uerba Christi: Vnus est enim uester doctor, nempe Christus.Matt.23.10,
units.tr: But who is the dispenser and keeper of them? The Son of God, the Word and Wisdom of the eternal Father, who under that name is called Prophet (Deut. 18.18, 19), and Apostle and High Priest of our confession (Heb. 1.1.). For "no man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (John 1.18). Therefore he is also called the Word who declares [ἐξαγγελτικὸς]. Basil rightly, in the second homily To the Rich, calls Christ "the truly teacher" [τὸν ἀληθῶς διδάσκαλον] and "the only true and good teacher" [μόνον ἀληθινὸν καὶ ἀγαθὸν διδάσκαλον], clearly alluding to the words of Christ: "For one is your teacher, even Christ" (Matt. 23.10).

units.la: Contrà, Matt.11.v.25. Patri æterno tri-buitur doctrinæ Euangelij dispensatio, quæ constat tum κρύψει & occultatione apud sapientes & intelligentes huius mundi; tum ἀποκαλύψει, quæ seruit paruulis. Ergo non Filius, sed Pater est præco τῆς ὑπο-φήτης suorum oraculorum.
units.tr: On the contrary, Matthew 11.25 attributes the dispensing of the doctrine of the gospel to the eternal Father. This consists both in hiding and concealment from the wise and understanding of this world, and in revelation, which serves little children. Therefore it is not the Son but the Father who is the herald [ὑποφήτης] of his own oracles.

units.la: λόγος
units.tr: Logos [λόγος]
