units.tr: 1. Just as a touchstone is to gold, so the terrors of mankind, which are sent by demons [δαιμόνιοι φόβοι], arise from sudden changes and from the greatest dangers.

units.la: Digna est memoria illa Plutarchi narratio de Aristippo navigante Corinthū: Cum tempestas subito orta, præsentem omnibus qui in navi erant, mortem intentaret, expalluit Aristippus. Sedata tempestate, cum scurra quidam, philosophici ordinis ofor, ei insultaret, dicens: Cur uos philosophi, qui mortis contemptum profitemini, expallescitis in discrimine, nos indocti non item? Respondit Philosophus: Non de pari anima tibi mihiqué cura est: significans, omnibus sanis communem esse mortis metum: sed tamen plurimùm interesse, hic an ille subito casu exstinguatur.
units.tr: Plutarch's narrative about Aristippus sailing to Corinth is worth remembering. When a storm suddenly arose and threatened death to everyone on board, Aristippus turned pale. When the storm had subsided, a certain jester, of the philosophical school, mocked him, saying: "Why do you philosophers, who profess contempt for death, turn pale in danger, while we unlearned men do not?" The philosopher replied: "You and I do not have the same concern for our souls," signifying that the fear of death is common to all sound people, but that it makes a great difference whether a man is snuffed out by a sudden accident here or there.

units.la: 2. Nam hominum alij, aduersis subitò ingruentibus, de præsidijs soliciti, tumul-tuantur: alij autem, veterno malæ conscientiæ mederi studentes, in utramuis aurem dormiunt. Ad priorem ordinem nautæ isti, & alij unà navigantes: ad posteriorem Ionas propheta referri debet. Illis hoc accidit, quod ijs qui incendio, terræmotu, aut alia re subita e profundo somno excitati, de aqua, de fuga cogitat: his uero idem quod illis, qui conscientiæ doloribus perpetua ingurgitatione & tumulentia nequicquam mederi conantur.
units.tr: 2. For some men, when adversity suddenly bursts upon them, grow anxious about their defences and make an uproar; others, trying to cure the lethargy of a bad conscience, sleep on whichever ear they like. The sailors and the others sailing with them belong to the first group; Jonah the prophet must be assigned to the second. The sailors experience what happens to those who, roused from deep sleep by a fire, an earthquake or some other sudden event, think about water and flight. Jonah experiences what happens to those who try in vain to cure the pains of conscience by constant gorging and drinking.

units.la: 3. Aduersa repentè ingruentia in magna hominum parte nō nisi timorem, sed metum maioris mali pariunt. Peccant autem homines, cum de effectu soliciti, causam eius negligunt. Non enim ex calamitate & poena culpam colligunt: sed ex leuiore calamitate, quam προλήψιν[?] esse statuunt, maiorem sibi imminere præ-fagiunt, & id dolenter ferunt.
units.tr: 3. In a great part of mankind, sudden adversities produce not mere fear but dread of a greater evil. People go wrong when, anxious about the effect, they neglect its cause. For they do not infer guilt from the calamity and punishment; instead, from a lesser calamity, which they take to be a foretaste [προλήψιν], they foresee a greater one hanging over them, and they bear this with grief.

units.la: 4. Metus maiorum malorum exprimit preces pro obtinenda incolumitate.
units.tr: 4. Fear of greater evils wrings out prayers for obtaining safety.

units.la: Perinde autem agùt homines malorum agmine circumuenti & attoniti, quemad modum ægroti, qui medicorû opem implorant, morbi autem quo tenentur causas & συμπτώματα dissimulat. Quasi verò medicus prudens, morbi ratione non cognita, medicam manum adhibere soleat.
units.tr: Men caught in a crowd of evils and stunned act in the same way as sick people who beg for the help of doctors while ignoring the causes of the disease they suffer from and its symptoms. As if a wise physician would ordinarily apply his remedy without knowing the reasoning of the illness.

units.la: 5. Primùm autem confugiunt ad Numen, idq; seu verum, seu commenticiu. Ita enim divinitús comparata est hominum na-tura, ut supra vires oppressa, ad causam omnipotetem & primam sibi confugiedum intelligat: quod cum facit, semetipsam perasta idololatriæ, & fiduciæ in cæteras creaturas iam deficientis coarguit. Nota est illa narratio Diogenis Laertij de Biante, & ἀθέοις qui in eadem cum ipso navi periclitabantur: Συμπλέων ποτὲ ἀσεβέσι, χειμαζομένης τῆς νεώς, ἐπικαλουμένων τὴν θεὸν: Σιγᾶτε, ἔφη, μὴ ἀκούοντα ὑμᾶς ἐνθάδε πλέοντας.
units.tr: 5. First they flee to a divinity, whether a true one or an invented one. For human nature is so constituted by God that, when it is overwhelmed beyond its strength, it understands that it must flee to the almighty and first cause; yet in doing so it convicts itself of idolatry and of trust in other creatures, which is already failing. The story told by Diogenes Laertius about Bias and the impious men who were in danger on the same ship with him is well known: "Once, when he was sailing with impious men, and the ship was storm-tossed while they called upon their gods, he said: 'Be silent, lest they hear you sailing here.'" [Συμπλέων ποτὲ ἀσεβέσι, χειμαζομένης τῆς νεώς, ἐπικαλουμένων τὴν θεὸν: Σιγᾶτε, ἔφη, μὴ ἀκούοντα ὑμᾶς ἐνθάδε πλέοντας.]

units.la: 6. Vt autem ęger animus semper errat: ita hi, cum suum quisque idolum implo-ret, bis peccant, cum & sibi pro arbitrio suo numina fingant, & si maximè unum Deum adorét, μονόφθαλμον esse uelint, qui ad ipsorum peccata uel cæcus sit, uel con-niueat, & laborantibus euestigiò succur-rens, molestia eos liberet. Quàntò re-ctius Ethnicus ille Xenophō statuit, Deū in secundis studiosè colendum, ut in ad-uersis dexter & propitius nobis adsit.
units.tr: 6. Just as a sick mind always wanders, so these men, each invoking his own idol, sin twice over: they fashion divinities for themselves at will, and even if they adore the one God, they want him to be one-eyed [μονόφθαλμον], blind or indulgent toward their sins, and to free them from trouble by rescuing them at once when they are in distress. How much more rightly did the heathen Xenophon judge that God should be zealously worshipped in prosperity, so that in adversity he may be present to us, favourable and propitious.

units.la: 7. Deinde confugiut ad alia salutis suæ præsidia, quæ à secundis causis subministrari uidentur. Vt cum nautæ, salute pro-pè desperata, ἀπολλύντι γε θυμῷ[?] iacturam faciunt. Ac si tale quid ex sententia succedat, & optato fine potiantur, ne sui domestici idoli (quod φίλαυτοι homines unicè colunt) obliti, suiq; dissimiles uideantur, numini aliquam, industriq; & labori suo optimam salutis suæ partem, non sine sacri-legio, adscribunt.
units.tr: 7. Then they flee to other means of safety, which seem to be supplied by secondary causes. When the sailors, with their safety almost despaired of, cast out their cargo [ἀπολλύντι γε θυμῷ], and if something of this sort turns out as they wished and they attain their desired end, then, forgetful of their own domestic idol, which self-loving men worship above all, and lest they seem unlike themselves, they ascribe to some divinity, and to their own industry and labour, the best part of their safety, and not without sacrilege.

units.la: 8. Qui uerò in utramuis indormiunt aurem, ne sensus malorum publicorum, cōscientiam torqueat, multis modis peccant & errant. Peccant, cum nec Deo glo-riam dant, nec sibi cōsulunt, nec aliis com patiuntur. Errant autem toto cœlo, cùm se latere posse, cum veternum malo inte-stino quo laborant mederi, opinantur.
units.tr: 8. Those who fall asleep with a deaf ear, so that the feeling of public evils does not torment their conscience, sin and err in many ways. They sin, since they give glory neither to God, nor care for themselves, nor show compassion to others. And they err utterly, since they suppose that they can hide and cure by sleep the lethargy from which they suffer within.

units.la: 9. Alia tamen est filiorum huius secu-li, alia Sanctorum offensa præoccupato-rum ratio. Illi enim postquam dedolue-runt, semetipsos dedunt proteruiæ, ad patrandam impuritatem omnem certatim: Eph. 4. 19. Hi autem, perspecta opportunitate, quòd scilicet tempestiuum iam sit expergisci à somno (Nunc enim propius nos est salus, quàm cum credidimus) nocte prætereunte, die autem adueniente, abijciunt arma tenebrarum, & induuntur habitu qui luci conueniat. induunt enim Dominum Iesum. Rom. 13. 11. 12. 13.
units.tr: 9. But the offence of the sons of this world is one thing, and the reasoning of the saints who have been forestalled is another. For the former, after they have become callous, give themselves over to shamelessness, eagerly committing every impurity: Eph. 4. 19. But the latter, having perceived the opportunity, namely that it is now high time to wake from sleep (for now our salvation is nearer than when we first believed), the night having passed and the day having come, cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light, which befits the day. For they put on the Lord Jesus. Rom. 13. 11. 12. 13.

units.la: VERSUS VI.
units.tr: VERSE VI.

units.la: Accessit autem ad eum magnus guber-nator, & dixit ei: Quid tibi soporato? Surge, clama ad Deum tuum: forte placa-bitur Deus ipse nobis, & non peribimus.
units.tr: And the great pilot came to him and said: Why are you sleeping? Arise, call upon your God: perhaps God will be appeased toward us, and we shall not perish.

units.la: Vt doctrina de reprehensionis acrimo-nia, qua Deus malè sibi cōsciorum veter-num καὶ ἀναλγησίαν[?] excutere solet, illustretur, primùm quid in ὑποθέσει[?] de Iona & Nauarcho nobis sit obseruādum, indica-bo: bo: deinde ad θέσιν[?] de Reprehensione peccatorum accedam. Dominus Iesus det, ut isthaec omnia nostrae instaurationi & emendationi seruiant.
units.tr: So that the doctrine concerning the sharpness of rebuke, by which God is accustomed to shake off the sluggishness of those who know they have sinned badly (and insensibility), may be made clear, I will first point out what in the hypothesis about Jonah and the shipmaster is to be observed, and then come to the thesis on the rebuke of sins. May the Lord Jesus grant that all these things serve our renewal and amendment.

units.la: Hypothesin, secundum personarum & rerum circumstantiam, διχοτομέιν[?] poteri-mus. Personæ sunt, Reprehensor & Reprehensus. Res, Obiurgatio & Exhorta-tio. De his ordine & breuiter agendum.
units.tr: We may divide the hypothesis according to the circumstances of persons and things. The persons are the rebuker and the rebuked; the things are the reproof and the exhortation. These are to be treated in order and briefly.

units.la: 1. Si Reprehensoris personam spectes, Ethnicus Israelitam, Nauclerus Prophetă Domini, merito reprehendit.
units.tr: 1. If you look at the person of the rebuker, the heathen sailor rightly rebukes the Israelite, the prophet of the Lord.

units.la: 2. Si Reprehensum, male sibi conscius arguitur. Videmus autem talionis poenam Ionam affectum. Qui enim nomine Domini exercituum Niniuitarum peccata arguere, & illos reos peragere recusauit, eaq; in parte Deo non obedijt, iusto eius iudicio uel ab Ethnico nauta redargutus fuit.
units.tr: 2. If you look at the one rebuked, Jonah is shown to be a man who knew his guilt. For he, who refused to denounce the sins of the Ninevites in the name of the Lord of hosts and to bring them to judgment as guilty, and in this respect did not obey God, was, by God's just judgment, rebuked even by a heathen sailor.

units.la: 3. Si obiurgationem, grauissima erat. Quid enim? An non supina negligentia est, si ipse cum multis aliis periclitēris, de salute non esse solicitum? Praeterea, an nō magna est iniustitia, non commoueri, si maximè alij quoq; tua causa in summo uitæ discrimine uersentur? Postremò, qui aliorum exemplo non commouetur, eti-am cum eos in summa consternatione versari videt, plus quàm ferreus est.
units.tr: 3. If you look at the reproof, it was most severe. For what? Is it not supine negligence, when you are in danger together with many others, not to be anxious about safety? Besides, is it not great injustice not to be moved, when others also are in the greatest peril of life on your account? Finally, whoever is not moved by the example of others, even when he sees them in utter dismay, is harder than iron.

units.la: 4. Si deniq; exhortationem ad preces, illa uerò & religiosa erat, & modis omnibus necessaria. In eo tamen nauclerus peccauit, quòd haesitás καὶ Διαχρινόμενος[?] de salute dixit: Forte placabitur Deus? & q; de sua salute seu uita magis, quàm de gloria Dei, laborauit. Atqui & viuedo & moriendo glorificadus nobis est Dominus.
units.tr: 4. If finally you look at the exhortation to prayer, it was indeed both pious and in every way necessary. Yet the sailor sinned in this, that, hesitating and doubting about salvation, he said: "Perhaps God will be appeased?" and that he was concerned about his own safety or life more than about the glory of God. And yet, both in living and in dying, the Lord is to be glorified by us.

units.la: THESIS.
units.tr: THESIS.

units.la: Iam uerò ut ad thesin de Reprehensi-one peccantium accedamus, initiò reprehensores, deinde reprehensos, tertiò ipsam reprehensionem, postremò salubre consilium, expedere conuenit. Vt piarum cogitationum materia subministretur, θετικῶς[?] rem exponam, & quidem iuxta causas.
units.tr: Now, to come to the thesis on the rebuke of sinners, it is fitting first to set out the rebukers, then the rebuked, third the rebuke itself, and last the salutary counsel. So that material for pious thoughts may be supplied, I will set out the matter by positions, and indeed according to its causes.

units.la: 1. Deus uel immediatè peccantes reprehendit, uel mediatè. Haec thesis de reprehensionum αἰτίῳ κυρίῳ[?] praecipuè agit, hoc est, de Deo. Exemplum immediatae reprehensionis occurrit Gen. 20. 3. Venit autem Dominus ab Abimelech noctu in somnis, & dixit ei: En mortuus es propter uxorem quam accepisti, quum ipsa maritata sit marito.
units.tr: 1. God rebukes sinners either immediately or mediately. This thesis deals chiefly with the principal cause of rebukes, that is, with God. An example of immediate rebuke occurs in Genesis 20:3: "But the Lord came to Abimelech by night in a dream and said to him: Behold, you are dead because of the woman whom you have taken, since she is married to a husband."

units.la: 2. Cum mediatè reprehendit, utitur ministerio seu creaturarū animatarum, seu actionum suarum. Actionem voco, cùm ferula filios, gladio alienos visitat. Virga, gladius, fames, pestis, bestiae, & alia Dei iudicia, quid aliud sunt, quàm conciones exhortatoriae ad refipiscentiam & eius fructus?
units.tr: 2. When he rebukes mediately, he uses the ministry either of animate creatures or of his own actions. I call it an action when he visits sons with the rod and aliens with the sword. The rod, the sword, famine, pestilence, beasts, and the other judgments of God, what else are they than exhortations to repentance and its fruits?

units.la: 3. Creaturae animatae vel sunt λογικοὶ[?], vel brutae. Annotauit hoc studiosè Petrus Apostolus 2. Epist. 2. 16. de Bileamo loquens: Sed redargutionem suae transgressionis sustinuit: nam subiugis asina muta, humana voce clamans, prohibuit Prophetae dementiam. Quis autem dubitet, αὐτῷ τῷ ἔργῳ[?] temulentorum hominū intemperantiam à brutis redargui, cum haec naturæ satisfaciunt potu necessario?
units.tr: 3. Animate creatures are either rational or brute. Peter the Apostle carefully noted this in 2 Peter 2:16, speaking of Balaam: "But he was rebuked for his transgression: for a dumb ass, speaking with a human voice, restrained the madness of the prophet." Who, indeed, would doubt that by the very deed the intemperance of drunkards is rebuked by brute beasts, since these supply the drink nature necessarily requires?

units.la: 4. Homines autem qui alios reprehendunt, eis pares aut impares sunt aetate, fide, officio, & aliis circumstantijs, quae reprehensionem non parum acuunt. Quis enim dubitet, grauius multò esse, si iure perstringatur senex à iuvene, Christianus ab infideli, doctor à discipulo: quàm si uel parem par(ut Petrum Paulus,Gal.2.) obiurget, uel superior ætate,fide,officio, inferiorem aliquem? Notum est exemplum Danielis, qui Senes accusauit: si modò historicum est.
units.tr: 4. Men who rebuke others are equal or unequal to them in age, faith, office, and other circumstances, which sharpen the rebuke not a little. For who would doubt that it is much more serious if an old man is justly censured by a young man, a Christian by an unbeliever, a teacher by a disciple, than if one equal rebukes an equal (as Paul rebuked Peter, Gal. 2), or a superior in age, faith, or office rebukes someone inferior? The example of Daniel, who accused the elders, is well known, if indeed it is historical.

units.la: 5. Iam si eos qui reprehenduntur spectes, uel bene sibi conscij sunt, uel male. Si bene, ἀνωαδιλησίαν[?] illam ob specialem innocentiam, non parum diluit communis reatus conscientia, quæ pungitur reprehensionis aculeo. Si male sibi conscij sunt, tum in eis animus sibi cōscius, uoce reprehensoris ad Dei omnium ἐπόψει[?] tribunal se pertrahi sentiens, αὐτοκατάκριτος est.
units.tr: 5. Now if you look at those who are rebuked, they are either conscious of being good or conscious of being bad. If good, the common consciousness of guilt, which is stung by the sting of rebuke, does not a little dilute that sense of special innocence. If they are conscious of being bad, then in them a mind conscious of itself, perceiving that by the voice of the rebuker it is dragged before the tribunal of the all-seeing God, is self-condemned.

units.la: 6. Porrò, cum sit mira ingeniorum uarietas, alij malum dissimulant, alij illud ingenuè fatentur. Quomodo utriqj tractandi sint, hæc Patrum dicta monent? Mansueti benignè corripiendi sunt, inquieti seuerè. Item: Iuuenes, inquit Ambrosius, plerumq; seueritas admonitionis ad profectum dirigit: senes uerò ad meliora opera deprecatio blanda componit.
units.tr: 6. Furthermore, since there is a remarkable variety of dispositions, some dissemble their fault, others frankly confess it. How they are to be handled, the sayings of the Fathers instruct us: the gentle are to be corrected kindly, the restless severely. Likewise: "Young people," says Ambrose, "are for the most part directed to improvement by the severity of admonition; but older people are better brought to better works by gentle entreaty."

units.la: 7. Iusta tamen sit & tempestiua reprehensio oportet. Iusta erit, si uituperanda & laudanda non sumantur promiscuè; sed illa reprehendantur aperte, hæc col-laudentur candidè. Tempestiua erit, si decori temporisq; habeatur ratio. Ebrius, cum non det locum reprehensioni, non nisi cum sobrius esse coepit, arguedus est. Ac rectè in uersu dicitur: Intempestiuè qui monet, ille nocet. Ac dulcior est, ut ait Ambrosius, religiosa castigatio, quàm blanda remissio.
units.tr: 7. Yet the rebuke must be just and timely. It will be just if things blameworthy and things praiseworthy are not treated indiscriminately; but the former are rebuked openly, the latter are commended frankly. It will be timely if regard is had for propriety and for the time. A drunkard, since he does not give room for rebuke, is not to be censured until he has begun to be sober. And rightly is it said in verse: "Whoever admonishes unseasonably does harm." And, as Ambrose says, a pious correction is sweeter than a flattering indulgence.

units.la: 8. Non autem satis est reprehendere quod merito displiceat, nisi etiam quid magnis de causis probetur, aperias. Correctio, inquit Ambrosius, errantes corripit, con-filium bonis datur. Non sunt autem in malorum numero habendi ij, quos reprehensione sancta ad meliorem frugem reuocare studemus.
units.tr: 8. However, it is not enough to rebuke what rightly displeases, unless you also set forth what is approved for great reasons. "Correction," says Ambrose, "rebukes those who err; counsel is given to the good." Yet those whom we labour to recall to a better course by holy rebuke are not to be counted among the wicked.

units.la: 9. Citra autem omnem hæsitationem, spem gratiæ Dei resipiscentibus facere debemus: cùm uera resipiscentia ab eadem Dei gratia dependeat. Vt maximè enim temporales pœnas pœnitentiam agentibus non remittat Deus, tamen eos vitæ æternæ hæredes esse vult.
units.tr: 9. Without any hesitation, we ought to give hope of God's grace to those who repent, since true repentance depends on that same grace of God. For although God does not remit temporal punishments to those who do penance, nevertheless he wills that they be heirs of eternal life.

units.la: De reprehensione securitatis magnæ partis hominum.
units.tr: On the rebuke of the great majority of men's security.

units.la: Quod Christus discipulis olim dixit [illegible, ~8 letters]: Dormite quod superest, & requiescite: Matth.26.45. id ne dubitemus maximae parti generis humani, quae etiā periculosissimo hoc tempore, asciticio lethargo correpta, in utramuis aurem indormit, quoque dictum esse.
units.tr: What Christ once said to his disciples [illegible, about eight letters]: "Sleep on now, and take your rest" (Matt. 26.45). Let us not doubt that the same words also apply to the greater part of the human race, which, even in this most dangerous age, seized by an acquired lethargy, sleeps on with both ears.

units.la: Si Hierophantas quosdam speētes, cū quasi iam debellato à maioribus Antichristianismo, profesionem Christianae religionis uentri & gloriae aucupādae serviire cupiant, de sinceritate doctrinae coelestis, de uitae integritate minimè soliciti, tales omnino sunt, quales depinxit Isaias, cuius haec uerba sunt: Speculatores eius caeci, uniuersi ipsi nihil norunt: uniuersi ipsi canes muti, qui non ualent latrare, dormitantes, iacentes, diligentes dormitare. Isa.56.10.
units.tr: If you look at certain hierophants, who, as though Antichristianism had already been overcome by our ancestors, wish to serve their bellies and seek glory by means of their profession of the Christian religion, and who are not at all anxious about the purity of heavenly doctrine or the integrity of their lives, they are altogether such as Isaiah described, whose words are these: "His watchmen are blind; they are all ignorant; they are all dumb dogs, unable to bark, lying down, dreaming, and loving to sleep" (Isa. 56.10).

units.la: Si sapientes huius seculi consideres, animaduertes ufqueadeò non esse solicitos de ueritate tuenda, & de eadem incorrupta ad posteros propaganda, ut etiā pacis (si Deo placet) studio ad manifestos errores, contumeliosos in filium Dei, connivendum dicant, ut irascantur ijs, uelut hominibus turbulentis, qui ueritatis defensione suscipiunt. Placet eis illud Erasmianū: Mihi adeò inuisa est discordia, dia, ut veritas etiam displiceat seditiosa. Itáne veritas, immenso Dei beneficio nobis indignis patefacta, seditiosa dici & haberi debet? Et an'non in Deum, qui veritas est, haec contumelia recidit, cùm ea dicitur seditiosa ?
units.tr: If you consider the wise men of this age, you will notice that they are so little concerned to defend the truth, and to pass it on uncorrupted to posterity, that for the sake of peace (God willing) they say that manifest errors, insulting to the Son of God, must be tolerated, and they grow angry at those who take up the defence of the truth, as though they were troublemakers. They like that saying of Erasmus: "I so dislike discord that even truth becomes displeasing when it is seditious." Is truth, which has been revealed to us unworthy people by the immense goodness of God, to be called and regarded as seditious? And does this insult not fall back upon God, who is the truth, when it is said to be seditious?

units.la: Hos duces ignara multitudo sequitur, & se necessitate discendi doctrinam cœ-lestem liberari laetatur, ac de peccatis publicè privatimque grassantibus secura, in utramuis aurem indormit.
units.tr: An ignorant crowd follows these leaders, and rejoices that it is freed by necessity from learning heavenly doctrine; and, careless about the sins that rage publicly and privately, it sleeps on with both ears.

units.la: Si qui itaque aures ad audiendum habent, somno excusso, meditentur haec dicta: Excitare qui dormis, & surge a mor-tuis, & illucescet tibi Christus. Eph. 5.14.
units.tr: If therefore anyone has ears to hear, let him shake off sleep and ponder these words: "Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you" (Eph. 5.14).

units.la: Vt Sole, rebus humanis lucem inferente, expergefacti accedimus ad occupationum nostrarum functiones: sic à ueterno securitatis experrecti, Christo qui Soliusticiæ est, cordibus nostris lucem inferete, ἀγγε-λῶς ambulemus: non ut insipientes, sed ut sapientes.
units.tr: As the sun, bringing light to human affairs, wakes us so that we go about our daily tasks, so, roused from the drowsiness of security, let us bring Christ, who is the Sun of righteousness, into our hearts as light, and let us walk carefully [ἀκριβῶς], not as fools but as wise.

units.la: VERSUS VII.
units.tr: VERSE 7.

units.la: Et dixerunt quisq; ad proximum suum: Venite, & proiiciamus sortes, ut sciamus propter quem (euenit) nobis malum istud.
units.tr: And they said every one to his neighbour: Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us.

units.la: € s Proie-
units.tr: Proie-

units.la: Proiecerunt itaque sors, & cecidit sors ipsa super Ionam.
units.tr: So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.

units.la: Si ita uobis uidetur, fratres carissimi, omissa ὑποθέσει[?], in qua nihil obscurum est, ad thesin progrediemur, ac de Sontium inquisitione miranda, dicemus. Iunio-res in transcursu obseruent hæc prouer-bia, quæ ad nostrum institutum faciunt: Reperit Deus nocentem: ἀνὴρ θεὸς τὸν ἀ-[?]λιτήριον[?]. Item: Vel mus mordeat improbum. Item: Ibyci grues.
units.tr: If it seems good to you, dearest brothers, let us set aside the narrative [ὑπόθεσις], in which nothing is obscure, and proceed to the thesis, and speak of the marvellous inquiry into the guilty. Younger readers should note in passing these proverbs, which suit our purpose: "God finds the guilty one"; "[illegible] ... a god finds the ... man"; likewise, "Even a mouse may bite the wicked man"; likewise, "the cranes of Ibycus."

units.la: 1. Sontium per sortes inquisitio, prouidentiæ (cui omnia manifesta sunt, etiam occulta hominum) mirado modo seruit. Id uidere est in hac narratione de Iona Propheta, qui sorte deprehensus est ab ijs, qui cum eo in eadem naui erant.
units.tr: 1. The inquiry into the guilty by lot serves divine providence, to which all things are manifest, even the hidden things of men, in a wonderful way. This can be seen in this narrative about the prophet Jonah, who was detected by lot by those who were in the same ship with him.

units.la: 2. Auctor huius rei Deus est, qui, cum interest ipsius gloriæ, fontes, ceu Cacos, in lucem protrahit.
units.tr: 2. The author of this matter is God, who, whenever it concerns his glory, drags the hidden deeds into the light as if into daylight.

units.la: Ita ingenium est hominum animaliū, ut φιλαυτίας[?] fascinati, non nisi à Deo cordium cognitore, rei peragi & conuinci possint. Homines enim facilè fallunt, simulando integritatem, & dissimulando peccata.
units.tr: Men are so much the kind of creatures that, bewitched by self-love [φιλαυτία], they can be exposed and convicted only by God, the knower of hearts. For men easily deceive, by feigning integrity and by concealing their sins.

units.la: Cum autē & tempestatem in mari excitauerit Dominus, & ipse solus regat sortes, nō est obscurum, Deum huius inquisitionis in Ionam prophetam, ἐργοδιώκτην[?] nobis esse statuendum.
units.tr: Since the Lord also stirred up the tempest at sea, and he alone governs the lots, it is not unclear that we must regard God as the taskmaster [ἐργοδιώκτης] of this inquiry against the prophet Jonah.

units.la: 3. Vtitur autem, cum ei uisum est, ad eā rem opera hominum, uel ordinarie, uel extra ordinem. Ordinarie, ut cum magistratuum ministerium adhibet: ut cū Io- suam inquirere iussit in sacrilegū Achan. Iof. 8.
units.tr: 3. He uses human agency, however, when it seems good to him for this purpose, either in the ordinary way or outside the ordinary way. In the ordinary way, as when he employs the ministry of magistrates, as when he ordered Joshua to inquire into the sacrilege of Achan (Josh. 7).

units.la: 4. Lucet autem Dei prouidentia mirā- do modo, cum extra ordinem politicum constituti, Deo hac in parte seruiunt.
units.tr: 4. God's providence also shines in a marvellous way when men who are not in any political office serve God in this matter.

units.la: Nam ut ei seruiant inscij, uicinis tan- tùm causis excitati & moti, & quidē magno consensu, conspirantes, siue finem, si- ue media spestes, id uerò singulari proui- dentia fieri, nihil dubium est. Fere enim fieri solet, ut quot sunt capita, tot sint & sententiæ.
units.tr: For that they serve God without knowing it, roused and moved only by immediate causes, and indeed in great agreement, conspiring together, whether they aim at the end or at the means, is beyond doubt done by singular providence. For it usually happens that there are as many opinions as there are heads.

units.la: Atqui (ut in ὑποθέσει[?] uidere est) nauigā- tes cum Iona, ignari præcipuarum causa- rum (uidelicet irę Dei aduersus Ionam, defugietem sanctam uocationem) & ma- lis doćti de quodam reo, magno consen- su inquisitionem istam instituerunt. Servierunt itaque providentiae divinae.
units.tr: Yet (as can be seen in the narrative) the sailors with Jonah, ignorant of the chief causes (namely the anger of God against Jonah, who fled from his holy calling), and taught by evil men about a certain guilty person, instituted this inquiry with great agreement. Thus they served the divine providence.

units.la: Fuit autem in illis, 1. προηγούμενον[?]. Calamitas praesupponit culpam. Item, Saepe fit, ut ob unius noxam multi laborent.
units.tr: Now in them there was, 1. the antecedent [προηγούμενον]: calamity presupposes guilt. Likewise, it often happens that many suffer on account of one man's offence.

units.la: 2. [illegible, ~12 letters], Tempestas praesentem intentans omnibus mortem.
units.tr: 2. [illegible, about twelve letters]: the tempest threatening death to everyone present.

units.la: 3. Finis proximus, Rei hominis agnitio: superior, eiusdem iusta poena: summus, incolumitas, qua se, nocente praesente, nec poenis affecto, potiri non posse, iudicabant.
units.tr: 3. The proximate end: the recognition of the man's guilt; the higher: his just punishment; the highest: safety, by which they judged that, if the guilty man remained present and unpunished, they could not secure themselves.

units.la: 5. Modi deprehendendi fontes, multiplices sunt. Hoc loco fortis mentio fit, de qua paulo post dicam.
units.tr: 5. The ways of detecting the guilty are many. In this passage mention is made of the lot, about which I will say a little later.

units.la: Olim fontes deprehendebatur per applicationem tribuum, familiarum, personarum. Iof. 7. Ac sunt, qui Arcam & pe-storale (in quo erat Urim & Thumim) adhibita fuisse dicant. Eodem fecit, Aqua zelotypiae, Sors, & alia quaedam.
units.tr: Formerly the guilty were detected by the application of tribes, families and persons (Josh. 7). There are also those who say that the Ark and the breastplate (in which were the Urim and Thummim) were used. To the same purpose belong the water of jealousy, the lot, and certain other things.

units.la: Cum mirabdis modis hominum occulta mala Deus retegat, studendum est ve-rae pietati, & orandus Dominus, ut ne patiatur nos labi in tetros furores & errores.
units.tr: Since God uncovers hidden evils of men in wonderful ways, we must devote ourselves to true piety and pray to the Lord that he may not allow us to slip into foul frenzies and errors.

units.la: 6. Nec est cur filij Dei putent, occultanda esse sua ἁμαρτήματα, caeterorum aut hominum errata & peccata retegeda. Nam quo maiora in illos, quam in hosce, χαρίσ-ματα[?] μετὰ[?] effundit, tanto plura pietatis ἀπολυτρώματα[?] ab eisdem iure optimo requirit. Atque haec causa est, cuius gratia lapsus summorum hominum Adae, Noah, Abrahae, Lothi, Mosis, Aaronis, Dauidis, Petri, Spiritus sanctus in sacra historia nequaquam praeteriuit, ut conspectiora essent uitia & delicta.
units.tr: 6. Nor is there any reason why the sons of God should think that their own sins ought to be hidden, while the errors and sins of others or of men should be uncovered. For the more abundant gifts [χαρίσματα] he pours out upon these men than upon those, the more numerous acts of piety he rightly demands from them in return. And this is the reason why the Holy Spirit, in sacred history, did not pass over the falls of the greatest men, Adam, Noah, Abraham, Lot, Moses, Aaron, David and Peter, so that their faults and offences might be more conspicuous.

units.la: METHODVS ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΙΚΗ DE SORTE, ac de reis per sortitionem deprehensis.
units.tr: THE DIDACTIC METHOD [ΔΙΔΑΣΚΑΛΙΚΗ] CONCERNING THE LOT, AND CONCERNING THE GUILTY DETECTED BY LOT.

units.la: Hebraei גּוֹרָל Gorol, Graeci κλῆρον[?], Latini Sortem uocant, speciem quandam rituum, in quibus ad rei dubiae dijudicationem, adhibitis notis, quae non nisi ex pacto ualent, Deo arbitrium permittitur.
units.tr: The Hebrews call it Gorol [גּוֹרָל], the Greeks klēron [κλῆρον], and the Latins sors. It is a certain kind of rite in which, to decide a doubtful matter, certain signs, which have force only by agreement, are used, and the judgment is left to God.

units.la: Est autem ὁμώνυμον Sortis uocabulum, ut quod significet, alias
units.tr: The word sors is, however, equivocal [ὁμώνυμον], so that it signifies at other times:

units.la: 1. Ceremoniam sortitionis, id est, actionem. ut in hoc dicto: Proiecerunt sortem super uestimenta mea. Psal. 22. 18.
units.tr: 1. The ceremony of casting lots, that is, the action itself, as in this saying: "They cast lots upon my garments." Ps. 22:18.

units.la: 2. Talionis poenam, seu passionem. Isa. 17. 14. Haec est sors diripientium nos.
units.tr: 2. The penalty of retaliation, or suffering. Isa. 17:14: "This is the lot of those who plunder us."

units.la: 3. Notas sortitionis seu relationem. Inde phrasis, Proijcere sortes, id est, tesseras. Ion. 1. 7.
units.tr: 3. The tokens of the lot, or the act of drawing. Hence the phrase proicere sortes, that is, to cast tokens. Jonah 1:7.

units.la: 4. Substantiam, uerbi gratia Populum. Psal. 125. 3. Non quiescet sceptrum impi-orum orum super fortem iustorum: ne exten-dant iusti ad iniquitatem manus suas. Est.13.17: Sorti tuæ esto propitius.
units.tr: 4. A substance, for example, a people. Ps. 125:3: "The sceptre of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity." Esth. 13:17: "Be gracious to your lot."

units.la: 5. Possessionem communem bonorū seu spiritualium, seu corporaliū. De spiritualium bonorū possessione dicitur: Gratias agentes Patri, qui idoneos nos fecit ad participandam sortem Sanctorum in luce. Col.1.12. De privatione autem horum bonorum dicitur: Non est tibi pars neque sors in hoc negotio. Act.8.21.
units.tr: 5. Common possession of goods, whether spiritual or bodily. Of the possession of spiritual goods it is said: "Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit to share in the lot of the saints in light." Col. 1:12. But of the deprivation of these goods it is said: "You have neither part nor lot in this matter." Acts 8:21.

units.la: 6. Officium. De Iuda Iscariota dicitur Act.1.17. Quia annumerabatur nobiscū, & sortitus erat partem (κλήρου[?]) ministerij huius, &c. Daniel.12. Tu autem stabis in sorte tua. De hoc dicto, an ne de officio accipi debeat, iudiciū alijs permitto.
units.tr: 6. An office. Of Judas Iscariot it is said, Acts 1:17: "For he was numbered with us, and had obtained a share [κλῆρον] of this ministry," etc. Dan. 12: "But you shall stand in your lot." Whether this saying ought to be taken of office, I leave to others to judge.

units.la: Sortes hoc loco significat ceremonias varias, in quibus, adhibitis ex pacto certis quibusdam testeris, Deo indicium iudiciumq; de personis aut reb. permittitur, ut finis sit suspicionum & controuersiarum. Hæc finitio per causarum & fortiū praxeos ἀντιγραφὴν[?] sic illustrabitur.
units.tr: Here sortes means various ceremonies in which, certain tokens having been agreed upon, judgment concerning persons or things is committed to God, so that there may be an end to suspicions and disputes. This definition will be illustrated as follows, by the practice of cases and lots compared with one another.

units.la: Proverb.16.33. In sinum proijcitur sors, sed a Iehoua est omne iudicium eius. παρὰ κυρίου[?], & gubernator euentus in forti-tioione est Dominus. Ideo Apostoli, cùm forte defignádus effet, qui in officio Apostolico Iudae succederet, duobus pro-positis & forte missa, precati sunt: Tu Do-mine, qui corda omnium nosti, oste-de u-trum elegeris ex his duobus, ut accipiat sortem ministerii huius & Apostolatus, à quo aberravit Iudas, ut abiret in locum suum.
units.tr: Prov. 16:33: "The lot is cast into the lap, but every judgment of it is from the LORD" [παρὰ κυρίου], and "the disposing of the lot is wholly from the Lord." So the Apostles, when someone had to be designated to succeed Judas in the apostolic office, after two had been proposed and lots cast, prayed: "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen, that he may take the lot of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas fell away, to go to his own place." Acts 1.

units.la: Caussæ [illegible, ~9 letters] & famulantes, sunt ii qui, non superstitione ducti, sortes ia-ciunt, parati stare iudicio divino. Act.1.
units.tr: Those who cast lots and serve, not led by superstition but prepared to stand before the divine judgment, are the ones who ... Acts 1.

units.la: Ceremoniae etiam meminit Salomon, de qua suo loco forsan viderimus. Pro.18.
units.tr: Solomon also mentions this ceremony, of which we shall perhaps see more in its place. Prov. 18.

units.la: 18. Lites cessare facit fors: & inter fortes diuidet. Ex hoc dicto colligere licet fi-nes & effectus fortitionis, bono consilio adhibitae. De his [illegible, ~9 letters] isthaec habetote:
units.tr: 18. The lot makes disputes cease, and it separates between the mighty. From this saying we may gather the ends and effects of the lot, when it is used with good counsel. Concerning these, take the following points:

units.la: 1. Lites oriuntur vel rerum, vel perso-narum nomine.
units.tr: 1. Disputes arise either over things or over persons.

units.la: 2. Quae si alias legitimè componi nequeant, bona conscientia sortes adhibe-ri possunt, si modò disceptates parati sint stare arbitrio Dei.
units.tr: 2. Those which cannot otherwise be settled lawfully may, with a good conscience, be submitted to the lot, provided the disputants are ready to abide by the judgment of God.

units.la: 3. Nonnunquam enim ignoratio divi-nitùs destinatae rei & iuris, sortitione re-quirit. quirit. Ut Israelitarum singulæ Tribus scire possent, quam cuique illarum Cananæ regionis Eparchiam Dominus desti nasset, mandatum de κληρ[?]ωσίας datum est, Num. 33. Ac Deus forte terram partitus est. Psal. 78. 55. Iosua autem σωφρων [?] καὶ ἀλλόφυλος [?] fuit. Iof. 14. 15.
units.tr: 3. For sometimes the lot is needed to learn what has been divinely appointed concerning a thing or a right. So that the individual tribes of Israel might know which province of the land of Canaan the Lord had assigned to each, a command concerning the allotment was given, Num. 33. And God divided the land by lot, Ps. 78:55. Joshua, however, was a wise man and a stranger [σωφρων καὶ ἀλλόφυλος] ... Josh. 14:15.

units.la: 4. Sors itaque suo indicio iusticiæ tam commutatiuæ, quàm distributiuæ seruire poterit. In illa arithmetica, in hac geometrica proportio locum habet.
units.tr: 4. The lot, therefore, by its own judgment, can serve both commutative and distributive justice. In the former, arithmetical proportion holds its place; in the latter, geometrical proportion.

units.la: 5. Commutatiuæ quidem, in diuisione familiæ hercisçundæ, Num. 36. in distinctione agrorum, & similibus.
units.tr: 5. Commutative justice, indeed, in the division of an inheritance, Num. 36, and in the marking out of fields and similar matters.

units.la: 6. Distributiuæ verò, in delectu personarum, qui seruit τῷ ἀφορισμῷ [?] bonorum & malorum.
units.tr: 6. Distributive justice, however, in the selection of persons, which serves the separation [τῷ ἀφορισμῷ] of good and bad.

units.la: 7. Eo nomine forte adhibita distinxit Dauid rex prudentissimus ἐφημερίας [?] sacerdotum, 1. Par. 24. 31. Cantorum, 1. Paral. 25. 8. Ianitorum, 1. Par. 26. 14.
units.tr: 7. For this purpose David, the most prudent king, used the lot to distribute the priestly courses, 1 Chr. 24:31; the singers, 1 Chr. 25:8; and the gatekeepers, 1 Chr. 26:14.

units.la: 8. Interdum autem factum est, ut forte adhibita, etiam fontes deprehenderentur: id quod universale & regulare non esse existimo. Præ aliis illustria sunt hæc exempla. Ionathan forte deprehensus fuit, cum contra temerarium uotum & edictum édistū patris mel gustasset,i.Sam.14. I-tem Ionas Propheta, cap.i.
units.tr: 8. Sometimes, however, it happened that the lot, when used, also detected faults; this I do not think is universal or the rule. Among others, these examples are notable. Jonathan was detected by lot when, against his father's rash vow and edict, he had tasted honey, 1 Sam. 14. Likewise Jonah the prophet, chapter 1.

units.la: De circūstantijs sortitionis,quibus ueteres sæpiùs usi sunt, ex hisce dictis nonnulla coniicere licet: Proijcere sortes. In sinum proijcere. Certo die sortiri. Sed quia ocio & tempore destituor,isthęc uobis peruestigandā relinquo.
units.tr: From these sayings we may conjecture some of the circumstances of casting lots, which the ancients often used: proicere sortes, to cast into the lap, to draw lots on a set day. But since I am lacking in leisure and time, I leave these matters for you to investigate.

units.la: VERSVS VIII.
units.tr: VERSE 8.

units.la: Dixerunt ergo ad eum: Indica nunc quaso nobis (tu) propter quē hoc malum (acci- dit) nobis:quod est opus tuum,& unde uenis,& quæ terra tua, & de quónam populo es?
units.tr: So they said to him: "Tell us now, we beg you, on whose account this evil has come upon us; what is your work, and where do you come from, and what is your country, and of what people are you?"

units.la: In ὑποθέσει hæc obseruanda sunt.
units.tr: Three things are to be observed in the hypothesis [ὑποθέσει].

units.la: 1. Genus & schema orationis plenū humanitatis, & alienum à Cyclopica asperitate. Benignè enim Ionam, forte iam deprehensum, & hauddubiè ualde consternatum, alloquuntur, dolentes, ut res ipsa doceat[?], cum dolente. Simile exemplū habetur Iof.7.19. Dixit Iofua ad Achan: Fili mi, da quæso gloriā Iehouæ Deo Israelis, & da ei confessionē, atq; indica nūc mihi quid feceris, ne abscondas à me.
units.tr: 1. The manner and form of the address are full of humanity and far from Cyclopean harshness. They speak kindly to Jonah, who has perhaps been caught and is surely greatly dismayed, and they sympathise with him as the situation itself teaches, as with one in distress. A similar example occurs in Josh. 7.19: "Joshua said to Achan, 'My son, give, I pray, glory to the LORD God of Israel, and make confession to him, and tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me.'"

units.la: Vtinam uerò omnes nominis Christiāni magistratus, cum in fontium crimina inquirendum est, seueritatem humanitate temperantes, non malint diris & tormentis veritatem ab attonitis extorquere, quàm religiosa persuasione uti, ut gloria (ingenua confessione elicita) Deo potius detur, quàm confessio cōsusanea tormentis accepta feratur.
units.tr: Would that all magistrates of the Christian name, when crimes must be investigated, would temper severity with humanity, and would rather not wring the truth from the terrified by dreadful torments. Would that they would use religious persuasion instead, so that glory is given to God through a free and ingenuous confession, rather than a confession extracted by torture is put forward.

units.la: Quod autem Arist. Top. 8, de altercantis quæstionibus dixit, Qui non sine litigatione interrogat, prave disputat: id de contentiosa inquisitione criminum quoque dici posse videtur.
units.tr: What Aristotle says in the Topics, book 8, about contentious questions, that one who questions without wrangling argues badly, seems also to apply to the contentious inquiry into crimes.

units.la: 2. Interrogatoria, de tanti mali auctore primario, de eius uitæ genere & functio-ne, de patria, de gente. Hæc omnia & eis cognata monent, ea quæ bonis ornamē-to sunt, per accidens eisdem dehonesta-mento esse: si videlicet virtutum decora ab ortu suo vitæq; instituto seiungant.
units.tr: 2. The questions concern the primary author of so great an evil: his manner of life and occupation, his homeland, his people. All these things, and those connected with them, warn that what adorns good people is by accident a disgrace to them, if indeed they separate the beauty of the virtues from their origin and from the pursuit of their life.

units.la: Sed ad Thesin nos accedere præstat, de qua hæc habetote.
units.tr: But it is better that we come to the thesis itself, concerning which take the following points.

units.la: 1. Deum pœnis publicis sic iram suam erga publicè grassantem impietatem & iniusticiam declarare, ut interim occulta seruorum suorum παραπτώματα[?] retegat. Non enim lynceis oculis aspicit mundi peccapeccata, & ad sanctorũ offensas coniuet[?] sed hos ceu filios castigat, ut ad peccato-rum suorum agnitionem adducat.
units.tr: 1. God thus declares his anger against impiety and injustice that spread publicly, so that meanwhile he may also lay bare the hidden transgressions of his servants. For he does not look upon the sins of the world with lynx's eyes, nor does he wink at the offences of the saints, but he chastises them as sons, so as to lead them to the acknowledgment of their own sins.

units.la: 2. Μονοφθάλμως[?] tamen esse istorum iudi-ces, qui sic in piorum offensas inquirunt, ut sui interim obliuiscantur, hoc est, ut se quoque graviter peccavisse non agnoscat. Severam enim in alios censuram instituunt & agunt, ut interim sibi ipsis innocentiae laudem acquirant: non dissimiles indoctis, qui dum alios carpunt, doctrinae opinionem apud alios captant.
units.tr: 2. Yet those judges are monophthalmōs [μονοφθάλμως], one-eyed, who inquire into the offences of the godly in such a way that they meanwhile forget themselves, that is, do not recognize that they too have sinned grievously. For they institute and carry out a severe censure of others, so that meanwhile they may win for themselves a reputation for innocence: not unlike the unlearned, who while they carp at others, seek among others a reputation for learning.

units.la: 3. Nequaquam enim Dominus severiter in servos suos inquirens & animadvertens, caeterorum impietatem & scelera pro nihilo ducit, aut iustificat.
units.tr: 3. For the Lord, inquiring into and punishing his servants severely, does not therefore count the impiety and crimes of others as nothing, nor does he justify them.

units.la: Itaq; Aristarchi isti sibi ipsis imponunt paralogismo secundum non causam ut causam. Deus, aiunt, istorum hominum lapsus particulares in lucem producit & vindicat: in nos autem talem censuram & animadversionem nō instituit. Igitur ipsis factis & illos reos peragit, & nos iustificat. Ad hoc λεπτολόγημα[?] praeclare respondet Petrus Apostolus: Nam tempus est, quo incipiat iudicium a domo Dei: quod si primum incipit a nobis, quis finis erit eorum qui non parent Dei Euan-gelio? Et, si iustus uix seruatur, impius & peccator ubi comparebit? 1.Pet.4.17.18.
units.tr: So those Aristarchuses impose on themselves a paralogism, a fallacy of the non-cause taken as cause. God, they say, brings to light and punishes the particular lapses of these men, but does not institute such a censure and punishment against us. Therefore by the very deeds he condemns those men and justifies us. To this subtle sophism the Apostle Peter replies admirably: "For the time has come for judgment to begin at the house of God; and if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not obey the gospel of God? And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?" 1 Pet. 4:17-18.

units.la: 4. Atque hac in re miranda iudiciorum Dei dispensatio elucet. Nam dum ad ea exequenda Critici isti ἐφωθὶν [?] censuram exercent in particularia aliorum errata: se-ipsos ἑαυτοὺς [?] (conscientiae propriae testimonio convicti) uniuersalis iniusticiae reos & αὐτοκατάκριτοι [?] esse, deprehendunt. Sic itaque affecti sunt, ut ij qui caedis aut furti reum damnant, parricidij interim vel sacrilegij sibi conscij. Ac de eiusmodi Aristarchis dicitur: Quid autem aspicis festucam, quae est in oculo fratris tui: trabem vero quae est in oculo tuo, non vides? Matt.7.3.
units.tr: 4. In this matter the wonderful arrangement of God's judgments shines forth. For while these critics exercise their censure in dealing with the particular errors of others, they discover themselves (convicted by the testimony of their own conscience) to be guilty of universal injustice and self-condemned. They are so affected as those who condemn a man for murder or theft are, meanwhile, aware of their own parricide or sacrilege. And of such Aristarchuses it is said: "Why do you look at the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the beam that is in your own eye?" Matt. 7.3.

units.la: 5. Sunt autem modis omnibus tum stolidi, tum infelices, cum in alios seueriore censuram instituendo, innocentiae umbram frustra captant, & immedicabile conscientiae vulnus non sanant, sed exa-sperat. Non enim asperitas erga eos quorum manifesta sunt peccata, lenit aut tollit dolores animi male sibi conscij: sed potius culpam & dolorem auget, cum hypocrisi seruiat, & cum charitate pugnet. Si, ait Augustinus, conscientia criminis mordet, laus mundi parum prodest.
units.tr: 5. Yet such people are in every way both foolish and unhappy: when they institute a harsher censure against others, they vainly seek the shadow of innocence, and they do not heal the incurable wound of conscience but make it worse. For harshness toward those whose sins are manifest does not soothe or remove the pains of a mind that is ill at ease with itself; rather it increases guilt and pain, since it serves hypocrisy and fights against charity. "If conscience bites with a crime," says Augustine, "the praise of the world does little good."

units.la: 6. Ex istis tamen malis Deus bona efficit, cum & suos ab errore in viam revocet, & caeterorum conscientias sic pulset, ut nō possint sibi ipsis blandiri, & ex peccatis delitias facere.
units.tr: 6. Yet God brings good out of these evils, since he both calls his own back from error into the way and so strikes the consciences of others that they cannot flatter themselves and make delights out of their sins.

units.la: 7. Præstat autem Sanctos, delicto aliquo pręoccupatos, coram hominibus rubore suffundi: quàm cum reprobis in conspectu Dei & angelorum in ęternum cofundi.
units.tr: 7. It is better for the saints, when they have been overtaken by some fault, to blush before men than to be confounded together with the reprobate in the sight of God and the angels for eternity.

units.la: Coronidis uice addam memorabile dictum Demonactis: Non tantum irascendum est delinquentibus, sed etiam, si fieri possit, uitia corrigenda, & quidem exemplo Medicorum, qui non indignantur ægrotis, sed morbo medentur.
units.tr: By way of a garland, I will add a memorable saying of Demonax: One must not only be angry with wrongdoers, but, if it can be done, correct their faults, and indeed after the example of physicians, who are not indignant at the sick but treat the disease.

units.la: VERSVS IX.
units.tr: VERSE 9.

units.la: Et dixit ad eos: Hebræus sum, & Ieho-vam Deum cæli timeo, qui fecit mare & aridam.
units.tr: And he said to them: I am a Hebrew, and I fear Jehovah, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.

units.la: Ex hoc & sequente versu colligere licet, Ionam hæc tria fassum esse. Primò, quòd gente Hebræus esset: secundò, quòd alienus à Getium idolomania, Iehovam universorum conditorem & conservato rem coleret: tertiò, quòd inobedientia reus effet, ut qui fugeret à facie Iehouæ.
units.tr: From this verse and the following one it can be gathered that Jonah confessed these three things. First, that he was a Hebrew by nation; second, that, being alien to the idolatry of the Gentiles, he worshipped Jehovah, the maker and preserver of all things; third, that he was guilty of disobedience, as one who fled from the face of Jehovah.

units.la: 1. Magnum est operæpretiũ scire, quid Sanctis faciendum sit, cum in aliqua of-sensa deprehensi, à Deo adiguntur, ut τοῖς ἔξω[?], seu à fide alienis, vitæ suæ, fidei & fa-ctorum rationem reddere cogantur. Atq; id, si permiserit Deus, ex hac Ionæ pro-phetæ confessione discemus.
units.tr: 1. It is of great importance to know what the saints ought to do when, caught in some offence, they are dealt with by God and compelled to render an account of their life, their faith and their deeds to those outside (that is, to those alien to the faith). And if God grants it, we shall learn this from the confession of the prophet Jonah.

units.la: 2. Meminerint itaq; Sancti, se non tam humana, quàm diuina auctoritate, ad e-dendam ingenuam confessionem adduci. Errant enim in iudicando, qui nō uident, nullam homines seu infideles, seu etiam inferiores auctoritatem in se habituros, nisi eam à Deo accepissent. Ideò Christus Dominus noster Pilato inter alia dixit: Non haberes potestatem aduersus me ullam, nisi datum tibi esset super-nè. Ioan. 19.11.
units.tr: 2. Let the saints therefore remember that they are led to make a frank confession not so much by human authority as by divine authority. For they err in judging who do not see that men, whether unbelievers or even inferiors, will have no authority over them unless they have received it from God. Hence Christ our Lord said to Pilate, among other things: "You would have no power against me at all, unless it had been given to you from above." John 19.11.

units.la: 3. Atq; eo nomine, ut sanctificetur Iehouah exercituum, interrogati testen-tur, primùm quę bona à Deo acceperint, deinde quomodo sese erga eundem gef-serint[?].
units.tr: 3. And for this reason, that the name of Jehovah of hosts may be sanctified, let those who are questioned bear witness, first to the good things they have received from God, and then to how they have conducted themselves toward him.

units.la: Confesio duabus partibus constare debet. Prima est, testimonium uerum de ornamentis & donis diuinitus cocesis. Vthocloco fatetur Ionas, se in ea gente natu, quæ tum temporis erat Dei peculi-um:se uerę religionis, quæ in Iehouæ có ditoris & redetoris agnitione posita est, sectatorem, alienum esse ab Ethnicorum δεισιδαιμονίας[?] & superstitione. Altera pars est, culpę specialis aut uniuersalis expo-sitio, quæ Deo gloriam dat.
units.tr: A confession ought to consist of two parts. The first is a true testimony concerning the ornaments and gifts divinely bestowed. In this place Jonah confesses that he was born in that nation which at that time was God's peculiar people; that he is a follower of the true religion, which rests on the acknowledgment of Jehovah the creator and redeemer; and that he is alien to the superstition and godlessness of the Gentiles. The second part is an exposition of guilt, either particular or universal, which gives glory to God.

units.la: 4. Itaq; ueteratoria & mutila confessio est, quæ bona sic recenset & amplificat, ut hominis industriæ & meritis potius, quàm Dei gratiæ, accepta ferat: mala autem uel dissimulando præterit, uel extenuando eleuat. Ac talis uidetur oratio Pharisæi apud Lucam, cap. 18. 11. 12.
units.tr: 4. Therefore that confession is deceitful and mutilated which so recounts and magnifies the good things as to credit them to human industry and merits rather than to the grace of God, while it either passes over the evils in silence or, by minimizing them, lightens them. Such seems to be the prayer of the Pharisee in Luke, chapter 18, verses 11 and 12.

units.la: 5. Quàm autè nihil agant Sancti, si quà-do carnis affectu ad tempus uicti, pecca-ta sua tegunt & dissimulant, suo exem-plo docet Dauid, cuius hæc uerba sunt: Quando tacui, uetustate collapsa sunt os sa mea, cum rugirem tota die. Quoniam interdiu & noctu ingrauescebat super me manus tua: uersus est uigor meus in siccitates æstatis. Itaq; peccatum meum tibi notum feci, & iniquitatem meam non abscondi. dixi enim: Confitebor aduersus me scelus meum Iehouae. Tu uero remi-sisti noxam peccati mei, Psal. 32.3.4.5.
units.tr: 5. How little the saints accomplish when, overcome for a time by the affection of the flesh, they cover and conceal their sins, David teaches by his own example, whose words are these: "When I kept silent, my bones grew old through my groaning all the day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my moisture was turned into the drought of summer. So I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said: I will confess my transgression to Jehovah. And you forgave the guilt of my sin." Ps. 32.3, 4, 5.

units.la: DE VERI DEI DE-scriptione.
units.tr: ON THE DE-scription OF THE TRUE GOD

units.la: Scriptura sancta Deu, nobis plane incomprehensibilem, varijs modis describit. Nos hoc tempore caeteris omisis, ἐκφρασιν[?] hoc loco traditam diligenter expendemus. Utinam vero nostrum studium, divini nominis sanctificationi serviat. Tria autem membra sunt descriptionis veri Dei, quę hoc loco tradita est, primum de essentia Dei, in nomine Iehouae: secundum de eius auctoritate & dominio in universa, in epitheto, Deus cœli: tertium de eius operibus, videlicet de creatione & coservatione universorum. De his ordine viderimus, sic ista perscrutantes, ut interim summa cum religione vota faciamus, ut nos luce sapientiæ Pa-ter ille cœlestis illuminare dignetur.
units.tr: Holy Scripture describes God, who is altogether incomprehensible to us, in various ways. At this time, setting the others aside, we will carefully weigh the description given here, the ekphrasis [ἔκφρασιν]. Would that our effort serve the sanctification of the divine name. The description of the true God given here has three parts: first, concerning the essence of God, in the name Jehovah; second, concerning his authority and dominion over the universe, in the epithet "God of heaven"; third, concerning his works, namely the creation and preservation of all things. We shall consider these in order, examining them in such a way that meanwhile we make our prayers with the utmost reverence, that that heavenly Father may deign to illuminate us with the light of wisdom.

units.la: I. DE NOMINE IEHOVAE ἀξιώματα,
units.tr: I. ON THE NAME JEHOVAH: AXIOMS [ἀξιώματα]

units.la: 1. Iehouae nomen in Scripturis sanctis tribuitur Deo vero, uni, ęterno, incompre-hensibili, omnipotenti, beato, habenti im-mortalitatem, luce habitanti inaccessam; juxta hæc testimonia, quibus σύμφωνα [?] colligere, religiosæ uestræ diligentiæ fuerit.
units.tr: 1. In the holy Scriptures the name Jehovah is ascribed to the true God, who is one, eternal, incomprehensible, almighty, blessed, having immortality, dwelling in light inaccessible. It will be a matter for your careful diligence to gather agreements [σύμφωνα] from these testimonies.

units.la: Ier.10.10. Iehouah autem Deus ueritas (seu uerus) est: ipse Deus uiuens, & rex æternus.
units.tr: Jer. 10.10. But Jehovah is God, the truth (or the true God): he is the living God and the eternal King.

units.la: Deut.6.4. Iehouah Deus noster, Iehouah unus est.
units.tr: Deut. 6.4. Jehovah our God, Jehovah is one.

units.la: Eph.4.5. Vnus Dominus, una fides.
units.tr: Eph. 4.5. One Lord, one faith.

units.la: Rom.16.26. Ex imperio æterni Dei.
units.tr: Rom. 16.26. By the command of the eternal God.

units.la: 2.Par.6.18. Sed nū uere habitabit Deus cum homine super terram? ecce, cœlum & cœli cœlorum non capiunt te, quanto minus domus hæc quam ædificaui?
units.tr: 2 Chron. 6.18. But will God indeed dwell with man upon the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you; how much less this house which I have built?

units.la: Gen.17.1. Ego Deus omnipotens.
units.tr: Gen. 17.1. I am God Almighty.

units.la: 1.Tim.6.15. Beatus ille & solus Princeps, Rex regum, & Dominus dominorum. 16. qui solus habet immortalitatem, lucem habitans inaccessam: quem uidit nemo hominum, neq; uidere potest; cui honor & robur æternum. Amen.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 6.15–16. The blessed and only Potentate, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, dwelling in light inaccessible, whom no man has seen or can see; to whom be honour and eternal power. Amen.

units.la: 2. Est enim Spiritus, qui solus αὐτάρκεια [?] obtinet immensam, liberrimam, omnipotentem, iustam, bonam, sapientem, &c. iuxta hæc dicta:
units.tr: 2. For he is Spirit, who alone possesses self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια], immense, most free, almighty, just, good, wise, etc., according to these sayings:

units.la: Ioan.4.24. Deus est Spiritus.
units.tr: John 4.24. God is Spirit.

units.la: Ier.23.24. An non cœlū & terram ego impleo, dicit Dominus?
units.tr: Jer. 23.24. Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord?

units.la: Pfal.115.3. Certè Deus noster est in cœ-lo: omnia quæ uoluit,fecit.
units.tr: Ps. 115.3. Certainly our God is in heaven; whatever he has willed, he has done.

units.la: Pfal.119.Iustus es Domine,& iusta sunt iudicia tua.
units.tr: Ps. 119. You are just, O Lord, and your judgments are right.

units.la: Matt.19.17.Nullus est bonus,nisi unus, nempe Deus.
units.tr: Matt. 19.17. No one is good but one, namely God.

units.la: Iac.1.5. Quòd fi cui uestrûm deest sapi-entia,postulet ab eo qui dat,nempe Deo, qui dat omnibus benignè, &c. Caussa non est effectu deterior. Deus autem petenti ex fide dat sapientiæ χαρίσματα[?]. Itaq; ipse sapientissimus est.
units.tr: James 1.5. But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of him who gives, namely God, who gives to all generously, etc. The cause is not inferior to its effect. God indeed gives gifts of wisdom [χαρίσματα] to him who asks in faith. Therefore he himself is most wise.

units.la: § Sic autem dicitur,tum fui ipsius,tum operum καὶ ἀποτελεσμάτων[?] respectu: ut ex hisce duobus dictis colligi potest.
units.tr: § But he is so called both with respect to himself and with respect to his works and effects [καὶ ἀποτελεσμάτων], as can be gathered from these two sayings.

units.la: Ex.3.13. Et dixit Mose ad Deum : Ecce ego ibo ad filios Israel,& dicam eis,Deus Patrum ueftrorû misit me ad uos. Et dicent mihi: Quod est nomen eius? quid tum respondebo eis? 14. Et dixit Deus ad Mosen: Ero,qui ero. Dixit prætereà: Sic dices filijs Israel,Ero misit me ad uos.
units.tr: Exod. 3.13–14. And Moses said to God: Behold, I will go to the children of Israel and say to them, "The God of your fathers has sent me to you." And they will say to me: What is his name? What then shall I answer them? 14. And God said to Moses: I am who I am. He added: Thus you shall say to the children of Israel, "I am has sent me to you."

units.la: Rom.11.36. Nam ex eo, & per eum, & in ipso sunt omnia.
units.tr: Rom. 11.36. For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.

units.la: Act.17.28.Peripsum uiuimus,& moue-mur, & sumus, &c.
units.tr: Acts 17.28. For in him we live, and move, and have our being, etc.

units.la: 4. Commune aut est Iehouæ nome τε-τραγράμμα-[?] [illegible, ~12 letters] Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto.
units.tr: 4. The name Jehovah is common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit [τετραγράμματον]: [illegible].

units.la: Pfal.110.1. Dixit Iehouah Domino meo, Sede à dextris meis.
units.tr: Ps. 110.1. The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.

units.la: Ioan.20.28. Dominus meus, & Deus meus.
units.tr: John 20.28. My Lord and my God.

units.la: Isa.63.14. Spiritus Iehouah deduxit Israelem.
units.tr: Isa. 63.14. The Spirit of Jehovah led Israel.

units.la: Nec tamen sunt tres Iehouae, sed unus Iehouah. Pie itaque dicitur in Symbolo Athanasij: Pater Dominus est, Filius Dominus est, & Spiritus sanctus Dominus est. Et tamen non sunt tres Domini, sed unus. Respondet enim Iehouae nomini, κύριος[?], Domini augustissima appellatio.
units.tr: Yet they are not three Jehovahs, but one Jehovah. Thus it is rightly said in the Athanasian Creed: the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord; and yet they are not three Lords, but one. For the name Jehovah corresponds to κύριος [kyrios], the most august title of Lord.

units.la: 5. Nulli vero creaturae nomen Iehouae competit. Nomen enim essentiae αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀπεριγράπτου[?], conditricis & conseruatricis uniuersorum, creaturae seu corporeae seu incorporeae non conuenit. Tale autem est Iehouae nomen.
units.tr: 5. The name Jehovah belongs to no creature. For the name of that essence which is self-existent and uncircumscribed [αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀπεριγράπτου], the creator and preserver of all things, does not fit any creature, whether corporeal or incorporeal. Such is the name Jehovah.

units.la: 6. Christo Iesu tamen congruit, sed respectu τῆς λόγος, non τῆς σαρκός. Iehouah enim est & dicitur respectu eius naturae, secundum quam est essentialis Dei inconspicui imago, splendor gloriae eius, character personae eius, magnus Deus, conditor omnium, [illegible, ~12 letters], neq; initium dierum, neque uitæ finem habens. Col.1.15.Heb.1.2.Tit.2.13.Heb.7.3.Ioan.1.
units.tr: 6. Yet it fits Christ Jesus, but with respect to the Word, not the flesh. For he is and is called Jehovah with respect to that nature according to which he is the essential image of the unseen God, the brightness of his glory, the express character of his person, the great God, the maker of all, [illegible], having neither beginning of days nor end of life. Col. 1.15; Heb. 1.2; Titus 2.13; Heb. 7.3; John 1.

units.la: Non autem ratione eius naturæ, quæ est creatura [illegible, ~9 letters], feme Abrahæ & Dauidis, [?], forma serui, seu hominū similitudo, id est, fratribus similis: Ioa.1.14. Caro: Matthæi 8.20. Filius hominis, cuius Matt.1.& 2. Luc.1.& 2. conceptio & natiuitas ex uirgine, motus localis, & alia documenta essentiæ, ut tempore, sic loco finitæ, occurrunt. Rom.1.3: De Filio suo, facto ex semine Dauid secundum carnem. Hebr.7.3. Phil.2.7. Hebr.2.17.
units.tr: Not, however, by reason of that nature which is a creature [illegible], the seed of Abraham and David, [?], the form of a servant, or the likeness of men, that is, made like his brothers: John 1.14, flesh; Matt. 8.20, Son of man; Matt. 1 and 2, Luke 1 and 2, his conception and birth from a virgin, local motion, and other proofs of an essence limited in time and in place, all occur. Rom. 1.3: concerning his Son, made from the seed of David according to the flesh. Heb. 7.3; Phil. 2.7; Heb. 2.17.

units.la: II. DE ELOGIO, Deus cœli.
units.tr: II. ON THE TITLE: God of heaven.

units.la: 1. Deus in Scripturis sanctis & uniuersarum creaturarum, & hominum Deus recte dicitur. Psal.24.1. Iehouæ est terra, & quicquid continet: orbis terrarum, & qui habitant in eo. Quia ipse super maria fundauit eam, &c. Ion.1.9. Deus cœli, [?] parte omnium pulcerrima pro toto sumta, uocatur.
units.tr: 1. God is rightly called the God of the Scriptures, of all creatures, and of men. Psal. 24.1: "The earth is Jehovah's, and all that it contains: the world, and those who dwell in it. For he founded it upon the seas, etc." Jon. 1.9: God is called "God of heaven," the most beautiful part of everything taken for the whole.

units.la: 2. Cum dicitur uniuersorū, Deus auctoritas Creatoris in creaturas designatur. Psal.47.2. Quoniam Iehouah excelsus, terribilis: Rex magnus super omne terrā.
units.tr: 2. When he is called the God of all, the authority of the Creator over creatures is indicated. Psal. 47.2: "For Jehovah is high and terrible, a great King over all the earth."

units.la: 3. Hanc auctoritatem ubique praefens exercet, alias quidem defendendo, alias uero perdendo. Atque ideo Deus non motium solum, sed & campestrium, omniumque in genere locorum, nuncupatur. 1.Reg.20.28. Accesserat uero uir Dei, & dixerat Regi Israel his uerbis: Sic dixit Iehouah, Propterea quod dixerunt Syri, Deus montium est Iehouah, & non Deus vallium est: dabo uniuersam multitudinem magnam hanc in manum tuam, ut sciatis quod ego sim Iehouah.
units.tr: 3. He exercises this authority everywhere present, sometimes by defending, sometimes by destroying. And so God is named not only of the mountains but also of the plains and of places in general. 1 Kings 20.28: "The man of God came near and said to the king of Israel: Thus says Jehovah, Because the Syrians have said, 'Jehovah is a God of the mountains, and not a God of the valleys,' I will deliver all this great multitude into your hand, so that you may know that I am Jehovah."

units.la: 4. Hominum tamen Deus peculiariter dicitur, quia eorum curam praecipue gerit. Psal.36.6. Hominem & bestias seruas Iehouah. Et rectissime Plutarchus alicubi scribit: Deus non φιλόφυις aut φίλανθρωπος, sed φιλανθρώπος est.
units.tr: 4. Yet he is called the God of men in a special way, because he chiefly cares for them. Psal. 36.6: "Jehovah, you preserve man and beast." Plutarch rightly writes somewhere that God is not a lover of nature [φιλόφυις] or a lover of humankind [φίλανθρωπος], but a lover of man [φιλανθρώπος].

units.la: 5. Aliter tamen hominum in genere, aliter uero Sanctorum in specie Deus esse dicitur: ut ex hoc Pauli dicto liquet: Spe fixam habeamus in Deo uiuo, qui est coseruator omnium hominum, maxime autem fidelium. 1.Tim.4.10.
units.tr: 5. Yet God is spoken of in one way as the God of men in general, and in another as the God of the saints in particular, as is clear from this saying of Paul: "We have set our hope on the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, especially of believers." 1 Tim. 4.10.

units.la: 6. Gratuitae enim adoptionis respectu, eorum Deus est, quos uocat & iustificat. Rom.3.29. An Iudaeorum Deus solum? An non & Gentium? Certè & Gentium. Rom.10.12. Non est distinctio uel Iudæi, uel Græcinam idem Dominus omnium, est dies in omnes, à quibus inuocatur. Psal.144.15. Beatus populus cuius sic: beatus est populus cuius Iehouah est Deus.
units.tr: 6. For in respect of gratuitous adoption, he is the God of those whom he calls and justifies. Rom. 3.29: "Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Certainly of the Gentiles also." Rom. 10.12: "There is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is over all and is rich toward all who call upon him." Psal. 144.15: "Blessed is the people whose God is Jehovah."

units.la: 7. Peculiariter itaq; eorum Deus dicitur, quia sunt ἀνμφύλοι Christi, & cocorpores, qui etiâ ab eode Spiritu reguntur. Eo nomine in Baptismo dicimur, Christi insititi fieri, participes nimirum mortis & uitæ, ac Spiritus eiusdem. Rom.6.
units.tr: 7. He is therefore called their God in a special way, because they are kinsmen of Christ [συμφύλοι] and fellow members of his body, who are also ruled by the same Spirit. By this title we are said in Baptism to be grafted into Christ, namely to become partakers of his death and life, and of his Spirit. Rom. 6.

units.la: 8. Homonymœ autè dicitur Deus eorum, qui in Ecclesia sunt, sed non ex ea: siue loquentium, siue sedetium partes obtineant. De illis dicitur: Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine Domine, introibit in regnum cœlorum, sed qui facit quod uult Pater meus, qui in cœlis est. Matth.7.21. De his autem accipi debet illud: Ex eo multi discipulorum eius pedem retulerunt, nec amplius cum eo uersabantur. Ioan.6.66.
units.tr: 8. But he is called the God of those who are in the Church, yet not from it, in a merely nominal sense, whether they hold the place of speakers or of listeners. Of these it is said: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." Matt. 7.21. But that saying must be understood of them: "From that time many of his disciples drew back and no longer walked with him." John 6.66.

units.la: De Cœli definitione quid statuis?
units.tr: What do you determine about the definition of heaven?

units.la: Loco cœlum illud ἀοχέον, in quod Deus nos omnes suscepturus est, definiendum, ex hisce colligo. 1. Quòd cœlum istud terrae opponitur.
units.tr: Concerning the place of that heaven [ἀοχέον], into which God will receive us all, I gather the following for its definition. 1. That this heaven is set over against the earth.

units.la: 2. Quòd ut cæteras creaturas, ita quoque cœlum Deus creauisse dicitur.
units.tr: 2. That, like the other creatures, heaven too is said to have been created by God.

units.la: 3. Quòd cœlum ceu sedè & thronû Deus occupasse, terrā hominibus concessisse dicitur.
units.tr: 3. That God is said to have occupied heaven as his seat and throne, and to have granted the earth to men.

units.la: 4. Quòd cœlos apertos legimus.
units.tr: 4. That we read of the heavens being opened.

units.la: 5. Quòd idem instar pellis aut aulæi extensum dicitur.
units.tr: 5. That it is said to be stretched out like a skin or a curtain.

units.la: 6. Quòd Christus diserte locum uocat, Ioan.14.
units.tr: 6. That Christ expressly calls it a place, John 14.

units.la: 7. Quòd nemo pius unquam beatorum æternum ἀϊδίῳ[?] loco definiendum dubitauit.
units.tr: 7. That no pious person has ever doubted that the eternal dwelling of the blessed [ἀϊδίῳ] is to be defined as a place.

units.la: 8. Ut in terris, ita in cœlis creaturæ esse dicuntur, Col.1.
units.tr: 8. That creatures are said to be in heaven just as they are on earth, Col. 1.

units.la: 9. Quòd ut in terra, sic etiam in cœlo Dei creaturæ esse dicuntur.
units.tr: 9. That, just as on earth, so also in heaven God's creatures are said to exist.

units.la: 10. Quòd cœli & terra renouabuntur, non gloria.
units.tr: 10. That heaven and earth will be renewed, not destroyed.

units.la: 11. Quòd nobis orandum est, ut sicut in cœlis, ita etiam in terris fiat Dei uoluntas.
units.tr: 11. That we must pray that God's will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

units.la: 12. Quòd Christo data est omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra.
units.tr: 12. That all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ.

units.la: 13. Quòd cœlum sursum, terra deorsum esse dicitur.
units.tr: 13. That heaven is said to be above and earth below.

units.la: 14. Quòd ut terræ, ita cœlo extremitas tribuitur, Matt.13.
units.tr: 14. That, as with the earth, so with heaven, extremity is attributed to it, Matt. 13.

units.la: III. DE OPERIBVS DEI, uidelicet de creatione & conseruatione uniuersorum.
units.tr: III. ON THE WORKS OF GOD, namely on the creation and preservation of all things.

units.la: Qui fecit mare & aridam. Discimus hoc loco:
units.tr: Who made the sea and the dry land. From this place we learn:

units.la: 1. Creationem uniuersorum nobis cū Scriptura sancta statuedam, ne quis mun-dum æternum fingat.
units.tr: 1. That the creation of all things must be held along with holy Scripture, lest anyone imagine the world to be eternal.

units.la: 2. Iehouæ autem soli eam tribuedam: ne quis cum Manichæis statuat duos cō-ditores, Deum bonum, conditorem bo-narum rerum: & Deum malum, auctore malarum & noxiarum seu rerum, seu actionum.
units.tr: 2. That it must be ascribed to Jehovah alone, lest anyone, with the Manichaeans, posit two creators: a good God, the creator of good things, and an evil God, the author of evil and harmful things, whether of things or of actions.

units.la: 3. Nec ab eadem segregandam conser-vationem totius uniuersitatis, quæ à creatione λόγῳ solum differes, eius cōtinuatio, &, ut ita dicamus, perpetuatio quædam est. Notum est illud Christi: Pater meus usque adhuc operatur, & ego operor. Ioan.5.17.
units.tr: 3. Nor is the preservation of the whole universe to be separated from creation; it differs from creation only in reason [λόγῳ], being a kind of continuation and, as we may say, perpetuation of it. That saying of Christ is well known: "My Father is working until now, and I am working." John 5.17.

units.la: DE VERA RELIGIONE.
units.tr: ON TRUE RELIGION.

units.la: Occurrit in hoc uersu breuisima verę religionis descriptio, in phrasi, Iehouam timere: quam non decet nos præterire. Methodo autem didascalica, selectisi-ma Scripturæ dicta de timore Iehouæ disponemus.
units.tr: A very brief description of true religion occurs in this verse, in the phrase "to fear Jehovah," which we should not pass over. By a didactic method, we will arrange the most select sayings of Scripture about the fear of Jehovah.

units.la: 1. Distinctio uocis in sua significata. Timor Iehouæ quomodo sit distinguedus, ex hisce testimonijs liquet. Gen.31.42. Nisi Deus patris mei, Deus Abrahā, & Timor Isaac mihi adfuisset. Eodē cap.v.53. Juravit Jacob per Timore patris sui Isaac. Isa.8.13. Jehovam exercituum sanctifica-bitis: & ipse sit timor vester, & pavor vester. In his & similibus dictis, Jehovah ipse, μετωνυμίας, Timor dicitur. Ac pij eo nomine Timentes dicutur. Psal.15.4. Vilis est in oculis eius homo nihili, sed timē tes Jehovam honorat.
units.tr: 1. The distinction of the word in its senses. How the fear of Jehovah is to be distinguished is clear from these testimonies. Gen. 31.42: "Unless the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the Fear of Isaac had been with me." Likewise Gen. 31.53: "Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac." Isa. 8.13: "You shall sanctify Jehovah of hosts; let him be your fear, and let him be your dread." In these and similar sayings, Jehovah himself is called "Fear" by metonymy, and the godly are called "fearers" from that name. Ps. 15.4: "A worthless man is contemptible in his eyes, but he honours those who fear Jehovah."

units.la: 1. Joan.4.18. Timor non est in charita-te: expleta charitas foras eijcit timorem seu metum: quoniam timor cruciatū habet. qui autem timet, non est perfectus in charitate.
units.tr: 1 John 4.18: "There is no fear in love; perfect love casts out fear or dread, since fear has torment. He who fears is not perfect in love."

units.la: Discimus, aliud esse timorem Jehovae, qui cum fiducia misericordiae, charitate & gaudio (ob conscientiae pacem) coniungitur, & filialis, propter adoptionis Spiritum, recte dicitur: aliud metum seu timorem servilem, qui charitatis expers, κόλασιν habet. In hoc tamen dicto speciem χαρίσματος Spiritus sancti significat.
units.tr: We learn that the fear of Jehovah is one thing, which is joined with confidence in mercy, with love and joy (arising from the peace of conscience), and is rightly called filial, on account of the Spirit of adoption. Another is servile dread or fear, which lacks love and has punishment. Yet in this saying it signifies the form of a gift of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Interesse autem inter Timorem seu reverentiam & Metum, etiam Spartiata ille monuit, qui cum interrogatus esset, Cur Lacones promte in acie periclitarentur, respondit: ὅτι ἀνδρείαν[?] τὰς[?] ἡγεμόνας ἐμα-χόμεθα[?], φοβεῖσθαι. Saepe tamen promiscuè in Scripturis illa verba [?]ἀνδρεῖσθαι καὶ φοβεῖσθαι fumi, sequentia testabuntur.
