units.tr: The difference between fear, or reverence, and dread was also pointed out by that Spartan, who, when asked why the Laconians readily faced danger in battle, replied: "Because we fear our leaders" [φοβεῖσθαι]. Yet often in the Scriptures those words are used interchangeably, as the following will show.

units.la: Psal.112.10. Initium seu caput sapientiæ est timor Iehouæ. In hoc dicto veram religionem, quæ in reuerentia erga Deum posita est, significatā statuo: ac de hac præ-cipuè propositum nobis est, quædam secundum Scripturas proponere.
units.tr: Ps. 111.10 (Psal. 112.10): "The beginning, or chief part, of wisdom is the fear of Jehovah." In this saying I take true religion, which consists in reverence toward God, to be signified; and it is chiefly about this that we propose to set out certain things according to the Scriptures.

units.la: Alias timoris species nunc non attingam, qualis illa est Rom.13.7, Cui timore, timore: cū de religione nobis sit agendū.
units.tr: I will not now touch on other kinds of fear, such as that in Rom. 13.7 ("fear to whom fear is due"), since we are to speak of religion.

units.la: 2. Notatio, Verbum Hebræum יִרְאָה timuit, nomen ab eo descendens יִרְאָה timor, Apostoli vocant φόβον ἢ εὐλαβείαν [?]. Act.9.32. Ecclesiæ ædificabatur, pergetes in timore Domini, τῷ φόβῳ τοῦ κυρίου [?]. Heb.5.7. καὶ εἰσακουσθεὶς ὑπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείας [?]. Ideo homines religiosi εὐλαβεῖς dicuntur. Luc.2.25: Symeon ἄνθρωπος δίκαιος καὶ εὐλαβής. Act.8.2: Extulerunt autē unà Stephanum ἄνδρες εὐλαβεῖς.
units.tr: 2. Notation. The Hebrew verb יָרֵא "he feared," and the noun derived from it, יִרְאָה "fear," the Apostles render as φόβος or εὐλάβεια. Acts 9.31: "The church was built up, walking in the fear of the Lord" [τῷ φόβῳ τοῦ κυρίου]. Heb. 5.7: "and was heard because of his godly fear" [εὐλαβείας]. Thus religious men are called "devout" [εὐλαβεῖς]. Luke 2.25: Simeon was "a just and devout man" [εὐλαβής]. Acts 8.2: "devout men" [εὐλαβεῖς ἄνδρες] carried Stephen out together.

units.la: 3. An sit. Deum nobis timendum esse, hæc eius mandata testantur. 1.Pet.2.17. τὸν θεὸν φοβεῖσθε, Deum timete. Apoc.14.7. Timete Deum, & date ei gloriam.
units.tr: 3. Whether it is so. That God is to be feared, his commands testify. 1 Pet. 2.17: "Fear God" [τὸν θεὸν φοβεῖσθε]. Rev. 14.7: "Fear God, and give him glory."

units.la: Vt autem, Augustino teste, timor est humilium: ita Paulus negat, impios Deum timere, seu reuereri: Non est, dicens, Dei timor coram oculis eorū: Rom.3.18. Me-tuunt tuunt quidem male sibi conscij Deum ut iudicem &ἱλωτὴν[?], & fugiunt à conspectu eius: sed non reuerentur eum ut Dominum, nec diligunt ut Patrem. Econtrà pij regnum assumentes, quod cocuti nō potest, tenent gratiam, per quam ita seruiunt Deo, ut ei placeant, cum reuerentia & religione. Heb.12.28.
units.tr: But, as Augustine testifies, fear belongs to the humble; so Paul denies that the wicked fear God, or revere him: "There is no fear of God before their eyes," Rom. 3.18. Those who are conscious of evil indeed fear God as judge and avenger, and flee from his sight; but they do not revere him as Lord, nor love him as Father. On the contrary, the godly, receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, hold fast to grace, by which they so serve God that they please him with reverence and godly fear. Heb. 12.28.

units.la: 4. Pulcerrimæ autem finitiones timoris Dei, κατ' ἐπαῖνον[?] & aliæ, passim in Scripturis sanctis occurrunt, inter quas hæc sunt. Prou.8.13. Timor Iehouæ est, odio habere malum, superbiam & arrogantiam, & uiam malam, & os loquens peruersita tes odi. Hæc est descriptio κατ' ἀφαίρεσιν τῆς σύνταξις[?], quæ congerie pugnantium constat. Pro.1.7.&9.10. Principium sapientiæ timor Iehouæ: & scientia sanctorum, intelligentia. Finitio ἀληθινὸς[?]. Vera enim Sapientia, quæ in Dei & nostri cognitione posita est, causa προσηγορικὴ[?] est timoris Dei. Pro.14.27. Timor Iehouæ, uena uitæ, ut recedatur à laqueis mortis. Finitio à salutari effectu, q̄ est euitare mortis laqueos.
units.tr: 4. The most beautiful definitions of the fear of God, both by praise and otherwise, occur throughout the holy Scriptures; among them are these. Prov. 8.13: "The fear of Jehovah is to hate evil, pride and arrogance, the evil way, and a mouth speaking perverse things." This is a description by negation, made up of a heap of opposites. Prov. 1.7 and 9.10: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Jehovah; and the knowledge of the holy is understanding." This is a true definition, for true wisdom, which lies in the knowledge of God and of ourselves, is the proper cause of the fear of God. Prov. 14.27: "The fear of Jehovah is a fountain of life, so that one turns away from the snares of death." This is a definition from its saving effect, which is to avoid the snares of death.

units.la: Hoc autem loco Timor Dei significat reuerentiam, quam prælucente fide, Deo tanquam Domino, serui religiosè præstamus, adipsius gloriam noftramq; emen-dationem.
units.tr: In this passage, the fear of God signifies the reverence which, with faith shining forth, we servants render religiously to God as Lord, for his glory and our own amendment.

units.la: 5. Τὸ ὅτι,
units.tr: 5. The "that" [Τὸ ὅτι].

units.la: Αἴτιον λύριον[?] est Deus, iuxta hæc dicta: Isa. 11.2. Spiritus scientiæ & timoris Dei. Hoc dictum monet id quod scite Lactantius alicubi dixit: Nullam sine veritate religionem esse posse. Scientia enim in dicto Isaiæ significat veram Dei agnitionem, quæ à religione seiungi nequit. Ier. 32. 40. Timorem meum dabo in corde eorum, ut non recedant à me. Hic unicus veriusculus efficientem principem causam timoris Dei, Iehouam: ὑπομένων[?], cor: finem, nō recedere à Iehouah, copletitur.
units.tr: The efficient cause is God, according to these sayings. Isa. 11.2: "The Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of God." This saying recalls what Lactantius somewhere well said: that there can be no religion without truth. For knowledge in Isaiah's saying signifies the true knowledge of God, which cannot be separated from religion. Jer. 32.40: "I will put my fear in their heart, so that they do not depart from me." Here the one true principal efficient cause of the fear of God, Jehovah, is set out; the subject is the heart; and the end, not to depart from Jehovah.

units.la: Προηγουμένη[?] tradita est in hoc dicto: Itaq; si Patrem cognominatis eū qui citra personarum respectum iudicat ex cuiusque opere, cum timore uersamini commorationis uestræ tempore: 1. Pet. 1.17. Reuereri nos decet eum Patrem, qui ἀπροσωπο-λήμψως[?] iudicat.
units.tr: The first cause is set out in this saying: "So if you call on him as Father, who judges without respect of persons according to each one's work, pass the time of your sojourning in fear." 1 Pet. 1.17. "We ought to revere that Father who judges without partiality" [ἀπροσωπολήμπτως].

units.la: Forma, ἐν ἁπλότητι καρδίας Deum timereut de seruis dicitur Col.3.22. Cum autem contrariorum sit eadem doctrina, ex querela Domini apud Malachiam colligere licet forma timoris Domini, Mal.1.6. Filius honorat patrem,& seruus dominũ suum(timet.) Quòd si Pater ego sum,ubi est honor mei?& si Dominus sum, ubi est timor mei? Colligimus formá uerę religionis esse, Deum ut Patre quidé fide honorare,ut autem Dominum per fidem reuereri. Sic enim diligi à nobis uult, ut non absit debita reuerentia.
units.tr: The form of the fear of God is said of servants: "serving with singleness of heart" (Col. 3.22). Since the teaching of contraries is the same, we may gather the form of the fear of the Lord from the Lord's complaint through Malachi. Mal. 1.6: "A son honours his father, and a servant his lord (fears him). If then I am Father, where is my honour? And if I am Lord, where is my fear?" We gather that the form of true religion is to honour God indeed by faith as Father, but to revere him as Lord through faith. For he wishes to be loved by us in such a way that due reverence is not absent.

units.la: Materia in qua, seu subiectum timoris Dei,est Cor fide purificatum. Vt enim corde credimus ad iusticiam,Rom.10.10. ita corde reueremur Deum. Atque eo sanè nomine Deus eorum religionem & cultum damnat, qui ore, non autem corde, Deo appropinquant: Matt.15.8.Isa.29.13. Et supra adduxi uerba Domini apud Ieremiam: Dabo timorem meum in corde eorum:cap.32.40.
units.tr: The matter in which, or the subject of, the fear of God is the heart purified by faith. For as with the heart we believe unto righteousness (Rom. 10.10), so with the heart we revere God. And indeed under this name God condemns the religion and worship of those who draw near to God with the mouth, not with the heart (Matt. 15.8; Isa. 29.13). And above I have adduced the words of the Lord through Jeremiah: "I will put my fear in their heart," ch. 32.40.

units.la: Fines proximi sunt: Perficere sanctificationem in timore Dei.2.Cor.7.1. Item, Cum timore & tremore salute suam conficere.Phil.2.12.
units.tr: The nearer ends are: to perfect sanctification in the fear of God (2 Cor. 7.1); likewise, to work out one's salvation "with fear and trembling" (Phil. 2.12).

units.la: Vltimus finis est,gloria Dei. Isa.8.13. Ie houam exercituum sanctificabitis:& ipse sit timor uester,& ipse pauor uester.
units.tr: The ultimate end is the glory of God. Isa. 8.13: "You shall sanctify Jehovah of hosts; let him be your fear, and let him be your dread."

units.la: 6. Cognata (si speciem spectes) sunt χαρίσμα]α[?] cętera Spiritus sancti,de quibus Ifa.ii.2. Requiescet super eum Spiritus Iehouæ, Spiritus sapientiæ & intelligentiæ, Spiritus consilij & fortitudinis, Spiritus scientiæ & timoris Iehouæ. Item 1.Pet. 3.15. Dominum autem Deum sanctificate in cordibus vestris. Estote autem semper parati ad respondendum cuilibet petenti rationem eius spei, quæ in vobis est, μετὰ πραΰτητος καὶ φόβου.
units.tr: 6. Cognate (if you look at the species) are the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, concerning which Isa. 11.2: "The Spirit of Jehovah shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Jehovah." Likewise 1 Pet. 3.15: "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Be always ready to answer anyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear" [μετὰ πραΰτητος καὶ φόβου].

units.la: 7. Pugnantia. Cum vero Dei timore pugnat, Epicureus Dei contemtus, quem ἄθεοι seu verbis & factis, ut Iulianus apostata: seu factis, non verbis, ut Pseudochristiani, profitentur. Ac de his dicitur Tit.1.16. Deum profitentur se scire, sed factis negant, quum sint abominandi & rebelles, & ad omne opus reprobi. De illis autem idem Apostolus: Non, ait, est timor Dei ante oculos eorum: Rom.3.18. Item: Dixit insanus in corde suo, Nō est Deus: corrupti sunt, abominabiles facti sunt studio, non est qui bene agat. Psal.14.1.
units.tr: 7. Contraries. Contempt of God opposes the fear of God. This is professed by the Epicurean and by atheists, either in words and deeds, like the apostate Julian, or in deeds but not words, like false Christians. Of these Titus 1.16 says: "They profess that they know God, but by their works they deny him, since they are abominable and rebellious, and reprobate for every good work." Of such the same Apostle says: "There is no fear of God before their eyes" (Rom. 3.18). Likewise: "The fool has said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have become abominable in their doing; there is none who does good." Ps. 14.1.

units.la: Pugnat etiam cum Dei timore uitiosus metus, seu Pseudoprophetarum, Leuit.18.22. uel aliorum minacium hominum, 1.Pet.3.14. Item, contraria timori ὑψηλο-φρονοῦντες[?], de qua Paulus: Ne effertor animo, sed time:Rom.11.20. Atqui haec hactenus [illegible, ~12 letters] Dominus det, ut ipsum solum toto corde, per fidem, reuereamur.
units.tr: Also opposed to the fear of God is sinful dread, whether of false prophets (Lev. 18.22 or similar) or of other threatening men (1 Pet. 3.14). Likewise, contrary to fear is being high-minded, of which Paul says: "Do not be haughty in mind, but fear" (Rom. 11.20). And so far these things [illegible]. May the Lord grant that we revere him alone with the whole heart, through faith.

units.la: VERSVS X.
units.tr: VERSE 10.

units.la: Timuerunt ergo uiri illi timore ingenti, & dixerunt ei: Cur hoc fecisti? sciebant enim uiri illi, quòd à facie Iehouæ fugeret: nam indicauerat ipsis.
units.tr: Those men therefore feared with great fear and said to him: "Why have you done this?" For those men knew that he was fleeing from the face of Jehovah, because he had told them so.

units.la: Ex antecedentibus & cōsequentibus liquet, τὰς συμπλέοντας[?] istos nequaquam prorsus alienos fuisse à ueri Dei agnitione & cultu, plurimum etiam in Crucis schola, in qua τὰ παθήματα fiunt μαθήματα, profecisse. Iuxta illud: Bonū est mihi Domine, quòd me humiliasti, ut discerem iustificationes tuas. Psal.119.
units.tr: From what precedes and what follows it is clear that those sailors were by no means entirely alien to the knowledge and worship of the true God, and that they had made considerable progress in the school of the cross, in which sufferings [τὰ παθήματα] become lessons [μαθήματα]. Accordingly: "It is good for me, O Lord, that you have humbled me, that I might learn your statutes." Ps. 119.

units.la: Thesis: Sensum irae Dei aduersus peccatum, ingens fidelium & aliorum consternatio, & alij motus sequuntur, cum sæpe unius ob noxiam multi alij malis publicis inuoluantur.
units.tr: Thesis: The sense of God's wrath against sin, great consternation among believers and others, and other emotions follow, since often, because of the offence of one person, many others are caught up in public calamities.

units.la: QVI MOTVS DIVINITVS EXcitantur in cordibus contritis hominum, qui non sunt ἀμετανόητοι[?];
units.tr: WHAT MOVEMENTS ARE STIRRED DIVINELY IN THE HEARTS OF CONTRITE PEOPLE, WHO ARE NOT unrepentant [ἀμετανόητοι]?

units.la: Hi de quibus Apostolus 2.Cor.7.10. ἡ γὰρ κατὰ[?] θεὸν λύπη μετάνοιαν εἰς σωτηρίαν ἀμέ[?]α-
units.tr: Those of whom the Apostle speaks, 2 Cor. 7:10: "For godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, not to be regretted" [ἡ γὰρ κατὰ θεὸν λύπη μετάνοιαν εἰς σωτηρίαν ἀμεταμέλητον].

units.la: μίλλ︎ονος ... (see note)
units.tr: ... (see note)

units.la: Quartò, metum, immò timorem, di-stis, factis & gestibus sic declarauerūt, ut nō solùm mortis metum, sed etiam Deo debitam reverentiam probarent.
units.tr: Fourthly, by their words, deeds and gestures they showed fear, indeed dread, so that they proved not only a fear of death but also the reverence owed to God.

units.la: Quintò, desiderij illud erat, quòd dicentes, Cur hoc fecisti? significarunt, se unicè hoc optare, ne factum illud unquam esset admissum.
units.tr: Fifthly, there was desire; for by saying, "Why have you done this?" they signified that they wished above all that this deed had never been committed.

units.la: Sextò, zeli erat, de tanti peccati expia-tione ferió & solicitè laborare.
units.tr: Sixthly, there was zeal: they laboured earnestly and anxiously to make expiation for so great a sin.

units.la: Postremò, quomodo ἐνδικῶς[?], seu vin-dicationem Deo probârint, Iona in mare misso, sequentia testantur.
units.tr: Lastly, they showed their justice [ἐνδικῶς], or vindication, toward God, as the following verses testify, when Jonah had been thrown into the sea.

units.la: Etsi autem ex superioribus liquet, ple-rosq; qui in eadem cum Iona naui erant, Ethnicos fuisse: cuius rei argumentum fuit, quòd singuli sua numina inuocauisse dicuntur: credibile tamen est, quosdam ex illis, malis istis doctos, profecisse in agnitione veri Dei, sic ut ei postea incolumitate acceptam ferentes, σωτήρια[?] immo larent. Interea statuo, Pauli dictū nō nisi ad eos q in Ecclesia sunt, referri debere.
units.tr: Although it is clear from what has gone before that most of those who were in the same ship as Jonah were Gentiles, the evidence for this being that each is said to have invoked his own gods, it is nevertheless credible that some of them, taught by those evils, advanced in the knowledge of the true God, so that afterwards, ascribing their safety to him, they offered sacrifices of salvation [σωτήρια], or rather praised him. Meanwhile I hold that Paul's saying must be referred only to those who are in the Church.

units.la: QVI AVTEM MOTVS EXCITAN-tur sensu irę Dei aduersus peccata, in cordibus hominum non renatorum?
units.tr: WHAT MOVEMENTS ARE STIRRED BY the sense of God's wrath against sins in the hearts of unregenerate men?

units.la: Primarius & generalis est, λύπης ἀδοῦς[?], trifticia mundi mortem afferes. Hæcsub se continet φόβου, seu metum impenden-tium pœnarum, fremitum aduersus iudi-cium Dei, & desperationem: ut testantur exempla Caini, Ahitophelis, Saulis, Iudæ proditoris, & similium.
units.tr: The primary and general one is worldly sorrow [λύπη τοῦ κόσμου], which brings death. This contains fear, that is dread of impending punishments, murmuring against the judgment of God, and despair, as the examples of Cain, Ahithophel, Saul, Judas the traitor, and similar cases testify.

units.la: Ex ijs autē quæ iam sunt dicta, liquet, quonam magistratui sit respiciendum, si quando negocium illi est cum ijs homi-nibus, qui pœnas publicas & capitales transgresione legum promeriti sunt.
units.tr: From what has now been said it is clear to what the magistrate must look when he has to deal with those men who have deserved public and capital punishment by transgressing the laws.

units.la: Reorum duo sunt genera: unum eorū qui trifticia secundum Deum afficiuntur, alterum eorum qui dolore mundi percel luntur.
units.tr: Offenders are of two kinds: one of those who are affected with sorrow according to God, the other of those who are overwhelmed by the sorrow of the world.

units.la: Magistratus erga utrosque probet pri-mùm se dignam ἀσεβείας, cum sunt perue-stiganda scelera: deinde ἀπολογίαν, ut probet se alienum ab eorum contagione, Deut. 21. 7. 8. tertiò ἀγανάκτησιν, seu νέμεσιν aduersus manifestam turpitudinē: quar-tò φόβον, ne unius ob noxiam non expia-tam Deus in omnes animaduertat: quin-tò ἐπιπόθησιν, desiderium probandi Deo integritatem: sextò, zelum pro gloria Dei; postremò ἐνδίκησιν, seu iu-stam ultionem.
units.tr: The magistrate, toward both kinds, should: (1) first show that he is worthy of hostility to impiety, when crimes are to be investigated; (2) then offer a defence [ἀπολογίαν], to show that he is free from their contagion, Deut. 21:7-8; (3) thirdly, show indignation, or retribution [νέμεσιν], against manifest baseness; (4) fourthly, feel fear, lest God punish everyone for one unexpiated offence; (5) fifthly, feel longing, the desire to prove his integrity before God; (6) sixthly, show zeal for the glory of God; and lastly, pursue just vengeance [ἐνδίκησιν].

units.la: VERSVS XI.
units.tr: VERSE 11.

units.la: Dixerunt ad eum: Quid faciemus ti-bi,ut sileat mare a nobis? Nam mare ibat & intumescebat.
units.tr: They said to him: What shall we do to you, that the sea may be quiet toward us? For the sea was growing rougher and swelling.

units.la: 1. Sontes eò adducedi sunt, ut nulla se iniuria affici intelligant,cum poenas dare coguntur. Peccant itaq; magistratus,qui sic saeuiunt in reos,ut fatali casu se opprimi putent,non autem poenas scelerum se dare animaduertat,cum nemo sit qui de magnitudine peccatorum,& de ira Dei aduersus illa, de lege diuina,miseros erudiat.
units.tr: 1. Sinners are to be brought to the point where they understand that no injury is done to them when they are compelled to pay penalties. Magistrates therefore sin when they rage against the guilty in such a way that the guilty think they are crushed by a chance fate, and do not perceive that they are paying the penalty for their crimes, since there is no one to instruct these wretched people about the greatness of sins, about the wrath of God against them, and about the divine law.

units.la: 2. Si adhibeatur grauis & tempestiua conscientiae appellatio,fructuilla non cerebit,siue eos qui resipiscunt, siue <bl>τὰς ἀμε- μετανοήτως</bl> spectes. Nam illi quidem,cum se peccauisse intelligat, iram Dei portabut, & Deo gloriam dabunt, spectatores autem & exemplo tristissimo & exhortatione a licentia peccandi dehortabuntur:hi uero,ut maxime se reos esse profiteri recusent,tamen in cordibus suis couincentur.
units.tr: 2. If a grave and timely appeal is made to the conscience, that fruit will not be lacking, whether you look at those who repent or at those who are unrepentant [ἀμετανόητοι]. For the former, when they understand that they have sinned, will bear the wrath of God and give glory to God; the spectators, however, will be turned away from licence in sinning by the most sorrowful example and by exhortation; while these, however much they refuse to profess themselves guilty, will nevertheless be convicted in their own hearts.

units.la: 3. Conscientiae appellationem <bl>αὐτοψίαν</bl>, & sensus publice,ob unius noxa,grassantium poenarum, efficacissimam reddit. Ideo nauigantes cum Iona maris tempestatem non sine summo horrore aspiciebant, uelut in oculos incurrens irae Dei τεκμήριον.
units.tr: 3. The appeal to conscience, together with the public sense of punishments raging because of one man's offence, makes it most effective. Therefore the sailors with Jonah beheld the tempest of the sea not without great horror, as a sign [τεκμήριον] of God's wrath running into their very eyes, an eyewitness [αὐτοψίαν].

units.la: 4. Nec syllogismus, a finali causa (Vt sileat mare a nobis) ductus, nobis praetereundus est. Non est aequum, ut insontes, sontium causa non modo periclitentur de uita, sed etiam pereant. Tu hac in parte reus es,nos uero innoxij. Quid igitur faciemus tibi, ut sileat mare a nobis? Huiusmodi ratiocinatione se quoq; conuictum sensit Dauid, cum peste grassante ob a se numeratum populum, precaretur: An non ego iussi numerari populum? & ego ipse sum qui peccaui, & male agendo male egi: istae autem oues quid fecerunt? O Iehouah Deus mi, sit quaeso manus tua in me & in domum patris mei, & in populum tuum ne sit plaga. 1.Paral.21.17.
units.tr: 4. Nor must we pass over the syllogism drawn from the final cause ("That the sea may be quiet toward us"). It is not fair that the innocent should be endangered of life, and even perish, for the sake of the guilty. You are guilty in this matter, but we are innocent. What then shall we do to you, that the sea may be quiet toward us? David too felt himself convicted by such reasoning, when, with plague raging because of the people he had numbered, he prayed: "Was it not I who commanded the people to be numbered? It is I who have sinned and done wrong; but these sheep, what have they done? O Jehovah my God, let your hand, I pray, be against me and against my father's house, but let there be no plague on your people." 1.Paral.21.17.

units.la: DE CONSCIENTIA.
units.tr: ON CONSCIENCE.

units.la: Conscientiam, Apostoli significantissimi mé συνείδησιν uocarunt: a uerbo συνοίδα, mihi conscius sum. Plato: ὁ σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ σοφὸς ὤν. ἄλλην γὰρ ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα· ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ ἀδικήματι[?]. Nullius enim rei mihi conscius sum: us sum: sed non per hoc iustificatus sum. 1.Cor.4.4. Dicitur etiam συνειδένα: unde ὁ συνειδὼς, conscius: καὶ τὸ συνειδὸς, conscientia. Chrysost. ἀδῆν ἔτως σύφφαίνειν εἰώθην: ὡς συνειδὸς λαθαρόν. De mala conscientia dicitur: καὶ ἐνοσφίσατο ἀπὸ τῆς τιμῆς: συνειδήσας, καὶ τῆς γυναικὸς αὐτῆς. Act.5.2.
units.tr: The Apostles, most expressive writers, called it syneidesin [συνείδησιν], from the verb synoida, I am conscious to myself. Plato says: "being wise, I am conscious to myself" [ὁ σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ σοφὸς ὤν]. For "I am conscious to myself of nothing else, but in the wrong" [ἄλλην γὰρ ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα· ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ ἀδικήματι]. "For I am conscious of nothing against myself; yet I am not thereby justified." 1 Cor. 4:4. The word syneidenai is also used, whence ho syneidōs, the one who is conscious, and to syneidos, conscience. Chrysostom: "I am accustomed to speak in this way, as a clear conscience" [ἀδῆν ἔτως σύφφαίνειν εἰώθην: ὡς συνειδὸς λαθαρόν]. Of an evil conscience it is said: "and he kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it" [καὶ ἐνοσφίσατο ἀπὸ τῆς τιμῆς, συνειδήσας καὶ τῆς γυναικὸς αὐτῆς]. Acts 5:2.

units.la: Iam ut doctrina de conscientia illustri-or sit, methodo ἐξηγήσει[?] eam exponemus. Dominus Jesus excitet in nobis & conferuet bonae conscientiae studium, ne unquam eo abiecto, etiam a fide aberremus, & ad μαλθαπολογίαν[?] deflectamus.
units.tr: So that the doctrine of conscience may be clearer, we shall set it out by a method of explanation [ἐξηγήσει]. May the Lord Jesus stir up in us, and preserve, the zeal for a good conscience, so that, casting that aside, we never stray even from the faith and turn aside to vain talk [μαλθαπολογίαν].

units.la: Propositum nobis est, Conscientiae finitionem petere ex hisce Pauli Apostoli verbis: οἵτινες ἐνδεικνύνται τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου γραπτὸν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν, συμμαρτυρούσης αὐτῶν τῆς συνειδήσεως, καὶ μεταξὺ ἀλλήλων τῶν λογισμῶν κατηγορούντων ἢ καὶ ἀπολογουμένων. Ut qui ostendant opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, una testimonium reddete eorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus, aut etiam excusantibus. Rom.2.15.
units.tr: Our purpose is to seek the definition of conscience from these words of the Apostle Paul: "who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness with them, and their thoughts between themselves accusing or else excusing one another" [οἵτινες ἐνδεικνύνται τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου γραπτὸν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν, συμμαρτυρούσης αὐτῶν τῆς συνειδήσεως, καὶ μεταξὺ ἀλλήλων τῶν λογισμῶν κατηγορούντων ἢ καὶ ἀπολογουμένων]. Rom. 2:15.

units.la: In his verbis observabimus ordine:
units.tr: In these words we shall observe the following in order:

units.la: 1. Definitum, videlicet conscientiam, quę est, ut Scholastici dicebant, adplicata scientia. Cum enim scientia actu primo, quae veluti somno sepulta in homine latebat, excitata obiecto aliquo ceu impellente causa, & expergefacta, hominem afficit, fit conscientia actu secundo. Nocrat Cain fratrem non esse interficiendum: sed haec noticia aliquamdiu in eo latuit, do nec excitata & applicata ad facinus admissum, conscientia esse coepit. τὸ καθόλου, verbi gratia, Summa cum diligentia officio nostro scholastico nobis defungendum esse, scimus omnes. Sed τὸ καθ' ἕκαστον, videlicet, mihi pia docendo, vobis eadem discendo, officium faciendum, conscientia dictat.
units.tr: 1. The definition, namely that conscience is, as the Scholastics used to say, applied knowledge. For when the knowledge which at first lies hidden in a person, as if buried in sleep, is aroused by some object, as by an impelling cause, and awakened, and affects the person, it becomes conscience in the second act. For example, Cain knew that his brother should not be killed; but this knowledge lay hidden in him for some time, until, aroused and applied to a deed committed, it began to be conscience. Thus, for instance, the general principle [τὸ καθόλου], that we must all discharge our scholastic duty with the greatest diligence, we all know. But the particular [τὸ καθ' ἕκαστον], that I must perform the duty of teaching you piously and you must learn the same, conscience dictates.

units.la: 1. Genus est, μαρτυρικόν. 2.Cor.1.12. τὸ μαρτύριον τῆς συνειδήσεως. Inde natum est proverbium: Conscientia mille testes. Et nō tum est illud Augustini dictum: Conscientia est codex, in quo quotidiana peccata conscribuntur. Sed meminerimus, etiam recte facta in eode codice annotari. Notum est τὸ
units.tr: 1. The genus is witnessing [μαρτυρικόν]. 2 Cor. 1:12: "the testimony of conscience" [τὸ μαρτύριον τῆς συνειδήσεως]. From this has arisen the proverb: "Conscience is a thousand witnesses." And that saying of Augustine is also true: "Conscience is a codex in which daily sins are written down." But let us remember that good deeds too are noted in that same codex. Well known is the line:

units.la: Hic murus aheneus esto,
units.tr: Let this be a bronze wall for me,

units.la: Nil conscire sibi, & nulla pallescere culpa.
units.tr: to be conscious of nothing to oneself, and not to turn pale at any fault.

units.la: 3. Differentia, quae respondet operi Legis, id est, Legi cordibus hominum diuinitus nitùs inscriptæ. Sed addere conuenit lumen fidei, in Euangelio accensum. iuxta dictum: Accedamus cum uero corde, & certa persuasione fidei, puris cordibus à conscientia mala. Hebr.10.22. Nam utin omnibus hominibus Legi naturæ, uelu-ti προσφάτου καὶ ἐφ' ὑπολιωνῆς[?], conscientia re-spondet:ita in filijs Dei, lumini fidei religiosè assentitur conscietia bona, & asper-sione sanguinis Christi emundata.
units.tr: 3. The difference, which corresponds to the work of the Law, that is, the Law divinely inscribed in the hearts of men. But it is fitting to add the light of faith, kindled in the Gospel, according to the saying: "Let us draw near with a true heart, in full assurance of faith, with hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience." Heb. 10:22. For just as in all men conscience answers to the law of nature, as to something fresh and [ἐφ' ὑπολιωνῆς?], so in the sons of God a good conscience assents devoutly to the light of faith and is cleansed by the sprinkling of Christ's blood.

units.la: Superuacaneam autem esse Scholasti-corum disputationem, de conscientia seu ad mentem, seu ad uoluntatem restrin-genda, cum ad utramq; referri debeat, ut Apostolus noster docuit, cum Menti iun-xit Conscietiam, de profanis hominibus loquens: Pollutis & infidelibus nihil est purum: sed polluta est eorum & mens & conscientia. Tit.1.15 [?].
units.tr: The disputation of the Scholastics, whether conscience is to be confined to the mind or to the will, is superfluous; for it ought to be referred to both, as our Apostle taught when, speaking of profane men, he joined conscience to the mind: "To the polluted and unbelieving nothing is pure, but both their mind and their conscience are polluted." Titus 1:15.

units.la: Constat, intelligetiam distingui secun-dum ea, circa quæ uersatur. Itaq; Nss in-telligentia θεωρητική[?], seu in contemplando occupata, est: & συλλογιστικὴ[?], propositionum legalium promum & condum complec-titur. Conscientia autem intelligentia πρακτική[?] est: & assumptiones ac complé-xiones subiugit & adplicat. Nec omnino male ideò Scholastici dixerunt; Conscientiam esse cum aliquo scientiam.
units.tr: It is agreed that intelligence is distinguished according to the things with which it is concerned. Thus intelligence which is theoretical [θεωρητική], occupied in contemplation, and syllogistic [συλλογιστικὴ], embraces the premises of the law, both taking and setting them forth. Conscience, however, is practical intelligence [πρακτική], and it subjoins and applies the assumptions and conclusions. Nor did the Scholastics speak wholly amiss when they said that conscience is knowledge together with something else.

units.la: 4. ὑπονόημα? est cor hominis, iuxta dicta: Et per hoc cognoscimus nos ex veritate esse, & coram ipso secura reddemus corda nostra. Nam si nos condemnet cor nostrum, potentior est Deus corde nostro, & novit omnia. Charissimi, si cor nostrū nos non condemnet, fiduciam habemus apud Deum. 1.Ioan.3.19.20.21. Recte itaque Philippus Melanchthon dicere solitus est, Conscientia esse in intellectu, &c.
units.tr: 4. The heart of man [ὑπονόημα?] is conscience, according to the words: "And by this we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him. For if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things. Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God." 1 John 3:19–21. Rightly, therefore, Philip Melanchthon used to say that conscience is in the intellect, etc.

units.la: 5. Materia circa quam, est legis operū & fidei observatio aut violatio. 1.Petr.3.16: Conscientiam bonam habentes, ut pro eo quod loquuntur adversus uos tanquam malefi-cos, pudefiat qui incessiunt uestram bonam in Christo conversationem. 1.Tim.4.2: In hypocrisi loquentium mendacium, & cauteriatā habentium conscientiā.
units.tr: 5. The matter with which conscience is concerned is the observance or violation of the works of the law and of faith. 1 Pet. 3:16: "having a good conscience, so that, in the things in which they speak against you as evildoers, those who revile your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame." 1 Tim. 4:2: "speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared with a hot iron."

units.la: 6. Propria conscientiæ sunt, primum testificari, secundum convincere, postremū obligare. iuxta hæc dicta: Simul attestan te eorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuò accusantibus aut excusantibus: Rom.2.15. Item: εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἀναπολογήτους[?]. Rom.1.20.
units.tr: 6. The proper functions of conscience are: first, to bear witness; second, to convict; last, to oblige. According to these words: "their conscience bearing witness with them, and their thoughts between themselves accusing or else excusing one another," Rom. 2:15. Likewise: "so that they are without excuse" [εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἀναπολογήτους]. Rom. 1:20.

units.la: Adiunctum conscientiae est, ratiocinari. Ideo enim Syllogismus practicus recte uocatur ab eodem Melanchthone. Cum autem Paulus λογιζόμεθα[?], pro συλλογιζόμεθα, dicat, Rom.3.28. uelim mihi non uitio dari, quòd in uerbis eiusdem Apostoli, Rom.2.15. λογισμοὺς[?] de syllogismis practicis accipiendos duco: cum res sit manifesta. Neque enim solùm cogitando, sed etiam aliud ex alio recte καὶ συλλογίζως[?] colligendo, conscientia suo in nobis munere defungitur. Duo hoc loco breuiter & dilucidè mihi tradenda statuo. Alterum est, quo pacto argumentetur conscientia: alterum, quotuplices eius syllogismi sint. Neq; uerò dubito, his duobus capitibus uerè expositis, illustrata iri totam de conscientia doctrinam.
units.tr: Reasoning belongs to conscience. For this reason Melanchthon rightly calls it the practical syllogism. But since Paul says "we reason" [λογιζόμεθα] for "we conclude by syllogism" [συλλογιζόμεθα], Rom. 3:28, I would wish not to be faulted for taking the word "reasonings" [λογισμούς] in the words of the same Apostle, Rom. 2:15, to mean practical syllogisms, since the matter is plain. For conscience discharges its office in us not only by thinking, but also by rightly drawing one thing from another by syllogism [καὶ συλλογίζως]. I resolve to set out two things here briefly and clearly. The first is how conscience reasons; the second is how many kinds of syllogism it has. Nor do I doubt that, once these two heads are truly explained, the whole doctrine of conscience will be made clear.

units.la: Si quando ἀδιαφόρων[?] scientia τῶν πρακτικῶν[?] ad hoc uel illud πρακτικόν[?] adplicatur actu, tunc in homine fit συνείδησις conscientia, uel de eo quod bonum est prosequendo, uel de malo fugiendo. Idem iudicium est de bonis uel malis iam peractis.
units.tr: When the knowledge of indifferent things [ἀδιαφόρων] of the practical kind [τῶν πρακτικῶν] is actually applied to this or that practical matter [πρακτικόν], then in the person there arises conscience [συνείδησις], either in pursuing what is good or in fleeing what is evil. The same judgment holds concerning good or evil deeds already done.

units.la: Iam uerò quemadmodum cum ratiocinamur in speculabilibus, tum tria concurrunt: Habitus principiorum seu Intellectus primum, deinde Διανοία seu ratio, postremo Scientia: & Intellectus quidem praebet Maiorem. verbi gratia: Omne totum est maius sua parte. Διανοία vero circa singularia discurrens, subsumit Minorem. ut: Circulus respectu semicirculi est totum. Scientia denique Complexioni insistens, colligit, Circulum semicirculo esse maiorem. Ita cum περὶ τῶν πραγμάτων argumentamur, haec tria itidem concurrunt. Primum Σύλληψις[?], Maiorem e Lege divina promens: Nemini inferenda est injuria. deinde Ratio, Minorem subiungens: Rem autem alienam invito domino accipere, injuria est. Conscientia tertio loco Complexionem dictat: Itaque a nullo res auferri debet ipso invito.
units.tr: Now, just as when we reason about speculative matters three things concur: first the habit of principles, or intellect; then discursive reason [Διανοία]; last, knowledge. The intellect supplies the major premise, for example: "every whole is greater than its part." Discursive reason, running through particulars, supplies the minor, for example: "a circle, with respect to a semicircle, is a whole." Finally knowledge, resting on the conclusion, infers that a circle is greater than a semicircle. So when we reason about practical matters, these three likewise concur. First, apprehension [Σύλληψις] sets forth the major premise from the divine law: "No one is to be wronged." Then reason adds the minor: "To take another's property against the owner's will is a wrong." Third, conscience dictates the conclusion: "Therefore nothing ought to be taken from anyone against his own will."

units.la: Quod si quis fines spectet, duo esse genera syllogismorum practicorum conscientiae animadvertet. Unum eorum, qui sunt ἀπολογητικοί: alterum eorum, qui sunt κατηγορικοί[?]. Diserte enim dicit Paulus: καὶ μεταξὺ ἀλλήλων τῶν λογισμῶν κατηγορούντων ἢ καὶ ἀπολογουμένων.
units.tr: If one considers the ends, one will notice that there are two kinds of practical syllogisms of conscience: one of those which are apologetic [ἀπολογητικοί], and the other of those which are accusatory [κατηγορικοί]. For Paul says plainly: "and their thoughts between themselves accusing or else excusing one another."

units.la: EXEMPLA SYLLOGIS-morum Apologeticorum.
units.tr: EXAMPLES OF APOLOGETIC SYLLOGISMS.

units.la: Sic argumentatur Paulus in apologia sua:
units.tr: Paul argues thus in his apology:

units.la: Quicunq; bonam habet conscientiam coram Deo, eos non est cur sanctae vocationis fideliter susceptae & administratae pudeat pigeatve.
units.tr: Whoever has a good conscience before God has no reason to be ashamed or weary of the holy calling faithfully received and administered.

units.la: Viri fratres, ego omni conscientia bona conuersatus sum ante Deum usq; in hodiernum diem. Act.23.1.
units.tr: Men and brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience up to this day. Acts 23.1.

units.la: Quare non est cur Apostolici muneris me pudeat,&c.
units.tr: Therefore there is no reason for me to be ashamed of the apostolic office, etc.

units.la: Dauid sic argumentatur 1.Sam.26.
units.tr: David argues thus, 1 Sam. 26.

units.la: Non est pij Principis, bene de se & de patria meritum hostiliter persequi.
units.tr: It is not the part of a pious prince to persecute with hostility one who has deserved well of himself and of his country.

units.la: Ego vero & bene meritus sum, & porro quoq; bene mereri de te, ô Rex, & de toto regno Israelis paratus sum.
units.tr: But I have deserved well, and I am also ready to go on deserving well of you, O King, and of the whole kingdom of Israel.

units.la: Quare non erat cur me persequereris? Vt quid dominus meus persequitur servum suum? quid enim feci? & quod in manu mea malum?v.18.
units.tr: Why then was there reason for you to pursue me? Why does my lord pursue his servant? For what have I done, and what evil is in my hand? v. 18.

units.la: Mardochæus, Hamanis molitiones adversus se & Iudaicum populum confide-rans[?], beneq; sibi conscius, sic argumentatus est: lectus primum, deinde Διάνοια seu ratio, postremò Scientia: & Intellectus quidem praebet Maiorem. verbi gratia: Omne totum est maius sua parte. Διάνοια vero circa singularia discurrens, subsumit Minorem. ut: Circulus respectu semicirculi est totum. Scientia deniq; Complexioni insistens, colligit, Circulum semicirculo esse maiorem. Ita cum περὶ τῶν πρακτῶν argumetamur, haec tria itidem concurrunt. Primùm Συλλογισμὸς, Maiorem è Lege divina promens: Nemini inferenda est iniuria. deinde Ratio, Minorem subiungens: Rem autem alienam inuito domino accipere, iniuria est. Conscientia tertio loco Complexionem dictat: Itaq; à nullo res auferri debet ipso inuito.
units.tr: Mordecai, considering the schemes of Haman against himself and the Jewish people, and conscious of his own good deeds, argued thus: first Intellect, then Reasoning (Dianoia, or ratio), and finally Knowledge. Intellect supplies the major premise, for example: every whole is greater than its part. Reasoning, running over particulars, supplies the minor premise, for example: a circle is, in relation to a semicircle, a whole. Knowledge, resting on the conclusion, infers that a circle is greater than a semicircle. So too when we argue about practical matters, these three likewise come together. First the syllogism, drawing the major premise from the divine Law: no one is to be wronged. Then Reason, adding the minor premise: to take another's property against the owner's will is a wrong. Conscience, in the third place, dictates the conclusion: therefore goods must be taken from no one against his will.

units.la: Quòd si quis fines spectet, duo esse genera syllogismorum practicorum conscientiæ animadvertet. Vnum eorū, qui sunt ἀπολογητικοί: alterum eorum, qui sunt κατηγορητικοί. Diserte enim dicit Paulus: καὶ μεταξὺ ἐν[?] ἀλλήλων τῶν λογισμῶν κατηγορούντων, ἢ καὶ ἀπολογουμένων.
units.tr: If one looks at the ends, one will notice that there are two kinds of practical syllogisms of conscience: one kind is apologetic (ἀπολογητικοί), the other accusatory (κατηγορητικοί). For Paul clearly says: "and between themselves the thoughts accusing or also excusing" [καὶ μεταξὺ ἀλλήλων τῶν λογισμῶν κατηγορούντων ἢ καὶ ἀπολογουμένων].

units.la: Sic argumentatur Paulus in apologia sua:
units.tr: Paul argues thus in his apology:

units.la: Quicunq; bonam habet conscientiam coram Deo, eos non est cur sanctæ vocationis fideliter suscepte & administratæ pudeat pigeatue.
units.tr: Whoever has a good conscience before God has no reason to be ashamed or weary of the holy calling faithfully received and administered.

units.la: Viri fratres, ego omni conscientia bona conuersatus sum ante Deu usq; in hodiernum diem. Act.23.1.
units.tr: Men and brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience up to this day. Acts 23.1.

units.la: Quare non est cur Apostolici muneris me pudeat,&c.
units.tr: Therefore there is no reason for me to be ashamed of the apostolic office, etc.

units.la: Dauid sic argumentatur 1.Sam.26.
units.tr: David argues thus, 1 Sam. 26.

units.la: Non est pij Principis, bene de se & de patria meritum hostiliter persequi.
units.tr: It is not the part of a pious prince to persecute with hostility one who has deserved well of himself and of his country.

units.la: Ego vero & bene meritus sum, & porro quoq; bene mereri de te, ô Rex, & de toto regno Israelis paratus sum.
units.tr: But I have deserved well, and I am also ready to go on deserving well of you, O King, and of the whole kingdom of Israel.

units.la: Quare non erat cur me persequereris.
units.tr: Therefore there was no reason for you to pursue me.

units.la: Vt quid dominus meus persequitur ser-[?]vum suum? quid enim feci? & quod in manu mea malum? v.18.
units.tr: Why does my lord pursue his servant? For what have I done, and what evil is in my hand? v. 18.

units.la: Mardochæus, Hamanis molitiones adversus se & Iudaicum populum considerans, benequ; sibi conscius, sic argumentatus est:
units.tr: Mordecai, considering the schemes of Haman against himself and the Jewish people, and conscious of his own good deeds, argued thus:

units.la: Qui Deum reuerentur,& de magistra- tu optime sunt meriti,non debent nimi- um metuere suos æmulos. iuxta dictum: Deo fido,quid faciet mihi caro?
units.tr: Those who revere God and have deserved best of the magistrate ought not to fear their rivals too much, according to the saying: "With God as my trust, what can flesh do to me?"

units.la: Ego uero & Deū reuereor, & regi As- suero olim aperui molitiones eorum qui uitæ illius insidiabantur.
units.tr: But I both revere God, and once revealed to King Ahasuerus the plots of those who lay in wait for his life.

units.la: Non itaque est, cur hunc nefarium ho- minem Hamanum nimium metuam.
units.tr: So there is no reason why I should fear this wicked man Haman too much.

units.la: Abimelech:Domine,inquit,numquid gentem etiam iustam occides? An non ipse dixit,Soror mea est?sed & ipsa dixit, Frater meus est. In perfectione cordis mei,& in mundicia manuum mearum fe ci hoc.Gen.20.5.
units.tr: Abimelech: "Lord," he said, "will you slay even a righteous nation? Did he not himself say, She is my sister? And she herself said, He is my brother. In the integrity of my heart and the cleanness of my hands I have done this." Gen. 20.5.

units.la: Iosephus per calumniam circumuen- tus, in carcere hoc practico syllogismo hau ddubie sese erexit:
units.tr: Joseph, overtaken by calumny, undoubtedly raised himself up in prison by this practical syllogism:

units.la: Iehouah educit sicut lucem, iusticiam cuiusq;, & iudicia eius quasi meridiem: ut etiam Dauid monet Psal.37.6.
units.tr: Jehovah brings forth the righteousness of each man like the light, and his judgments like the noonday, as David also admonishes, Ps. 37.6.

units.la: Ego sane præter meum meritū,sceleris attentati insimulor,& in carcere uersor.
units.tr: I am indeed accused of an attempted crime beyond my desert, and I am in prison.

units.la: Spero itaq; futurum,ut me liberet Deus meus.
units.tr: I hope therefore that my God will set me free.

units.la: Paulus Act.28.17.18.19.
units.tr: Paul, Acts 28.17-19.

units.la: Digni sunt cômiseratione bonorum,
units.tr: They are worthy of the compassion of good men,

units.la: qui feré totius alicuius gentis odio laborant, cum in eam nō modò non deliquerint,sed etiam ex animo fuerint officiosi.
units.tr: who labour under the hatred of almost an entire nation, when they have not only given it no offence but have even been dutiful to it with their whole heart.

units.la: Me uerò odio prosequuntur,&in uincula coniectum, ad Cæsarem prouocare coegerunt Iudæi.
units.tr: But they pursue me with hatred, and the Jews, having thrown me into chains, forced me to appeal to Caesar.

units.la: Itaq; uestra τῇ συμπαθείᾳ [?] dignus sum.
units.tr: Therefore I am worthy of your sympathy [συμπάθεια].

units.la: SYLLOGISMI ΚΑΤΗΓΟΡΙΚΟΙ [?]
units.tr: SYLLOGISMS OF ACCUSATION

units.la: 1. Primorum Parentum.
units.tr: 1. Of the first parents.

units.la: Synterefis. Transgressores Legis morte multandi sunt.
units.tr: Synteresis. Transgressors of the Law are to be punished with death.

units.la: Conscientia. Nos Legem Domini transgressi sumus.
units.tr: Conscience. We have transgressed the Lord's Law.

units.la: Itaq; nobis moriendum erit.
units.tr: Therefore we must die.

units.la: 2. Caini fratricidæ.
units.tr: 2. Of Cain the fratricide.

units.la: Synterefis. Maledictus est qui fratrē occidit.
units.tr: Synteresis. Cursed is he who kills his brother.

units.la: Conscientia. Ego Abelem fratrem occidi.
units.tr: Conscience. I have killed my brother Abel.

units.la: Sum igitur maledictus.
units.tr: I am therefore cursed.

units.la: 3. Dauidis,post adulterium & homicidium admissum.
units.tr: 3. Of David, after adultery and murder had been committed.

units.la: Synterefis. Digni sunt adulteri & homicidæ,quos Deus à facie sua abijciat,& à quibus Spiritum sanctum auferat,&c.
units.tr: Synteresis. Adulterers and murderers are worthy to be cast by God from his presence, and to have the Holy Spirit taken from them, etc.

units.la: Conscientia. Atqui ego adulterium & homicidium perpetraui.
units.tr: Conscience. But I have committed adultery and murder.

units.la: Quare dignus sum tantis poenis.
units.tr: Therefore I am worthy of such punishments.

units.la: 4. Studiosi ὁμωνύμως sic dicti.
units.tr: 4. Of students, so called homonymously.

units.la: Synterefis. Frugi adolescenti in timore Dei, summo studio in bonis literis versandum, nec frustranda spes paretum & propinquorum, nec fides magistratui data fallenda est.
units.tr: Synteresis. A good young man who fears God must devote himself with the greatest zeal to good letters; neither should the hope of parents and relatives be disappointed, nor the trust given to the magistrate be betrayed.

units.la: Conscientia. Tu vero nec pietatem erga Deum, nec diligentiam in studijs, nec reuerentiam praeceptoribus debitam, nec alias virtutes studioso homine dignas, unquam praestare & probare stu-duisti.
units.tr: Conscience. But you have never striven to show or prove piety toward God, diligence in your studies, the reverence due to your teachers, or the other virtues worthy of a studious man.

units.la: Quare non dubium est, te iratu habere Deum, & maledictu esse, ac poenas aeternas daturum, nisi resipiscas.
units.tr: Therefore there is no doubt that God holds you in anger and that you are accursed, and will suffer eternal punishments, unless you repent.

units.la: 8. Finis est, ut fit conscientia illustre testimonium de iudicio Dei, quod tum maxime lucet, cum male sibi conscios in mediis successibus, [illegible, ~14 letters] & anxios reddit:bene autem sibi conscios, in morte ipsa exhilarat & reficit. Prodest autem ex historijs petere exempla euentuum, qui fuerunt testimonia de syllogismis [?]istis. Cain, Ahitophel, Iudas Iscariotes, Saul malae conscientiae furijs ad desperationem & necem sibijpsis consciscédam adacti sunt.
units.tr: 8. The end result is that conscience becomes a clear testimony of the judgment of God, which shines most when, amid worldly successes, it makes those evilly conscious of themselves troubled and anxious; but it cheers and restores those well conscious of themselves even in death. It is useful to seek from histories examples of outcomes that served as testimonies of these syllogisms: Cain, Ahithophel, Judas Iscariot and Saul, driven by the furies of an evil conscience to despair and to inflicting death upon themselves. [illegible]

units.la: 9. Effectus,bonae quidem conscientiae, laeticia: malae autem,horribilis consternatio & alia mala.
units.tr: 9. The effect of a good conscience is joy; of a bad one, horrible dismay and other evils.

units.la: Exijs quae iam dixi,talis Conscientiae finitio cōstitui potest: Conscientia est te stimonium diuinitus cordibus hominū inscriptum,Legis & fidei lumini respondens,ut recte factorum memoria ἡ λογισμῷ[?],lętitiam: secus factorum,dolore,in homine αὐτοκατακρίτῳ[?],ad Dei gloriā pariat.
units.tr: From what I have already said, a definition of conscience may be framed thus: Conscience is a testimony inscribed by God in the hearts of men, answering to the light of the Law and of faith, so that the memory of right deeds, through reasoning, produces joy, and of the contrary, grief, in a man who condemns himself, to the glory of God.

units.la: VERSVS XII.
units.tr: Verse 12.

units.la: Quibus dixit: Tollite me, & proijcite me in mare: & silebit mare à uobis. scio e-nim ego,quòd propter me tempestas hæc su[?] peruenit uobis.
units.tr: They said to him: Take me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will become calm for you. For I know that this great storm has come upon you because of me.

units.la: Ionas αὐτοκατάκριτος[?], sententiam mortis de semetipso fert,exemplo ualdè inusita to. Tria uerò breui oratione complectitur. 1. Sententiam de morte sua & eius circumstantijs. 2. Praedictionem de sedanda maris tempestate. 3. αἰτιολογίαν[?], ab æquo ductam.
units.tr: Jonah, self-condemned [αὐτοκατάκριτος], pronounces sentence of death upon himself, an example quite unusual. In a short speech he embraces three things: (1) his sentence concerning his death and its circumstances; (2) a prediction that the storm at sea will be calmed; (3) a reason drawn from fairness [αἰτιολογία].

units.la: Obseruabitis autē initiō has quatuor ὑποθέσεις[?] de Iona.
units.tr: You will notice at the outset these four points about Jonah.

units.la: 1. Per fidem Ionas sententiam mortis de seipso tulit, nec recusauit sese subiicere eorum potestati, in quorum manus diuinitus sese traditū esse statuebat. Quinimò ut ne parcerent hac in parte, circumstantijs supplicij expositis eos hortatus est.
units.tr: 1. Through faith Jonah pronounced sentence of death upon himself, and he did not refuse to submit to the power of those into whose hands he believed God had delivered him. Indeed, so that they would not spare him in this matter, he urged them, having set out the circumstances of the punishment.

units.la: 2. Fulsit autē in eodem Prophetiae Spiritus: quo suggerēte, prędixit, fore ut ipso in mare proiecto, tempestas sedaretur.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, the Spirit of prophecy shone in the same man, and at its prompting he foretold that once he had been thrown into the sea the storm would be calmed.

units.la: 3. Erat etiā æquitatis illustre argumentum, quòd reatum fassus, sua causa neminem alium periclitari voluit.
units.tr: 3. There was also a notable argument of fairness: by confessing his guilt, he did not want anyone else to be endangered on his account.

units.la: 4. In eo etiam Christi typus fuit, quòd mori maluit solus, ut ne alijs moriendum esset. Ioan. 11.50. Expedit ut unus homo moriatur pro populo, & tota gens nō pe-reat. Hoc tamen interest, quòd Ionæ af-flictio τιμωρία fuit, Christi passio λύτρον e-jus qui non peccauerat.
units.tr: 4. In this there was also a type of Christ, in that he preferred to die alone, so that others would not have to die. John 11:50: "It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish." Yet there is this difference: Jonah's affliction was a punishment, while Christ's passion was a ransom paid by one who had not sinned.

units.la: Quia verò hic occurrit insigne exemplum obedientiæ fidei in pœnis, illud αὐτῷ θεῷ[?], ad nostram ædificationem, [illegible, ~8 letters] tra-stabimus.
units.tr: Since here occurs a remarkable example of the obedience of faith under punishment, we shall pass on to it, for our edification.

units.la: 5. Fides nec dissimulat, nec diffitetur culpam etiam speciale, idq; coram Deo & hominibus, Pro.18.17. Iustus, prior est in causa sua: venit autem socius eius, & inuestigat eum. Dauid dicebat ad Iehouam: Tibi soli peccaui: Psal.51.6. ad Nathane Prophetā: Peccaui Iehouae: 2.Sam, 12.13. Idem uidere est in Ionae exemplo.
units.tr: 5. Faith neither hides nor denies its guilt, even a special guilt, and that both before God and before men. Prov. 18:17: "The righteous man is first in his own cause, but his neighbour comes and examines him." David said to Jehovah: "Against you alone have I sinned," Ps. 51:6; and to the prophet Nathan: "I have sinned against Jehovah," 2 Sam. 12:13. The same can be seen in the example of Jonah.

units.la: 2. Et cum intelligat, distinctam esse remissionem culpae a remissione poenae temporalis in hac vita: sic accipit donum remissionis peccatorum, ut tamen subijciat hominem iudicio Dei poenisq; temporalibus, quae tamen scit non esse compensationes aut merita pro aeternis poenis. Ideo Ionas non defugiendā censuit mortem, quam se promeritū esse agnoscebat.
units.tr: 2. And since he understands that the remission of guilt is distinct from the remission of temporal punishment in this life, he receives the gift of forgiveness of sins in such a way that he nonetheless submits himself to God's judgment and temporal punishments, which he knows are not compensations or merits for eternal punishments. Therefore Jonah did not think that death should be avoided, since he acknowledged that he had deserved it.

units.la: 3. Quia verò gloriae Dei magis est, quā caducae vitae studiosa, suggerit Sanctis, offensa aliqua praeoccupatis, iustam sententiam, carni quidem molestam, spiritui verò iucundam. Vt hoc loco Ionas: Tollite, ait, me, & proijcite in mare, &c.
units.tr: 3. Since, however, it is more for the glory of God than for the eager preservation of this brief life, he sets before the saints, when some offence has gone before, a just sentence: troublesome to the flesh, but pleasing to the spirit. So Jonah here: "Take me," he says, "and throw me into the sea," etc.

units.la: 4. Sic autem Deus pro infinita sua bonitate temperat τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων[?] ἀμαρτωρέ[?], ut cum quid boni ex ijs secuturū sit, ipso suggerente praeuideant, aequioribus animis iram Dei, cui peccauerunt, etiam portent, tent. Vt Ionæ solatio esse potuit, quòd mare, ipso è naui præcipitato, quieturum præsciret.
units.tr: 4. God, in His infinite goodness, so tempers the consequences of sins that, when at His prompting they foresee whatever good is to follow from them, they bear even the wrath of God, against which they have sinned, with more equable minds. This could be a comfort to Jonah, that the sea would become quiet once he had been thrown from the ship, as he knew beforehand.

units.la: 5. Erumpit itaq; in charitatis ἀπολελυμένη fides, dum sic apud homines urget exe cutione iudicij diuini, ut interim aliorū incolumitati gratuletur eam prænunci- ando. Quibus hoc præstare datum est, ij reuera fide mũdum uicerunt. iuxta illud: Hæc est uictoria quæ uicit mũdum, nem- pe fides nostra. Quis est qui uincit mun- dum, nisi qui credit Iesum esse filiũ Dei? 1.Ioan.5.4.5.
units.tr: 5. Thus faith breaks forth in unfeigned [ἀπολελυμένη] charity, while it so urges upon men the execution of divine judgment that meanwhile it rejoices in the safety of others by proclaiming it in advance. Those to whom this has been granted have truly conquered the world by faith, according to that saying: "This is the victory that overcomes the world, namely our faith. Who is he that overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?" 1 John 5:4, 5.

units.la: 6. Solicite autem cauere solet, ne cui- quam periculo sit: quòd malit aliorum caussa plurimum laborare & pati, quàm suo nomine cuiquam male esse. Atq; eo nomine dicitur, διὰ ἀγάπης ςνεργοῦντα, per charitatem agens. Gal.5.6.
units.tr: 6. Faith is also accustomed to take careful precautions that it bring danger to no one, since it prefers to labour and suffer much for the sake of others rather than that anyone should be harmed on its account. And for this reason it is called [διὰ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη], working through love. Gal. 5:6.

units.la: 7. Coronidis uice hoc addam, aliud esse, si cui fides αὐθαίρετον huiusmodi de sei- pso sententia dictet: aliud, si conscientiæ dolore extorqueat tristè sententia, ut finis dolorū (ut ipsis uidetur) tandè subsequi posit. Huius posterioris exemplum com- memorabile, quod in archiuis clarissimæ cuiusdā Reipub. extare audio, recitabo. Pandochaeo, seni honesto, unica erat filia heres, bonis moribus & re mediocri: cuius nuptias οἰκέτης [?], homo caeteroquin frugi & industrius, ea de causa frustra ex petierat, quòd peregrinus, quòd pauper, & quòd servus esset. Et tamè eo loco ob fidelitatem apud Patrem familiās erat, ut hic cum uxore & filia ad thermas profectus, oeconomiam illi administrandā crederet. Factum autem est, ut absente Sene, diverteret Mercator in eo diversorio: quē prima statim nocte Famulus ille, qui domui praefuerat, nefariē obtrucat, & in equili sepelit, equo & vestimetis postero die diuenditis. Nemini mortalium, praeterquam auctori, de tanto constabat facinore. Ubi domum Pandochaeus revertisset, omnia recte à servo administrata putans, maiore illum benevolentia prosequi coepit. Nec multo post infelix ille latro hac commentus est technam. Conscribit literas, quasi à propinquis suis de morte parentis, reditūq; in patriam scriptas ad se. Eas è foro reversus, unà cum mediocre pecunia (opinor fuisse 8o coronatos) offert Patrifamiliās. Ait se nec equuum emturum, ut propinqui moneret, nec tot tent. Vt Ionæ solatio esse potuit, quòd mare,ipso è naui præcipitato,quieturum præsciret.
units.tr: 7. By way of a crown, I will add this: it is one thing if faith dictates such a self-chosen sentence against oneself, and another if a sad sentence is wrung out of someone by the pain of conscience, so that an end to the sorrows (as they seem to him) may at last follow. I shall recount a memorable example of this latter kind, which I hear exists in the archives of a most distinguished commonwealth. Pandochaeus, an honest old man, had one daughter as his sole heir, of good character and modest means. A servant [οἰκέτης], otherwise a thrifty and industrious man, had sought her hand in marriage in vain, for the reason that he was a foreigner, poor, and a servant. Yet he was held in such trust by the head of the household for his fidelity that, when the old man set out with his wife and daughter for the baths, he entrusted him with the management of the household. It happened that, while the old man was away, a merchant lodged at that inn. On the very first night that servant who was in charge of the house wickedly murdered him and buried him in the stable, selling the horse and clothes the next day. No mortal knew of so great a crime except the perpetrator. When Pandochaeus returned home, thinking that everything had been properly managed by the servant, he began to treat him with greater kindness. Not long after, that unhappy robber devised this trick. He wrote letters, as though from his relatives, about the death of the parent and the return home, addressed to himself. Returning from the forum, he offers these letters, along with a modest sum of money (I think it was 80 crowns), to the head of the household. He says that he will not buy a horse, as his relatives advised, nor take so many crowns with him for the journey.

Quibus hoc præstare datum est,ij reuera fide mūdum uicerunt.iuxta illud: Hæc est uictoria quæ uicit mūdum,nem- pe fides nostra. Quis est qui uincit mūn- dum, nisi qui credit Iesum esse filiū Dei? 1.Ioan.5.4.5.

Those to whom this has been granted have truly conquered the world by faith, according to that saying: "This is the victory that overcomes the world, namely our faith. Who is he that overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?" 1 John 5:4, 5.

Faith is also accustomed to take careful precautions that it bring danger to no one, since it prefers to labour and suffer much for the sake of others rather than that anyone should be harmed on its account. And for this reason it is called [διὰ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη], working through love. Gal. 5:6.

Sed tandem malæ conscientiæ doloribus sic excruciatus est, ut homo αὐτοκαταχείρητος[?] mori mallet, quàm diutius in tantis ver-sari angustijs. Die quadam præstituta iu-dicio capitali, homicidæ cuiusdam nomi-ne, quòd ipse quoq; è iudicum numero esset, iussus est adesse. Ibi miser manè sum-mo Missam de more aditurus, uxorem, qua cum bellè ipsi semper conuenerat, rogat, ut ferculum aliquod sibi nò ingra-tum tum apparaꝛet,quod molesta iudicij capi talis prouincia sibi defungedum esset eo die,nec ita bene haberet. Ubi è teplo domum regressus esset, audit interea allatu caput vitulinū,de quo aliquid libeter gustare solebat. Eius videndi studio ductus, arculam in qua illud repositum iacebat, aperit, & horrore perfusus, caput hominis ibi reconditum queritur. Quaeso tamen etiam atq; etiam, ut iusto capitis supplicio affectú, ab atrocissimis istis conscientiæ doloribus, quos multis iam annis sustinui, supplicio quod promeritum statuo, liberetis: efficiatisq;, ut satisfiat iufticiæ Dei. Factum itaq; est, ut eo loco quem indicârat, olim obtruncati Mercatoriū[?] ossibus inuentis, homo αὐτο- [illegible, ~9 letters] una cum homicida illo uolens duceretur & decollaretur.
units.tr: Pandochaeus, an honest old man, had one daughter as his sole heir, of good character and modest means. A servant [οἰκέτης], otherwise a thrifty and industrious man, had sought her hand in marriage in vain, for the reason that he was a foreigner, poor, and a servant. Yet he was in such favour with the head of the household for his fidelity that, when the old man set out with his wife and daughter for the baths, he entrusted him with the management of the household. It happened that, while the old man was away, a merchant lodged at that inn. On the very first night that servant who was in charge of the house wickedly murdered him and buried him in the stable, selling the horse and clothes the next day. No mortal knew of so great a crime except the perpetrator. When Pandochaeus returned home, thinking that everything had been properly managed by the servant, he began to treat him with greater kindness. Not long after, that unhappy robber contrived this scheme. He wrote letters, as though from his relatives, about the death of the parent and the return home, addressed to himself. He offers these, with a moderate sum of money (I think 80 crowns), to the head of the household, saying that he would take this for the journey. He adds that he would be unwilling to go elsewhere than to that city, where he had lived very comfortably for some years. What more? With a good part of the money deposited with the head of the household, and with the hope of a return, he set out on his journey. It was very inconvenient for the head of the household to let the man go at that critical time, but it seemed that he must yield to kindness. Not long after he returned, deposited the remaining money with the same man, and disclosed some matters concerning the paternal property; and at last, by these clever means, he arranged to become son-in-law and succeed to the father-in-law when he died. Because his character was honest, he was raised to a senatorial dignity and so conducted himself for a long time that he was regarded as blameless. But at last he was so tormented by the pains of a guilty conscience that, as a man who would rather die than remain longer in such distress, he chose to be a self-condemned man. On a day fixed for a capital trial, he was ordered to appear, since he too was among the judges, in the case of a certain murderer. There, the wretched man, going to hear Mass in the morning as was his custom, asked his wife, with whom he had always got on very well, to have some dish prepared for him that would not be unpleasant, since the unpleasant business of the capital trial had to be discharged that day, and he did not feel so well. When he returned home from the temple, he heard that a calf's head had been brought in, of which he was accustomed to taste with pleasure. Led by the desire to see it, he opened the little chest in which it lay, and, overcome with horror, he found there a man's head hidden. But admonished kindly by his wife that it was a mistake, he restrained himself, went to the court, and sat down in his place among the judges. When the order of business required him to give his sentence, as soon as he had declared, according to the prescription of the laws, that the murderer should be punished by beheading, he rose, and testifying that he pronounced the same sentence upon himself, and having set out the circumstances of a robbery he had once committed, he humbly asked that he not be compelled to undergo a heavier punishment. Some who thought the man was suffering from melancholy urged him to go home and attend to his health. But he said: "I know you do not suspect me, and indeed I am conscious of no other atrocious crime. Yet I beg you again and again that, since I have been sentenced to a just capital punishment, you free me from these most atrocious pangs of conscience, which I have endured for many years, by the punishment which I judge I have deserved, and that you make it so that justice of God is satisfied." And so it came about that, at the place he had indicated, the bones of the merchant, long since murdered, were found, and the man, wishing it, was led away together with that murderer and beheaded.

units.la: Audio etiam nō multis abhinc annis, Lypsiæ quendam ultrò adijsse iudicem, & fassum,quòd Principis Electoris plau-strorum direptioni interfuisset, moriqué mallet,quàm dolores conscientiæ diutius sustinere.
units.tr: I also hear that, not many years ago, a certain man at Leipzig went of his own accord to a judge and confessed that he had taken part in the plundering of the Elector's wagons, and he preferred to die rather than bear the pangs of conscience any longer.

units.la: Hæc & similia exempla intuentes, militemus bonam militiam, retinentes fidè & bonam conscientiam. Ne indulgea-mus iracundiæ, inuidiæ, ambitioni, & a-lijs cæcis & uiolentissimis affectibus. Dominum autem Iesum Christum precemur, ut nobis det, secundum Spiritum in-cedere, & carnis concupiscentijs non sa-tisfacere.
units.tr: Let us follow these examples and fight the good fight, holding fast to faith and a good conscience. Let us not give way to anger, envy, ambition, and other blind and violent passions. Let us pray the Lord Jesus Christ to grant us to walk according to the Spirit and not to satisfy the desires of the flesh.

units.la: VERSVS XIII.
units.tr: Verse 13.

units.la: Nitebantur autem remis uiri illi, ut reducerent (nauem) ad aridam, sed non ualuerunt: luerunt: quia mare ibat, & intumescebat super eos.
units.tr: Nevertheless those men strove with the oars to bring the ship back to dry land, but they could not prevail, because the sea kept rising and swelling over them.

units.la: THESIS.
units.tr: Thesis.

units.la: Quemadmodum praepostera est cle-mentia, quę voluntati & iudiciis Dei ad-uersatur: ita nulla hominum consilia, nullae uires, nulli deniq; conatus, executio-nem iudiciorum Dei remorari possunt. iuxta dictum: Consilium meum stabit, & omnem voluntatem meam faciam: Isa. 46.10. Consilium Iehouae in aeternū perstat: Psal.33.11. Ite: Non est sapientia, neq; intelligentia, neq; consilium contra Iehouam: Prouerb.21.30. In iis qui Ionae parcendum iudicabant, causa impulsiua erat, Commiseratio erga tantum virum: causa finalis, Incolumem eum seruare, siqua fieri posset: modus, Strenuè remigando ad littus contendere: euentus con silio & conatui repugnans, Maris tempestas magis ac magis inualescens. Haec omnia monent, saepenumero fieri, ut animi hominum errore ducti Deo aduersen tur, dum hominibus gratificari & succurere studeant. Occurrunt autem in hoc uersu duo Loci communes, De bona intentione: coronatos ἐφοδίῳ[?] gratia secum sumturū. Addit se illibenter alibi, quàm in ea urbe, in qua percommodè annis aliquot uixis-set, actūrum[?]. Quid multis? Bona parte pecunię penes Patremfamiliâs deposita, & spe reditus facta, iter ingreditur. Erat perquàm incommodum Patrifamiliâs, eo te poris articulo hominem dimittere[?]. Sed humanitati id dandum uidebatur. Nec multo post redux, reliquam pecuniam penes eundem deponit, nonnulla de facultatibus paternis aperit: & tandem tinnulis istis rationibus perficit, ut gener factus, socero demortuo succederet. Quòd autem honesti esset illius mores, ad Senatoriam dignitate euectus, diuq; ea sic functus est, ut haberetur ἀνέγκλητος[?]. Sed tandem malae conscientiae doloribus sic excruciatus est, ut homo αὐτοκατάκριτος[?] mori mallet, quàm diutiùs in tantis uersari angustijs. Die quadam praefituta iudicio capitali, homicidae cuiusdam nomine, quòd ipse quoq; è iudicum numero esset, iussus est adesse. Ibi miser mane summo[?] Missam de more aditurus, uxorem, qua cum belle ipsi semper conuenerat, rogat, ut ferculum aliquod sibi nō ingratum appararet,quód molesta iudicij capitalis prouincia sibi defungedum esset eo die,nec ita bene haberet. Vbi è tèplo domum regressus esset, audit interea allatū caput uitulinū,de quo aliquid libéter gustare solebat. Eius uidendi studio ductus, arculam in qua illud repositum iacebat, aperit, & horrore perfusus, caput hominis ibi reconditum quaeritur. Sed ab uxore benignè de errore admonitus, sese repressit: & in curiam progressus, suo loco iudicibus assedit. Cum ordo postularet, ut sententiā suā proferret, statim ubi secūdum Legum pręscriptum capite mulctādum homicidam pronunciauisset, assurgit, & eandem sententiam de semetipso sese ferre testatus, expositisq; latrocinij olim à se commissi circumstantijs, suppliciter petijt, ne supplicium grauius subire cogeretur. Erant,qui melancholia hominem laborare putarent,auctoresq; essent ut domum reuersus sui rationem haberet. Verùm ille: Scio,inquit, uos me suspectum non habere, necsanè alterius alicuius atrocis sceleris mihi cōscius sum. Quaeso tamen etiam atq; etiam, ut iusto capitis supplicio affectū, ab atrocisimis istis conscientiæ doloribus, quos multi# iam annis sustinui, supplicio quod promeritum statuo, liberetis: efficiatisq;, ut satisfiat iusticiæ Dei. Factum itaq; est,ut eo loco quem indicârat, olim obtruncati Mercatoriš ossibus inuentis, homo αὐτο-καταδικαστος una cum homicida illo uolens duceretur & decollaretur.
units.tr: As mercy that opposes the will and judgments of God is perverse, so no counsels, strength, or efforts of men can delay the execution of God's judgments, according to the saying: "My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure" (Isa. 46.10); "The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever" (Psal. 33.11); "There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD" (Prov. 21.30). In those who judged that Jonah should be spared, the impelling cause was pity for so great a man; the final cause was to keep him safe, if that could be done; the means was to row vigorously toward the shore; the outcome, which opposed their counsel and effort, was a storm at sea growing ever stronger. All this warns that it often happens that men, led astray by their feelings, set themselves against God while they strive to please and help other men. Two common topics arise from this verse: concerning good intention. [The text here is garbled:] He takes with him, as travel money [ἐφόδιον], some sum of money out of kindness. He adds that he would be unwilling to go anywhere else than to that city in which he had lived very comfortably for some years. To make a long story short: with a good part of the money deposited with the master of the household, and with hope of return, he sets out on his journey. It was quite inconvenient for the master of the household to let the man go at that juncture, but it seemed that this had to be granted to kindness. Soon after returning, he deposits the remaining money with the same man, discloses some matters concerning his father's property, and at last by such specious arguments brings it about that, having become a son-in-law, he succeeds his father-in-law when he dies. Moreover, his manners were honest; raised to the dignity of senator and long functioning in it, he was so regarded as blameless [ἀνέγκλητος]. But at last he was so tortured by the pains of a bad conscience that, as a man self-condemned [αὐτοκατάκριτος], he preferred to die rather than remain longer in such distress. On a certain appointed day, when a capital trial was in progress against a certain murderer, he was ordered to be present, since he too was among the number of the judges. There the wretched man, going to Mass early in the morning as was his custom, asked his wife, with whom he had always got on well, to prepare for him some dish he would not dislike, because the unpleasant duty of a capital trial had to be discharged by him that day and he was not feeling well. When he returned home from the temple, he heard that a calf's head had been brought in, of which he was used to gladly taking some. Drawn by the desire to see it, he opened the chest in which it lay, and, struck with horror, he searched for a human head hidden there. But, kindly admonished by his wife about his mistake, he restrained himself, went on to the court, and took his seat among the judges in his place. When the order of proceedings required him to pronounce his sentence, as soon as he had pronounced that the murderer should be punished by death according to the prescription of the laws, he rose, testified that he was pronouncing the same sentence upon himself, and, having set out the circumstances of a robbery he had once committed, begged humbly that he not be forced to undergo a more severe punishment. Some who were there thought the man was suffering from melancholy, and advised him to go home and look after himself. But he said: "I know you do not suspect me, nor am I conscious of any other atrocious crime. Yet I beg you again and again: let me be punished by the just penalty of execution, and free me from these most atrocious pangs of conscience which I have endured for many years, and which I judge I deserve to be punished for; and bring it about that the justice of God be satisfied." So it came about that, at the place he had named, where bones of a murdered merchant had been found long before, he was led off, willingly, together with that murderer, and beheaded, the man being self-condemned [αὐτο-καταδικαστος].

units.la: Audio etiam nō multis abhinc annis, Lypsiæ quendam ultrò adijsse iudicem, & fassum,quòd Principis Electoris plau-strorum direptioni interfuisset, moriqué mallet,quàm dolores conscientiæ diutius sustinere.
units.tr: I also hear that, not many years ago, a certain man at Leipzig went of his own accord to a judge and confessed that he had taken part in the plundering of the Elector's wagons, and he preferred to die rather than bear the pangs of conscience any longer.

units.la: Hæc & similia exempla intuentes, mi litemus bonam militiam, retinentes fidē & bonam conscientiam. Ne indulgeamus iracundiæ, inuidiæ,ambitioni,& aliis cæcis & uiolentissimis affectibus. Dominum autem Iesum Christum precemur,ut nobis det, secūdum Spiritum incedere, & carnis concupiscentijs non satisfacere.
units.tr: Let us follow these examples and fight the good fight, holding fast to faith and a good conscience. Let us not give way to anger, envy, ambition, and other blind and violent passions. Let us pray the Lord Jesus Christ to grant us to walk according to the Spirit and not to satisfy the desires of the flesh.

units.la: VERSVS XIII.
units.tr: VERSE 13.

units.la: Nitebantur autem remis uiri illi, ut reducerent (nauem) ad aridam, sed non ualuerunt: luerunt[?]: quia mare ibat, & intumescebat super eos,
units.tr: But those men rowed hard to bring the ship back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea kept rising and swelling against them,

units.la: THESIS.
units.tr: THESIS.

units.la: Quemadmodum praepostera est cle-mentia, quæ uoluntati & iudicijs Dei ad-uersatur: ita nulla hominum consilia, nulla uires, nulli deniq; conatus, executionem iudiciorum Dei remorari possunt. iuxta dictum: Consilium meum stabit, & omnem uoluntatem meam faciam: Isa. 46.10. Consilium Iehouæ in æternũ perstat: Psal.33.11. Ité: Non est sapientia, neq; intelligentia, neq; consilium contra Iehouam: Prouerb.21.30. In ijs qui Ionæ parcendum iudicabant, causa impulsiua erat, Commiseratio erga tantum uirum: causa finalis, Incolumem eum seruare, si qua fieri posset: modus, Strenuè remigando ad littus contendere: euentus consilio & conatui repugnans, Maris tempestas magis ac magis inualescens. Hæc omnia monent, sæpenumerò fieri, ut animi hominum errore ducti Deo aduersen-tur, dum hominibus gratificari & succurrere studeant. Occurrunt autè in hoc uer-su duo Loci communes, De bona inten-tione: tione:&,De infelici eorum lusta,qui cus-sum & executione iudiciorum Dei vel remorari,vel etiam impedire conantur.
units.tr: Just as it is absurd for mercy to oppose the will and judgments of God, so no human counsels, no strength, and finally no efforts can delay the carrying out of God's judgments. This accords with the saying: "My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure" (Isa. 46.10). "The counsel of Jehovah stands for ever" (Ps. 33.11). Again: "There is no wisdom, nor understanding, nor counsel against Jehovah" (Prov. 21.30). Among those who judged that Jonah should be spared, the moving cause was pity for so great a man; the final cause was to keep him safe, if that could be done; the means was to strive toward the shore by rowing vigorously; the outcome, which opposed their counsel and effort, was a storm at sea growing ever fiercer.
