units.la: Qui fidelibus Dei seruis, Domini sui uerbum praedicantibus, auscultat & credit, Deo ipsi auscultat & fidem habet. iuxta dictum: Qui uos audit, me audit: & qui uos reijcit, me reijcit: qui uero me reijcit, reijcit eum qui me misit: Luc.10. uerf.16. Sunt enim os Iehouae, quemadmodum Dominus Ieremiam moestum erigens inquit: Si eduxeris pretiosum a uili, tanquam os meum eris: conuertentur ipsi ad te, & tu non conuerteris ad illos: Ierem.15.19. Est autem & illa Ionae nostri φράσις, Niniuitae crediderunt Deo: instar sacramentalium loquendi formularum, quarum nonnullae signo tribuunt id quod est rei signatæ, quædam rei signatæ id tribuunt quod est signi, propter sacramentalem unionem, quæ est χρῖσμα[?] & relatiua. Niniuitæ ἐξωθὲν[?] à Iona, ἐνωθὲν[?] à Spiritu Christi edocti, crediderunt Deo: id est, tam comminationes, quàm promissiones eius ratas esse, sibi persuaserunt. De Israelitis recens ex Ægypto ductis dicitur: Vidit Israel manu magnam quam fecit Iehovah in Ægyptios, & timuit populus Iehovam: crediderunt autem Iehovae & Mosi servo eius: Exod. 14. 31. In Deum redemtorem crediderunt, non dubitantes ab eo missum Mosen virum sanctum. Atq; id est quod Auctor Epistolae ad Hebraeos docuit, cap. 11. 6. Fieri non potest, ut sine fide quisquam placeat: nam qui accedit ad Deum, hunc credere oportet esse (Deum,) & præmium largiri iis qui ipsum requirunt. Niniuitas autem Deo placuisse, vel ex eo colligi potest, quod is pro sua infinita misericordia eis, quibus & dedit ut ad ipsum converteretur, ignovit & pepercit.
units.tr: Whoever listens to and believes the faithful servants of God, who preach the word of their Lord, listens to God himself and has faith in him. This accords with the saying: "He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me; and he who rejects me rejects him who sent me" (Luke 10:16). For they are the mouth of Jehovah, as the Lord, raising up the grieving Jeremiah, says: "If you bring forth the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth; they shall turn to you, and you shall not turn to them" (Jer. 15:19). And this manner of speaking of our Jonah is also a figure: "the Ninevites believed God," in the manner of sacramental forms of speech, of which some attribute to the sign what belongs to the thing signified, and some attribute to the thing signified what belongs to the sign, on account of the sacramental union, which is relational. The Ninevites, taught externally by Jonah and internally by the Spirit of Christ, were persuaded that both his threats and his promises were sure. Of the Israelites newly led out of Egypt it is said: "Israel saw the great hand which Jehovah had shown against the Egyptians, and the people feared Jehovah; and they believed Jehovah and his servant Moses" (Exod. 14:31). They believed in God their redeemer, not doubting that Moses, a holy man, had been sent by him. And this is what the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews taught, ch. 11:6: "It is impossible to please God without faith; for whoever comes to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him." That the Ninevites pleased God may also be gathered from this, that he, in his infinite mercy, forgave and spared them, to whom he had also given the grace to turn to him.

units.la: Prædicatio publici ieiunij, & sacci, [illegible, ~8 letters] conversionis præconium denotat. notat. Similia autem exempla exstant Iud.20.26. 1.Sam.7.6. de Israelitis omnibus. Item, de Iosaphato & Iudaeis dicitur 2.Chron.20.3. Timuit itaq;, & posuit Iehosaphat faciem suam ad quaerendum Iehouam, & praedicauit ieiunium uniuerso Iehudah. 4. & congregati sunt (uiri) Iehudah, ut quaererent Iehouam: etiam de uniuersis urbibus Iehudah uenerunt ad quaerendum Iehouam. Et Dominus per Ioelem populum suum ad resipiscentiam reuocat grauissimo edicto: Et etiam nunc dicit Iehouah, Conuertimini ad me toto corde uestro, & in ieiunio, & fletu, & planctu[?]: & scindite cor uestrum, nō[?] autem uestimenta. Ioel.2.12.13.
units.tr: The proclamation of a public fast and of sackcloth [illegible, about 8 letters] denotes a herald of repentance. Similar examples exist: Judges 20:26 and 1 Sam. 7:6, concerning all the Israelites. Likewise, it is said of Jehoshaphat and the Jews, 2 Chron. 20:3-4: "Jehoshaphat feared, and set his face to seek Jehovah, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah. And the men of Judah gathered together to seek Jehovah; indeed, they came from all the cities of Judah to seek Jehovah." And through Joel the Lord calls his people back to repentance with a most solemn edict: "Even now, says Jehovah, turn to me with your whole heart, and with fasting, and weeping, and mourning; and rend your heart, and not your garments" (Joel 2:12-13).

units.la: THESIS
units.tr: Thesis

units.la: Ex fidei fonte conuersio uera promit-tiat[?], cuius externa documenta & τεκμήρια[?] piis non sunt negligenda.
units.tr: From the fountain of faith a true conversion arises, whose outward evidences and signs are not to be neglected by the godly.

units.la: DE VOCATIONIS œconomia.
units.tr: On the economy of vocation.

units.la: Vt haec thesis illustretur, aphorismis aliquot uocationis ordine completi studebimus. Loquimur autem de efficaci uocatione, de qua Paulus: Quos, ait, uocauit, eos etiam iustificauit: Rom.8.30. Item: Deus servavit nos, & vocavit vocatione sancta: non ex operibus nostris, sed ex suo proposito & gratia, &c. 2.Tim.1.9.
units.tr: To illustrate this thesis, we shall try, in an order of several aphorisms, to work through the calling. We are speaking, however, of the effectual calling, of which Paul says: "Those whom he called, them he also justified" (Rom. 8:30). Likewise: "God saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace," and so on (2 Tim. 1:9).

units.la: Aphorismus 1.
units.tr: Aphorism 1.

units.la: Deus vocat nos verbo suo. Quae sit verbi Dei ἐνέργεια [?] & efficacia, haec dicta ostendunt. Isa.55.11. Verbum meum, quod egredietur ex ore meo, nō revertetur ad me vacuum, sed facit quod volo, & prosperatur in his ad quae misi ipsum. Rom.1.16. Euangelium est δύναμις θεοῦ. Heb.4.12. ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ [?], καὶ ἐνεργὴς, καὶ τομώτερος ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν μάχαιραν, &c.
units.tr: God calls us by his word. The energy and efficacy of the word of God are shown by the following sayings. Isa. 55:11: "My word, which goes forth from my mouth, shall not return to me empty, but it shall do what I desire, and shall prosper in that for which I sent it." Rom. 1:16: the gospel is the power of God [δύναμις θεοῦ]. Heb. 4:12: For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and so on [ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ ἐνεργὴς, καὶ τομώτερος ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν μάχαιραν, &c.].

units.la: Aphorismus 2.
units.tr: Aphorism 2.

units.la: Verbo Dei respondet fides: quia haec illius correlatiuum est. Rom.10.14. Quomodo autem credent ei, de quo non audierint? Quomodo autem audient absq; praedicante?
units.tr: Faith answers to the Word of God, because faith is its correlative. Rom. 10. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?

units.la: Frustra autem praedicari verbum iis, qui fide illud nō apprehendunt, haec verba testantur: At non profuit illis auditus sermo, ut qui fidei nō mixtus fueritipsis qui audierant: Hebr.4.2. Inde à contrario colligimus, λόγον συγκεκραμένον τῇ πίστει prodesse auditoribus. Idem autem iudicium cium est & de uisibilibus Dei ueibis, seu de Sacramentis.
units.tr: That preaching the Word is in vain for those who do not grasp it by faith is shown by these words: "But the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in those who heard it," Heb. 4.2. From this we conclude, conversely, that a word mixed with faith [λόγον συγκεκραμένον τῇ πίστει] profits the hearers. The same judgment holds also for the visible words of God, that is, for the sacraments.

units.la: Aphorismus 3.
units.tr: Aphorism 3.

units.la: Porrò fides parit poenitentiam. Nam fi des Dei & nostri agnitione completes, abnegationem nostri suadet, ut nosmet- ipsos ad Dei pedes abijcientes, corde contrito & Spiritu humiliato ueniam petamus, & per ipsius gratiam in nouitate uitae ambulemus.
units.tr: Moreover, faith produces repentance. For faith, joined with the knowledge of God and of ourselves, urges self-denial, so that, casting ourselves at the feet of God with a contrite heart and a humbled spirit, we seek pardon and, by his grace, walk in newness of life.

units.la: Aphorismus 4.
units.tr: Aphorism 4.

units.la: Habet autem poenitentia sua documenta, ieiunium, preces, cofefsionem & alia, de quibus suo tempore agendum erit.
units.tr: Repentance has its own marks and exercises: fasting, prayers, confession, and others, of which something will have to be said in its proper place.

units.la: DE FIDE, METHODUS ἐξηγητική.
units.tr: ON FAITH: THE EXEGETICAL METHOD [ἐξηγητική]

units.la: Propositum nobis est, duas παραλλήλους definitiones fidei, à Paulo Apostolo traditas, logice καὶ ὡς ἐν τύπῳ explicare.
units.tr: Our purpose is to explain logically, and as it were in a figure, the two parallel definitions of faith handed down by the Apostle Paul.

units.la: Prima haec est. Tit. 1. 1. & 2.
units.tr: The first is this: Titus 1.1–2.

units.la: Fides electorum Dei, est agnitio ueritatis, quae est secundum pietatem, ad spem uitae aeternae, quam promisit Deus ille mentiri nescius. In hac pulcerrima definitione,
units.tr: The faith of God's elect is the knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, leading to the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, has promised. In this most beautiful definition:

units.la: 1. Definitum est, πίστις, fides, à qua πιστοί, fideles dicimur. Alia autem ratione Deus [?]λόγος[?] dicitur. 1.Cor.10.13: [?]λόγος ὁ θεός[?] alia nos [?]λόγοι[?] vocamur. Ille [?]λόγος[?] est, quia dictorum & conventorum constantiam & veritate nunquam non probat: nos autem [?]λόγοι[?] sumus, quia fide amplexi Christū, credentes Dei promissis, quae [?]λόγῳ[?], id est, veraci & fide digno, nobis annunciantur. Nec Dei fides, hominū incredulitate irrita fieri potest. Rom.3.3: Num incredulitas eorum Dei fidem inanem reddet? Quasi dicat, Nequaquam.
units.tr: 1. The thing defined is faith [πίστις], from which we are called faithful [πιστοί]. God is called faithful [πιστὸς ὁ θεός] in another sense, as in 1 Cor. 10.13, and we are called faithful in another. God is faithful because he always proves the constancy and truth of what he has said and agreed. We are faithful because, having embraced Christ by faith and believing God's promises, which are announced to us in the Word [λόγῳ], that is, by one who is true and worthy of belief. Nor can the faithfulness of God be made void by the unbelief of men. Rom. 3.3: Will their unbelief make the faithfulness of God without effect? As if to say, By no means.

units.la: 2. [?]ὑπολειμμένος[?], homo electus. Non enim omnium est vera illa fides: 2.Thessal.3.2. sed eorum qui sunt praordinati ad vitam aeternam: Act.13.48. Historica quidem fides etiam daemonis, Jac.2.19. temporaria autem assensio reprobis hypocritis, Matt. 13.21. Luc.8.13. communis est: haec autem de qua nunc loquimur, electorum Dei filiorum propria est, & ab electione dependet. Credunt enim hi in Christum, quia in eodem electi sunt. Eph.1.4. & 5.
units.tr: 2. The one who is chosen [ὑπολειμμένος], the elect man. For that true faith is not everyone's (2 Thess. 3.2), but belongs to those who are foreordained to eternal life (Acts 13.48). Historical faith belongs even to the devil (James 2.19), and temporary assent is common to the reprobate and hypocrites (Matt. 13.21; Luke 8.13). But the faith of which we now speak is the proper possession of the elect children of God and depends on election. For they believe in Christ because they were chosen in him (Eph. 1.4–5).

units.la: 3. Genus est, [?]ἐπίγνωσις[?], agnitio. Haec agnitio primum non [?]τῇ καταλήψει[?], qua percipitur quid hic vel ille dicat, definienda est. Nam fides non est naturalis aliqua in homine facultas, sed donum Spiritus sancti: deinde, eadem non circa ea quae caro & sanguis possunt inuestigare & cognoscere, sed quae Pater qui in coelis est retegit, uersatur. Deinde, nec solum τὴν ἐπι-γνῶσιν [?] qua non solum quod fit, sed cur fit, cognoscitur, definiri debet. Nam uera illa fides, electorum propria est: hæc autem ἐπίγνωσις, etiam reprobis nonnullis communis est. Ergo cum Paulo τῇ πληροφορίᾳ ea definiamus, Hebr.10.22. Accedamus, ait ille, cum uero corde ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πίστεως, & certa persuasione fidei, puris cordibus à conscientia mala.
units.tr: 3. The genus is knowledge [ἐπίγνωσις], recognition. This recognition must first be defined not as the comprehension [τῇ καταλήψει] by which one perceives what this or that man says. For faith is not some natural faculty in man but the gift of the Holy Spirit. Then, it is concerned not with those things which flesh and blood can search out and know, but with those which the Father who is in heaven reveals. Next, it must be defined not only as that knowledge [ἐπίγνωσις] by which not merely what is done but why it is done is known. For true faith is proper to the elect, whereas this knowledge is common also to some of the reprobate. Therefore, with Paul, we define it by full assurance [πληροφορία]: Heb. 10.22. Let us draw near, he says, with a true heart in full assurance of faith [ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πίστεως], and with a certain persuasion of faith, with hearts cleansed from an evil conscience.

units.la: Vocatur autem etiam τῆς συνέσεως πληροφορίας, Col.2.2. Vt consolationem accipiant eorum corda, ipsis charitate compactis, & omni opulentia certò persuasæ intelligentię, ad cognitionem mysterij Dei & Patris & Christi. Est itaq; fides, qua iustus uiuit, certissima persuasio & fiducia, quæ à Spiritu sancto in nobis accenditur, fouetur & augetur, cum transformamur per renouationem mētis nostræ, ad hoc ut probemus quæ sit uoluntas Dei, bona illa, accepta ac perfecta. Ro-man.12.2.
units.tr: It is also called the full assurance of understanding (Col. 2.2): that their hearts may be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the knowledge of the mystery of God, both the Father and Christ. Faith, therefore, by which the righteous lives, is a most certain persuasion and confidence, which is kindled in us by the Holy Spirit, nourished and increased, when we are transformed by the renewing of our mind, so that we may prove what is the will of God: that which is good, acceptable and perfect (Rom. 12.2).

units.la: Differentia est,Veritatis. Veritas hoc loco omni commenticiae [?] [?] opposita, veram religione significat. Vt etiam haec testimonia ostendunt. Ioan.17.17. Sanctifica eos tua veritate: fer-mo[?] tuus veritas est. Qui enim veram religionem profitentur, à profanis segregati, & Deo consecrati sunt. Paulus etiam Iudaeos de vera religione gloriari ait, dicens, [?] [?] [?] [?] [?] eos sibi ipsis tribuere: Rom.2.20. Et Gal.3.1. dicitur, eos non obsequi veritati, id est, veram & incorruptam religionem non retinere, qui ex lege iustificari volunt. Porrò, summam verae religionis Paulus [?] [?] uocat, fidei & operum legem: Rom.3.27.
units.tr: The difference is taken from truth. Truth in this place, opposed to all fictitious religion, signifies true religion, as these testimonies also show. John 17.17: Sanctify them through thy truth; thy word is truth. For those who profess true religion are set apart from the profane and consecrated to God. Paul also says that the Jews gloried in true religion, claiming it for themselves (Rom. 2.20). And Gal. 3.1 says that those who wish to be justified by the law do not obey the truth, that is, do not hold to the true and uncorrupted religion. Moreover, Paul calls the sum of true religion the law of faith and works (Rom. 3.27).

units.la: 5. Proprium est, [?] [?] pietas. Religio vera & pietas nullo modo seiungi possunt. Itaque ne religionis [?] omissa pietatis [?] meditemur. Nam fides per charitatem efficax est: Gal.5.6. ac sine operibus mortua: Iac.2.26. Videtur autem Paulus pietatem, fidei obedientiam vocasse, Rom.1.5. & 16.26. Positam autem esse pietatem in interioribus motibus cordis, quos Spiritus sanctus excitat, [?] [?] Pietatis & Corporalis exercitationis testatur.1.Tim.4.8. Corporalis exercitatio paululum habet utilitatis:at pietas ad omnia utilis est, ut quæ promissionem habeat uitæ præsentis & futuræ.
units.tr: 5. The property is piety [pietas]. True religion and piety can in no way be separated, so let us not, while meditating on religion, neglect piety. For faith is effective through love (Gal. 5.6), and dead without works (James 2.26). Paul seems to have called piety the obedience of faith (Rom. 1.5; 16.26). That piety lies in the inner motions of the heart, which the Holy Spirit stirs up, is attested by 1 Tim. 4.8: Bodily exercise profits a little, but piety is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come.

units.la: 6. Finis est,spes uitæ æternæ. Si,inquit Apostolus,in hac solùm uita speramus in Christum, miserrimi omnium hominum sumus. 1.Cor.15.19.
units.tr: 6. The end is the hope of eternal life. "If," says the Apostle, "in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable" (1 Cor. 15.19).

units.la: 7. Fundamentū fidei est,promissio Dei qui mentiri nescit. Qui itaq; dubitat de promissionum Dei firmitate & complemento,Deum mendacem scelerate facit. At qui de utroque plenè persuasus est,ut Abraham, is demum dat Deo gloriam. Rom.4.20.
units.tr: 7. The foundation of faith is the promise of God, who cannot lie. Therefore whoever doubts the firmness and fulfilment of God's promises makes God a liar, and does so wickedly. But he who is fully persuaded of both, as Abraham was, at last gives glory to God (Rom. 4.20).

units.la: Alia fidei descriptio,quæ exstat Heb.11.1.
units.tr: Another description of faith, which occurs in Heb. 11.1.

units.la: Ἐστι δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμά-τῶν ἔλεγχος ὁ[?] βλεπομένων.
units.tr: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. [Ἐστι δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων.]

units.la: Fides primùm est τῶν ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστα-sis. Est enim non modò plena persuasio & fiducia de rebus quæ sperantur: sed etiam,ut ea exstent,efficit.
units.tr: First, faith is the substance of things hoped for [τῶν ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις]. For it is not only a full persuasion and confidence about the things that are hoped for, but also brings it about that they exist.

units.la: Τῆς[?] ὑπόστασεως[?] uocabulum, quod generis in hac descriptione rationem obtinet, sexies,ut arbitror, in Epistolis Apostolicis occurrit: sed diuersa tamen significatione. Heb.1.3.significat personam,id est, ὑφιστάμενον[?], seu subsistens, uiuum, intelligens, incommunicabile, non suftetatum ab alio:ac tum opponitur τῇ ὑποστάσει. Verba sunt: Qui cum sit splendor gloriæ, & character hypostafeos,id est personæ,illius. Sed 2.Cor.9.4.&11.17. ὑπόστασις fiducia: & ὑπόστασις τῆς καυχήσεως, præsidente gloriationem, sine dubio significat. Hebr.2.14. fulcrum significat in hoc nobili dicto: Christi enim participes facti sumus, si modò principium illud quo sustetamur (τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως) firmum tenuerimus ad finem usque. In eadem significatione ὑποστάσεως uocabulum in descriptione fidei sumtum esse, magni nominis Doctores Ecclesiæ exististimauerunt. Parum tamen inter secundam & tertiam significationem interesse, non est obscurum. Fides enim fiducia rectè definitur: quia cū nitatur promissione Dei qui mentiri nescit, ipsa quoq; fulcri & sustetaculi instar nobis est. Scholiastes Græcus, ad fidei ἐνέργειαν & effecta respiciens, fidem ὑπόστασιν dictam ait, quòd efficiat ut exstent quæ sperantur. Eius hæc verba sunt: νῖς[?] ἐχὶν αὐτῇ ἡ ὑπόστασις ἡ ὁσία τῶν ἐλπιζομένων πραγμάτων, ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τὰ εἰ ἐλπίζομεν αὐνυπόστατα ἐστὶν,[?] ἐγὶμ, ὡς τίως μὴ ϖαρόντα, ἡ ϖίςις ὁσία τὶς αὐτῶν καὶ ἡ ὑπόςασις γίνε[?]σθαι, εἶναι αὐτὰ ἡ ϖαρεῖναι τρό[?]πον τινὰ παραπαυσάμενα, διὰ τῆ ϖίςεως εἶναι.
units.tr: The word hypostasis, which holds the place of the genus in this description, occurs six times in the Apostolic Epistles, as I think, but with different meanings. In Heb. 1.3 it signifies a person, that is, a subsistent being that is living, intelligent, incommunicable, and not sustained by another; and in this sense it is set over against ousia. The words are: "Who, being the brightness of his glory and the express image of his hypostasis, that is, of his person." But in 2 Cor. 9.4 and 11.17 hypostasis means confidence, and hypostasis tēs kauchēsēs undoubtedly means the ground of boasting. In Heb. 2.14 it means a support, in this noble saying: "For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold firm the beginning of our hypostasis [τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως] to the end." Those Doctors of the Church of great name have thought that the word hypostasis is used in the description of faith with the same meaning. It is not unclear, however, that there is little difference between the second and the third sense. For faith is rightly defined as confidence, since, resting on the promise of God who cannot lie, it is for us also like a prop and support. The Greek scholiast, looking to the working and effects of faith, says that faith is called hypostasis because it brings it about that the things hoped for exist. His words are: "Faith itself is the substance of things hoped for; for since the things we hope for have no substance, faith makes them, as it were, substantial and present, setting them before us in a certain way, so that they exist through faith." [νῖς ἐχὶν αὐτῇ ἡ ὑπόστασις ἡ ὁσία τῶν ἐλπιζομένων πραγμάτων, ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τὰ εἰς ἐλπίζομεν ἀνυπόστατά ἐστιν, ἡ πίστις οἷόν τις αὐτῶν καὶ ἡ ὑπόστασις γίνεται, εἶναι αὐτὰ ἢ παρεῖναι τρόπον τινὰ παραστήσασα, διὰ τῆς πίστεως εἶναι.]

units.la: Videntur autem hæc ex Chrysostomo transscripta, cuius hæc verba sunt: Quoniam ea quæ sunt in spe, sine substantia esse putantur, fides eis tribuit substantiam: magis autem eis non tribuit, sed ipsa est essentia eorum. Utputa, resurrectio nondum est facta, & necdum est in substantia, sed spes facit eam subsistere in anima nostra, hoc est quod dixit Substantia.
units.tr: These things seem to have been copied from Chrysostom, whose words are: "Since the things that are in hope are thought to be without substance, faith gives them substance; or rather, it does not give it to them, but is their very essence. For instance, the resurrection has not yet happened and is not yet in substance, but hope makes it subsist in our soul; this is what he meant by substance."

units.la: Basilius Magnus alicubi sic definit fidem: πίστις ἐγγυνα[?]θέσεως ἀδιακρίτος τῶν ἀ[?]νυσθ[?]ἰν[?]των, ἐν πληροφορίᾳ ἀληθείας τῶν ὑπερχθέν[?]των θεῷ χάριτι.
units.tr: Basil the Great somewhere defines faith thus: faith is an undoubting assurance of things not seen, in the full assurance of the truth of things that are beyond the reach of the senses, by the grace of God. [πίστις ἐγγύησις ἀδιάκριτος τῶν ἀνυποστάτων, ἐν πληροφορίᾳ ἀληθείας τῶν ὑπερκειμένων θεῷ χάριτι.]

units.la: Τὰ ἐλπιζόμενα, sunt materia fidei. Verbi gratia, malorum mitigatio & ab eisdem liberatio, carnis resurrectio, futurum iudicium, vita æterna: ut annotavit Theodor. Beza.
units.tr: The things hoped for are the matter of faith: for example, the mitigation of evils and deliverance from them, the resurrection of the flesh, the future judgment, eternal life, as Theodore Beza noted.

units.la: Itáne verò, dicet aliquis, communis est fidei & spei materia? Respondeo, eadem illa Dei beneficia, πίστει primum dici, quia certò intelligimus & persuasum habemus, Deum, qui ea nobis promisit, veracem esse, eoque de eorum possessione & fruitione tione tam non esse dubitandum, quàm non dubium nobis est, Mundum & nos eius incolas Dei verbo consistere: deinde ἐλπιζόμενα[?] vocari, quòd spes fidei luce accensa, bona illa quae differuntur in suum tempus, exspectando prosequatur, confirmata omnipotentiae Dei meditatione.
units.tr: "But is the matter of faith and hope therefore common?" someone will say. I answer: those same benefits of God are first said to be of faith, because we understand with certainty and hold it persuaded that God, who has promised them to us, is truthful, and therefore we ought to doubt their possession and enjoyment no more than we doubt that the world and we who dwell in it stand by the word of God. Then they are called hoped for because hope, kindled by the light of faith, pursues with expectation those good things that are deferred to their proper time, being strengthened by meditation on the omnipotence of God.

units.la: Sed cur addit Paulus, fide esse ἐλεγχ[?] Quia eius, veritate divina subnixae, tanta est πληροφορία[?] & certitudo, ut hominem convincat, & efficiat ut non possit necue lit contradicere. iuxta haec dicta, quibus mihi videtur Paulus elenchi vocem pulcerrimè declarauisse: 1.Cor.14.24. Sed si omnes prophetet, ingrediatur autem infidelis quispiam autidiota, arguitur, ἐλέγχεται[?] ab omnibus, dijudicatur ab omnibus, ἀνακρίνεται ὑπὸ πάντων. 25.Et ita occulta cordis eius manifesta fiunt. Atque ita procidens in faciem, adorabit Deum, renuncians Deū vere in vobis esse. Item: Dum ratiocinationes evertimus, omnemq; sublimitatem quae extollitur adversus cognitionem Dei: & captiuamducimus omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo: 2.Cor.10.5. Porrò Christo obediunt, qui in eum vere credunt: & eo sane nomine fidei obedientia celebratur Rom.1.& alibi.
units.tr: But why does Paul add that faith is elenchos? Because, resting on divine truth, it has such full assurance and certainty that it convinces a man and brings it about that he cannot, or does not dare, to contradict. In accordance with these words, by which Paul seems to me to have most beautifully explained the meaning of elenchus: 1 Cor. 14.24: "But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or unlearned man enters, he is convicted [ἐλέγχεται] by all, he is judged [ἀνακρίνεται] by all. 25. And thus the secrets of his heart are made manifest; and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you." Likewise: "Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ," 2 Cor. 10.5. Moreover, those who truly believe in Christ obey him, and it is under this very name that the obedience of faith is praised, Rom. 1, and elsewhere.

units.la: Quid vocat Paulus τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα[?]: Naturam Dei, & angelicam, Christi Iesu historiam, electorum Ecclesiam, &c. Fides enim nos convincit, unam esse essentiam divinam, & tamen tres in ea distinctas personas: Mundum à Deo conditum esse: Deum in carne patefactum esse, &c.
units.tr: What does Paul call things not seen [τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα]? The nature of God, and that of the angels, the history of Christ Jesus, the Church of the elect, etc. For faith convinces us that there is one divine essence and yet three distinct persons in it; that the world was created by God; that God was made manifest in the flesh, etc.

units.la: Libet autem hoc loco addere Glossema in Proœmium Decretalium Gregorij, ut videant pij & studiosi iuuenes, quàm parum honorificè Paulinam fidei descriptionem, ductam ab effectis & materia circa quam, Canonistæ quidam tractaue[?] rint. Vt maximè enim aliquis det, non totam fidei naturam integra definitione, sed partem solùm, instituto de patientia & spe accommodatam, à Paulo expositā esse: tamen honorificentius Dei oraculū explicandū esse, nemo sanus inficias ibit. Verba Glossatoris hæc sunt:
units.tr: Here it is worth adding a gloss on the Proem of Gregory's Decretals, so that pious and earnest young men may see how little honourably certain Canonists have treated the Pauline description of faith, which is drawn from its effects and from the matter about which it is concerned. For although one may grant that Paul described not the whole nature of faith in a complete definition, but only a part, suited to his purpose concerning patience and hope, yet no sane person will deny that the oracle of God ought to be explained more respectfully. The words of the Glossator are these:

units.la: Fides vero sic describitur ab Apostolo Hebr.11.[?] Fides est substantia rerum sperandarum, argumentū non apparentiū.
units.tr: Faith, however, is described thus by the Apostle, Heb. 11: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen."

units.la: Et dicitur substantia sperandarum rerum, quia sperare debemus, quod dictum est à Prophetis esse futurum. Atqui fi-des non hoc solùm efficit, ut nobis per-suadeamus, futurum ut euētus responde-ant uaticinijs Prophetarum: sed etiam, ut nobis mira quadam ratione exstent, quę alioqui speramus. Addit Glossa:
units.tr: It is called the substance of things hoped for because we ought to hope for what the Prophets have said will be. But faith does not only bring it about that we are persuaded that the outcomes will correspond to the prophecies of the Prophets, but also that the things we hope for in some wonderful way come to exist. The Gloss adds:

units.la: Argumentum non apparentium dici-tur, quia per prophetias iam completas debemus habere argumētum, id est, pro-bationem non apparētem, de futuris co-plendis, scilicet de die iudicij, & de uita æterna.
units.tr: It is called the evidence of things not seen because, through prophecies already fulfilled, we ought to have evidence, that is, a proof not seen, concerning the things to be fulfilled, namely the day of judgment and eternal life.

units.la: Neque uerò illo solùm nomine fidei ἔλεγχος dicitur, sed etiam quia uoce & au-ctoritate Dei, qui ἀψευδὴς est, & per Spiri-tum sanctum cor alloquitur, se conuinci, ut promissioni gratiæ assentiatur & ac-quiescat, reipsa experitur. Illa tamen su-periora minus sunt indigna, quàm ea quæ bonus ille Censor subiūxit, dicens:
units.tr: Nor is faith called elenchos only on this account, but also because a man experiences in fact that he is convinced by the voice and authority of God, who is unfailing [ἀψευδής], and through the Holy Spirit who speaks to the heart, so that he assents and acquiesces in the promise of grace. Yet these things above are less unworthy than those which that good Censor added, saying:

units.la: Sed uidetur, quòd ista definitio non sit bona: quia uera definitio conuertibilis esse debet cum suo definito. Sed hæc nō est conuertibilis: quia spes est similiter substantia rerum sperandarum. Vnde uideatur inferendum, quòd fides sit spes: quod est falsum. Respondeo ad Minoris probationem, id quod à Paulo λο[?] dictum est, de fide, quatenus ea cum probatione, patientia & spe coniuncta est, perperam à Canonistis, quasi sit ἁπλῶς dictum, accipi. Enimuero si Paulus fidem tantum circa τὰ ἐλπιζόμενα [?] uersari censuit, cur statim addidit, esse demonstratione eorum quæ non uidentur? An ne enim hæc quoq; non nisi si futura & sperata sunt? Non arbitror. Iam uerò, quis homo intelligens sic à parte totum colligat, ut eo nomine fidem esse spem colligat, quòd huic ex illa ortum ducenti quædam cum eadem communia sunt? Porrò integra definitio cum suo definito conuertibilis est: descriptio autem κατ' ἐπαινον [?], aut à communi materia ducta, non semper est conuertibilis. Intellectus noster circa uerum & bonum uersatur: idè dicitur & de uoluntate. An ne ex eo recte colligitur, uel illud uere non dici, uel intellectum esse ipsam uoluntatem? Addit Glossator:
units.tr: "But it seems that this definition is not good, because a true definition ought to be convertible with what it defines. But this one is not convertible, because hope is likewise the substance of things hoped for. Whence it seems to follow that faith is hope, which is false. I answer to the proof of the minor premise that what Paul said about faith, insofar as it is joined with proof, patience and hope, has been wrongly taken by the Canonists as if it were said absolutely." Indeed, if Paul judged that faith is concerned only with the things hoped for, why did he immediately add that it is the proof of things that are not seen? Surely these things too are not only future and hoped for? I do not think so. Now, what intelligent man so collects the whole from a part that he concludes faith is hope under this name, because certain things which arise from the one are common to both? Moreover, a complete definition is convertible with what it defines, but a description taken kat' epainon, or from a common matter, is not always convertible. Our intellect is concerned with the true and the good; for this reason it is also said of the will. Does it follow from this rightly either that the true is not truly so called, or that the intellect is the will itself? The Glossator adds:

units.la: Item ista definitio uidetur tantum loqui de futuris: cum fides sit tam de præ-sentibus, quàm de præteritis & futuris: eo quòd habet se ad omnia. Ad præteri-ta, ta, quia credendum est Christum fuisse natum & passum: ad praesentia, quia credendi est quod ipse sit qui in altari quotidie conficitur (Habetis hoc loco insigne exemplum petitionis principij.) Et ad futura, quia credere debemus ipsum uenturum & iudicaturum uiuos & mortuos, Et ita uidetur insufficiens ista definitio.
units.tr: Likewise, this definition seems to speak only of future things, whereas faith concerns present things as much as past and future, since it applies to all things. To past things, because we must believe that Christ was born and suffered; to present things, because we must believe that he is the one who is daily consecrated on the altar (here you have a notable example of begging the question). And to future things, because we must believe that he will come and judge the living and the dead. And so this definition seems insufficient.

units.la: Respondeo, τὸ Videtur, soluì per Non uidetur. Etsi enim fides facit, ut exstent ea quae sperantur ac futura sunt: eadem tamen demonstratio quoq; est πραγμά-τῶν ὑ[?] βλεπομένων. Unde colligimus, sententia Pauli fidem circa praeterita, praesentia & futura uersari, cum hominem ad patientiam & spem hortatur: ut ex hisce dictis liquet,
units.tr: I answer: the "It seems" (τὸ Videtur) is resolved by "It does not seem." For although faith makes those things exist which are hoped for and are yet future, it is also a demonstration of things not seen (πραγμάτων ... βλεπομένων). From this we gather that Paul's meaning is that faith is concerned with the past, the present and the future, when he exhorts a man to patience and hope, as is clear from these sayings:

units.la: 1. Fides recolit exempla Patrum. Psal. 22,4. In te sperauerunt Patres nostri: spe-rauerunt, & liberasti eos.
units.tr: 1. Faith recalls the examples of the Fathers. Ps. 22:4: "In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them."

units.la: 2. Eadem praesentia bona agnoscit. Psal. 1,18.43. Liberasti me à seditionibus populi: imposuisti me caput gentibus.
units.tr: 2. Faith also recognises present blessings. Ps. 18:43: "You have delivered me from the strivings of the people; you have made me head over the nations."

units.la: 3. Fides etiam spem fouet de futuris, id est, de mitigatione malorum, & de liberatione. Psal. 9.18. Quoniam non perpetuò obliuioni tradetur pauper:spes eorū qui opprimūtur, nō peribit perpetuō.
units.tr: 3. Faith also nourishes hope for the future, that is, for the easing of evils and for deliverance. Ps. 9:18: "For the poor shall not be forgotten for ever; the hope of the afflicted shall not perish for ever."

units.la: Ideo autem in hunc modum hoc quidem loco fidei vocabulum usurpandum est, quia illud institutæ exhortationi Paulinæ ad patientiam seruire debet.
units.tr: Moreover, the word faith is used in this passage in this way because it must serve the exhortation to patience that Paul has set out.

units.la: Videamus iam quàm lepidū colophonem addiderit: Et licet diuersa tempora comprehendat, una tamen fides esse uidetur. Vnde satis potest dici, quòd non est uera definitio, sed quædam notificatio fidei ab Apostolo dicta.
units.tr: Let us now see what a neat colophon he has added: "And although it embraces different times, faith nevertheless seems to be one." Whence it can fairly be said that this is not a true definition, but a certain notification of faith given by the Apostle.

units.la: Si fatetur Glossator, fidem præterita, præsentia & futura respicere, tum sophisma suum secundum ipsemet subuertit, &c, quod dici solet, propria vineta cædit.
units.tr: If the Glossator admits that faith looks to the past, the present and the future, then he overturns his own sophism, and (as the saying goes) cuts down the vine with its own pruning-knife.

units.la: Deinde, non est ἀδύνατον dicere unam esse fidem: Eph.4.5. & tamen cùm τῇ ἑνότητι μὴ ἡ τῇ πολυφορφίᾳ[?] constet, fateri quòd diuersa tempora comprehendat.
units.tr: Next, it is not impossible to say that there is one faith (Eph. 4:5); and yet, since it consists in unity and not in diversity [τῇ ἑνότητι μὴ ἡ τῇ πολυφορφίᾳ], to confess that it embraces different times is a contradiction.

units.la: Ut tamen Ecclesiæ rectius, si Deo placet, quàm Paulus olim fecit, consulat Glossator, quomodo nobis magistraliter sit definienda fides, his verbis docet: Potest, ait ille, magistraliter sic definiri: Fides est voluntaria certitudo absentium, infra scientiam & supra opinionem constituta. Scientia enim habet cognitionem, fides uerò non. Vnde dicit Augustinus: Fides est, credere quod non uides. Hæcille.
units.tr: Yet so that the Glossator may consult the Church more correctly, if it pleases God, than Paul once did, he teaches in these words how faith is to be defined magisterially for us: "It can," he says, "be defined magisterially thus: Faith is a voluntary certainty of things absent, established beneath knowledge and above opinion. For knowledge has cognition, but faith does not." Whence Augustine says: "Faith is to believe what you do not see." So far he.

units.la: Etsi abstinedum nobis est à λογομαχίας[?], & fatendum uocabula quædam aliter in Philosophia, quàm in Theologia, usurpa-ri:tamen in hac definitione illud probari non debet, quòd sic definit fidem, ac si es-set τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν[?], seu ut magis theologicè loquar, ac si à natura eiusq; uiribus, tanquàm suis principijs, non autem à gratia diuina, ortum ea duceret. Constat autem, fidem esse eximium & gratuitum Dei donum. Sed ad singula eius membra quædam διὰ βραχέων[?] annotabimus.
units.tr: Although we must abstain from logomachy, and admit that certain words are used differently in philosophy than in theology, yet in this definition it should not be granted that he defines faith as if it were among the things in our power [τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν], or, to speak more theologically, as if it derived its origin from nature and its powers as from its own principles, and not from divine grace. It is certain, however, that faith is an outstanding and gratuitous gift of God. But we shall briefly annotate some particulars of its several parts [διὰ βραχέων].

units.la: •. Si fides certitudo est, cur Pontificij fideles iubent ambigere, an'ne in gratia sint? cur nobis temerariæ præsumtionis notam aspergere conantur, cum audiunt affirmantes, Certò persuasos nos esse de bere de Dei erga nos beneuolentia? Pugnant extremè fides quæ certitudine definitur, & dubitatio. Quomodo ergo pœnantia in gradibus excellentibus, possunt esse in eodem subiecto, uidelicet in corde hominis?
units.tr: 1. If faith is certainty, why do the Papists bid the faithful to doubt whether they are in grace? Why do they try to fix on us the mark of rash presumption when they hear us affirm that we are firmly persuaded of God's goodwill towards us? Faith, which is defined by certainty, and doubt are utterly opposed. How then can they exist together in the highest degrees, namely in the same subject, the heart of man?

units.la: 2. Si etiam uoluntariam ideo uocant, quòd ab intelligentia & uoluntate humana mana oriatur & pendeat, errant toto cœ-lo. Nam animalis homo non percipit eâ quæ sunt Spiritus Dei: 1.Cor.2.14. uersa-tur in uanitate mentis suæ, cogitationem habens obscuratam & abalienatam à uita Dei, propter ignorantiam quæ est in eo ex obduratione cordis: Eph.4.17.18. Itaque nequaquam potest credere, quòd cę[?] ci sint oculi eius, & cor obduratum: Ioan. 12.39.40.
units.tr: 2. If they call it voluntary because it arises from and depends on human understanding and will, they are wrong by the whole heavens. For "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Cor. 2:14); he "walks in the vanity of his mind, having the understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God, through the ignorance that is in him, because of the hardening of his heart" (Eph. 4:17–18). Therefore he can by no means believe, since his eyes are blind and his heart hardened (John 12:39–40).

units.la: Sed si uoluntariam certitudinem esse dicit, quòd à Spiritu sancto mente illustrata, & uoluntate ad Deum conuersa, homo renatus sciens & uolens assentiatur promissioni gratiæ, & in ea acquiescat, libenter subscribemus. Spiritualis enim homo dijudicat, id est, intelligit ac discernit omnia: 1.Cor.2.15. Vult bonum facere, & delectatur Lege Dei secundum interiorem hominem: Rom.7.21.22.
units.tr: But if he says that it is a voluntary certainty, in the sense that the renewed man, his mind enlightened by the Holy Spirit and his will turned to God, knowingly and willingly assents to the promise of grace and rests in it, we shall gladly subscribe. For "the spiritual man judges all things, that is, understands and discerns them" (1 Cor. 2:15). He "wills to do good, and delights in the Law of God according to the inner man" (Rom. 7:21–22).

units.la: 3. Addit Definitor ille, Absentium. Fi-des, interveniente Spiritus sancti submi-nistratione, res absentes præsentes facit, & quodámodo sistit, sed pro diversa eâ-rum natura. Remissionem peccatorum & imputatione iustitiæ Christi, fides sic impetrat & applicat homini fideli, ut adsint, non absint illa Dei dona. Viuifica Christi caro, etsi ea actu primo in coelis est: quatenus tamen est ἐνεργητικὴ[?] & nos uiuificans caro, fide percipitur.
units.tr: 3. That Definer adds "of things absent." Faith, with the help of the ministry of the Holy Spirit, makes absent things present and in a certain way sets them before us, but according to the different nature of each. The forgiveness of sins and the imputation of Christ's righteousness faith so obtains and applies to the believing man that these gifts of God are present to him and not absent. The life-giving flesh of Christ, although in its first act it is in heaven, is nevertheless received by faith insofar as it is the active [ἐνεργητικὴ] flesh that quickens us.

units.la: 4. Toto autem coelo errat, cum fingit fidem scientia (quae est noticia conclusionum, quibus propter demonstrationem assentimur) inferiorem esse. Quid enim? An non fides est ἐπίγνωσις τῆς ἀληθείας; Tit. 1. 1. An non est ἔλεγχος; Hebr. 11. 1. An non ei summa certitudo tribuitur à Spiritu sancto in diuinis Scripturis? Quae, malum, haec uaesania est, fidem scientia inferiore fingere, cū credere nos gloriemur in Deum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum?
units.tr: 4. He errs by the whole heavens when he imagines that faith is inferior to knowledge (which is the recognition of conclusions to which we assent because of demonstration). For what? Is not faith "the knowledge of the truth" (Titus 1:1)? Is it not "a proof" (Heb. 11:1)? Is not the highest certainty ascribed to it by the Holy Spirit in the divine Scriptures? What madness, pray, is this, to imagine faith inferior to knowledge, when we glory in believing in God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit?

units.la: 5. Fidem autem ueram, non modò superiorem esse etiam opinione ea, quam Philosophus ἰσχυρὰν ὑπόληψιν nucupat, ex his dictis liquet: Vnusquisque in animo suo plenè persuasus est: Rom. 14. 15. Item: Qui disceptat, similis est fluctui maris, qui uentis agitatur & iactatur.
units.tr: 5. That true faith is not only superior to that opinion which the Philosopher calls a strong supposition [ἰσχυρὰν ὑπόληψιν], but is also above it, is clear from these sayings: "Let each one be fully persuaded in his own mind" (Rom. 14:5). Likewise: "He who disputes is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the winds" (cf. Jas. 1:6).

units.la: DE CONVERSIONE ad Deum Methodus.
units.tr: ON CONVERSION TO GOD: A Method.

units.la: Antequam ad aphorismos de conuersione, quibus illius caussas συλλήβδην compl ecti mihi propositum est, accedam, illud monere libet, idem Prophetis & Apostolis significare hæc duo illustria uocabula, ἐπιστροφὴν conuersionem, & μετανοίαν resi-piscentiam, ut uel ex hisce dictis liquet. Ier.31.19. Postquā enim conuersus sum, & pœnituit me. Act.11.18. Ἄρα γε καὶ τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ὁ θεὸς τὴν μετάνοιαν ἔδωκεν εἰς ζωήν; Ergo etiam Gentibus dedit Deus resipiscentiam ad vitam? Act.15.3. Paulus & Barnabas de ducti[?] ab Ecclesia, peragrárūt Phœnicem & Samariam, ἐνδιηγούμενοι[?] τὴν ἐπιστροφὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν. Ac nihil aliud esse conuerti, quàm μετανοεῖν resipiscere, hæc loca monent: Matt.13.14. & 18.3. Luc.1.16. Ier.31.19. Act.3.19. Μετανοήσατε οὖν[?] καὶ ἐπιστρέψατε.
units.tr: Before I come to the aphorisms on conversion, in which I intend to set out its causes briefly (συλλήβδην), I wish to point out that these two famous words, conversion [ἐπιστροφὴν] and repentance [μετανοίαν], mean the same thing to the Prophets and Apostles, as these sayings make clear. Jer. 31.19: "For after I was converted, I repented." Acts 11.18: "Then God has also granted repentance unto life to the Gentiles [Ἄρα γε καὶ τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ὁ θεὸς τὴν μετάνοιαν ἔδωκεν εἰς ζωήν]?" Acts 15.3: "Paul and Barnabas, brought on their way by the Church, travelled through Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles." And these passages show that to be converted is nothing other than to repent [μετανοεῖν] and turn back: Matt. 13.14; 18.3; Luke 1.16; Jer. 31.19; Acts 3.19: "Repent therefore and be converted [Μετανοήσατε οὖν καὶ ἐπιστρέψατε]."

units.la: Distinguenda etiam nobis sunt testi-monia de conuersione, quorū alia de prima hominis uocatione ad regnum Dei, alia autem de ciuium regni lapsu præoccupatorum instauratione loquuntur.
units.tr: We must also distinguish the testimonies about conversion. Some speak of the first calling of a man into the kingdom of God; others speak of the restoration of citizens of the kingdom who have been overtaken by a fall.

units.la: Prioris ordinis hæc exempla sufficiat in præsentia. 1.Thess.1.9. Siquidem ipsi de nobis annunciant, qualem ingressum habuerimus ad uos, & quomodo conuersi fueritis ad Deum, relictis idolis, ut seruiretis Deo uiuo & uero. Eph.2.11. Propterea memetote uos quondam gentes in carne,&c. 12.13. At nunc in Christo Iesu, uos qui olim eratis procul, propinqui facti estis per sanguine Christi. Act.14. 15. Euangelizantes, ut à uanis istis rebus conuertamini ad Deum illum uiuum.
units.tr: For the first kind, these examples will suffice for the present. 1 Thess. 1.9: "For they themselves report concerning us what manner of entrance we had among you, and how you were converted to God from idols, to serve the living and true God." Eph. 2.11: "Therefore remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, etc." 2.12–13: "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ." Acts 14.15: "Preaching the gospel to you, that you should turn from these vain things to the living God."

units.la: Ad posteriorem autem ordinem perti net hæc dicta. Luc.22.32. Ego rogaui pro te,ne deficiat fides tua: tu igitur aliquando conuersus,cōfirma fratres tuos. Gal. 6.1. Fratres,etiamsi præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliqua offensa, uos spirituales instaurate huiusmodi hominem cum spiritu mansuetudinis: considerans temetipfum, ne & tu tenteris. Iac.5.19. Fratres, fi quis inter uos aberrârit à ueritate, & conuerterit eum quispiam, sciat eum qui auerterit peccatorem ab errore uiæ suæ, seruaturum animam à morte, & obtecturum multitudinem peccatorum.
units.tr: To the second kind belong these sayings. Luke 22.32: "I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; you therefore, once converted, strengthen your brothers." Gal. 6.1: "Brothers, even if a man is overtaken in some offence, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted." Jas. 5.19: "Brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth, and someone converts him, let him know that whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins."

units.la: APHORISMI DE VE- ra conuersione.
units.tr: APHORISMS ON TRUE CONVERSION.

units.la: 1. De causa efficiente.
units.tr: 1. On the efficient cause.

units.la: Conuersio ad Deum, nō est αὐτοτέλεσμα naturæ, sed Dei donum. Hoc est, ij demū ad Deum uerè conuertuntur, quibus Deus pro sua immensa gratia id dedit. Vnde liquet, liquet,auctorem couersionis esse Deum. Hanc sententiam sic probo.
units.tr: Conversion to God is not an automatic result [αὐτοτέλεσμα] of nature but a gift of God. That is, only those to whom God has given this by his immense grace are truly converted to God. Hence it is clear that God is the author of conversion. I prove this opinion as follows.

units.la: 1. A' testimonis. Psal.85.4. Conuerte nos Deus saluator noster. Ier.31.18. Fac me conuerti, & conuertar, quia tu es Iehouah Deus meus. Act.11.18. [?] Nempe etiam Gentibus Deus resipiscentiam dedit adui tam. 2.Tim.2.25. Ecquando det illis Deus, ut resipiscentes agnoscant veritatem.
units.tr: 1. From testimonies. Psal.85.4. "Convert us, O God our Saviour." Jer.31.18. "Cause me to be converted, and I shall be converted, for you are Jehovah my God." Act.11.18. Indeed, God gave repentance unto life to the Gentiles also. 2 Tim.2.25. "If perhaps God may give them repentance, so that they may acknowledge the truth."

units.la: 2. Rectè ei soli conuersio tribuitur, qui à Deo alienos ei sic iungit, ut corda eorum illuminet ac innouet, sublata duricie seu contumacia & caligine. Sed Jehouah Deus noster id praestat, iuxta dicta: Dabo eis cor ut sciant me, quòd sim Iehouah: eruntq; mihi in populum, & ego ero eis in Deum: quia reuertentur ad me toto corde: Jer.24.7. Item: Dabo legem meam in medio eorum, & in corde eorum describam eam: Jer.31.33. Item: Daboq; uobis cor nouum, & Spiritum nouum dabo in medio uestri: & auferam cor lapideum è carne uestra, daboq; uobis cor carneum: Ezech.36.26.
units.tr: 2. Conversion is rightly ascribed to him alone who joins those alienated from God to himself in such a way that he enlightens and renews their hearts, taking away hardness, obstinacy and darkness. But Jehovah our God does this, according to the words: "I will give them a heart to know me, that I am Jehovah; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart." Jer.24.7. Likewise: "I will put my law in the midst of them, and write it on their heart." Jer.31.33. Likewise: "I will give you a new heart, and put a new spirit within you; I will take the stony heart out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh." Ezek.36.26.

units.la: Obiectio.
units.tr: Objection.

units.la: Deus conuersionem à nobis requirit, & pollicetur præmia resipiscentibus, pœnas
units.tr: God requires conversion from us, promises rewards to those who repent, and

units.la: has autem contumacibus καὶ ἀμετανοήτοις denunciat: ut uel ex unico hoc dicto liquet: Si uolueritis & audieritis, bonum terræ comedetis: si autem renueritis & irritaueritis, gladio deuorabimini: quia os Iehouæ locutum est: Isa.1.19.20. Ergo resipiscentia à natura & eius uiribus proficiscitur.
units.tr: announces punishments to the obstinate and unrepentant [ἀμετανοήτοις], as is clear from this one saying alone: "If you are willing and obey, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be devoured by the sword, for the mouth of Jehovah has spoken." Isa.1.19.20. Therefore repentance proceeds from nature and its powers.

units.la: Respondeo, esse fallaciam fecundum non causam ut causam. Ex debito enim non rectè colligitur facultas. Vt seruus il-le, qui decem milia talentorum domino debuit, non ideo quia debuit, soluendo fuit. Dignum autem memoria est dictum Augustini: Det Deus quod iubet, & iubeat quod vult. Item: O homo, in præceptione disce quid debeas habere: in correptione, tuo te uitio non habere: in precatione, à quo petere debeas id quod debes habere. Etsi autem nobis ἀδύνατα præcipit Deus, tamen non est in nos iniurius, cum tales condiderit, ut præstare illam obedientiam possemus: ipsi autem nostris peccatis ἀδικίαν illam accersiuerimus, quæ nos non soluit ab illa obligatione perfectè obedien-di Deo.
units.tr: I answer that this is the fallacy of taking what is not the cause for the cause. For ability is not rightly inferred from obligation. Thus that servant who owed his lord ten thousand talents was not able to pay merely because he owed it. It is worth remembering Augustine's saying: "God, give what you command, and command what you will." Also: "O man, in the precept learn what you ought to have; in the rebuke, learn that you do not have it through your own fault; in prayer, learn from whom you ought to ask what you ought to have." Although God commands us impossible things [ἀδύνατα], he is not unjust toward us, since he created us such that we could render that obedience; but we, by our sins, have brought upon ourselves that unrighteousness [ἀδικίαν], which does not free us from the obligation to obey God perfectly.

units.la: 2. Definibus conuersionis.
units.tr: 2. On the definition of conversion.

units.la: Ideo ad Dei laudem potissimùm, deinde & ad hominis restitutionem facit.
units.tr: Therefore it serves chiefly the praise of God, and then also the restoration of man.

units.la: Quemadmodum initiò conditi sunt homines ad gloriam Dei, opificis sapientissimi & optimi: ita post Adæ lapsum, præordinati ad uitam æternam, ad eiusdem Dei redemtoris laudē instaurantur, & fiunt καινὴ κτίσις: Gal. 6.15. iuxta dictū: Vt nos simus laudi gloriæ ipsius, qui priores sperauimus in Christo: Eph. 1.12. Itē: Sed Deus, qui diues est misericordia, propter multam charitatē suam, qua dilexit nos, etiam cum per offensas mortui essemus, unà uiuificauit nos per Christū, cuius gratia estis seruati: unaq; excitauit, unaq; collocauit in cœlis in Christo Iesu: ut ostenderet seculis succedētibus summas opes suæ gratiæ, sua erga nos benignitate in Christo Iesu. Eph. 2. 4. 5. 6. 7.
units.tr: Just as men were created at the beginning for the glory of God, the most wise and best Maker, so after Adam's fall, those predestined to eternal life are restored to the praise of the same God, their Redeemer, and become a new creation [καινὴ κτίσις], Gal.6.15, according to the saying: "That we should be to the praise of his glory, we who first hoped in Christ." Eph.1.12. Likewise: "But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our offences, made us alive together with Christ (by grace you are saved), and raised us up together and seated us together in the heavens in Christ Jesus; so that in the ages to come he might show the surpassing riches of his grace in his kindness toward us in Christ Jesus." Eph.2.4.5.6.7.

units.la: 3. De subiecto, seu de materia in qua.
units.tr: 3. On the subject, or the matter in which.

units.la: Vt autem nonnisi electorum est fides: ita eorū tantum est uera μετάνοια, seu resipiscētia, ut quæ ex fidei fonte promanet.
units.tr: Just as faith belongs only to the elect, so too true repentance [μετάνοια], or repentance, belongs only to them, since it springs from the fountain of faith.

units.la: Quibuscunq; Deus largitur fidei donum num, ijsdem & refipiscentiæ χαρίσματα[?] dat. Ideo præconisi fidei & conuersionis coniunguntur Act.22.21: Testificans Iudæis simul ac Græcis conuersionem ad Deum, & fidem in Dominum nostrum Iesum. Et Ioannes Baptista prædicans, dicebat: Resipiscite, appropinquauit enim regnū cœlorum: Matt.3.2. Ac uniuersalis omnium piorū cōuersio testatur, eos simul & credidisse in Christū, & pœnitētiam egisse.
units.tr: To whomever God grants the gift of faith, to the same he also gives the gifts [χαρίσματα] of repentance. Therefore faith and conversion are joined together: Act.22.21, "testifying to Jews and Greeks alike conversion to God and faith in our Lord Jesus." And John the Baptist, preaching, said: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." Matt.3.2. And the universal conversion of all the godly shows that they both believed in Christ and repented.

units.la: Atqui non omnium est fides: 2.Thess. 3.2. sed electorum Dei: Tit.1.1. hoc est, præordinatorum ad uitam æternam: Act.13.48. Itaq; refipiscentiam ad uitam ijsdem solis dari certum est. Act.11.18.
units.tr: But faith is not of all, 2 Thess.3.2, but of the elect of God, Tit.1.1, that is, of those predestined to eternal life, Act.13.48. Therefore it is certain that repentance unto life is given to these alone. Act.11.18.

units.la: Quid tibi uidetur de eorum sententia, qui dicunt in conuersione concurrere uoluntatem hominis?
units.tr: What do you think of the opinion of those who say that the will of man concurs in conversion?

units.la: Præstat te fateri, humanam uoluntatem esse principale subiectum, quod ab alio conuertitur, non à seipso. Ac ubi uoluntas conuersa & uiuificata est, ipsa quoq; acta à Spiritu sancto sine mora agit. Ex subiecto igitur quod conuertitur, ne facias caussam efficientem conuersionis: in qua si spectes non initia, sed τὴν ἀναγεννητικὴν[?] uoluntas regenerata demum, & à Spitu sancto acta, ipsa quoque agit.
units.tr: It is better to confess that the human will is the principal subject, which is converted by another and not by itself. When the will has been converted and quickened, it too, being acted upon by the Holy Spirit, acts without delay. Therefore do not make the subject that is converted the efficient cause of conversion; and if you look not at the beginnings but at the regenerating [τὴν ἀναγεννητικὴν] will, once regenerated and acted upon by the Holy Spirit, it too acts.

units.la: 4. De forma.
units.tr: 4. On the form.

units.la: Ut autem hominem à fictitiis & cadu-cis bonis revocat ad Deum, qui est infinitum bonum: sicut illa extenuet, hoc autē merita prosequatur laude, mortificatio-ne carnis & spiritus vivificatione cōstat.
units.tr: Now, as he calls man back from false and perishable goods to God, who is the infinite good, so that he weakens the former, and pursues the latter with praise, it consists in the mortification of the flesh and the vivification of the spirit.

units.la: Testimonia,
units.tr: Testimonies,

units.la: 1.Thess.1.9. Quomodo conversi fueritis ad Deum, relictis idolis, ut serviretis Deo vivo & vero.
units.tr: 1 Thess. 1:9. How you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God.

units.la: Act.14.15. Evangelizantes, ut à vanis istis rebus convertamini ad Deum illum vivum, qui fecit cœlum & terram & mare, & omnia quæ in eis sunt.
units.tr: Acts 14:15. Preaching to you that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea, and all that is in them.

units.la: Gal.4.8. Imò tum quidem ignorantes Deum, serviebatis ijs qui natura nō sunt Dij: 9. At nunc cum cognoscatis Deum, imò potius edocti stis [?] à Deo, quomodo convertimini retrorsum ad impotetia & egena elementa, quibus retrorsus ab initio servire vultis?
units.tr: Gal. 4:8-9. Indeed, at that time, not knowing God, you served those who by nature are not gods; but now, since you know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you wish to be in bondage again from the beginning?

units.la: Idem autem colligi è contrario potest. De idololatris enim dicitur: Deo mala fecit populus meus: me dereliquerunt ve-nam aquæ vivæ, ut effoderent sibi cister-nas, nas,cisternas confractas, quæ non valent continere aquas.Hier.2.13.
units.tr: The same can be gathered from the opposite. For of idolaters it is said: My people have done evil to God; they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, to dig themselves cisterns, broken cisterns, which cannot hold water. Jer. 2:13.

units.la: Iam verò quòd resipiscentia vera consistet mortificatione carnis & viviificatione spiritus, Apostolus noster his verbis docuit: Col.3.5. Mortificate igitur membra vestra terrestria,&c. 10.Et induceritis novum illum hominem, qui renovatum[?] in agnitionem congruetem imagini eius qui ipsum condidit.
units.tr: Now, that true repentance consists in the mortification of the flesh and the vivification of the spirit, our Apostle taught in these words: Col. 3:5. Mortify therefore your earthly members, etc. v. 10. And put on that new man, who is renewed in knowledge after the image of the one who created him.

units.la: Oremus autem toto pectore Deum æternum,Patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ut nobis per Spiritum suum sanctum det, pœnitentia dignos fructus proferre, ad ipsius divini nominis sanctificationem, & nostram aliorumq; ædificationem. Nam ut de publicis & politicis miseriis nihil jam dicam, cum vastent apri sylvestres vineam Jehouæ exercituum, qui interim πρωτοστάται[?] populi Dei videri volunt, & jam pellatur è medio sapientia,viq[?] omnia generantur, nihil dubium est nostra peccata obstare, quo minus quaprimum Dominus laboranti Ecclesiæ manum auxiliatricem & protectricem è cœlo porrigat. Convertamur itaq; ad Dominum optimo jure nos percutientem:scindamus corda nostra, & non vestimenta: precemur eum, ut hostes veritatis vel convertat, vel cofundat: ipsi autem usq; ad mortem pro veritate pugnemus: nec magis afficiamur sensu privatarum miseriarum, quàm Ecclesiae & praeclari depositi caelestis doctrinae cura & studio.
units.tr: Moreover, we pray with our whole heart to the eternal God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that through his Holy Spirit he may grant us to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, for the sanctification of his divine name and for our own and others' edification. For, to say nothing now of the public and political miseries, while the wild boars lay waste the vineyard of the LORD of hosts, and those who meanwhile want to be seen as the leaders of the people of God, and while wisdom is now driven from the midst and all things are thrown into confusion, there is no doubt that our sins stand in the way of the Lord stretching out from heaven a helping and protecting hand to his afflicted Church as soon as possible. Let us therefore turn to the Lord, who strikes us with the best right: let us rend our hearts and not our garments; let us pray that he either convert or confound the enemies of the truth; and let us fight for the truth even unto death. Nor should we be moved more by the sense of private miseries than by the care and zeal for the Church and for the excellent heavenly deposit of doctrine.

units.la: VERSVS VI,
units.tr: Verse 6,

units.la: Et pervenit verbum illud ad Regem Ni-nive: qui surrexit de solio suo, & deposuit vestimentum suum à se, operuitq; sese sacco, & sedit in cinere.
units.tr: And the word came to the king of Nineveh, and he rose up from his throne, and laid his robe aside from him, and covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.

units.la: Conijcio, hunc regem Ascrapacen vocari. Fuit enim is xxxvii Rex Assyriorum, qui circiter 42 annos regnavit. Regnare coepit anno ab orbe condito 3088. ante Christum natum 883. Ionas enim eo regnante floruit. Sardanapalus autem regnū Assyriorū obtinuit anno Mundi 3129; ante Christū natum 842. Huius temporibus Nahum propheta Niniuitis ad vomitum relapsis, urbis excidium & regni periodum praenunciauit.
units.tr: I conjecture that this king was called Ascrapacen. For he was the 37th king of the Assyrians, and reigned about 42 years. He began to reign in the year from the creation of the world 3088, before the birth of Christ 883. For Jonah flourished under his reign. Sardanapalus, however, obtained the kingdom of the Assyrians in the year of the world 3129, before the birth of Christ 842. In his time Nahum the prophet foretold to the Ninevites, who had relapsed into their vomit, the destruction of the city and the end of the kingdom.

units.la: Hic potentissimus Rex, edoctus de conversione Ionae, & de periculis impendentibus, serio resipuit, & suâ conversionem ad Deum ueris documetis declarauit, Tria autem illi Spiritus sanctus tribuit.
units.tr: This most powerful king, instructed about the conversion of Jonah and about the dangers hanging over him, seriously repented, and declared his conversion to God by true evidences. The Holy Spirit, however, bestowed three things upon him.

units.la: 1. Fidei obedientiam, Non enim patu-las solum aureis Dei uerbo praebuit, nequaqua aulicis uoluptatibus ebrius: sed etiam puro corde illud excepit, eique fidem habuit.
units.tr: 1. The obedience of faith. For he did not merely offer his ears to the golden word of God, nor was he, drunk with courtly pleasures, merely hearing it; but he received it with a pure heart and gave it his trust.

units.la: 2. Summissionem regiae maiestatis sub poteti manu Dei, quam e folio regali descendens, & in cinere sedens, declarauit.
units.tr: 2. The submission of his royal majesty under the mighty hand of God, which he declared by coming down from his royal throne and sitting in ashes.

units.la: 3. Agnitionem sui ipsius. Nam ut Deo quidem gloriam daret, seipsum uero peccatis pollutum, cinerem pulueremque, seu χοϊκόν [?], terrenum esse profiteretur, induit saccum, & sedit in puluere: commemorabili sane, & omnibus Regibus & Principibus imitando exemplo.
units.tr: 3. The knowledge of himself. For while he indeed gave glory to God, and professed that he himself, polluted by sins, was ashes and dust, that is, earthly, he put on sackcloth and sat in the dust: a truly memorable example, and one for all kings and princes to imitate.

units.la: THESIS.
units.tr: THESIS.

units.la: Exemplo poenitentiae summos homines caeteris mediocribus & infimis praelucere, non modo aequum, verum etiam salutare est.
units.tr: It is not only fair but also salutary that eminent men shine before others of middling and lowly rank by the example of repentance.

units.la: Verisimum est id quod Plato his uerbis testatus est: Eorum qui Reipub. praesunt, non modo singula uerba, nec res tantum publicitus gestae, animaduerti notant[?]; sed uirtus quoq;, iociq; simul &feria quoq;, domus ipsa,familia,uxor, cubile curiosius perquiruntur. Nam,ut Cicero Platoni subscribens ait: Studiosè pleriq; facta Principum imitantur. Neq; uerò quicquâ imitandũ sibi ducũt,quod non notauerũt,nondum commoti exemplo aut similitudine: quæ duo maximè commouere, rectè idem Cicero monuit.
units.tr: What Plato attested in these words is true: the notes of those who preside over the commonwealth take account not only of single words and of the things publicly done, but more carefully inquire into their virtue and their jests, their leisure too, their household, family, wife and bed. For, as Cicero, agreeing with Plato, says: most people eagerly imitate the deeds of princes. Nor do they think anything should be imitated by themselves which they have not observed, not yet moved by example or by likeness; and these two things, as the same Cicero rightly warned, most of all move people.

units.la: Danda itaq; opera est ijs, quos in illustri dignitatis gradu Deus eminere voluit, ut non tantùm auctoritate & gloria superiores sint, sed etiam iufticiæ, prudentiæ, fortitudinis & aliarum uirtutum exemplo laudatisimo excellât. Sed nō minori studio, fidei & pietatis [illegible, ~8 letters] eosdem agere æquum est. Rectè enim Bernardus: Sermo,ait,uiuus & efficax exemplum operis est.
units.tr: Therefore care must be taken that those whom God has wished to stand out in an illustrious rank of dignity are not only superior in authority and glory, but also excel by the most praiseworthy example of justice, prudence, fortitude and the other virtues. But it is fair that they also act with no less zeal for faith and piety. For Bernard rightly says: "A living and effective word is the example of a deed."

units.la: Sedenim, dicet aliquis, cur æquum & salutare esse censes,ut magistratus & Ec-clesiæ pastores exemplo pietatis & pulcerrimarum uirtutum alijs præluceant?
units.tr: But, someone will say, why do you think it fair and salutary that magistrates and ministers of the Church should shine before others by the example of piety and most excellent virtues?

units.la: Respondeo, Id eò requiri,quòd munerum,quibus utriq; defunguntur,ratio postulet,ut nō tantùm illi quidem legibus, edictis,præmijs & pœnis: hi uerò institutione è uerbo Dei petita, exhortatione, obiurgatione, agant: sed etiam amabili laudatae uitae exemplo, suae fidei commissos meliores reddere studeant. Itaq; eximia sane laus ceteri ea debet, quam Origeni Adamantio Eusebius tribuit, dicens: οἷος ἦν τῷ λόγῳ, τοῖος ἦν ἡ τῷ τρόπῳ, &c.
units.tr: I answer: this is required because the nature of the offices which both perform demands that they not only act, the former with laws, edicts, rewards and punishments, the latter with instruction drawn from the Word of God, exhortation and rebuke, but also strive to make better those committed to their trust by the lovable example of a praised life. Hence the outstanding praise which Eusebius gives to Origen Adamantius deserves to be given to all: "such as he was in word, such was he in manner," etc. [οἷος ἦν τῷ λόγῳ, τοῖος ἦν ἡ τῷ τρόπῳ]

units.la: Quomodo autem summi homines mediocribus & infimis praelucere debent?
units.tr: But how ought eminent men to shine before those of middling and lowly rank?

units.la: Respondeo: Primùm quidem uera fidei obedientia, sic ut ad se quoq; doctrinam, comminationes & promissiones diuinas pertinere, reipsa testentur. Exemplo est Dauid, qui homicidij & adulterij reus, obiurgante eum Nathan propheta, ingenuè respondit: Peccaui. Ac deinde absolutioni à peccatis, annunciatae his uerbis, Dominus abstulit peccatum tuum; idem ex animo fidem habuit.
units.tr: I answer: first of all, by true obedience of faith, so that by their deeds they bear witness that the teaching, threats and promises of God pertain also to themselves. David is an example, who, guilty of murder and adultery, when the prophet Nathan rebuked him, frankly answered: I have sinned. And then, when absolution from sins was announced in these words, The LORD has taken away your sin, he believed this from his heart.

units.la: Secundò, praelucere eos decet non fucata sui agnitione. Hanc autem testantur, cum uelut obliti ciuilis dignitatis, sese humiliant coram Deo & hominibus.
units.tr: Second, they ought to shine forth with an unfeigned knowledge of themselves. They attest this when, as if forgetting their civil dignity, they humble themselves before God and men.

units.la: Postremò, cùm ea τῆς ταπεινοφροσύνης & doloris ob admissa peccata specimina edunt, quorum αὐτοψία aliorum instaurationi plurimum seruire poterit.
units.tr: Finally, when they show such tokens of humility [τῆς ταπεινοφροσύνης] and of sorrow for sins committed, whose seeing for oneself [αὐτοψία] will be able to serve greatly for the restoration of others.

units.la: Etsi autem res uestiaria ad φραστικὰ ζωῆς ψυχικοῖς[?] pertinet, quemadmodum & sessio in cinere: si tamen exemplum utriusq;, aut similium rerum & circumstatiarum, moribus laudatis receptum sit, & multorum emendationi seruire possit, non est cur summi homines caeteris exemplo es-se recusent.
units.tr: Although the matter of clothing pertains to outward things of life, as does sitting in ashes, yet if the example of either, or of similar things and circumstances, is received with approval as praiseworthy conduct, and can serve the correction of many, there is no reason why eminent men should refuse to be examples to others.

units.la: An ne conuersio ad Deum,uiribus humanis ac-cepta ferri possit: cum hoc dicatur, Regem Niniuitarum serio resipuisse?
units.tr: Whether conversion to God can be attributed to human powers, since it is said that the king of the Ninevites seriously repented?

units.la: Aientem opinionem Pelagiani & eorum sequaces probare conantur, argumēto ducto à consideratione mandatorum Dei,& exemplorum tum obedientiae in conuersione,tum contumaciae.
units.tr: The Pelagians and their followers, and the Papists of this age, try to prove the affirmative opinion by an argument drawn from the consideration of God's commandments, and from examples both of obedience in conversion and of obstinacy.

units.la: Quæcunq; Deus serio à nobis requirit:& ab aliis quidem magno eorum bono præstantur,ab aliis autem summo eorum malo negliguntur: ea uideri possunt in humanis posita uiribus, & in τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν numero. Ratio huius propositio-nis gemina dari posse uidetur. Nam,ne nobis crudeliter illudat Deus, non requirit à nobis ἀδύνατα, cum intelligat ea à nobis miseris præstari non posse: & a-liorum quidem obedientia, aliorum autem contumacia, manifestum argumentum est,quod nos cõuincitut statuamus, illos quidem potuisse & uoluisse resipiscere,hos uerò noluisse conuerti ad Deũ: ut de Hierosolymitanis dicitur,[?] καὶ οὐκ ἠθε-λήσατε: Matt.23.37.
units.tr: Whatever God seriously requires of us, some men perform to their great good, while others neglect it to their great harm. Such things can seem to lie within human powers and to belong to the number of things in our power [τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν]. This proposition seems to be supported in two ways. First, God does not cruelly mock us by requiring of us things that are impossible [ἀδύνατα], since he knows that we wretched creatures cannot perform them. Second, the obedience of some and the obstinacy of others is a plain proof that compels us to hold that the former were able and willing to repent, while the latter were unwilling to be converted to God. This is said of the people of Jerusalem: "and you would not" [καὶ οὐκ ἠθελήσατε], Matt. 23.37.

units.la: Sed ut conuertamur ad se ex toto corde, Dominus Deus noster ferió efflagitat.iuxta dictum: Resipiscite,& conuertimini,ut deleatur peccata uestra: Act.3.19.
units.tr: But that we should turn to him with our whole heart, the Lord our God earnestly demands, according to the saying: "Repent and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out," Acts 3.19.

units.la: Et hæc Ionæ historia illustre exemplum Regis potentissimi μετανοοῦντος[?] resipiscentis continet. Paulus etiam quibusdam tribuit σκληρότητα duritie, [?] ἀμετανόητον καρδίαν, cor resipiscere nescium, Rom.2.5.
units.tr: The history of Jonah also contains the notable example of a most powerful king who repented [μετανοοῦντος]. Paul, too, ascribes to some "hardness" [σκληρότητα] and "an unrepentant heart" [ἀμετανόητον καρδίαν], a heart unable to repent, Rom. 2.5.

units.la: Ex his sequi videtur,in humanis situm esse viribus, resipiscere & nō resipiscere: id quod cum Pelagianis veteribus Pontificij huius ætatis statuunt.
units.tr: From these things it seems to follow that it lies within human powers to repent or not to repent. The Papists of this age, like the old Pelagians, hold this.

units.la: Respondeo,
units.tr: I answer:

units.la: 1. Ad Maiorem,in qua est τὸ λεγόμενον, Esse in argumentatione paralogismum secundum non causam ut causam. Ex mandato enim Dei non rectè colligitur facultas præstandi ea, quæ ille optimo sanè iure à nobis flagitat, cum ad gloriam suam nos condiderit. Porrò,ut exempla resipiscentiæ,non hominū uires, sed Dei donum & Spiritus sancti efficaciam commendant: sic eorum qui non resipuerunt exempla ostendunt,tum quàm sit depravata hominum natura & per se ἀμεταπ[illegible, ~6 letters]τος,tum quòd impijs nō sint mutationes, & quòd Deum non timeant: id est,quòd nequaquam in melius mutent mentes sũas & mores, & quòd posterioribus curis neutiquam locum dent.Psal.55.19.
units.tr: 1. To the major premise, in which lies what is called the fallacy of taking what is not the cause for the cause in argument. For it is not rightly inferred from God's commandment that there is a power to do what he most justly demands of us, since he created us for his own glory. Moreover, just as the examples of repentance commend not human powers but the gift of God and the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, so the examples of those who did not repent show both how depraved human nature is and how unchangeable [ἀμετάπτωτος] it is in itself, and that the wicked have no changes of mind, and do not fear God; that is, they by no means change their minds and manners for the better, and they never give place to later concerns. Ps. 55.19.

units.la: 2. Ad primam rationem per inficiationem. Nequaquam enim crudeliter nobis illudit Deus,cum Legis suæ obseruationem à nobis requirit. Primùm enim Deus tales initiò homines condidit,ut legi satisfacere possent: ipsi autem sponta-nea defectione ἀδικίᾳ[?] sibi accersiuerunt tantam,ut Legi satisfacere nequeat. Deinde, ut debitores non esse desinunt, qui suo scelere effecerunt ut soluedo nō sint:ita nec nos ideo debitores Legis non sumus,quia ei non plenè satisfacere possumus. Tertiò,nobis qui per Spiritum & aquam renati sumus,ideo lex obseruanda præscribitur,quia,ut loquitur Augustinus,Deus nobis dat qd̃ pręcipit,sic ut imputatione & incoatione Legè pstemus.
units.tr: 2. To the first argument, by denial. For God by no means cruelly mocks us when he requires us to keep his law. For first, God created men at the beginning so that they could satisfy the law; but by their own voluntary defection, they brought upon themselves such great unrighteousness [ἀδικίᾳ] that they cannot satisfy the law. Next, just as those who by their own crime have made themselves insolvent do not cease to be debtors, so we are not for that reason not debtors of the law because we cannot fully satisfy it. Third, for us who have been born again through the Spirit and water, the law is prescribed to be kept for this reason: as Augustine says, God gives us what he commands, so that we may fulfil the law by imputation and by a beginning.

units.la: 3. Ad secundam rationem, ab exemplis eorum qui uel resipiscunt, uel in peccatis manent, ductam, Esse eam ἀσυλλόγιστον[?]. Neque enim sequitur: Niniuitae resipuerunt. Igitur suis uiribus hoc praestiterūt nec à Deo acceperunt donum, ut poenitentiam agerent. Certum enim est, resipiscentiam donum Dei esse, quod non nisi filijs lucis confertur.
units.tr: 3. To the second argument, drawn from the examples of those who either repent or remain in their sins, I say that it is inconclusive [ἀσυλλόγιστον]. For it does not follow that the Ninevites repented, therefore they accomplished this by their own powers and did not receive from God the gift of repenting. For it is certain that repentance is a gift of God, which is bestowed only on the children of light.

units.la: 4. Ad postremum de Ierosolymitanis, qui dicuntur noluisse amplecti oblatum Christi beneficium, Matt.23.37. Si cum quibusdam agat Dominus externo solùm ministerio, non autem σῴζειν[?] alloquatur cor hominis, & illud aperiat & mundū creet, mirum non debere uideri, si prauum & peruersum ac lapideum hominis cor, sui simile, hoc est contumax & refractarium esse pergat, sic ut non nisi in testimonium ei cedat ministerium publicum & commune.
units.tr: 4.
