To the last point, about the people of Jerusalem, who are said to have been unwilling to embrace the benefit of Christ offered to them, Matt. 23.37: if the Lord deals with some only by external ministry, and does not address the heart of man to save [σῴζειν] it, open it and create it clean, it should not seem strange if the man's heart, perverse, crooked and stony, and like itself, that is, stubborn and refractory, continues to be so, so that the public and common ministry serves only as a testimony against it.

units.la: Negantem uero sententiam, quæ negat humanis uiribus conuerti hominem, quibus, quæsote, rationibus diuina Scriptura demonstrat?
units.tr: But on the opposing view, which denies that man can be converted by human powers, by what reasons does holy Scripture prove it?

units.la: Recitabo è multis maximè illustres & euidentes,
units.tr: I will recite some of the most notable and evident of many:

units.la: 1. Quia eiusdem est nostra per refipiscentiam instauratio, cuius est & creatio. Neque enim minus habere debet uirtutis & omnipotentiae diuinae ἀποτέλεσμα[?], Instauratio nostri post grauissimum lapsum & corruptionem, quàm Creatio. Atqui Deus ipse nos fecit, & nō ipsi nos:Psal.100.3. Itaque & de nostra recreatione & regeneratione cum Apostolo nostro concludamus: Ipsius sumus opus, cōditi in Christo Iesu ad opera bona, quae praeparauit Deus ut in eis uersaremur:Eph.2.10.
units.tr: 1. Because our restoration through repentance belongs to the same one to whom our creation belongs. For the restoration of ourselves after the most grievous fall and corruption ought to show no less the power and omnipotence of God than the creation does. But God himself made us, and not we ourselves: Ps. 100.3. So, with our Apostle, let us also conclude about our re-creation and regeneration: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them," Eph. 2.10.

units.la: 2. Mortui in offensis & peccatis seipsos non possunt, ad Deum sponte sua couersi, uiuificare. Omnes autem homines, cū ex carne nati sint, in offensis & peccatis mortui sunt: Ioan.3. Eph.2.1. Itaq; nulli homines seipsos uiuificare possunt: & per consequens, nulli homines suis uiribus conuerti ad Deū, seu uiuificari possunt. Quis ergo nos uiuificat? Deus ipse, ut eum celebrans Paulus testatur: Etiam, dicens, cū per offensas mortui essemus, una uiuificauit nos per Christum, cuius gratia estis seruati:Eph.2.5.
units.tr: 2. Men dead in trespasses and sins cannot, by turning to God of their own accord, make themselves alive. But all men, since they are born of the flesh, are dead in trespasses and sins: John 3; Eph. 2.1. Therefore no men can make themselves alive, and consequently no men by their own powers can be converted to God, or be made alive. Who then makes us alive? God himself, as Paul bears witness in praising him, saying: "even when we were dead through trespasses, he made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved," Eph. 2.5.

units.la: 3. Mens ignara Dei, & uoluntas ab eodem auersa, non dici possunt causae con-uersionis uersionis ad Deum. Ratio 1.Conuersio enim fine luce gratiae & fidei peragi nequit. Illa uero in no renatis nequaquam est: qui eo nomine in tenebris & umbra mortis sedere dicuntur, Matt. 4.16. Ratio 2. de uoluntate: Subiectum principale conuersionis no debet confundi cu eiusdem efficiente principali. Sed uoluntas est conuersionis principale ὑποκείμενον: ut uel nomen ipsum Conuersionis docet.
units.tr: 3. A mind ignorant of God, and a will turned away from him, cannot be called the causes of conversion to God. The first reason: conversion cannot be carried out without the light of grace and faith. But these are by no means in the unregenerate, who are said to sit in darkness and the shadow of death, Matt. 4.16. The second reason concerns the will: the principal subject of conversion must not be confused with its principal efficient cause. But the will is the principal subject [ὑποκείμενον] of conversion, as the very name of conversion teaches.

units.la: Atqui in no renato homine mens ignara est Dei, & uoluntas contumax, διεστραμμένη[?] & à Deo auersa. iuxta hæc dicta: Hoc igitur dico & obtestor per Dominum, ne amplius uersemini sicut reliquae Gentes uersantur in uanitate mentis suae, cogitationem habentes obscuratam, & abalienatam à uita Dei, propter ignorantiä quę est in ipsis ex obduratione cordis eorū: Eph. 4.17.18. Item: Animalis autem homo non est capax eorū quae sunt Spiritus Dei:sunt enim illi ftulticia. 1.Cor.2.14.
units.tr: But in the unregenerate man the mind is ignorant of God, and the will is obstinate, perverted [διεστραμμένη] and turned away from God, according to these words: "This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles walk, in the futility of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God, because of the ignorance that is in them, due to the hardening of their hearts," Eph. 4.17-18. Likewise: "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him," 1 Cor. 2.14.

units.la: Fateamur itaq; id quod res est, nostris uiribus nos neutiquā cōuerti ad Deum.
units.tr: Let us therefore confess what is the case: by our own powers we are by no means converted to God.

units.la: VERSVS VII.
units.tr: VERSE 7.

units.la: Et proclamare inssit,& dicere in Nini- ueh ueh[?] edicto regio & magnatu eius, dicedo: Homines & iumenta, boues & pecudes ne gustent quicquam, neque pascantur, et aquâ non bibant.
units.tr: And he caused it to be proclaimed and said throughout Nineveh, by the king's edict and that of his nobles, saying: Let men and beasts, oxen and sheep, taste nothing, nor be fed, nor drink water.

units.la: In hoc uersu & duobus sequentibus uersibus, summam regij edicti de poenitentia agenda descripsit Ionas. Duo autem hæc obseruanda sunt: Circumstantiæ personarum, & Edictum.
units.tr: In this verse and the two that follow, Jonah sets out the substance of the royal edict concerning the performance of repentance. Two things are to be observed here: the circumstances of the persons, and the edict itself.

units.la: Edicti duæ partes sunt: altera περὶ τῶν πραγμάτων, seu de rebus agendis: altera περὶ τῶν ἐλπισομένων, seu de spe veniæ & diuinæ misericordiæ. Obseruandus autem est ordo. Resipiscentiam & eius fructus comitatur mitigatio malorum: cor autem ἀμετανόητον seu poenitere nescium, & opera carnis, sequuntur poenæ. Ideo Rex prudenter initiò poenitentiam requirit, & eius exercitium præscribit.
units.tr: The edict has two parts: one concerning the things to be done (περὶ τῶν πραγμάτων), that is, the actions required; the other concerning the things to be hoped for (περὶ τῶν ἐλπισομένων), that is, hope of pardon and divine mercy. The order must be observed. Repentance and its fruit are accompanied by the easing of evils, whereas an unrepentant heart (ἀμετανόητον, one that does not repent) and the works of the flesh are followed by punishments. Therefore the king wisely first requires repentance and prescribes its practice.

units.la: Τῶν πραγμάτων, & couersionis exercitiorum ac documentorum hic ordo est: Initiò præscribitur ieiunium commune: deinde, lugubris habitus, uelut reatus & humiliationis signum: tertiò, preces ardentissimæ: postremò, odium & fuga mali, cum quo iungi debet amor studiumq; boni. Hæc omnia uers.7.& 8.occurrunt.
units.tr: Of the things to be done, and of the exercises and instructions of conversion, the order here is this. First, a common fast is prescribed; then mourning dress, as a sign of guilt and humiliation; third, most fervent prayers; last, hatred and flight from evil, to which must be joined love and zeal for good. All of these occur in verses 7 and 8.

units.la: Quid sperandum sit de clementia Dei & malorum mitigatione, postrema edi-cti istius pars, uers.9.ostendit.
units.tr: What is to be hoped for concerning the mercy of God and the lessening of evils, the last part of this edict, shows in verse 9.

units.la: DE PERSONIS [?]EARVM-que circumstantijs.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE PERSONS AND THEIR CIRCUMSTANCES.

units.la: Si ὑπόθεσιν uers.7.ad thesin reducas, occurret hæc doctrina: Decreta magistra-tus exercitijs pœnitentiæ seruire debent.
units.tr: If you reduce the hypothesis of verse 7 (ὑπόθεσιν) to a thesis, this doctrine will emerge: Decrees of the magistrate ought to serve the exercises of repentance.

units.la: Vt hoc loco dicitur, Regem Assyriorum eiusq; ξυμπαρακλήτας [?], regni Proceres, edi-ctum de resipiscentiæ exercitijs præscri-psisse subditis, ut ad laudabile Regis ad Deum conuersi exemplum, salutaris eiusdem per edictum exhortatio accederet.
units.tr: As is said in this place, the King of the Assyrians and his associates (ξυμπαρακλήτας), the nobles of the realm, prescribed to the subjects by edict the exercises of repentance, so that the salutary exhortation carried by the edict might be joined to the king's praiseworthy example of conversion to God.

units.la: Noti sunt elegantes hi uersus:
units.tr: These elegant verses are well known:

units.la: Tu ciuem patremq; geras, tu consule cunctis: In commune iubes si quid censesq; tenendum, Primus iussa subi. tunc obseruantior æqui Fit populus, nec ferre uetat, cum uiderit ipsum Auctorem parere sibi. componitur orbis Regis ad exemplum: nec sic inflectere sensus Humanos edicta ualent, quam uita regentis. Mobile mutatur semper cum Principe uulgus.
units.tr: You bear both the citizen and the father, you take thought for all. If you command something to be kept in common, you yourself first submit to the commands. Then the people becomes more observant of what is fair, and does not refuse to bear it when it sees the author himself obeying. The world is arranged after the king's example; edicts cannot bend human minds as much as the life of the ruler does. The fickle crowd always changes with the prince.

units.la: Nonnihil simile est exemplum Nebu-cadnezaris magni, qui à Deo graujter correptus, ubi ad sanitaté mentis reuocatus esset,edictum de pœnis,quibus ob su-perbiam & alia peccata affectus erat, & de earum relaxatione, deq; veri Dei agnitione & cultu,in subiectorum gratiam promulgari curauit: Dan.4. Item illud Iudaeorum e Babylone reducum,& poenitentiam Ezra hortante agetium exemplum, de quo agitur Nehem.9.
units.tr: Somewhat similar is the example of the great Nebuchadnezzar, who, severely chastised by God, when he was restored to sanity of mind, took care to have published for the good of his subjects an edict concerning the punishments with which he had been afflicted for pride and other sins, and concerning their remission, and concerning the knowledge and worship of the true God: Dan. 4. Likewise the example of the Jews returned from Babylon, who carried out repentance at Ezra's exhortation, of which it is spoken in Neh. 9.

units.la: Sedenim consensus Regis Assyriorum & Optimatum eius, magna laude dignus est. Saepe enim diuersa sunt Regum & Procerum consilia & studia, sic ut pijs conatibus quorundam, pars altera adversetur, seu vi, seu artificio Sinonio.
units.tr: Indeed, the agreement of the king of the Assyrians with his nobles is worthy of great praise. For often the counsels and aims of kings and nobles differ, so that one part opposes the pious endeavours of certain others, either by force or by the artifice of Sinon.

units.la: DE IEIVNIO.
units.tr: CONCERNING FASTING.

units.la: Propositum nobis est, Ieiunij, proprie sic dicti, finitione & causas aliquot paucis tradere. Det autē nobis Dominus Iesus Christus, ne de nobis quoq; dici possit illud Hieronymi: Delicatus magister est, qui pleno ventre de ieiunijs disputat.
units.tr: It is our purpose to set out briefly the definition and some causes of fasting, properly so called. May the Lord Jesus Christ grant that that saying of Jerome may not be applied to us as well: "He is a pampered teacher who discourses on fasts with a full belly."

units.la: ι. Quid non sit ieiunium. ἀπόφασις.
units.tr: 1. What fasting is not. (ἀπόφασις)

units.la: 1. Non est solùm temperantia in cibo & potu. Nam haec per omnem vitam nobis est sectanda, iuxta dictum: Cauete, ne grauentur corda vestra crapula, &c.
units.tr: 1. It is not merely temperance in food and drink. For this must be pursued by us throughout our whole life, according to the saying: "Take heed that your hearts are not weighed down with surfeiting," etc.

units.la: 2. Non est abstinentia à prandio aut à cœna. Nam & Plato dicit infelices eos esse, qui bis saturi fiunt eodem die. Acue teribus Græcis usitatum fuit, semel tantùm interdiu cibum sumere.
units.tr: 2. It is not abstinence from lunch or supper. For Plato too says that those are unhappy who become sated twice in the same day. Among the Greeks it was customary to take food only once, in the daytime.

units.la: 3. Nec est ciborum delectus. Neque enim ieiunium fuerit à certa cibi specie abstinere, & delitijs genio satisfacere.
units.tr: 3. Nor is it a choice of foods. For fasting would not consist in abstaining from one particular kind of food while indulging the appetite with delicacies.

units.la: 2. Quid sit ieiunium.
units.tr: 2. What fasting is.

units.la: Est, cùm sponte nostra aliquid usitatæ diætæ subtrahimus, ut ea res seruiat carni in nobis mortificandæ, precibus ardenter ad Deū fundendis, & nostræ summisi oni sub potenti manu Dei. Hæc finitio αὐτιολογικὴ docet utrumq;, & quæ sit ratio seu forma ieiunij ueri, & quæ sint eius caussæ finales.
units.tr: It is when, of our own accord, we withhold something from our usual diet, so that this thing serves the mortifying of the flesh within us, while we pour out prayers earnestly to God, and humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God. This causal definition (αὐτιολογικὴ) teaches both what the reason or form of true fasting is and what its final causes are.

units.la: Forma & modus quantitatem, qualitatem & tempus complectitur, Ieiunates enim nec alias usitata cibi & potus copia, nec delitijs cõsuetis, nec eodem tempore, uti debent: ut συλλήβδην multa complectar.
units.tr: The form and manner comprise quantity, quality and time: fasters ought to use neither their usual amount of food and drink, nor their customary delicacies, nor the usual time for eating. To sum up, I may comprise many things.

units.la: Fines sunt, ut carnis mortificationi, ut precibus, ut deniq; τὴν ταπεινοφροσύνη seruiat.
units.tr: Its ends are that it serve the mortification of the flesh, serve prayer, and finally serve humility (τὴν ταπεινοφροσύνην).

units.la: Cum autem ieiunium σωματικῆς γυναικείας species quædam sit, illud non quasi sit cultus Dei, sed quia præstantioribus illis finibus, de quibus diximus,feruit, commendamus & requirimus. Iuxta haec dicta Patrum:
units.tr: But since fasting is a kind of bodily exercise, we commend and require it not as if it were worship of God, but because it serves those higher ends of which we have spoken. In accordance with these sayings of the Fathers:

units.la: Modicus & temperatus cibus, & animae & corpori utilis est: Hieronymus ad Rusticum Monachum. Ieiunio alae duae sunt, orationis uidelicet & iusticiae: Bernardus de Quadr. Quid prodest tenuari corpus abstinentia, si animus intumescit superbia? Hieronymus ad Celatiam. Ieiunium, humilitatis signum: Augustinus epist.176. Ieiunium est abstinentia a uitijs: Chrysostomus. Ieiunium modestiae principium: Idem ad Antioch. hom.43.
units.tr: Moderate and temperate food is useful both to soul and body: Jerome to the monk Rusticus. Fasting has two wings, namely prayer and righteousness: Bernard, On Lent. What good is it for the body to be thinned by abstinence if the mind swells with pride? Jerome to Celantia. Fasting is a sign of humility: Augustine, letter 176. Fasting is abstinence from vices: Chrysostom. Fasting is the beginning of modesty: the same, to the Antiochenes, homily 43.

units.la: Sed cur iumentis & pecoribus quoq; subtrahendum censuerunt pabulum & potum, cum illis nec culpa imputari, nec ieiunij finis innotescere potuerit?
units.tr: But why did they think that fodder and drink should be withheld from beasts of burden and flocks also, since no guilt could be imputed to them, nor could they know the purpose of fasting?

units.la: Quia inferiorum ordinum creaturę,ut bruta animantia, cum hominis causa condita sint,non melius quam ille habere debent,etsi non assequantur destinatum rei alicuius finem. Iam uero,ex praescripto edicti regij,omnium ordinum & ætatu homines ieiunare, saccis operiri, in cinere sedere oportuit. Itaq; nequaquam brutorum maior quàm hominum habenda erat ratio.
units.tr: Because creatures of the lower orders, such as the brute animals, were created for the sake of man, they ought to have no better lot than he does, even if they do not attain the end appointed for them. Indeed, by the prescription of the royal edict, men of every order and age had to fast, be covered with sackcloth, and sit in ashes. Therefore by no means ought a greater regard to be had for brutes than for men.

units.la: Porrò, si æquum est, post lapsum primorum parentum, tot seculis mundi, res creatas uanitati subijci,nō sua sponte,sed propter eum qui subiecit eas isti uanitati:sub spe,quōd & ipsę uindicabuntur ex seruitute interitus,sic ut unà nobiscum su spirent & parturiát:Rom.8.20.21.22. quis intelligens miretur, armentis,pecoribus &iumentis Niniuitarum tempore ieiunij & resipiscentiæ ac supplicationum,ali quandiu pabulo potuq; caredum fuisse?
units.tr: Moreover, if it is fitting that after the fall of our first parents, through so many ages of the world, created things should be subjected to vanity, not of their own will but on account of him who subjected them to it, in hope that they too will be set free from the bondage of corruption, so as to groan and travail together with us (Rom. 8:20–22), who that understands would wonder that the herds, flocks and beasts of burden of the Ninevites were for a time kept without fodder and drink, in the time of fasting, repentance and supplication?

units.la: Est & illud notandum, ieiunio, operimento sacci, sesione in cinere & puluere, corpora potisimùm affici & macerari. Eorum itaq; respectu,bruta minus bene habita, male affici possunt,& homini ni συγναιυχείδαι,
units.tr: It is also to be noted that by fasting, the covering of sackcloth, and sitting in ash and dust, bodies above all are afflicted and worn down. Therefore, with regard to these, beasts that are less well treated can be affected badly, and to share the feeling with man (συναισθάνεσθαι).

units.la: VERSVS VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 8.

units.la: Operiantur sacciis homines ipsi, & ipsa iumenta, atq; clament ad Deum fortiter: & conuertantur quisq; à uia sua mala, & ab iniquitate quæ est in manibus eorum.
units.tr: Let men and beasts alike be covered with sackcloth, and let them cry mightily to God. Let every one turn from his evil way and from the iniquity that is in his hands.

units.la: Inter τὰ πρῶτα secundo loco, habitus lugubris: tertiò, preces: quartò, cōuersio, quæ odio mali & studio boni constat, recensetur: ut ex hoc uersu liquet. Nos de his ordine agemus.
units.tr: Among the first things (τὰ πρῶτα), the second place is given to a mourning habit, the third to prayers, and the fourth to conversion, which consists in hatred of evil and zeal for good. This is clear from the verse. We shall take these up in order.

units.la: DE SACCO, SEV DE lugubri habitu.
units.tr: ON SACKCLOTH, OR ON MOURNFUL DRESS.

units.la: 1. Vsitatissimum fuit iam olim apud Israelitas, sacco, seu uili & lugubri habitu uti, si quando uel publicæ uel priuatæ calamitates ansam præberent. In exequijs Abneri dolo perempti: Scindite, dicebat Rex Dauid ad suos familiares, uestimenta uestra, & accingite uos saccis, & plangite ante Abner; 2.Sam.3.31. Et in historia Nehemiæ, cap.9.1. Vicesimaquarta die mensis huius, congregauerunt sese filij Israelis in ieiunio, & cum saccis, ac terra erat super eos, &c. Hunc morem ritum q; etiam Ethnici quidam nonnunquam obseruasse uidentur, ut Plutarchus [?]περὶ δεισιδαιμονίας[?], his uerbis hominem superstitiosum graphicè depingens, docet;
units.tr: 1. Among the Israelites, from of old, it was very common to wear sackcloth, that is, coarse and mournful clothing, whenever public or private calamities gave occasion for it. At the funeral of Abner, who was treacherously slain, King David said to his servants: "Tear your garments, and gird yourselves with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner" (2 Sam. 3:31). And in the history of Nehemiah, chapter 9:1: "On the twenty-fourth day of this month the children of Israel assembled themselves with fasting, and with sackcloth, and earth was upon them," etc. Some of the heathen also seem sometimes to have observed this custom and rite. Plutarch, describing the superstitious man vividly in these words, teaches this in his work On Superstition [περὶ δεισιδαιμονίας]:

units.la: ἐξω [?]ἱματίου[?] ἔχων, ἢ προσιζωσμένος ῥάκεσι ῥυπαροῖς, πολλάκις δὲ γυμνὸς[?] ἐν πηλῷ κυλινδούμενος[?].
units.tr: Having his cloak off, or girt about with filthy rags, and often naked, rolling in the mud [ἐξω ἱματίου ἔχων, ἢ προσιζωσμένος ῥάκεσι ῥυπαροῖς, πολλάκις δὲ γυμνὸς ἐν πηλῷ κυλινδούμενος].

units.la: Fortasis inde ortum duxit proverbium, Vestem mutare: quod luctus indicium est.
units.tr: Perhaps from this arose the proverb "to change one's clothes," which is a sign of mourning.

units.la: 2. De caussa finali sacci citra superstitio nem sumti, hoc breuiter monere libet, Vt corporis lasciuiam, inedia & ieiunio domari: sic eiusdem fastum nimiumq; cultum, uili operimento non parum minui. Cultus, inquit ille, & victus familiaris uitam indicant. Itaque utriusq; habenda ratio est ijs, qui uita & mores serio emendare student. Sordidae, inquit Hieronymus, uestes, candidae mentis indicia sunt. Hau ddubie autem sordidas dixit, nō pretiosas nimium. His enim cur nonnulli utantur, uere docuit Gregorius, cuius haec uerba sunt: Quòd pro sola inani gloria ueftimetum pretiosius quaeritur, res ipsa testatur: quia nemo uult ibi pretiosis uestibus indui, ubi ab alijs nō possit uideri.
units.tr: 2. On the final purpose of sackcloth, taken up without superstition, it is worth briefly noting this: just as it tames the wantonness of the body by fasting and abstinence, so by a coarse covering it no little diminishes its pride and excessive finery. "Dress and a plain way of life," he says, "indicate the character; so both must be taken into account by those who earnestly strive to amend their life and morals." "Dirty clothes," says Jerome, "are signs of a pure mind." Doubtless he called them dirty, not excessively costly. Why some people use them, Gregory truly taught, in these words: "That the more costly garment is sought for mere empty glory, the thing itself bears witness: for no one wishes to be clothed in costly garments where he cannot be seen by others."

units.la: Caeterum saccus primum humilitatis index erat: quia cultus & ornatus, eo sum to uefteq; mutata, corpori detrahitur: deinde, signum reatus & doloris. Luc. 10. 13. Vae tibi Corazin: uae tibi Beth-saida, nam siin Tyro & Sidonae editae fuissent uirtutes quae editae sunt apud uos, olim cum sacco & cinere sedentes resipuissent.
units.tr: Moreover, sackcloth was first a sign of humility, because adornment and finery are taken off the body when the garment is changed; then it was a sign of guilt and sorrow. Luke 10:13: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes."

units.la: Absit autem superstitio & magnificentia nimia a fidelium habitu, qui debet esse ἐσθῆτι σεμνῆς; & habeatur decori ratio. Etsi enim uerum est uetus illud prouerbium, Vestis facit uirū: tamé pie docuit Bernardus, Sub quauis ueste bene coli pietate.
units.tr: Yet let superstition and excessive magnificence be far from the dress of the faithful, which ought to be "in honourable clothing [ἐσθῆτι σεμνῆς]," and let regard be had for decency. For although that old proverb is true, "Clothes make the man," yet Bernard piously taught: "Under any garment true piety may be well cultivated."

units.la: DE CLAMORE AD DEVM, seu de Supplicationibus publicis.
units.tr: ON THE CRY TO GOD, OR ON PUBLIC SUPPLICATIONS.

units.la: In Regis Assyriorum edicto, tertium in numero τῶν προσπλῶν[?] locum supplicationes publicae sibi uendicant.
units.tr: In the edict of the kings of Assyria, public supplications claim for themselves the third place among the [things] that come first (τῶν προσπλῶν).

units.la: Clament ad Deum fortiter. Requiritur autem hac parte edicti, ut non solum singuli uotis cordis, gemitibus, suspirijs, lacrymis agant, sed etiam ad alios excitandos & exacuedos, uoce clarisima preces co-cipiant, omnesq; uno ore & Spiritu commune negocių agant.
units.tr: Let them cry mightily to God. In this part of the edict it is required that individuals not only pursue their prayers in the heart, with groans, sighs and tears, but also, to stir up and sharpen others, that they offer prayers with the loudest voice, and that all, with one mouth and one Spirit, carry on the common business.

units.la: Αἴτησις Paulo est supplicatio, qua petimus à Deo, ut uel ab molestijs quæ nos grauiter premunt liberet, uel ab impendentibus malis præseruet. 1.Tim.2.1. Facit huc illud Iacobi 5.16. Confitemini a-lij alijs offensas, & orate alij pro alijs, ut sanemini: multũ enim ualet deprecatio iusti assidua.
units.tr: Paul calls supplication (αἴτησις) that by which we ask God either to free us from troubles that press heavily upon us, or to preserve us from impending evils (1 Tim. 2:1). To this belongs James 5:16: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that you may be healed; for the earnest prayer of a righteous man avails much."

units.la: Cognatum ei uocabulum ἱκετηρία est, quod exstat Hebr.5.7. Christus cū in diebus carnis suæ, deprecationes & supplicationes, δεήσεις τε καὶ ἱκετηρίας[?], apud eum qui po-terat terat eum seruare à morte,cum clamore ualido & lacrymis obtulisset,&c.
units.tr: A related word is ἱκετηρία (supplication), which occurs in Heb. 5:7: "Christ, in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications [δεήσεις τε καὶ ἱκετηρίας] to him who was able to save him from death, with strong crying and tears," etc.

units.la: Ad quem autem instituendæ sunt ab ijs qui resipiscunt, supplicationes istæ?
units.tr: To whom, then, ought supplications of this kind to be directed by those who repent?

units.la: Ad Deum solum: ut hæ subiectæ grauissimæ rationes docent.
units.tr: To God alone, as these very weighty reasons show.

units.la: 1. Cuicunque soli competit adorationis cultus, eidem & supplicatio feria debetur.Deo autem soli adorationis cultus debetur, iuxta legem: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ei soli seruies: Deut.6. 13.Matt.4.10. Quare & ad eum solum cōcipiendæ sunt supplicationes.
units.tr: 1. Whatever is due to God alone as the worship of adoration, to the same alone is due also the supplication of the same kind. But the worship of adoration is due to God alone, according to the law: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him only" (Deut. 6:13; Matt. 4:10). Therefore supplications also are to be directed to him alone.

units.la: 2. Ipsa recta ratio docet, Reorum esse; supplices fieri ei in quem grauiter peccauerunt, & eius offensam deprecari. Peccamus autem in Deum præcipuè. Ideo Dauid, etsi in Uriam quoq; se grauiter deliquisse non ignorabat, tamen in Deum præcipuè respiciens: Tibi,tibi,inquam,soli peccaui, & malum in oculis tuis feci: Psal.51.6. Et Niniuitæ Deo supplices facti, fortiter ad eum clamauisse dicuntur.
units.tr: 2. Right reason itself teaches that it is the duty of those who are guilty to make supplication to the one against whom they have grievously sinned, and to beg for his favour. But we sin chiefly against God. Therefore David, although he was not unaware that he had grievously offended also against Uriah, nevertheless, looking chiefly to God, said: "Against you, you only, have I sinned, and done this evil in your sight" (Ps. 51:6). And the Ninevites are said to have made supplication to God and to have cried mightily to him.

units.la: Ex his liquet, grauiter peccare Pontificios, cū ad limina diuorum supplicationes instituunt, & honorem Deo soli debitum, creaturis deferunt. enim verum est vetus illud proverbium, Vestis facit virū: tamē piè docuit Bernar-dus, Sub quavis veste bene coli pietatē.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that the Papists sin grievously when they institute supplications at the thresholds of the saints and transfer to creatures the honour due to God alone. For although that old proverb is true, "Clothes make the man," yet Bernard piously taught: "Under any garment true piety may be well cultivated."

units.la: DE CLAMORE AD DEVM, seu de Supplicationibus publicis.
units.tr: ON CRYING OUT TO GOD, or on Public Supplications.

units.la: In Regis Assyriorum edicto,tertium in numero τῶν πραγμάτων[?] locum supplicationes publicæ sibi vendicant.
units.tr: In the edict of the king of the Assyrians, public supplications claim third place among the things [τῶν πραγμάτων] that are to be done.

units.la: Clament ad Deum fortiter. Requiritur autem hac parte edicti,ut non solum singuli votis cordis,gemitibus,suspirijs,lacry-mis agant,sed etiam ad alios excitandos & exacuedos,voce clarissima preces cō-cipiant,omnesq; vno ore & Spiritu com-mune negocių agant.
units.tr: Let them cry out to God mightily. This part of the edict requires that individuals not only pray in the wishes of their hearts, with groans, sighs and tears, but also, to arouse and stir up others, that they offer their prayers with the loudest voice and carry on the common business with one mouth and one Spirit.

units.la: Δέησις[?] Paulo est supplicatio, qua peti-mus à Deo, ut vel ab molestijs quæ nos graviter premunt liberet, vel ab impen-dentibus malis præserveret. 1.Tim.2.1. Fa-cit huc illud Iacobi 5.16. Confiteminia-lij alijs offensas, & orate [illegible, ~12 letters] aliis,ut sanemini: multū eni[illegible, ~10 letters] iusti assidua.
units.tr: Supplication [δέησις], according to Paul, is the request we make to God that he either free us from troubles that press heavily upon us, or preserve us from impending evils. 1 Tim. 2.1. To this belongs James 5.16: Confess your offences to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed; for the earnest prayer of a righteous man avails much [...].

units.la: Cognatum [illegible, ~10 letters] ꝗ exstat He[illegible, ~8 letters] carnis su[illegible, ~3 letters] nes,[illegible, ~6 letters] terat eum seruare à morte,cum clamore ualido & lacrymis obtulisset,&c.
units.tr: [...] which is found in [...] the flesh [...] to save him from death, having offered it with a strong cry and tears, etc.

units.la: Ad quem autem instituendæ sunt ab ijs qui resipiscunt, supplicationes istæ?
units.tr: But to whom must these supplications be directed by those who repent?

units.la: Ad Deum solum: ut hæ subiectæ gravissimæ rationes docent.
units.tr: To God alone, as these very weighty reasons below show.

units.la: 1. Cuicunque soli competit adorationis cultus, eidem & supplicatio feria debetur.Deo autem soli adorationis cultus debetur, iuxta legem: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ei soli seruies: Deut.6.13.Matt.4.10. Quare & ad eum solum cōcipiendæ sunt supplicationes.
units.tr: 1. Worship of adoration is due to whatever being alone; supplication is owed to the same being. But worship of adoration is due to God alone, according to the law: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone (Deut. 6.13; Matt. 4.10). Therefore supplications are also to be addressed to him alone.

units.la: 2. Ipsa recta ratio docet, Reorum esse, supplices fieri ei in quem grauiter peccauerunt, & eius offensam deprecari. Peccamus autem in Deum præcipuè. Ideo Dauid, etsi in Vriam quoq; se grauiter deliquisse non ignorabat, tamen in Deum præcipuè respiciens: Tibi, tibi, inquam, soli peccaui, et [illegible, ~12 letters]alum in oculis tuis feci: [illegible, ~10 letters]æ Deo supplices fa-[illegible, ~8 letters]mauisse dicuntur. [illegible, ~6 letters]r peccare Pontifi[illegible, ~8 letters]um supplicatio-[illegible, ~6 letters]eo soli de-
units.tr: 2. Right reason itself teaches that it is the duty of the guilty to make supplication to the one against whom they have sinned gravely, and to beg for his pardon. But we sin chiefly against God. Therefore David, although he was not unaware that he had also grievously wronged Uriah, nevertheless looking chiefly to God said: Against you, you alone, I have sinned, and done what is evil in your eyes [...] they are said to have been suppliants to God [...] the Papists' supplication [...] to God alone [...].

units.la: [illegible, ~8 letters]catu

1. Quia eiusdem est nostra per resipiscentiam instauratio, cuius est & creatio. Neque enim minus habere debet uirtutis & omnipotentiae diuinae ἀποτέλεσμα[?], Instauratio nostri post grauissimum lapsum & corruptionem, quàm Creatio. Atqui Deus ipse nos fecit, & nō ipsi nos: Psal.ioo.3. Itaque & de nostra recreatione & regeneratione cum Apostolo nostro concludamus: Ipsius sumus opus, cōditi in Christo Iesu ad opera bona, quæ præparauit Deus ut in eis uersaremur: Eph.2.10.
units.tr: 1. Because our restoration through repentance belongs to the same one to whom our creation belongs. For the restoration of us after the gravest fall and corruption ought to show no less of the power and omnipotence of God than creation does. And indeed God himself made us, and not we ourselves (Ps. 100.3). Therefore, with our Apostle, let us also conclude concerning our re-creation and regeneration: We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them (Eph. 2.10).

units.la: 2. Mortui in offensis & peccatis seipsos non possunt, ad Deum sponte sua conuersi, uiuificare. Omnes autē homines, cū ex carne nati sint, in offensis & peccatis mortui sunt:Ioan.3. Eph.2.1. Itaq; nulli homines seipsos uiuificare possunt: & per consequens, nulli homines suis uiribus conuerti ad Deũ, seu uiuificari possunt. Quis ergo nos uiuificat? Deus ipse, ut eum celebrans Paulus testatur: Etiam, dicens, cū per offensas mortui essemus, unà uiuifi-cauit nos per Christum, cuius gratia estis seruati:Eph.2.5.
units.tr: 2. Those who are dead in offences and sins cannot, by their own will, turn themselves to God and make themselves alive. But all men, since they are born of flesh, are dead in offences and sins (John 3; Eph. 2.1). Therefore no men can make themselves alive, and consequently no men can by their own strength be converted to God or be made alive. Who then makes us alive? God himself, as Paul, celebrating him, bears witness, saying: even when we were dead through offences, he made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved (Eph. 2.5).

units.la: 3. Mens ignara Dei, & uoluntas ab eo-dem auersa, non dici possunt causae con-uersionis uersionis ad Deum. Ratio 1.Conuersio enim fine luce gratiæ & fidei peragi nequit. Illa uerò in nõ renatis nequaquam est: qui eo nomine in tenebris & umbra mortis sedere dicuntur, Matt. 4. 16. Ratio 2.de uoluntate: Subiectum principale conuersionis nõ debet confundi cũ eiusdem efficiente principali. Sed uoluntas est conuersionis principale ὑποκείμενον: ut uel nomen ipsum Conuersionis docet.
units.tr: 3. A mind ignorant of God and a will turned away from him cannot be called the causes of conversion to God. The reason for the first: conversion cannot be carried out without the light of grace and faith. But these are by no means in the unregenerate, who are said for that reason to sit in darkness and the shadow of death (Matt. 4.16). The reason for the second, concerning the will: the principal subject of conversion must not be confused with its principal efficient cause. But the will is the principal subject [ὑποκείμενον] of conversion, as the very name of conversion teaches.

units.la: Atqui in nõ renato homine mens ignara est Dei,& uoluntas contumax, διεστραμμένη & à Deo auersa. iuxta hæc dicta: Hoc igitur dico & obtestor per Dominum,ne amplius uersemini sicut reliquæ Gentes uersantur in uanitate mentis suæ,cogita-tionem habentes obscuratam,& abalie-natam à uita Dei,propter ignorantiā quę est in ipsis ex obduratione cordis eorū: Eph.4.17.18. Item: Animalis autem ho-mo non est capax eorū quæ sunt Spiritus Dei:sunt enim illi stulticia. 1.Cor.2.14.
units.tr: Yet in the unregenerate man the mind is ignorant of God, and the will is stubborn, perverted [διεστραμμένη] and turned away from God, according to these words: This therefore I say and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened and alienated from the life of God, because of the ignorance that is in them, due to the hardening of their hearts (Eph. 4.17–18). Likewise: But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him (1 Cor. 2.14).

units.la: Fateamur itaq; id quod res est,nostris uiribus nos neutiquā cōuerti ad Deum.
units.tr: Let us therefore confess what is the case: by our own strength we are in no way converted to God.

units.la: VERSVS VII.
units.tr: VERSE VII.

units.la: Et proclamare iussit, & dicere in Ninineh edicto regio & magnatu eius, dicedo: Homines & iumenta, boues & pecudes ne gustent quicquam, neq; pascantur, et aquâ non bibant.
units.tr: And he caused it to be proclaimed, and to say in Nineveh by the king's decree and that of his nobles, saying: Let neither men nor beasts, oxen nor sheep, taste anything, nor feed, nor drink water.

units.la: In hoc uersu & duobus sequentibus uersibus, summam regij edicti de poenitentia agenda descripsit Ionas. Duo autem hæc obseruanda sunt: Circumstantiæ personarum, & Edictum.
units.tr: In this verse and the two following, Jonah sets out the substance of the royal edict concerning the repentance to be undertaken. Two things are to be observed here: the circumstances of the persons, and the edict.

units.la: Edicti duæ partes sunt: altera περὶ τῶν προαγωγῶν, seu de rebus agendis: altera περὶ τῶν ἐλπισμένων, seu de spe ueniæ & diuinæ misericordiæ. Obseruandus autè est ordo. Refipifcentiam & eius fructus comitatur mitigatio malorum: cor autem ἀμετανόητον seu poenitere nescium, & opera carnis, sequuntur poenæ. Ideo Rex prudenter initiò poenitentiam requirit, & eius exercitium præscribit.
units.tr: The edict has two parts: one concerning the things to be done [περὶ τῶν προαγωγῶν], that is, the duties to be performed; the other concerning hope [περὶ τῶν ἐλπισμένων], that is, the hope of pardon and divine mercy. The order is to be observed. Repentance and its fruits are accompanied by the mitigation of evils; but an impenitent heart, unable to repent, and the works of the flesh, are followed by punishments. Therefore the king prudently first requires repentance and prescribes its practice.

units.la: Τῶν προαγωγῶν, & couersionis exercitiorû ac documentorû hic ordo est: Initiò præscribitur ieiunium commune: deinde, lugubris habitus, uelut reatus & humiliationis signum: tertiò, preces ardetissimæ: postremò, odium & fuga mali, cum quo iungi debet amor studiumq; boni. Hæc omnia uerf.7.& 8.occurrunt.
units.tr: The order of these things to be done [Τῶν προαγωγῶν] and of the exercises and instructions of conversion is this: first, a common fast is prescribed; then, mourning dress, as a sign of guilt and humiliation; third, most fervent prayers; last, hatred and flight from evil, joined with love and eagerness for good. All these occur in verses 7 and 8.

units.la: Quid sperandum sit de clementia Dei & malorum mitigatione, postrema edi-cti istius pars, uerf.9.ostendit.
units.tr: What is to be hoped for from the clemency of God and the mitigation of evils, the final part of this edict, verse 9, shows.

units.la: DE PERSONIS EARUM-que circumstantijs.
units.tr: On the persons and their circumstances.

units.la: Si ὑπόθεσιν [?] uersus 7.ad thesin reducas, occurret haec doctrina: Decreta magistratus exercitijs poenitentiae seruire debent.
units.tr: If you refer the hypothesis [ὑπόθεσιν; ?] of verse 7 to the thesis, this doctrine emerges: the decrees of the magistrate ought to serve the exercises of repentance.

units.la: Vt hoc loco dicitur, Regem Assyriorum eiusq; συμπαραστάτας [?], regni Proceres, edictum de resipiscentiae exercitijs praescri-psisse subditis, ut ad laudabile Regis ad Deum conuersi exemplum, salutaris eiusdem per edictum exhortatio accederet.
units.tr: As is said in this passage, the king of the Assyrians and his companions [συμπαραστάτας; ?], the nobles of the kingdom, prescribed to the subjects an edict on the exercises of repentance, so that, following the king's praiseworthy example of turning to God, a salutary exhortation through the same edict might be added.

units.la: Noti sunt elegantes hi uersus:
units.tr: These elegant verses are well known:

units.la: Tu ciuem patremq; geras, tu consule cunctis: In commune iubes si quid censesq; tenendum, Primus iussa subi. tunc obseruantior æqui Fit populus, nec ferre uetat, cum uiderit ipsum Auctorem parere sibi. componitur orbis Regis ad exemplum: nec sic inflectere sensus Humanos edicta ualent, quàm uita regentis. Mobile mutatur semper cum Principe uulgus.
units.tr: You bear the citizen and the father, you look after all: if you command anything to be held in common, be the first to submit to your orders. Then the people becomes more observant of what is right, and does not refuse to bear it when it sees the author himself obeying. The world is shaped after the example of the king; and edicts cannot bend human minds as much as the life of the ruler does. The fickle crowd always changes with the prince.

units.la: Nonnihil simile est exemplum Nebucadnezaris magni, qui à Deo grauiter correptus, ubi ad sanitatem mentis reuocatus essET,edictum de poenis,quibus ob su perbiam & alia peccata affectus erat, & de earum relaxatione,deq; ueri Dei agni tione & cultu,in subiectorum gratiam pro- mulgari curauit:Dan.4. Item illud Iudæ- orum è Babylone reducum,& poenitentiam Ezra hortante agetium exemplum, de quo agitur Nehem.9.
units.tr: Something rather similar is the example of the great Nebuchadnezzar, who, severely corrected by God and recalled to soundness of mind, saw to it that an edict was published concerning the punishments with which he had been afflicted on account of pride and other sins, and concerning their remission, and concerning the knowledge and worship of the true God, for the benefit of his subjects: Dan. 4. Likewise there is the example of the Jews returning from Babylon, and of Ezra exhorting them to repentance, of which Nehem. 9 speaks.

units.la: Sedenim consensus Regis Assyriorum & Optimatum eius,magna laude dignus est. Sæpe enim diuersa sunt Regum & Procerum consilia & studia,sic ut pijs conatibus quorundam,pars altera aduersetur,seu ui,seu artificio Sinonio.
units.tr: Indeed, the agreement of the king of the Assyrians and of his nobles is worthy of great praise. For the counsels and endeavours of kings and nobles are often at odds, so that the pious efforts of some are opposed by the other part, whether by force or by Sinonian trickery.

units.la: DE IEIVNIO.
units.tr: ON FASTING.

units.la: Propositum nobis est, Ieiunij, proprie sic dicti,finitione & causas aliquot paucis tradere. Det autē nobis Dominus Iesus Christus,ne de nobis quoq; dici possit illud Hieronymi: Delicatus magister est,qui pleno uentre de ieiunijs disputat.
units.tr: It is our purpose to set out briefly the definition and some causes of fasting, properly so called. May the Lord Jesus Christ grant that that saying of Jerome cannot be applied to us as well: "He is a pampered teacher who discourses on fasting with a full belly."

units.la: 1. Quid non fit ieiunium. ἀποφάσις.
units.tr: 1. What fasting is not. ἀποφάσις.

units.la: 1. Non est solùm temperantia in cibo & potu. Nam hæc per omnem uitam no bis est sedanda.iuxta dictum: Cauete,ne grauentur corda ueστra crapula,&c.
units.tr: 1. It is not merely moderation in food and drink. For this must be observed by us throughout our whole life, according to the saying: "Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting," etc.

units.la: 2. Non est abstinentia à prandio aut à cœna. Nam & Plato dicit infelices eos esse, qui bis saturi fiunt eodem die. Ac veteribus Græcis usitatum fuit, semel tantùm interdiu cibum sumere.
units.tr: 2. It is not abstinence from dinner or supper. For Plato also says that those are unhappy who become full twice in the same day; and it was customary among the ancient Greeks to take food only once during the day.

units.la: 3. Nec est ciborum delectus. Neque e-nim ieiunium fuerit à certa cibi specie ab stinere, & delitijs genio satisfacere.
units.tr: 3. Nor is it a choice of foods. For fasting would not consist in abstaining from a particular kind of food and gratifying the appetite with delicacies.

units.la: 2. Quid sit ieiunium.
units.tr: 2. What fasting is.

units.la: Est, cùm sponte nostra aliquid usitatæ diætæ subtrahimus, ut ea res seruiat carni in nobis mortificandæ, precibus ardé-ter ad Deū fundendis, & nostrę summissi oni sub potenti manu Dei. Hæc finitio αἰτιολογικὴ[?] docet utrumq;, & quæ sit ratio seu forma ieiunij ueri, & quæ sint eius caussæ finales.
units.tr: It is when we of our own accord withdraw something from our usual diet, so that this matter serves to mortify the flesh within us, while we pour out prayers earnestly to God and humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God. This definition, which is aetiological [?], teaches both things: what the reason or form of true fasting is, and what its final causes are.

units.la: Forma & modus quantitatem, qualitatem & tempus complectitur, Ieiunates enim nec alias usitata cibi & potus copia, nec delitijs cōsuetis, nec eodem tempore, uti debent: ut συλλήβδην multa complectar.
units.tr: The form and manner comprise quantity, quality and time: for those who fast ought not to take the usual amount of food and drink, nor their customary delicacies, nor at the usual time; to sum up briefly, I shall embrace many things.

units.la: Fines sunt, ut carnis mortificationi, ut precibus, ut deniq; τῇ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ[?] seruiat.
units.tr: The ends are that it serve the mortification of the flesh, that it serve prayers, and finally that it serve humility [τῇ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ].

units.la: Cum autem ieiunium σωματικῆς γυμνα-σίας species quædam sit, illud non quasi sit cultus Dei, sed quia præstantioribus illis finibus, de quibus diximus, feruit, commendamus & requirimus. Iuxta hæc dicta Patrum:
units.tr: Since fasting is a certain kind of bodily exercise, we commend and require it not as if it were a worship of God, but because it serves those more excellent ends of which we have spoken. In accordance with these sayings of the Fathers:

units.la: Modicus & temperatus cibus, & animæ & corpori utilis est: Hieronymus ad Rusticum Monachum. Ieiunio alæ duæ sunt, orationis uidelicet & iusticiæ: Bernardus de Quadr. Quid prodest tenuari corpus abstinentia, si animus intumescit superbia? Hieronymus ad Celatiam. Ieiunium, humilitatis signum: Augustinus epist.176. Ieiunium est abstinentia a vitiis: Chrysostomus. Ieiunium modestiæ principium: Idem ad Antioch. hom.43.
units.tr: Moderate and temperate food is useful both to the soul and to the body: Jerome to Rusticus the monk. Fasting has two wings, namely of prayer and of righteousness: Bernard, On the Quadragesima. What does it profit for the body to be made thin by abstinence, if the mind swells with pride? Jerome to Celantia. Fasting is a sign of humility: Augustine, Letter 176. Fasting is abstinence from vices: Chrysostom. Fasting is the beginning of modesty: the same, homily 43 on Antioch.

units.la: Sed cur iumentis & pecoribus quoq; subtrahedum censuerunt pabulum & potum, cum illis nec culpa imputari, nec ieiunij fi-nis innotescere potuerit?
units.tr: But why did they judge that fodder and water should also be withheld from beasts of burden and cattle, since no guilt can be imputed to them, nor can the purpose of fasting be made known to them?

units.la: Quia inferiorum ordinum creaturę, ut bruta animantia, cum hominis causa condita sint, non melius quàm ille habere debent, etsi non assequantur destinatum rei alicuius finem. Iam vero, ex præscripto edicti regij, omnium ordinum & ætatum homines ieiunare, saccis operiri, in cinere sedere oportuit. Itaq; nequaquam brutorum maior quàm hominum habenda erat ratio.
units.tr: Because creatures of the lower orders, such as brute animals, were created for the sake of man, and ought to have no better than he does, even if they do not attain the end appointed for them. Indeed, by the prescription of the royal edict, men of all orders and ages were required to fast, to be covered with sackcloth, and to sit in ashes. Therefore by no means ought a greater regard to be had for brutes than for men.

units.la: Porrò, si æquum est, post lapsum primorum parentum, tot seculis mundi, res creatas uanitati subiici, nō sua sponte, sed propter eum qui subiecit eas isti uanitati: sub spe, quòd & ipsæ uindicabuntur ex seruitute interitus, sic ut unà nobiscum sui spirent & parturiat: Rom. 8.20.21.22. quis intelligens miretur, armentis, pecoribus & iumentis Niniuitarum tempore ieiu-nij & refipiscentiæ ac supplicationum, ali quandiu pabulo potuq; caredum fuisse[?]
units.tr: Furthermore, if it is fitting that, after the fall of our first parents, created things should for so many ages of the world be subjected to vanity, not of their own will but on account of him who subjected them to that vanity, in hope that they themselves also will be freed from the bondage of corruption, so that they groan and travail together with us (Rom. 8:20–22), who that understands would wonder that the herds, flocks and cattle of the Ninevites, at the time of fasting, repentance and supplications, were for a while deprived of fodder and water?

units.la: Est & illud notandum, ieiunio, operi-mento sacci, sessione in cinere & pulue-re, corpora potissimum affici & macera-ri. Eorum itaq; respectu, bruta minus bene habita, male affici possunt, & homini [illegible, ~12 letters].
units.tr: It is also to be noted that by fasting, by the covering of sackcloth, and by sitting in ashes and dust, bodies chiefly are afflicted and worn down. With respect to these, therefore, beasts that are not well treated can be afflicted badly, and for man [illegible, ~12 letters].

units.la: VERSVS VIII.
units.tr: VERSE 8.

units.la: Operiantur saccis homines ipsi, & ipsa iumenta, atq; clament ad Deum fortiter: & conuertantur quisq; à uia sua mala, & ab iniquitate quæ est in manibus eorum.
units.tr: Let man and beast alike be covered with sackcloth, and let them cry mightily to God; and let every one turn from his evil way, and from the violence that is in his hands.

units.la: Inter τὰ πρῶτα[?] secundo loco, habitus lugubris: tertiò, preces: quartò, cōuersio, quæ odio mali & studio boni constat,re-censetur: ut ex hoc uersu liquet. Nos de his ordine agemus.
units.tr: Among the first things, in second place, a mournful habit is listed; third, prayers; fourth, conversion, which consists in hatred of evil and zeal for good; as is clear from this verse. We shall treat these in order.

units.la: DE SACCO, SEU DE lugubri habitu,
units.tr: ON SACKCLOTH, OR ON MOURNFUL DRESS.

units.la: 1. Visitatissimum fuit iam olim apud Is-raelitas, sacco, seu uili & lugubri habitu uti,si quando uel publicæ uel priuatæ ca-lamitates ansam præberent. In exequijs Abneri dolo perempti: Scindite, dicebat Rex Dauid ad suos familiares, ueftimen-ta uestra, & accingite uos saccis, & plan-gite ante Abner; 2.Sam,3.31. Et in hifto-ria Nehemiæ, cap.9.1. Vicefimaquarta die mensis huius,congregauerunt sese fi-lij Israelis in jeiunio,& cum saccis,ac ter-ra erat super eos,&c. Hunc morem ri-tumq; etiam Ethnici quidam nonnun-quam observasse uidentur,ut Plutarchus περὶ δεισιδαιμονίας, his uerbis hominem su-perstitiosum graphicè depingens, docet: ἐξω νηστείαν φανιον ἐχων, ἢ περιεσπασμένος ῥάκεσι ῥυπαροῖς, πολλάκις δὲ γυναικὸς ἐν πηλῷ κυλινδούμενος. Fortassis inde ortum duxit proverbium, Vestem mutare: quod luctus indi-cium est.
units.tr: 1. It was already very common long ago among the Israelites to wear sackcloth, or coarse and mournful dress, whenever public or private calamities gave occasion. At the funeral of Abner, slain by treachery, King David said to his familiars: "Rend your garments, gird yourselves with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner" (2 Sam. 3:31). And in the history of Nehemiah, chapter 9, verse 1: "On the twenty-fourth day of this month the children of Israel assembled themselves with fasting, and with sackcloth, and earth was upon them," etc. Some Gentiles also seem sometimes to have observed this custom and rite, as Plutarch, in his work On Superstition, graphically depicting the superstitious man in these words, teaches: "Having a fast in appearance, or wrapped in filthy rags, and often rolling himself in the mud, like a woman." Perhaps from this arose the proverb "to change one's clothes," which is a sign of mourning.

units.la: 2. De causa finali sacci citra superstitio [?]em sumti, hoc breuiter monere libet, Vt corporis lasciuiam, inedia & ieiunio domari: sic eiusdem fastum nimiumq; cultum, uili operimento non parum minui. Cultus, inquit ille, & victus familiaris uitam indicant. Itaque utriusq; habenda ratio est ijs, qui uitā & mores serió emendare student. Sordidæ, inquit Hieronymus, uestes, candidæ mentis indicia sunt. Hauddubiè autem sordidas dixit, nō pretiosas nimium. His enim cur nonnulli utantur, uerè docuit Gregorius, cuius hæc uerba sunt: Quòd pro sola inani gloria ueftimetum pretiosius quæritur, res ipsa testatur: quia nemo uult ibi pretiosis uestibus indui, ubi ab alijs nō possit uideri.
units.tr: 2. Concerning the final purpose of taking sackcloth, without superstition, it is pleasing to advise briefly this: that the wantonness of the body is tamed by scant food and fasting, and likewise its pride and excessive finery are not a little diminished by a coarse covering. "Dress," he says, "and the manner of life of a household reveal one's way of life." Therefore both must be taken into account by those who seriously strive to amend their life and morals. "Squalid garments," says Jerome, "are signs of a pure mind." Certainly he called them squalid, not excessively costly. Why some people use these, Gregory truly taught, whose words are these: "That a costlier garment is sought for mere empty glory, the thing itself bears witness: for no one wishes to be dressed in precious clothes where he cannot be seen by others."

units.la: Cæterum saccus primum humilitatis index erat: quia cultus & ornatus, eo sum to uestēq; mutata, corpori detrahitur: deinde, signum reatus & doloris. Luc.10.13. Væ tibi Corazin: uæ tibi Bethsaida, nam si in Tyro & Sidonæ editæ fuissent uirtutes quæ editæ sunt apud uos, olim cum sacco & cinere sedentes resipuissent.
units.tr: Moreover, sackcloth was first a sign of humility, because adornment and finery are taken away from the body when the garment is changed; then, a sign of guilt and sorrow. Luke 10:13: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works which have been done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes."

units.la: Absit autem superstitio & magnificentia nimia à fidelium habitu, qui debet esse [?]; & habeatur decori ratio. Etsi enim verum est vetus illud proverbium, Vestis facit virû: tamé pie docuit Bernardus, Sub quavis veste bene coli pietate.
units.tr: But let superstition and excessive magnificence be far from the dress of the faithful, which ought to be [?]; and a regard for decency should be had. For although that old proverb is true, "Clothes make the man," nevertheless Bernard piously taught: "Under any garment, godliness is well cultivated."

units.la: DE CLAMORE AD DEVM, seu de Supplicationibus publicis.
units.tr: ON CRYING TO GOD, or on Public Supplications.

units.la: In Regis Assyriorum edicto, tertium in numero τῶν πρακτῶν[?] locum supplicationes publicae sibi vendicant.
units.tr: In the edict of the King of the Assyrians, public supplications claim the third place among the acts [τῶν πρακτῶν].

units.la: Clament ad Deum fortiter. Requiritur autem hac parte edicti, ut non solum singuli votis cordis, gemitibus, suspirijs, lacrymis agant, sed etiam ad alios excitandos & exacuedos, voce clarissima preces cō-cipiant, omnesq; uno ore & Spiritu commune negocii agant.
units.tr: "Let them cry mightily to God." This part of the edict requires that people not only pray privately with the desires of the heart, groans, sighs and tears, but also, to rouse and sharpen others, that they lift up prayers with the clearest voice, and that all carry on the common business with one mouth and one Spirit.

units.la: Δέησις[?] Paulo est supplicatio, qua petimus à Deo, ut vel ab molestijs quae nos graviter premunt liberet, vel ab impendentibus malis praefervet. 1.Tim.2.1. Facit huc illud Iacobi 5.16. Confiteminia-lij alijs offensas, & orate alij pro alijs, ut sanemini: multū enim valet deprecatio iusti assidua[?].
units.tr: Supplication [δέησις] is Paul's term: it is the petition by which we ask God either to free us from troubles that press hard upon us, or to guard us against impending evils. 1 Tim. 2.1. James 5.16 belongs here: "Confess your faults to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed; the earnest prayer of a righteous person has great power."

units.la: Cognatum ei vocabulum ἱκετηρία[?] est, quod exstat Hebr.5.7. Christus cū in diebus carnis suae, deprecationes & supplicationes, δεήσεως τε καὶ ἱκετηρίας[?], apud eum qui poterat eum seruare à morte, cum clamore ualido & lacrymis obtulisset, &c.
units.tr: The cognate word is supplication [ἱκετηρία], found in Heb. 5.7: "Christ, in the days of his flesh, offered up prayers and supplications [δεήσεις τε καὶ ἱκετηρίας] to him who was able to save him from death, with strong crying and tears," etc.

units.la: Ad quem autem instituendæ sunt ab ijs qui resipiscunt, supplicationes istæ?
units.tr: To whom should those who repent direct these supplications?

units.la: Ad Deum solum: ut hæ subiectæ grauissimæ rationes docent.
units.tr: To God alone, as the following very weighty reasons teach.

units.la: 1. Cuicunque soli competit adorationis cultus, eidem & supplicatio seria debetur. Deo autem soli adorationis cultus debetur, iuxta legem: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ei soli seruies: Deut.6.13.Matt.4.10. Quare & ad eum solum cōcipiendæ sunt supplicationes.
units.tr: 1. Worship of adoration is due only to the one to whom alone it belongs, and earnest supplication is due to the same. But the worship of adoration is due to God alone, according to the law: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone": Deut. 6.13; Matt. 4.10. Therefore supplications too are to be addressed to him alone.

units.la: 2. Ipsa recta ratio docet, Reorum esse supplices fieri ei in quem grauiter peccauerunt, & eius offensam deprecari. Peccamus autem in Deum præcipuè. Ideo Dauid, etsi in Viam quoq; se grauiter deliquisse non ignorabat, tamen in Deum præcipuè respiciens: Tibi, tibi, inquam, soli peccaui, & malum in oculis tuis feci: Psal.51.6. Et Niniuitæ Deo supplices fa-cti, fortiter ad eum clamauisse dicuntur.
units.tr: 2. Right reason itself teaches that guilty persons ought to make supplication to the one against whom they have grievously sinned, and beg for his pardon. But we sin chiefly against God. So David, though he did not ignore that he had also grievously wronged men, nevertheless looking chiefly to God said: "Against you, you alone, have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight": Ps. 51.6. And the Ninevites, made suppliants before God, are said to have cried mightily to him.

units.la: Ex his liquet, grauiter peccare Pontificios, cū ad limina diuorum supplicationes instituunt, & honorem Deo soli debitum, creaturis deferunt.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that the Papists sin gravely when they institute supplications at the shrines of the saints, and transfer to creatures the honour due to God alone.

units.la: Quomodo autem publicè Deo supplicandum, si quando ingens & publicum periculum precibus auertendum est?
units.tr: But how is God to be supplicated publicly, if some great and public danger must be averted by prayer?

units.la: Clamandum est fortiter ad Deum. Etsi autem est etiam interior quidam clamor cordis, in Spiritu & veritate orantis; ut monet exemplum Mosis, Exodi 14.15. quia tamen Deo soli καρδιογνώστης [?] de illo constare potest: si externa uox, animi resipiscentis index, aedificationi & emendationi aliorum seruire possit, clamandum est fortiter, ut nos aliorum precibus nostras, & alij suas nostris possint coniungere.
units.tr: One must cry out mightily to God. Although there is also a certain inward cry of the heart, of one who prays in spirit and truth, as the example of Moses in Exod. 14.15 shows, nevertheless, since only God, the searcher of hearts [καρδιογνώστης], can be certain of that, an outward voice, the sign of a repentant mind, can serve the edification and amendment of others. So we must cry out mightily, so that our prayers may be joined to those of others, and theirs to ours.

units.la: DE CONVERSIONE.
units.tr: On Conversion.

units.la: Et conuertantur quisque à uia sua mala, & ab iniquitate quae est in manibus eorum. Vt tota haec doctrina de Conuersione illustretur, primùm uocabula quaedam exponemus; deinde, de hominis auersione & conuersione ad Deum ἀποφατικῶς [?] agemus: postremò, capita doctrinae de hominis uia subiungemus. Dominus Iesus det, ut piè omnia prosequamur.
units.tr: "Let every one turn from his evil way and from the iniquity that is in their hands." So that this whole doctrine of conversion may be made clear, we will first explain certain words; then we will treat of man's aversion from God and conversion to him in a negative manner [ἀποφατικῶς]; finally we will add the heads of doctrine concerning man's way. May the Lord Jesus grant that we pursue all these things piously.

units.la: Via hoc loco significat uitae rationem: ut Psal.1.6. Nam agnoscit Iehouah uiam iustorum: via autem malorum peribit. Via mala significat peruersum vivendi modu, qui exorbitat a praescripto legis divinae.Huic viae insistit natio ἄπιστος ἡ διεστραμμένη [?], incredula & peruersa: Matth.17.17. Porro etiam Pythagoras, monens vulgi errores sapienti non esse sequendos, dixit: λεωφόρῳ μὴ βαδίζειν [?].
units.tr: Here "way" means the manner of life, as in Ps. 1.6: "For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish." An evil way signifies a perverse manner of living that strays from the precept of divine law. The unbelieving and perverse generation [ἄπιστος ἡ διεστραμμένη] walks in this way: Matt. 17.17. Moreover Pythagoras, warning that the errors of the crowd are not to be followed by the wise, said: "Do not walk on the public highway" [λεωφόρῳ μὴ βαδίζειν].

units.la: Via autem Domini,Psal.119. pacis,Roman.3.17. sanctum vitae institutum, quod ad amusim Legis Dei (quoad eius fieri in hac nostra imbecillitate potest) exigitur, significat. Psal.15.2. Qui incedit integer, & facit iusticiam: & loquitur veritatem in corde suo. 3.Qui non detrahit lingua sua, &c. Phil.2.15.Vt sitis irreprehensi & sinceri,filij,inquam,Dei,inculpa-ti, in medio nationis pravae & tortuosae: inter quos (homines) splendetis ut luminaria in mundo.
units.tr: The way of the Lord, Ps. 119, and the way of peace, Rom. 3.17, signify the holy course of life which is required by the rule of God's Law (as far as this can be done in our weakness). Ps. 15.2: "He who walks blamelessly and does what is right, and speaks the truth in his heart." 3: "who does not slander with his tongue," etc. Phil. 2.15: "That you may be blameless and innocent, children of God, unblemished in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world."

units.la: Quid autem sit iniquitas quae est in manibus, liquet ex his distis. Psal.26.9. Ne colligas cum peccatoribus animam meam, & cum viris sanguinolentis vitam meam: 10.in quorum manibus est malum consilium, & quorum dextera plena est muneribus. Dicitur ergo in eorum manibus iniquitas esse, qui male cogitata promte exequuntur, & qui sunt [illegible, ~8 letters]γοι ἡ [illegible, ~8 letters]. Pfal.58.2. Quin potius in corde iniquitates agitatis, in terra uiolentiā manuū uestrarū appenditis. Eiusmodi hominibus tribuuntur & pedes uelōces ad effundendum sanguinem, Rom. 3.15. Interdum autem specioso iuris praetextu, nonunquam perfricta fronte grassantur & saeuiunt in pios. Ista paucis de uocabulis dicere uisum est.
units.tr: What the iniquity in their hands is becomes clear from these passages. Ps. 26.9-10: "Do not gather my soul with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men, in whose hands is an evil plan, and whose right hand is full of bribes." So iniquity is said to be in the hands of those who promptly carry out evil thoughts, and who are [illegible]. Ps. 58.2: "Indeed, you work iniquities in your hearts; in the land you weigh out the violence of your hands." To such men are also ascribed swift feet for shedding blood, Rom. 3.15. Sometimes under the specious pretext of law, sometimes with brazen face, they rage and storm against the godly. It seemed worth saying these few things about the words.

units.la: Aphorismi breues de Aucersione & Conuer-sione hominis ad Deum.
units.tr: Brief Aphorisms on the Turning Away and the Conversion of Man to God.

units.la: 1. Certum est, homini opus esse uero stabiliq; bono, quod semper uelut in Cynosuram respiciat, & in quo tuto acquiescat. Ratio: Quia non est per se αὐτάρκης πρὸς εὐδαιμονίαν[?], ut Deus: ut autem felix fortunatusq; fit, pręcipuo quodam bono fruatur necesse est.
units.tr: 1. It is certain that man needs a true and stable good, which he may always look to as to the Cynosure, and in which he may rest safely. Reason: because he is not self-sufficient for happiness [αὐτάρκης πρὸς εὐδαιμονίαν] as God is; but to be happy and fortunate he must enjoy some chief good.

units.la: 2. In seipso aute acquiescere nō potest. Ratio 1. Quia sua causa non est conditus & redemtus. Pro.16.4. Omnia operatus est Iehouah propter seipsum. Rom.9.22. Deus pertulit multa lenitate uasa irae coagmetata ad interitum.23.Et ut notas fa-ceret diuitias gloriae suae erga uasa mise-ricordiæ, ricordiæ,quæ præparavit ad gloriā. Ratio 2. Quia malus est, & natura filius iræ. Eph.2.3.
units.tr: 2. But he cannot rest in himself. Reason 1: because he was not made and redeemed for his own sake. Prov. 16.4: "The LORD has made all things for himself." Rom. 9.22: "God endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, and that he might make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy, which he has prepared for glory." Reason 2: because he is evil and by nature a child of wrath, Eph. 2.3.

units.la: 3. Cum in Deu respicit, & in eo acquiescit, optime habet. Huius sententiæ expositio extat Psal.123.2[?]. Ecce sicut oculi servorum ad manu dominorum fuorū,sicut oculi ancillæ ad manum dominę suę: ita oculi nostri ad Iehouā Deum nostrū, donec misereatur nostri.
units.tr: 3. When he looks to God and rests in him, all is well. An exposition of this sentiment appears in Ps. 123.2: "Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to Jehovah our God, until he have mercy upon us."

units.la: 4. Cum autem creaturas præ Creatore colit, maledictus est. Hier.17.5.Sic dicit Iehouah: Maledictus vir qui fidit homini, & ponit carnē brachium suum, & à Iehouah recedit cor eius. 6.Erit enim tanquam myrica in deserto, neq; videbit cū venerit bonum,&c.
units.tr: 4. But when he worships creatures before the Creator, he is cursed. Jer. 17.5–6: "Thus says Jehovah: Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from Jehovah. For he shall be like a juniper in the desert, and shall not see when good comes," etc.

units.la: 5. Tribuitur autē conversioijs, qui jam antea à Deo aversi erant. Rom.5.10. Nam si,cum inimici essemus, reconciliati suimus Deo per morte filii eius, multo magis reconciliati servabimur per vitam ipsius. 1.Pet.2.25. Nam eratis velut oves errantes:sed conversi nunc estis ad pastore & curatorem animarum nostrarum.
units.tr: 5. Conversion is ascribed to those who were previously turned away from God. Rom. 5.10: "For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved by his life." 1 Pet. 2.25: "For you were like sheep going astray, but now you have returned to the shepherd and guardian of your souls."

units.la: 6. Aversi à Deo infideles sunt & ἀντιλο-γικοί, Rom.10.21. Toto die expandi ma-nus nus meas ad populū rebellem & contradicentem. Incredulitas causa auersionis est: contradictio, eiusdem effectum.
units.tr: 6. Those turned away from God are unbelieving and contrary (ἀντιλογικοί). Rom. 10.21: "All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people." Unbelief is the cause of turning away; contradiction is its effect.

units.la: 7. Conuersi ad Deum, quod corde credunt, id ore profitentur, & manibus seu factis exprimunt. Rom.10.10.Corde enim creditur ad iusticiam, ore autem confesio fit ad salutem. Phil.1.11. Pleni fructibus iusticię[?], qui(insunt vobis) per Christum Iesum, ad gloriam & laudem Dei.
units.tr: 7. Those converted to God believe in the heart, confess with the mouth what they believe, and express it with their hands or deeds. Rom. 10.10: "For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Phil. 1.11: "Filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are in you through Christ Jesus, to the glory and praise of God."

units.la: 8. Conuersio vera odio fugaq; mali, & studio boni constat. Psal.34.12. Quis est vir appetens vitæ[?]amans dies quibus videat bonum? 13.Cohibe linguam tuam a re mala, & labia tua ne loquantur dolum. 14.Declina a malo, & fac bonum: inquire pacem, & persequere eam.
units.tr: 8. True conversion consists in hatred and flight from evil, and in zeal for good. Ps. 34.12–14: "Who is the man who desires life and loves days in which he may see good? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it."

units.la: DE VIIS HOMINVM, & de Viatoribus.
units.tr: ON THE WAYS OF MEN, AND ON TRAVELLERS.

units.la: 1. Hominem certæ cuidam viæ insiste-re, par est. Ratio: Est enim non ἄλογος, ut bruta, sed rationalis creatura: & diuinitus inscriptum est cordi eius opus Legis, simul attestante ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuò accusantibus aut excusantibus: Rom.2.15. Itaque ne sit sicut equus & sicut mulus, quibus nō est intelliintelligentia: capistro & freno constringis maxillam eorum, ne accedant ad te: Psal.32.9.
units.tr: 1. It is fitting for a man to keep to a certain way. Reason: for he is not unreasoning like the beasts, but a rational creature; and the work of the Law is written by God in his heart, their own conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or excusing one another, Rom. 2.15. Therefore, do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding; bind their jaw with bit and bridle, lest they come near you, Ps. 32.9.

units.la: 2. Finis autem seu Boni cuiusdam consideratione sic commouetur, ut uiam aliquam sibi probatam ingrediatur. Notum est monostichon:
units.tr: 2. A man is moved by consideration of some end or good so as to enter upon a way that he has approved. There is a well-known one-line verse:

units.la: Quicquid agis, prudenter agas, & respice finem.
units.tr: Whatever you do, do it prudently, and look to the end.

units.la: Jam uero finis non solum est ultimum rei, sed etiam optimum: ut recte Philosophus docuit Phys. 2. Tenendae autem nobis sunt Boni distinctiones. Aliud est increatum, immensum & aeternum: ut Deus. Matth. 19.17. Ac recte ei accommodauerimus finitionem Aristotelis: Διὸ [?]καλῶς [?]ἀπεφήναντο τ' ἀγαθὸν [?]ἢ πάντα ἐφίεσθαι. Aliud est creatum bonum, quod in physicum, ethicum, & theologicum subdiuidere licet. Et physicum quidem animali uitae tuendae seruit: ethicum facit, ut uitam hominibus non indignam agamus: theologicum & diuinum illud est, quod ad aeternam uitam consequendam facit. De his tribus speciebus loquitur Jacobus capite 1.17. Omne munus bonum, & omne donum est perfectum, descendens à Patre luminum. Est & haec distinctio memoria digna,quam Aristoteles tradidit in Ethi-cis ad Eudemum: Bonum uel est simpli-citer bonum: uel relatiue, quatenus alicui bonum est. Ac Deus,cum sit ipsa bonitas, & cum sit idem summè beneficus, utroq; modo bonus recte dicitur. Sede-nim huic nostro instituto maxime est ac-commoda Boni distinctio in uerum & in apparens bonum, ut ex sequentibus colligere licet.
units.tr: Now the end is not only the last thing of a matter but also the best, as the Philosopher rightly taught in Physics 2. We must also keep to the distinctions of good. One good is uncreated, immense and eternal, as God is (Matt. 19.17). And we may rightly apply to him Aristotle's definition: Therefore they rightly declared the good to be that which all things desire [Διὸ καλῶς ἀπεφήναντο τ' ἀγαθὸν ἢ πάντα ἐφίεσθαι]. Another is created good, which may be subdivided into physical, ethical and theological good. The physical good serves the preservation of animal life; the ethical good makes us lead a life not unworthy of men; the theological and divine good is that which helps us to attain eternal life. James speaks of these three kinds in chapter 1.17: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights." There is also a distinction worth remembering, which Aristotle set out in the Ethics to Eudemus: good is either simply good, or relatively good, insofar as it is good for someone. God, since he is goodness itself and is supremely beneficent, is rightly called good in both ways. But for our present purpose the distinction between the true good and the apparent good is most suitable, as may be gathered from what follows.

units.la: 3. Qui uerum bonum, à Spiritu sancto edocti elegerunt, ij Christo Iesu (qui uia & ueritas est) duce, in uia mandatorum Dei ambulant. Ratio: Quia Deo se iungi,& eidè hac ratione συμμόρφως[?] fieri, intelligunt, & cum Dauide dicunt: Quinam emendabit adolescens uiam suam? si custodiat uerbum tuum. Item: Via testimoniorum tuorum delector, sicut super omnes diuitias. Psal.119.9.&14.
units.tr: 3. Those who, taught by the Holy Spirit, have chosen the true good, walk in the way of God's commandments, with Christ Jesus (who is the way and the truth) as their guide. Reason: because they understand that they are joined to God and are made conformed to him [συμμόρφως] in this way, and say with David: "How shall a young man cleanse his way? By keeping your word." Likewise: "I delight in the way of your testimonies, as much as in all riches." Ps. 119.9, 14.

units.la: 4. Qui verò apparens solùm & fucatū bonum sectantur, ingrediuntur uiam malam & latam, iuxta dicta: Pro.12.15. Via stulti recta est in oculis eius. Et cap.14.12. Est uia recta coram uiro: & exitus eius, uiae mortis. Exemplo sunt auari, qui dū in terris opes congerunt, coelestia bona amittunt: item, φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι & qui gloriam apud hominess, uerae gloriae quae apud Deum est praeferunt, & horum similes. Matth.7.13.Lata & spatiosa uia est quę abducit in exitium, multiq; sunt qui introeunt per eam.
units.tr: 4. But those who pursue only the apparent and false good enter the evil and broad way, according to the sayings: Prov. 12.15, "The way of a fool is right in his own eyes." And 14.12: "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." Examples are the covetous, who while they heap up riches on earth lose heavenly goods; likewise those who love pleasure more than God (φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι), and those who prefer glory among men to the true glory which is before God, and others like them. Matt. 7.13: "Wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it."

units.la: 5. Caeterum uiatorum quatuor sunt ordines: si uidelicet spectes perseueratiam in bono, contumaciam in malo, salutare μετάνοιαν eorum qui iuxta prouerbium, πάλιν [illegible, ~9 letters] malunt [illegible, ~10 letters]: & exitiosam à bono defectionem.
units.tr: 5. Moreover, there are four orders of travellers, if you look at perseverance in good, obstinacy in evil, the saving repentance of those who, as the proverb has it, prefer to return again, and the destructive falling away from good.

units.la: 6. Sunt enim quibus dedit Deus, ut inde usq; ab initio suę uocationis, inoffenso pede incedant usq; ad finem. De horum felicitate dicitur Pfal.9i.u.[?] Quoniam angelis suis mandauit de te, ut custodiant te in omnibus uijs tuis. 12. Super manus portabunt te, ne offendas pedem tuum.
units.tr: 6. For there are those to whom God has given that, from the very beginning of their calling, they should go on with unstumbling foot to the end. Of their happiness it is said, Ps. 91.11–12: "For he will give his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways. They shall bear you up in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone."

units.la: 7. Sunt qui semper extra Legis orbitã per auia ferantur: ut impij Mahometistae & alij, quos Deus non dignatur sua gratia & luce.
units.tr: 7. There are those who are always carried wandering outside the orbit of the Law through pathless places, like the impious Mahometans and others, whom God does not deign to favour with his grace and light.

units.la: 8. Sunt qui à Domino ab errore in uiã reuocetur, & salui fiant: ut Saulus, Petrus, & adolescens ille quem Ioannes Euangelista è latronum contubernio in Ecclesiae societasocietatem reduxit, cuius meminit Eusebius: item Philosophus ille, quem idiota quidam conuertit ad fidem in Christum, in Nicena synodo.
units.tr: 8. There are those whom the Lord calls back from error to the way, and they are saved: such as Saul (Paul), Peter, and that youth whom the Evangelist John led back from the company of robbers into the fellowship of the Church, whom Eusebius mentions; likewise that philosopher whom a certain unlearned man converted to faith in Christ at the Council of Nicaea.

units.la: 9. Sunt denique, qui à regia uia diuini scripti defleƨtunt in errores, & pereunt. 2.Pet.2.21. Satius enim fuisset eis, non cognouisse uiam iusticiæ, quàm cognita illa regredi à sancta doctrina ipsis tradita.
units.tr: 9. Finally, there are those who turn aside from the royal road of the divine Scriptures into errors, and perish. 2 Pet. 2.21: "For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them."

units.la: 22.Sed accidit illis quod uero prouerbio dici solet, Canis reuersus est ad suum ipsius uomitum: &, Sus lota ad uolutabrum cœni. Talis fuit Ecebolus.
units.tr: 22. But what happens to them is what the true proverb says: "The dog has returned to his own vomit," and "the washed sow to wallowing in the mud." Such was Ecebolus.

units.la: 10. Videamus igitur quomodo accuratè incedamus, non ut insipientes, sed ut sapientes: redimentes occasionem, quoniā dies mali sunt: Eph.5.15.16.
