Et cum ἀκριβῶς περιπατεῖν [?], non sit in nostris uiribus positum, iuxta illud Ieremiae, Scio Domine, quòd non sit hominis uia eius: precemur cum Dauide, Vias tuas edoce me, &c.
units.tr: 10. Let us therefore see how we may walk carefully, not as fools but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Eph. 5.15–16. And since walking accurately (ἀκριβῶς περιπατεῖν) is not within our own powers, according to that saying of Jeremiah, "I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not his own" (Jer. 10.23), let us pray with David: "Teach me your ways," etc.

units.la: Vtinam uerò ipsi quoq; uiam doctrinæ quam profitemur, & uitæ quâ sectamur, expendamus: & omnia dicta factaq; nostra ad Dei gloriam, ac nostram aliorúq; emendationem referamus. Amen.
units.tr: Would that we also weighed the way of the doctrine we profess and of the life we follow, and referred all our words and deeds to the glory of God and to our own and others' amendment. Amen.

units.la: Restat hemistichij uersus 8. pars po-strema, ftrema, in qua per [illegible, ~10 letters] dicitur: Et ab iniquitate quæ est in manibus eorum.
units.tr: There remains the last part of the eighth verse, the second half of the verse, in which [illegible] is said: "And from the violence that is in their hands."

units.la: Etsi uocabulum Viæ γνώσεως[?] cogitationes, dicta & facta complectitur: quia tamen manuum ἀποτελέσματα maximè incurrunt in oculos & alios sensus, requiritur edicto regio, ut ne quisquam uiolentas manus cuiquam inijciat, ut ui aut dolo ademta restituantur, utq; præstentur ea humanitatis officia, quæ interueniente manuum ministerio præstari solent.
units.tr: Although the word "way" embraces thoughts, words and deeds, the works of the hands [ἀποτελέσματα] especially strike the eyes and the other senses. For this reason the royal edict required that no one lay violent hands on anyone, that things taken by force or fraud be restored, and that those acts of humanity be performed which are usually done through the service of the hands.

units.la: Plurimum huc facit illa Dauidis deprecatio: Ne inuadant me pedes superborum: & ne manus impiorum detrudat me: Psal.36.11. Cupiunt enim θεόμαχοι & hostes Sanctorum, hos manibus uiolentis prosternere, & pedibus calcare. Et illa oratio, in qua idem regius Propheta abusum membrorum corporis humani ad seuitiam exercendam, scitè depingit: Acuunt linguas suas sicut serpens: uenenum aspidis sub labijs eorum. Serua me Iehouah de manu improbi, à uiris uioletis serua me, qui cogitant depręcipitandis gressibus meis: Psal.140.3.4. Ex his & simi-libus locis colligere licet, quæ sint occupationes hominum non renatorum. Ho-mo homo homini lupus est tantisper, donec animalis homo est. Sic enim seipsum suspicit & colit, ut non nisi eos utcunq; ferat, quos suis commodis, honoribus & desiderijs seruire opinatur. Caeterorum infelicitate & calamitatibus suam felicitate homo ἐπιχαιρέκακος[?] illustrari vult. Renatus econtrà homo homini deus est. In Deum enim & eius voluntatem respici-ens, ut [illegible, ~10 letters] ex animo alijs omnibus, maximè tamen fidei domesticis consultum esse cupit: & alienarum miseriarum ferio sensu afficitur. Ut autè ille ge-statimaginem terreni patris: ita hic ima-ginem cœlestis patris refert. 1.Cor.15.49.
units.tr: David's prayer bears heavily on this point: "Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the wicked drive me away" (Ps. 36:11). For the enemies of God and of the saints desire to overthrow them with violent hands and to trample them under foot. And in another prayer the same royal prophet vividly describes the misuse of the members of the human body for the exercise of cruelty: "They sharpen their tongues like a serpent; the poison of an asp is under their lips. Lord, keep me from the hand of the wicked; preserve me from violent men, who plan to trip up my steps" (Ps. 140:3–4). From these and similar passages we may gather what the occupations of unregenerate men are. "Man is a wolf to man," for as long as he is merely an animal. For he so regards and honours himself that he tolerates others only so far as he thinks they serve his advantages, honours and desires. He wants his own happiness to shine out from the unhappiness and misfortunes of others. The regenerate man, on the contrary, is a god to man. For looking to God and his will, he wishes, from his heart, to provide for all others, and most of all for the household of faith, and he is deeply moved by the miseries of others. As the one bears the image of the earthly father, so the other bears the image of the heavenly Father (1 Cor. 15:49).

units.la: Illud autem in edicto regio de poeni-tentia non est prætereundum, quòd non paucis quibusdam, sed omnibus in universum civibus & magistratibus Niniui-tarum resipiscétia & eius exercitia ac documenta præscripta sunt. Dissimilis sanè fuit hic Rex Assyriorum, ijs Principibus & Politarchis, qui leges severas de vitanda temulentia, scortatione & alijs sceleribus subditis præscribút, quas ipsimet in aulis domibusq; suis nequaquam observant. Enimverò si, sententia Hera-cliti, cliti, civibus non minus pugnandum est pro legibus, quàm pro mœnibus: quòd absq; mœnibus, nō autem absq; legibus incolumis esse possit civitas: non minus religiosè elaborandum, ut salutaria edicta de pietatis exercitijs, de fuga vitiorū, de disciplina & progymnasmatis virtutum, locum habeant in Ecclesia, quæ sanctorum ἁγίων κοινωνία[?] id est, societas est.
units.tr: Something in the royal edict concerning repentance must not be passed over: that repentance and its exercises and precepts were prescribed not to a few particular persons but to all the citizens and magistrates of Nineveh without exception. This king of the Assyrians was certainly unlike those princes and magistrates who prescribe severe laws against drunkenness, fornication and other crimes for their subjects, yet by no means observe them in their own courts and houses. Indeed, following the saying of Heraclitus, that citizens must fight for their laws no less than for their walls, since a city can be safe without walls but not without laws, so we must labour no less diligently that the salutary edicts concerning the exercises of piety, the flight from vices, and the training and exercise of virtues, may have their place in the Church, which is the communion of saints [ἁγίων κοινωνία].

units.la: VERSVS IX.
units.tr: VERSE IX.

units.la: Quis scit si convertatur, et pœniteat Deum, avertaturq; à furore iræ suæ: & non peribimus?
units.tr: "Who knows whether God will turn and repent, and turn away from the fierceness of his anger, so that we shall not perish?"

units.la: Hæc est altera pars regij edicti, in qua agitur περὶ τῶν πιστῶν[?] ἢ[?] ἐλπιζομένων, id est, de iis quæ credenda & sperānda essent conversis ad Deum.
units.tr: This is the second part of the royal edict, in which is treated what is to be believed and hoped for by those converted to God (περὶ τῶν πιστῶν ἢ ἐλπιζομένων).

units.la: Poterant Niniuitæ dicere: Cur ad ieiunium, ad saccum, ad supplicationes, denique ad conversionem ipsis factis contestandam nos vocas? Respondetur: Quia spes est, Deum pro infinita sua clementia nobis parsurum esse, si resipiscamus. Eodem sane modo Dominus per Ieremiam Israelitis resipiscentibus pollicetur veniam. Si reversus fueris Israel, dixit Ieho-vah, uah,ad me,quiescestes: & si abstuleris abominationes tuas à facie mea, non demigrabis. cap.4.1.
units.tr: The Ninevites might say: why do you call us to fasting, to sackcloth, to supplications, and finally to a conversion to be attested by our deeds? The answer is that there is hope that God, in his infinite mercy, will spare us if we repent. In exactly the same way the Lord, through Jeremiah, promises pardon to the Israelites when they repent: "If you return, Israel, says the LORD, to me you shall return; and if you take away your abominations out of my sight, you shall not be moved" (Jer. 4:1).

units.la: Sed hæc de orationis forma quæritur. An ne dubitantis oratio fit: Quis scit si conuertatur, &c. an uero affirmatis, bene de misericordia Dei & de uenia Niniuitis sperandum? Respondeo: Cùm studio uerae resipiscentiae nulla res magis aduerse-tur, quàm dubitatio de misericordia Dei, & de uenia & mitigatione malorum: non est consentaneum, Regem, qui unicè uellet & optaret suos ciues una secum resipiscere, hoc orationis schemate dubios de salutari fructu conuersionis relinquere uoluisse. Immò contrà, ut τὰ [?], sic τὰ ἐλπιζόμενα certa uideri & haberi uolebat. Aduersatur igitur consilio Regis, dubitationis illud commentum.
units.tr: But it may be asked whether this is a prayer of one who doubts: "Who knows whether he will turn," etc., or whether it affirms that the Ninevites may well hope for God's mercy and pardon. I answer: since nothing is more opposed to the zeal for true repentance than doubt about the mercy of God and about pardon and the mitigation of evils, it is not consistent to suppose that a king who wished and desired above all that his citizens repent together with him would have wanted, by this form of speech, to leave them doubtful about the saving fruit of conversion. On the contrary, just as he wanted the things of God [τὰ θεῖα] to be seen and held as certain, so he wanted the things hoped for [τὰ ἐλπιζόμενα] to be seen and held as certain. Therefore that invention of doubt is contrary to the king's purpose.

units.la: Etsi autem non semper distinguitur remissio pœnæ temporalis à remissione culpæ: ut ostendunt exempla, Dauidis, qui homicidij & adulterij graues dedit pœ-nas: Mosis, qui, quòd ad petram diffiden-tia peccasset, non potuit impetrare copi-am introeundi terram Patribus promis-sam: sæpe tamen Deus etiam temporales poenas vel relaxat, ut Niniuitarum exemplum monet: vel differt, ut Ezechiæ & posterorum historia testatur: Esa.39.8.
units.tr: Although the remission of the temporal punishment is not always distinguished from the remission of the guilt, as the examples show: David, who paid heavy penalties for murder and adultery; Moses, who, because he sinned by distrust at the rock, could not obtain entry into the land promised to the fathers. Nevertheless God often either relaxes even temporal punishments, as the example of the Ninevites warns, or defers them, as the history of Hezekiah and his successors testifies (Isa. 39:8).

units.la: Porrò, Si dubitatiuè ista a Rege pronū-ciata fuissent, qui nam,te quaeso,Deo,ad quem accedentes credere oportet, pro-bata fuissent? Nam qui disceptat, similis est fluctui maris, qui ventis agitatur & ia-statur[?]. Neigitur existimet homo ille, se quicquam accepturum a Deo: Iac.1.6.7. Fieri non potest, ut sine fide quisquâ Deo placeat. nam qui accedit ad Deum, hunc oportet credere esse Deum, & pręmia lar-giri ijs qui ipsum requirut: Heb.11.6. Placuerunt autem Niniuitæ Deo, & impetra-verunt relaxationem denunciatæ pœnę: ut historia eorum docet. Itaque statua-mus, Deum illis dedisse, ut citra hæsitati-onem ad eum conversis veniam spe de-sponderent.
units.tr: Moreover, if these things had been pronounced by the king in a doubtful manner, I ask you, what proofs would there be of God, to whom those who approach him must believe? For one who wavers is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the winds. Let that man not think that he will receive anything from the Lord (Jas. 1:6–7). It is impossible for anyone to please God without faith; for whoever comes to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him (Heb. 11:6). Now the Ninevites pleased God and obtained the relaxation of the threatened punishment, as their history teaches. Therefore let us establish that God gave them this, that those who turned to him without hesitation might be assured of pardon.

units.la: Obiectio: Apud quę non est transmu-tatio, aut conversionis obumbratio, ei nō re-ctè tribuūtur conversio, poenitentia, a-versio à furore iræ, & similia πάθη[?].
units.tr: Objection: to those in whom there is no change, nor any shadow of turning, conversion, repentance, turning away from the fury of wrath and similar affections are not rightly attributed.

units.la: Sed apud Deum non est παραλλαγὴ ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα[?]: Iac.1.17. Item: Fortitudo Israelis non mentietur, nec pœnitudine duceducetur:non enim homo est,ut poeniteat illum.1.Sam.15.29.
units.tr: But with God there is no "variation or shadow of turning" (Jas. 1:17). Likewise: "The Strength of Israel will not lie, nor be moved to repentance; for he is not a man, that he should repent" (1 Sam. 15:29).

units.la: Quare non recte ei tribuuntur conuer-sio,poenitentia,auersio a furore irae,&c.
units.tr: Therefore conversion, repentance, turning away from the fury of wrath, etc., are not rightly attributed to him.

units.la: Respondeo, esse fallaciam ἀμφιβολογίας [?] in argumento, nec ualere confequetiam mutato praedicationis genere. Nam conuersio,poenitudo,& alia πάθη [?], per ἀνθρωπικὰ [?] πάθη [?] Deo tribuuntur, no proprie: ut ex his argumentis colligi potest.
units.tr: I answer that there is a fallacy of equivocation in the argument, and that the consequence does not hold when the kind of predication has been changed. For conversion, repentance and the other affections are attributed to God in a human manner, not properly; as can be gathered from these arguments.

units.la: 1. Cuicunq; non competunt ignorantia,error in cofilijs,& alia ἁμαρτήματα [?], quae ex illis oriuntur: is proprie loquendo poenitudine non ducitur. Deo autem illa no competunt. Igitur,&c.
units.tr: 1. Whoever is not subject to ignorance, error in counsels, and the other sins which arise from these, is not, properly speaking, moved to repentance. But these things do not apply to God. Therefore, etc.

units.la: 2. Cuius propositum suo fine nunqua frustrari potest,is ἀμεταμέλητος [?] est.
units.tr: 2. Whose purpose can never be frustrated by its end, that one is unrepentant [ἀμεταμέλητος].

units.la: Deus autem propositi fui fine frustrari nequit: alioquin nec omnipotens,nec omnifcius effet.
units.tr: But God cannot be frustrated in his purpose by its end; otherwise he would be neither omnipotent nor omniscient.

units.la: Ad ea quae nuper diximus de Deo pro positum suum exequente, plurimum facit allegatio principij Theologici: Deus est immutabilis. Num.23.19.Non est homo Deus,ut mentiatur:& filius hominis, ut poeniteat eum.ipse dixit,& non faciet? locutus est,& non praestabit illud?Itaque id demum accidit, quod ipse ab omni æternitate decreuit: nec ipse in consilijs suis potest falli aut præpediri. Recte igitur dicimus, eum proprie loquendo ἀμετανόητον τῷ ἀμεταμελήτῳ[?] esse, cum omnia iuste re-steq; decernat & prosequatur. Sed addamus aliud argumentum.
units.tr: To what we have just said, that God carries out his purpose, the principle of theology is very relevant: God is unchangeable. "God is not a man, that he should lie; nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said it, and will he not do it? Has he spoken, and will he not fulfil it?" (Num. 23:19). Thus that comes to pass which he has decreed from all eternity, and he himself cannot be deceived or hindered in his counsels. Therefore we rightly say that, properly speaking, he is unrepentant [ἀμετανόητον], to the unchangeable one [τῷ ἀμεταμελήτῳ], since he decrees and carries out all things justly and rightly. But let us add another argument.

units.la: 3. Passio Deo tribui nequit: est enim μακάριος ἢ μόνος δυνάστης[?] 1.Tim.6.15. Sed poenitudo passio est: magnum enim ex erro-re in consilijs & actionibus, & utrorumq; exitu, dolorem is percipit, qui ducitur pœnitetia.
units.tr: 3. Passion cannot be attributed to God, for he is "the blessed and only Potentate" (1 Tim. 6:15). But repentance is a passion; for he who is moved to repentance feels great grief from error in counsels and actions and from their outcome.

units.la: ¶ Instantia. Malach.3.6. Ego enim Ie-houah non mutor.
units.tr: ¶ Instance: "For I am the LORD, I do not change" (Mal. 3:6).

units.la: Pœnitetia autem & auersio ab ira, mu-tatio quædam est.
units.tr: But repentance and turning away from wrath are a kind of change.

units.la: Pugnat itaq; Ionæ dictum, & multa alia dicta similia, cum dicto Malachiæ.
units.tr: Therefore the saying of Jonah, and many other similar sayings, conflict with the saying of Malachi.

units.la: Respondeo ad Maiorem primum, quod[?] hoc solum sibi vult, Deum quidem sibi ipsi semper esse similem: Israelitas autem mire mutabiles fuisse. ac futurum, ut nisi resipiscant, Deum iratum sentiant: si vero ad Deum convertantur, propitium experiantur. vers.7. Stat enim illud: Erga be-nignu exhibes te benignu; & erga virum integrum exhibes te integrũ. Erga purũ exhibes te purum: & aduersus distortũ te distortũ præbes: Psal.18.25.26. Deus sane non mutatur: sed sui similis, ignoscit resipiscenti, irascitur contumaci: quemadmodum diserte edixit. Ac esset (ut hoc κατὰ βίαιον[?] adducam) in Deo mutatio, si resipiscenti irasceretur, non resipiscenti propi-tius esset.
units.tr: I answer to the major premise, first, that this means only that God is always like himself, while the Israelites were wonderfully changeable; and that it would come about, unless they repented, that they would feel God angry, but if they turned to God they would experience him as favourable (v. 7). For this stands: "With the merciful you show yourself merciful, and with the upright man you show yourself upright; with the pure you show yourself pure, and with the crooked you show yourself crooked" (Ps. 18:25–26). Certainly God is not changed; but being like himself, he pardons the repentant and is angry with the stubborn, as he plainly declared. And there would be a change in God (to bring in this point by force [κατὰ βίαιον]) if he were angry with the one who repents and favourable to the one who does not repent.

units.la: Sicut autem essentia Dei simplicissima & perfectissima, ita etiam arcana eius uoluntas nunquam mutatur. Patefacta tamen uoluntas si mutetur, mirum uideri non debet. nam & hypothesin tacitam, ac conditionem annexam habet, quam ex euentu colligere licet: & mutatio illa non tam in Deo, quàm in re fit. Ut, Si non egerint Niniuitæ pœnitentiam, post dies quadraginta peribunt. Ita dicitur Ier.7.3. Sic dixit Iehouah exercituum Deus Israel: Bonas facite uias uestras, & opera uestra, & habitare uos faciam in loco isto. Item cap.26.13. Nunc igitur bonas facite uias uestras & opera uestra, & obedite uoci Iehouę Dei uestri, & pœnitebit Iehouam mali quod locutus est aduersus uos.
units.tr: Just as the essence of God is most simple and most perfect, so his secret will never changes. Yet if a revealed will is changed, that should not seem strange. For it also carries an implied condition attached to it, which can be inferred from the outcome, and that change occurs not so much in God as in the thing itself. For example, "If the Ninevites do not repent, they will perish after forty days." So it is said in Jer. 7.3: "Thus said the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Amend your ways and your doings, and I will cause you to dwell in this place." Likewise in chap. 26.13: "Now therefore amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, and the LORD will repent of the evil that he has spoken against you."

units.la: Minorem quod attinet, uera est, si proprie fumas pœnitetiæ uocabulum de hominū pœnitentia, quæ mortificatione carnis & uiuificatione spiritus constat. Deo autem ἀνθρωποπαθῶς[?] tribuitur. Vt enim ipsi, cum mutamus rem aliquam, pœnitentia ductiid fecisse dicimur: ita cū uoluntatis suæ non plane nobis patefactæ decretum Deus, re mutata, eidem accommodat, pœnitentia affectus dicitur.
units.tr: As for the minor premise, it is true if you take the word "repentance" properly, as the repentance of men, which consists in the mortifying of the flesh and the quickening of the spirit. But it is attributed to God in a human manner [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς]. For just as we ourselves, when we change something, are said to have done it moved by repentance, so God, when he changes a thing and accommodates his decree, which was not plainly disclosed to us, to that changed thing, is said to be affected by repentance.

units.la: Quomodo ad nos conuerti dicitur Deus?
units.tr: In what sense is God said to be turned towards us?

units.la: Cùm se nobis adesse præsentia suæ gratiæ, sereno vultu nos respicere & illuminare, lætitiam in corde dare, resipiscentibus ignoscere, reipsa testatur.
units.tr: When he bears witness by his deed that by the presence of his grace he is near us, that with a serene countenance he looks upon us and enlightens us, that he gives joy in the heart, and that he pardons those who repent.

units.la: Quomodo dicitur pœnitudine duci?
units.tr: In what sense is it said that God is led by repentance?

units.la: Quando interueniete & impleta conditione, id omittit, quod illa non adimpleta, se facturum esse denunciauerat. Vt cùm Niniuitis ad se conuersis parceret, pœnitentia ductus esse dicitur. Cum autem ad eum modū agit Deus, non mutat arcanam suam uoluntatem & decretū, sed id quod ex comminatione aut promissione conditionali, nos certò futurum esse, nobis persua-feramus.
units.tr: When, the condition having intervened and been fulfilled, he omits what he had declared he would do if that condition were not fulfilled. Thus when he spares the Ninevites, who have turned to him, he is said to be led by repentance. But when God acts in this way, he does not change his secret will and decree; rather, he persuades us that what we are certain to be going to happen from a conditional threat or promise is what will happen.

units.la: Aversio autem à furore ira, quomodo praedicatur de Deo?
units.tr: How is turning away from wrath and fury predicated of God?

units.la: Cum Deus nullis perturbationibus sit obnoxius, ira, furor, & alij similes motus, Deo non nisi, ut toties dictum est, κατ' ἀν-θρωποπάθειαν tribuuntur. ut in Psal. 2.12. Osculamini filium, ne quando irascatur, & pereatis ex via, quando exarserit subito ira eius. Psal.18.8. Ascendit fumus per nares eius, & ignis vorax ex ore eius: prunę ardebant coram eo. Definit irasci Deus, cum vel condonat poenas, vel eas mitigat. Caetera, quae huc faciunt, alio tempore, si dabit & volet Deus, exponam.
units.tr: Since God is subject to no passions, anger, fury and other similar emotions are attributed to God only in a human manner [κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν], as has been said so often. So in Ps. 2.12: "Kiss the Son, lest he be angry and you perish from the way, when his wrath is suddenly kindled." Ps. 18.8: "Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; coals were kindled before him." God ceases to be angry when he either remits the punishments or moderates them. I shall expound the other matters that bear on this at another time, if God gives and wills it.

units.la: VERSVS X.
units.tr: VERSE 10

units.la: Vidit autem Deus opera eorum, quòd conversi essent à via sua mala: & poenituit Deum ipsum mali quod locutus fuerat se facturum ipsis, & non fecit.
units.tr: "And God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil which he had said he would do to them, and he did it not."

units.la: Hoc loco occurrit commemorabile exemplum oraculi: Nunquid desiderando desidero ut moriatur impius, dixit Dominus Iehouah? An nō, si aversus fuerit à viis suis, viuet? Ezech. 18.23. Niniuitis enim ad se conversis ignovit & pepercit Deus, qui copia benignitatis, lenitatis tolerantię ad refipiscentiam deducit: Roman.2.4.
units.tr: Here occurs a memorable example of the oracle: "Do I at all desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord GOD? Is it not rather that he should turn from his ways and live?" (Ezek. 18.23). For God forgave and spared the Ninevites when they turned to him, he who through the riches of his goodness, forbearance and patience leads to repentance (Rom. 2.4).

units.la: Nos,ut doctrina hoc loco tradita illu-stretur,duas nobilissimas quaestiones tra-ctabimus: quarum altera est de causis propter quas poenitentiam agetibus De-us parcit: altera de firmitate divini pro-positi,& de immutabilitate decretorum eius. Faxit Dominus Iesus, ut pie & ve-re omnia tractemus.
units.tr: So that the doctrine delivered in this place may be illustrated, we shall treat two most noble questions: the first concerns the causes on account of which God spares those who repent; the second concerns the firmness of the divine purpose and the immutability of his decrees. May the Lord Jesus grant that we treat all these things piously and truly.

units.la: I. QUID CAUSSAE EST, QUOD resipiscentibus Deus parcit?
units.tr: I. WHAT IS THE CAUSE WHY GOD SPARES THOSE WHO REPENT?

units.la: Respondeo, Deum parcere refipiscen-tibus, sic ut culpam, & simul poenas temporales & aeternas remittat: vel culpa co-donet,& poenas aeternas relaxet, non autem temporales: ut monet Dauidis exe-plum. Hoc autem loco quaeritur, quam ob causam Deus refipiscetibus ignoscat & parcat? Sic autem argumentor: Deus in gratiam refipiscetes recipit, aut eo-rum merito motus, aut sua gratia & mi-sericordia. juxta dictum: Ita igitur & hoc tempore reseruatio secundum electionem gratuitam facta est. Quod si per gratiam, non jam ex operibus: alioquin gratia jam non est gratia. Sin ex operibus, jam non est gratia:alioquin opus iam non est opus:Rom.11.5.6. Atqui nemo hominū ob sua merita in gratiam recipitur.Ratio: Quia nullum est hominum meritum,nisi malum, & quod poenas meretur,non praemia. Itaque cum Apostolo Paulo dicamus: Non ex operibus iustis quae fecerimus nos,sed ex sua misericordia servauit nos,&c.Tit.3.5. Item: Gratia enim estis seruati per fidem : idq; non ex uobis. Dei donum est.Non ex operibus,ne quis glorietur.Eph.2.8.9.
units.tr: I answer that God spares those who repent in such a way that he remits both the guilt and the temporal and eternal punishments together; or he pardons the guilt and relaxes the eternal punishments, but not the temporal ones, as the example of David warns. Here, however, the question is: for what reason does God forgive and spare those who repent? I argue thus: God receives those who repent into favour either moved by their merit, or by his own grace and mercy. According to the saying: "So too at this present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace. And if by grace, then it is no more of works; otherwise grace is no more grace. But if of works, then it is no more grace; otherwise work is no more work" (Rom. 11.5-6). Yet no man is received into favour on account of his own merits. The reason: because there is no merit of men except evil, and what deserves punishment, not rewards. Therefore, with the Apostle Paul we say: "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, etc." (Titus 3.5). Likewise: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God. Not of works, lest anyone should boast" (Eph. 2.8-9).

units.la: Constituta hac pia sententia,uideamus quid Sophistae ex uerbis Ionae,quę in manibus habemus, conentur ad eam conuellendam euincere. Sic enim illi paralogizant:
units.tr: This pious opinion being laid down, let us see what the Sophists try to overturn it with, drawing from the words of Jonah which we have before us. For they argue thus:

units.la: Remissio peccatorum & relaxatio poenae,ei caussae accepta ferri debet,quam re spiciens Dominus Niniuitis ignouit, & decretum de illis perdendis rescidit.
units.tr: The remission of sins and the relaxation of punishment must be credited to the cause which the Lord regarded when he forgave the Ninevites and rescinded the decree to destroy them.

units.la: Atqui diserte dicitur, quod Deus Ninivitarum opera respiciens,poenitudine duci coeperit.
units.tr: But it is plainly stated that God, regarding the works of the Ninevites, began to be moved by repentance.

units.la: Fuerunt igitur opera Niniuitarū caussa remissionis peccatorum, & relaxationis poenarum. Vnde colligitur,opera bona mena mereri veniam & liberationem à malis impendétibus: ut Pelagiani & eorum sequaces volunt.
units.tr: Therefore the works of the Ninevites were the cause of the remission of sins and the relaxation of punishments. From this it is gathered that good works of men merit pardon and deliverance from impending evils, as the Pelagians and their followers maintain.

units.la: Respondeo, in hoc argumento esse paralogismum secundum non causam ut causam. Non enim hoc dicitur, Propter opera bona Deum Niniuitis pepercisse: sed, Deum παντων[?] ἐφορον καὶ καρδιογνώστην[?], fructus poenitentia dignos animaduertis-se in Niniuitis: quibus alioquin ex mera sua gratia & misericordia poenitentiae donum largitus fuerat, veniam dedit, & poenas relaxauit.
units.tr: I answer that in this argument there is the paralogism of taking what is not the cause as the cause. For it is not said: "On account of good works God spared the Ninevites"; rather, God, the overseer of all and searcher of hearts [πάντων ἐπόπτην καὶ καρδιογνώστην], noticed in the Ninevites fruits worthy of repentance, to whom otherwise, out of his mere grace and mercy, he had granted the gift of repentance, and whom he pardoned, and whose punishments he relaxed.

units.la: Etsi autem cordium scrutator Deus fidem potissimùm respicit: tamen humano more loquendo, eius effectus, videli-cet bona opera respicere dicitur, quòd hæc sint testimonia fidei per caritatem efficaciter agentis, per quæ etiam aliis innotescere potest fides.
units.tr: Although God, the searcher of hearts, chiefly regards faith, nevertheless, speaking in human fashion, his effect, namely good works, is said to be regarded, because these are the testimonies of faith working effectually through love, through which faith can also become known to others.

units.la: Instantia: Probabile videri posset id quod affirmas, nisi obstaret pronomen Eorum, quod monet operibus hominū potius, quàm operi quod Dei proprium est, (videlicet, parcere resipiscenti) acceptam esse ferendam veniam & liberationem è tanto periculo. Qui hoc pacto instant, non vident se τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ λαμβάνειν: cum idem opus bonum diverso respectu, Deo ut αὐτῷ ἐνεργοῦντι[?] homini ut instrumento tribuatur. Iam verò si Deus efficiens causa est bonorum operum, quae resipiscentes praestant: ei sanè uni, si quae laus est bonorum operum, non autem organicis caussis, quae multis modis illa cōtaminant, tribui debet. Re-ste igitur Augustinus, Deum non merita nostra, sed sua dona in nobis coronare, alicubi docuit.
units.tr: Objection: What you affirm might seem probable, were it not that the pronoun "their" points to the works of men rather than to the work which is proper to God (namely, sparing the one who repents), and that pardon and deliverance from so great a danger ought to be credited to it. Those who press this objection do not see that they are begging the question [τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ λαμβάνειν], since the same good work is attributed to God, who works by himself [αὐτῷ ἐνεργοῦντι], and to man as an instrument, under a different respect. Indeed, if God is the efficient cause of the good works which those who repent perform, then, if there is any praise of good works, it ought to be given to him alone, and not to the instrumental causes, which in many ways contaminate those works. Therefore Augustine taught somewhere that God crowns not our merits but his own gifts in us.

units.la: Est autem in Instantia coccysmus prę-supponens falsò, Deum propter opera, seu propter pœnitentiæ fructus Niniuitis ignouisse.
units.tr: There is, moreover, a sneering jibe in the objection, which presupposes falsely that God forgave the Ninevites on account of their works, or on account of the fruits of repentance.

units.la: Instantia: Contrariorum eadem est ratio. Sed propter malefacta hominū irascitur Deus & vindicat iniquitate. iuxta dicta: Et dabo eos in commotionem universis regnis terræ, propter Manassen filium Ezechiæ Regem Iuda, propter ea quæ fecit Ierosolymis: Ier.15.4. Item: Visitans iniquitate patrum super filios, in tertiam & quartam generationem odio habetibus me. Exod.20.5. Ergo etiam propter benefacta Deus ignoscit & pœnas remittit. Nego sequi, cum contraria illa nō sint utrinq; plena. Nam mala opera ab homine perpetrantur, & poenas merentur: bona autem opera primum à Spiritu sancto efficiuntur, quatenus sunt bona: deinde, imperfecta pariter & peccatorum sordibus respersa & contaminata sunt. Unde liquet, nec nostra proprie dici, nec mereri praemia illa, quae non nisi ex gratia Dei operantibus contingunt. Vocantur autem filiorum praemia, quae gratis dantur; Deo se nobis gratuita promissione, ad illa praemia nobis largienda, obligante.
units.tr: Objection: The reasoning is the same for contraries. But God is angry at, and avenges, the wicked deeds of men on account of their iniquity, according to the sayings: "And I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh the son of Hezekiah king of Judah, for what he did in Jerusalem" (Jer. 15.4); and: "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me" (Exod. 20.5). Therefore God also forgives and remits punishments on account of good deeds. I deny the consequence, since the contraries are not full in both respects. For evil works are committed by man, and deserve punishments; but good works are first effected by the Holy Spirit, in so far as they are good; and then they are likewise imperfect and stained and contaminated with the filth of sins. Whence it is clear that those rewards are neither properly called ours nor merited, since they come only to those who work by the grace of God. But they are called the rewards of the sons, which are given freely, God having bound himself by a gratuitous promise to bestow those rewards upon us.

units.la: ¶ Priusquam ad sequentia accedam, de eo paucis agam, cuius memoriam hodierna dies nobis refricare potest. Etsi hesterna die Ecclesia pie repetiuit ἀνάλ-ψιν[?] τῇ Iesu Christi: quia tamē eam in quintū die Maij incidisse, uiri quidā religiosi & eruditi ostenderunt, paucis de ea agam.
units.tr: Before I come to what follows, I will say a few words about the event whose memory today can renew for us. Although yesterday the Church piously commemorated the ascension [ἀνάλημψιν] of Jesus Christ, certain religious and learned men have shown that it fell on the fifth of May, so I will speak briefly about it.

units.la: Initiò, ut Dei in carne reuelationi, & eiusdem τῇ ἀναλήψει[?], certa temporum momenta diuinitus fuerunt praestituta: sic dies à resurrectione Iesu Christi 40 eiusdē in coelum ascensioni praefinitus fuit.
units.tr: At the outset, just as certain moments of time were divinely appointed for God's revelation in the flesh and for his ascension [ἀνάλημψιν], so the interval of forty days after the resurrection of Jesus Christ was fixed for his ascent into heaven.

units.la: Neque uero est cur putemus, ea ratio-ne Christum Iesum in coelos ad Patrem ascendisse, qua ratione Deus ascendisse aut descendisse sæpenumero dicitur. Dei enim essentia infinita est, sic ut non nisi ἀνθρωποπαθῶς[?] ascensio & descensio illi tri-buatur. Humana autem natura cùm spi-ritu finito & corpore organico constet, localis est,& proprie de loco in locum trās-ferri dicitur.
units.tr: Nor is there any reason to think that Christ Jesus ascended into the heavens to the Father in the same way that God is so often said to have ascended or descended. For the essence of God is infinite, so that ascent and descent are attributed to him only in a human manner [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς]. But human nature, consisting of a finite spirit and an organic body, is local, and is properly said to be transferred from place to place.

units.la: Euexit λόγος naturam humanam supra omnes cœlos, ad dextram Patris. Et a-scensio quidem, si carnem spectes, localis fuit,sicut & ipsa caro localis ac circum scripta est.
units.tr: The Word raised human nature above all the heavens, to the right hand of the Father. And the ascension, if you regard the flesh, was local, just as the flesh itself is local and circumscribed.

units.la: Etsi autem Christi caro iam tum glori-ficata fuit:tamen gloria ei non naturæ ue-ritatem, sed infirmitatem ademit. Utq; articulus symboli de ascensione, de locali motu in cœlestem ufq; regionem: sic is qui est de sessione, ad imperij cōsortium referri debet. Non nouimus nunc Christum secundum carnem, quæ ubicunque actu primo & corporaliter est, ibidem videri & tangi potest. Sed interim non ne-gamus,totum Christū nobis adesse: quia idem uerus Deus, & proinde infinitus & ubique est.
units.tr: Although Christ's flesh was already then glorified, glory did not take away from it the reality of its nature, but its weakness. Just as the article of the creed concerning the ascension refers to local movement into the heavenly region, so the article concerning the session must be referred to the sharing of dominion. We do not now know Christ according to the flesh, which, wherever it is actually and bodily present, can be seen and touched in that place. Yet meanwhile we do not deny that the whole Christ is present with us, because he is the same true God, and therefore infinite and everywhere.

units.la: Neq; uerò Christi personam cum Ne-storio storio diuidimus, quando dicimus, λόγῳ sic σωματικῶς seu personaliter assumtæ naturæ adesse, ut tamen extra eam sit. Vnionis enim duarum illarum naturarum differentia specifica non est, simul ubiq; esse, ut nec simul ab æterno esse: sed unam personam efficere.
units.tr: Nor indeed do we divide the person of Christ with Nestorius when we say that the Word is present to the assumed nature bodily or personally [σωματικῶς], and yet is outside it. For the specific difference of the union of those two natures is not that they are at once everywhere, any more than they were at once from eternity, but that they make up one person.

units.la: Oportuit autem Christi carnem, quæ nostræ ὁμοούσιος est, in cœlum traduci, ut nobis, qui filij Dei & cohæredes Christi sumus, pignoris loco esset, spemq; possessionis eiusdem cœlestis patriæ in nobis accederet & foueret per Spiritum sanctum, qui est arrhabo hæreditatis nostræ.
units.tr: It was fitting that Christ's flesh, which is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with ours, be carried up into heaven, so that it might serve as a pledge to us, who are sons of God and co-heirs with Christ, and so that hope of possessing that heavenly fatherland might be kindled and nourished in us through the Holy Spirit, who is the earnest of our inheritance.

units.la: Hęc paucis monere uisum est, etiá eam ob caussam, ut nō modò ipsi fidei simplicitate contenti, periculosis de ascensione allegoriis (quæ euanefcentiæ commento & delirio de inuisibili corpore Christi stabiliendo parum sanè seruiunt) locum non demus: sed etiam, Deum precemur, ut eis qui in hoc capite à nobis dissentiût, pro infinita sua bonitate det in ueritatis uiam redire, & in ipso unà nobiscum τὸ ἓν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν.
units.tr: I have thought it right to remind you of these things briefly, and also for this reason: that we, content with the simplicity of faith itself, may give no place to dangerous allegories concerning the ascension, which serve very poorly to establish the vaporous fiction and delirium of an invisible body of Christ. And we pray God that, in his infinite goodness, he may grant to those who dissent from us on this article to return to the way of truth, and in him to be of one mind with us [τὸ ἓν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν].

units.la: Si quis uolet Neoterici alicuius ἀξιολόγῳ[?] Scriptoris, orthodoxæ Ecclesiæ de ascesione Christi in coelos cosensum unà nobi-fcu adprobantis, teftimoniu inspicere,le-gat Philippi Melanchthonis postrema in cap.3.Epiftolęad[?] Colloffenfes[?] Enarratio ne. Sed iam ad inftitutu de cotrouerfijs quae sunt de bonis operibus, accedamus.
units.tr: If anyone wishes to examine the testimony of some noteworthy modern writer who, together with us, approves the consensus of the orthodox Church concerning Christ's ascension into the heavens, let him read Philip Melanchthon's last commentary on chapter 3 of the Epistle to the Colossians. But now let us proceed to the plan of the controversies concerning good works.

units.la: ¶ Existimo mei esse officij,fontes praecipuarũ controuerfiarũ inter nostras Ec-clefias & Pontificios, uelut exerto digito comonftrare,ut quo ordine praecipua fo-phismata nobis diftribueda,& quo pacto dijudicanda sint, intelligamus. Breuiter itaq; treis nobiles quaestiones, de origi-ne,speciebus & utilitate bonorū operū, proponā,ac de ijs ordine & logicè agam.
units.tr: I think it is my duty to point out, as with an outstretched finger, the sources of the chief controversies between our Churches and the Papists, so that we may understand in what order the principal sophisms are to be distributed and how they are to be judged. Briefly, then, I will set forth three important questions concerning the origin, kinds and usefulness of good works, and I will treat them in order and logically.

units.la: 1. De efficientibus caussis; An'ne gra-tiae & liberi arbitrij concursus opera bo-na producat,nécnè?
units.tr: 1. Concerning the efficient causes: does the concurrence of grace and free will produce good works or not?

units.la: 2. De forma : An'ne praeter ea bona opera,quae Deus praescripsit,alia quoq; esse possint hoc nomine digna?
units.tr: 2. Concerning the form: can there be other works, besides those which God has prescribed, that are worthy of this name?

units.la: 3. De finibus:An'ne,fi negetur iustifica-tio operum bonorum haec, fructu carere, eoq; negligi posse,fit existimandum?
units.tr: 3. Concerning the ends: if the justification of good works is denied, is it to be thought that they lack fruit and so may be neglected?

units.la: De prima quaestione, in qua agitur de bonorum operum origine,
units.tr: Concerning the first question, in which the origin of good works is treated,

units.la: Vt haec quaestio,An'ne liberi arbitrij gratiae concursus opera bona producat, an uero non ?illustretur,tria nobis obser-uanda erunt.
units.tr: So that this question, whether the concurrence of free will and grace produces good works or not, may be made clear, three things must be observed.

units.la: 1. Status hominis plane animalis. In quo nihil est praeter tenebras & odium Dei,ei(cum de prima origine boni,quod in homine incoari potest,disseritur) non potest tribui naturae διάθεσις [?] ad primam gratiam suscipiendam,quae postea a succedente altera gratia adiuuetur. Sed in animali homine tenebrae & odium Dei & alia mala grassantur. Quare non potest ei tribui physica dispositio ad suscipiendam gratiam,quae sit initium bonorum operum.
units.tr: 1. The state of man is altogether animal. In that state there is nothing but darkness and hatred of God. Therefore, when we are discussing the first origin of the good that can begin in man, no natural disposition toward receiving the first grace, which a second, following grace would then assist, can be attributed to him. But in the animal man darkness, hatred of God and other evils rage. Therefore a physical disposition to receive grace, which would be the beginning of good works, cannot be attributed to him.

units.la: Item: Quicquid non est ex fide,peccatum est: Rom.14.23. Sed opera hominis renati non sunt ex fide. Neque enim effectus praecedit causam, sed sequitur: ut umbra corpus. Itaque non renati hominis opera,sunt peccata.
units.tr: Likewise: whatever is not from faith is sin: Rom. 14.23. But the works of a man who has been reborn are not from faith. For the effect does not precede its cause but follows it, as a shadow follows a body. Therefore the works of an unregenerate man are sins.

units.la: Item: Putris arbor fert fructus malos: Matt.7.17. Non renatus homo arbor putris est. Quare no nisi fructus malos,quos Paulus Carnis opera uocat,producit: Galat.5.19.
units.tr: Likewise: a rotten tree bears bad fruit: Matt. 7.17. An unregenerate man is a rotten tree. Therefore he produces only bad fruits, which Paul calls the works of the flesh: Gal. 5.19.

units.la: 2. Prima couersio hominis. Quod nusquam est,non concurrit ad hominem cõ-uertendum. In prima hominum conuer-sione,nullũ est liberũ arbitrium: tum de-mũ enim Spiritus sanctus homines manu mittit à peccato,cũ Christi per fidē insiti-tios facit,ut uitā ex eo haurientes,Deo uiuere incipiant, Quare nō concurrit ad ho-mine conuertendum liberum arbitrium.
units.tr: 2. The first conversion of man. What is nowhere does not concur in converting a man. In the first conversion of men there is no free will, for then at last the Holy Spirit releases men from sin, when through faith he grafts them into Christ, so that, drawing life from him, they begin to live to God. Therefore free will does not concur in converting a man.

units.la: Item: Certum est,præclara χαρίσματα[?] & eorū ἀποτελέσματα[?] ei qui eorū auctor est,tri-buenda esse. Atqui Deus est is qui efficit in nobis & ut uelimus,& ut perficiamus, pro gratuita sua beneuolentia: Phil.2.13. Ideo & dona & effecta quæ ab illis proficiscuntur, Deo soli accepta ferenda sunt.
units.tr: Likewise: it is certain that excellent gifts and their effects are to be ascribed to the one who is their author. But God is the one who, out of his free goodwill, works in us both to will and to accomplish: Phil. 2.13. Therefore both the gifts and the effects that proceed from them are rightly credited to God alone.

units.la: 3. ἐνδελέχεια[?] conuersionis. Id quod altę-ri gratiæ debetur, nō est humanis uiribus tribuendum. Atqui quòd uoluntas libe-rata à seruitute peccati incipit bene uelle,& in eo cursu perseuerat, alteri gratiæ acceptū ferri debet. Phil.1.6.Persuasum habes hoc ipsum,fore ut qui cœpit in uo-bis opus bonum,perficiat usque ad diem Iesu Christi. Ut igitur Deo debitam laudem tribuamus, fateamur id quod res est,uidelicet, conuersionem & opera bona à solo Deo proficisci.
units.tr: 3. The perseverance [ἐνδελέχεια] of conversion. What is owed to another grace must not be attributed to human powers. But that the will, freed from the slavery of sin, begins to will well and perseveres in that course, must be credited to the other grace. Phil. 1.6: "Being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion by the day of Jesus Christ." So, that we may give God the praise due to him, let us confess what is the case: namely, that conversion and good works proceed from God alone.

units.la: De secunda quæstione, in qua de forma bonorum operum agitur.
units.tr: On the second question, which concerns the form of good works.

units.la: Ea demum opera in cẽfu[?] bonorum locum obtinent, quæ respondent voluntati diuinæ. Est enim illa certissima regula, ad quam exigenda sunt omnia opera, sic ut, quæ ei quadrant, probari; quæ vero repugnant, improbari debeant. Sed opera utriusq; Tabulæ Decalogi eiusmodi sunt. Ac ideo inscriptum est opus Legis cordibus nostris; Rom.2.15. & eam etiam ob causam lex diuina in monte Sina repetita est, ut exstaret certissimus canon discernens bona & mala opera.
units.tr: Only those works hold a place in the reckoning of good works that correspond to the will of God. For that is the most certain rule, by which all works must be measured, so that those that agree with it are approved and those that conflict with it are to be rejected. Now the works of both tables of the Decalogue are of this kind. Therefore the work of the Law is written on our hearts (Rom. 2.15), and for this reason also the divine law was repeated on Mount Sinai, so that there might stand a most certain canon distinguishing good works from evil.

units.la: De postrema quæstione, in qua agitur de utilitate bonorum operum.
units.tr: On the last question, which concerns the usefulness of good works.

units.la: Qui ex eo quòd negamus, Bonorum operum merito nos iustificari, colligunt, nullam esse eorum utilitatem, paralogismo secundum plures interrogationes, sibijpsis & aliis imponunt. Etsi enim negamus, operibus Legis quenquam iustificari; non tamen negamus, magnam & multiplicem esse bonorum operum utilitatem. Bonorum autem operum, quæ à fide per caritatem efficaçe[?], ductu sancti Spiritus peraguntur, hæ sunt præcipuæ utilitates.
units.tr: Those who infer from our denial that we are justified by the merit of good works that such works are of no use at all deceive both themselves and others by a paralogism of many questions. For although we deny that anyone is justified by the works of the Law, we do not deny that good works are great and manifold in their usefulness. The chief uses of those good works which, proceeding from faith through love and carried out under the leading of the Holy Spirit, are these.

units.la: 1. Sunt testimonia de nostra salute & eius causis antegressis. Cum enim ad sanctificationem proprie spectent, κατ' ἀ-νάλυσιν [?] ex illa iustificatio, ex iustificatione uocatio, & ex hac electio colligitur. Rom.8.30.
units.tr: 1. They are evidence of our salvation and of its antecedent causes. For since they properly pertain to sanctification, [κατ' ἀνάλυσιν] from this we infer justification, from justification calling, and from this election (Rom. 8.30).

units.la: 2. Deus ea mercede gratuita remunera ri dignatur. Itaque fructu non carent.
units.tr: 2. God deigns to reward them with a gracious wage, and so they are not without fruit.

units.la: 3. Seruiunt aedificationi proximorum, iuxta dictum: Sic splendeat lux uestra, ut uideant homines bona uestra opera, & glorificent Patrem uestrum qui est in coelis. Matt.5.16.
units.tr: 3. They serve the edification of our neighbours, according to the saying: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven" (Matt. 5.16).

units.la: Hæc breuiter attingere uisum est in tā-ta temporis angustia. Dominus Iesus det, ut inoffenso cursu per bonorum operum stadium festinemus ad coelestem patriā, cuius ius & possessionem sanguinis sui pretiosi λύτρῳ Christus Dominus nobis parauit. Amen.
units.tr: It has seemed right to touch on these matters briefly, given the narrowness of the time. May the Lord Jesus grant that, with an unhindered course, we hasten through the race-course of good works towards the heavenly fatherland, whose right and possession Christ our Lord has prepared for us by the ransom [λύτρῳ] of his precious blood. Amen.

units.la: II. DE FIRMITATE PRO-positi & decreti diuini.
units.tr: II. On the firmness of the divine purpose and decree.

units.la: Cum Deus sui propositi fine nunquam frustretur, eo quod is & omniscius & omnipotens est: ἀμεταμέλητος ἡ μὴ παλινάγρητον [?] est, quicquid ille se facturum denunciat. Sic ergo illa Scripturae loca, in qui-bus bus Deus aliquid se facturum prænūcia-uit, quod tamen postea non fecit, accipi-enda & interpretanda nobis sunt, ne ei tribuatur transmutatio aut conversionis obumbratio. Iac.i.17.
units.tr: Since God is never thwarted in the end of his purpose, because he is both all-knowing and all-powerful, whatever he declares he will do is [ἀμεταμέλητος ... παλινάγρητον], unchangeable and irrevocable. Therefore those passages of Scripture in which God announced that he would do something which he afterwards did not do must be received and interpreted by us in such a way that no change or shadow of turning is ascribed to him (Jas. 1.17).

units.la: Ut autem doctrina de firmitate decre-torum Dei illustretur, demonstrationes aliquot eam confirmantes præmittam: deinde respondebo ad obiectionem de Ninivitis non deletis. Vestrum fuerit, o-mnia religiose ἁγιοπρεπῶς[?], & ad verbi divini canonem exigere.
units.tr: In order that the doctrine of the firmness of God's decrees may be made clear, I shall first set out some demonstrations confirming it, and then I shall answer the objection concerning the Ninevites who were not destroyed. It is your business to examine everything religiously, [ἁγιοπρεπῶς], in a manner befitting holiness, and by the canon of the divine Word.

units.la: 1. Qualis est natura Dei, talis est & eius voluntas. Atqui Dei natura est immutabilis. Psal.102.26. Omnia quasi vestimentum veterascet, quasi vestem mutabis ea, & mutabuntur. 27. At tu idem es: & anni tui non deficient. Hæc Dei creatoris & creaturarum ἀντιθέσεως[?] monet, res conditas mutabiles esse, Deum vero sibi semper similem & plane ἀναλλοίωτον esse. Quare & eius voluntas est immutabilis.
units.tr: 1. Such as God's nature is, such also is his will. But God's nature is unchangeable (Ps. 102.26): "They shall perish, but thou remainest; they shall all wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed. But thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end" (27). This passage, by way of contrast [ἀντιθέσεως] between the Creator and creatures, teaches that created things are changeable, but that God is always like himself and altogether [ἀναλλοίωτον], unchangeable. Therefore his will is also unchangeable.

units.la: 2. Iam vero divinæ voluntati decreta, quæ ab ea dependent, respondere, nemo sanus negabit. Illam autem immutabilem esse, ex antedictis liquet. Ac invictam[?] esse eandem, Paulus à consensu omnium homi-
units.tr: 2. Now that the decrees which depend upon the divine will correspond to that will, no sane person will deny. That the will itself is unchangeable is clear from what has been said. And that it is irresistible, Paul shows from the agreement of all men

units.la: hominum ostendit, Rom.9.19. Voluntati eius quis resistit? Rectè ergo colligimus, etiam decreta eius firma esse. iuxta dictū: Consilium meum stabit, & omnem voluntatem meam faciam.Isa.46.10.
units.tr: of men (Rom. 9.19): "Who resists his will?" Rightly, therefore, we conclude that his decrees also are firm, according to the saying: "My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure" (Isa. 46.10).

units.la: 3. Id quod Spiritus sancti testimonia ἀνταππήτως confirmant, non est in dubiū uocandum. Confirmant autem illa, Dei decreta esse immutabilia: iuxta hęc dicta. Malach.3.6. Ego Deus, &non mutor. Perinde pronunciat, ac si diceret, Iudaeos & omnes homines mutabiles esse, Deū autem tam essentia quàm voluntate immutabilem. Iesa.14.24. Iurauit Iehouah exercituū, dicendo: Si non secundum quod cogitaui, sic fiet: & secūdum quod decreui, consurget. Haec loquēdi & iurisiurandi forma τὸ τῆς βιβλίας θεῦ ἀμετάθετον diserte confirmatur, Act.2.23. Huc definito Dei consilio & prouidētia deditū, &c. Non solùm definito Dei consilio Christus passus est; sed etiā alia Dei decreta τῆ τῆς θεοῦ ωρισμένη βουλῇ nituntur. Prouerb.19.21. Multę cogitationes sunt in corde uiri: consiliū aut Iehouae permanet. Vt rerum, ita uoluntatū humanarū mirae sunt couersiones & mutationes: Dei autem χαρίσματα ἀμεταμέλητα decreta irreuocabilia sunt. Act.5.39.Si ex Deo est, dissolui non poterit. Digna etiam est memoria Persae cuiusdam uox apud Herodotum: ὅτι ἀεὶ ἐν θεῷ γενέσθαι ἀμή-χανον ἀποτρέψαι, &c. His testimonijs contenti, demus Deo gloriam, agnoscetes ut delicet immutabilitatem consiliorum & decretorum eius.
units.tr: 3. What the testimonies of the Holy Spirit in harmony [ἀνταππήτως] confirm cannot be called into doubt. Now those testimonies confirm that God's decrees are immutable, according to these sayings: "I am the LORD, I change not" (Mal. 3.6). He speaks in such a way as if he were saying that the Jews and all men are changeable, but that God is immutable both in essence and in will. "The LORD of hosts hath sworn, saying: Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand" (Isa. 14.24). This form of speaking and swearing the unchangeableness of God's counsel [τὸ τῆς βιβλίας θεῦ ἀμετάθετον] is expressly confirmed in Acts 2.23: "delivered up by the determinate counsel [τῆ τῆς θεοῦ ωρισμένη βουλῇ] and foreknowledge of God," etc. Christ suffered not only by the determinate counsel of God, but other decrees of God also rest on the determinate counsel of God. "Many devices are in a man's heart; but the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand" (Prov. 19.21). As with things, so with human wills, there are wonderful changes and reversals; but the decrees of God are irrevocable gifts [χαρίσματα ἀμεταμέλητα], that is, irrevocable (Rom. 11.29). "If it is of God, it cannot be overthrown" (Acts 5.39). The saying of a certain Persian reported by Herodotus is also worth remembering: that it is impossible to avert what has been determined by God, etc. Content with these testimonies, let us give glory to God, acknowledging, namely, the immutability of his counsels and decrees.

units.la: Obiectio prima.
units.tr: First objection.

units.la: Deus temporibus ueteris Testamenti praescripsit & obseruari uoluit liturgiam Leuiticam Sacramentorum, sacrificiorum, dierum festorum, quam in Nouo foedere abrogauit. Est igitur mutabilis eius uoluntas, cum alias alio modo coli uelit.
units.tr: God, in the times of the Old Testament, prescribed and willed to be observed the Levitical liturgy of sacraments, sacrifices and festival days, which he abrogated in the New Covenant. Therefore his will is changeable, since at one time he wishes to be worshipped in one way and at another time in another.

units.la: Respondeo per distinctionem Literae & Spiritus, corporalis exercitationis & pietatis. Omnibus mundi temporibus in spiritu & veritate coli & adorari voluit Deus. Psal.50.Ies.1.Ioan.4.Rom.12. Non autem valet argumentum à mutatione quarundam rerum & effectuum, ad causarum ἐν προσκαιρέοις[?] agentium mutationem. Quemadmodum peritus medicus, eundem hominem saepius curans, medicamenta aetati puerili, iuuenili, uirili, senili congruentia exhibere solet, nequaquam mutato voluntatis suae destinato: ita De-us paedagogiam legis suo tempore vigere, ceremoniarium cultum observari voluit: idem, Christo exhibito, circumcisionem, esum Paschalis agni, sacrificia Leuitica abrogari item voluit, citra omnem voluntatis mutationem.
units.tr: I answer by distinguishing letter from spirit, bodily exercise from piety. In every age of the world God willed to be worshipped and adored in spirit and truth (Ps. 50; Isa. 1; John 4; Rom. 12). The argument from the change of certain things and effects does not, however, hold for a change in the causes acting in temporal [ἐν προσκαιρέοις] matters. A skilful physician who treats the same man many times customarily gives medicines suited to his boyhood, youth, manhood and old age, without any change in his settled purpose. So God willed that the paedagogy of the law should hold sway in its own time and that the ceremonial worship be observed. The same God, once Christ had been revealed, willed that circumcision, the eating of the Passover lamb and the Levitical sacrifices be likewise abrogated, with no change of his will whatsoever.

units.la: Obiectio secunda.
units.tr: Second objection.

units.la: Qui quae se facturum denunciat, praetermittit, eius decreta mutabilia esse videntur. Atqui Deus denunciat[?] Ninivitis impendentem post 40 dies interneci-onem. Ergo decreta eius mutabilia videri possunt.
units.tr: One who announces that he will do something and then leaves it undone seems to have changeable decrees. But God announced to the Ninevites that destruction was impending after forty days. Therefore his decrees may seem changeable.

units.la: Respondeo primum ad Maiorem, interesse plurimum inter decretum Dei, & inter denunciationem divinam, qualis ea fuit, cuius praeconem egit Ionas.
units.tr: I answer first to the major premise: there is a great difference between the decree of God and the divine announcement of the kind that Jonah was sent to proclaim.

units.la: Decretum enim incommutabilem καὶ ἀμετακίνητου[?] Dei voluntatem, quae aeternę Dei sapientiae & consilio semper respondet, significat.
units.tr: For a decree signifies the unchangeable and immovable [ἀμετακίνητον] will of God, which always corresponds to the eternal wisdom and counsel of God.

units.la: Denunciatio autem saepe sic secundis causis respondet. Hae autem cum sint mutabiles, fit ut denunciatio quoq; nonnunquam mutetur. Etsi ergo cum res muta-tur, denunciatio quoq; mutatur: tamen decredecretum Dei,æterno Dei consilio & uoluntati (quę prima rerum omnium causa est) respondens, nunquam mutatur.
units.tr: An announcement, however, often corresponds to secondary causes. Since these are changeable, it follows that the announcement too is sometimes changed. Although, when the thing changes, the announcement also changes, yet the decree of God, which corresponds to the eternal counsel and will of God (the first cause of all things), never changes.

units.la: Ad Minorem quod attinet, dico in ea esse paralogismum à dicto secundum quid, ad simpliciter dictum. Non enim simpliciter & absolute denunciata est Niniuitis [illegible, ~9 letters] & excidium: sed [?]κατά τί[?] uide licet non respicerent. Hanc tacitam conditionem subintelligendam esse, euentus docuit. Non pepercisset Deus Niniuitis, si absolute decreuisset eos perdere: nec etiam Ionam resipiscentiæ præconem ad eosdem ablegauisset, nisi & pœnitentiæ donum eis largiri, & resipiscentibus ignoscere, eidem propositum fuisset.
units.tr: As for the minor premise, I say that it contains a fallacy from what is said in a certain respect [secundum quid] to what is said absolutely. For the destruction was not announced to the Ninevites simply and absolutely [illegible], but in some respect [κατά τί], namely on condition that they did not look back. The event has taught that this tacit condition must be understood. God would not have spared the Ninevites had he absolutely decreed to destroy them; nor would he have sent Jonah, a herald of repentance, to them, unless it had been his purpose both to bestow on them the gift of repentance and to forgive those who repented.

units.la: Obiectio tertia.
units.tr: Third objection.

units.la: Deus Ezechię Regi per Isaiam prophetā indicari voluit, adesse iam mortis illius tempus: Præcipe, dicens, domui tuę, quia morieris tu, &c nō uiues. Postea exoratus uitæ illius adiecit annos quindecim: Isa. 38.1.&c 5. Ergo & uoluntas diuina, & eius denunciationes non sunt immutabiles.
units.tr: God wished to indicate through the prophet Isaiah to King Hezekiah that the time of his death was now at hand: "Give orders to your house, for you shall die and not live" (Isa. 38). Afterwards, when he had been entreated, he added fifteen years to his life (Isa. 38:1, 5). Therefore both the divine will and its announcements are not immutable.

units.la: Respondeo, Aliud esse, si quæras quid ferant secundæ causæ: & aliud, si species[?] diuinæ uoluntatis decretum. Lethalis erat Ezechiae morbus, à quo nullis naturae viribus liberari poterat: ac eius respectu denunciata est mors Regi Ezechiae. Deo autem visum erat usuram vitae illius ad annos quindecim prorogare. Itaque id demum factum est, quod Deo visum fuit.
units.tr: I answer: it is one thing if you ask what secondary causes bring about, and another if you consider the decree of the divine will in itself. Hezekiah's illness was deadly, and he could not be freed from it by any powers of nature; and with respect to this, death was announced to King Hezekiah. But it seemed good to God to extend the span of that life by fifteen years. So what finally happened was what seemed good to God.

units.la: Coronidis loco addam Gregorij dictū memorabile: Nouit Deus mutare sententiam, sed non nouit mutare consilium. Quod Lucas uocat [?]βουλήν, Act.2. 17. id Gregorius consilium dixit. Consilia sunt, immutabilia Dei decreta de creatione mundi: de missione Filij, qui est Deus in carne patefactus: de collectione & protectione Ecclesiae, de resuscitatione mortuorum, de iudicio extremo, de aeterna vita.
units.tr: By way of conclusion I will add a memorable saying of Gregory: God knows how to change his judgement, but he does not know how to change his counsel. What Luke calls counsel [βουλήν] (Acts 2:17) Gregory called counsel. The counsels are the unchangeable decrees of God concerning the creation of the world; concerning the sending of the Son, who was revealed as God in the flesh; concerning the gathering and protection of the Church; concerning the resurrection of the dead, the final judgement, and eternal life.

units.la: Sententiam autē uocat, pronunciatum de poenis aut praemijs dispensandis, ex cōditione, non autē ex absoluto decreto & [?]ἀνάλυσις. Verbi gratia: Si Iudęi resipuerint, non abducentur in Babylonem: contra si in idolomania & iniustitia perstiterint, abducentur. Item: Niniuitae post 40 dies peribunt: si uidelicet non resipiscat. Videmus ut sententiae ad causas secundas, & rerum mutationes referantur.
units.tr: He calls a judgement [sententia] a pronouncement concerning the dispensing of punishments or rewards, made on a condition, and not from an absolute decree and [ἀνάλυσις]. For example: if the Jews repent, they will not be led away to Babylon; but if they persist in idolatry and injustice, they will be led away. Likewise: the Ninevites will perish after forty days, that is, if they do not repent. We see that judgements are referred to secondary causes and to changes in things.

units.la: IN CAPVT QVARTVM tum τὰ προλεγόμενα[?].
units.tr: ON CHAPTER FOUR, together with the prefatory matters [τὰ προλεγόμενα].

units.la: 1. Iudiciale caussæ genus in hoc toto capite dominatur. Hominis enim pij,sed tamè carnis intelligentia & affectu nonnihil laborantis,& per impru-dentiam Deo ex aduerso respondentis, exemplum,cum ei opposita iudiciorum Dei grauissima defensione,nobis propo-nitur,ut discamus intelligetiam nostram frenare,& Dei iudicia adorare,ac nō mo-dò famæ & existimationi nostrae,sed etiā omnibus rebus huius mundi præferre.
units.tr: 1. The judicial kind of cause dominates this whole chapter. For we are set before an example of a godly man, yet one who is somewhat troubled by the understanding and feelings of the flesh, and who, through imprudence, answers God back in opposition. Against him is set the most serious defence of God's judgements, so that we may learn to bridle our understanding, to adore God's judgements, and to prefer them not only to our reputation and good name but to all the things of this world.

units.la: 2. Status est iuridicialis. Quæritur,Iu-réne, an uerò iniuria Ionas commouea-tur & irascatur ob Niniuitas à Domino non deletos?
units.tr: 2. The status is juridical. The question is whether Jonah was moved and angry, rightly or wrongly, because the Lord had not destroyed the Ninevites.

units.la: Thesis : Non est cur quisquam piorum sic indulgeat suo dolori,ut etiam Dei,qui nunquam non rectè agit,iudiciis oblo-quatur.
units.tr: Thesis: There is no reason why any of the godly should so indulge his grief that he finds fault with the judgements of God, who never does anything other than rightly.

units.la: Hypothesis:Peccauit Ionas,tantam fidei & existimationis suę ratione habens,ut etiam indignè ferret,quòd Niniuitis resipiscétibus Deus pro immensa sua bo-nita[illegible, ~2 letters]pepercisset.
units.tr: Hypothesis: Jonah sinned, having such regard for his faith and reputation that he took it ill and unworthily that God, when the Ninevites repented, had spared them in his immense goodness.

units.la: 3. Syllogismi principales, thesim illam defendentes, hi sunt.
units.tr: 3. The principal syllogisms defending this thesis are these.

units.la: 1. Id quod Deo placuit, homini pio displicere non debet. Illius enim, qui sum-me bonus & summe sapiens est, iudicio hominem stare, æquum est. Atqui Deo ut [?] sum erat, Niniuitis ad se conuersis ignoscere. Itaque non erat cur Ionæ id di-spliceret.
units.tr: 1. What has pleased God ought not to displease a godly man. For it is right that a man should abide by the judgement of one who is supremely good and supremely wise. But it pleased God to forgive the Ninevites when they turned to him. Therefore there was no reason why this should displease Jonah.

units.la: 2. Non maior est habenda ratio alie-næ opinionis de nostra veracitate & sin-ceritate, quàm voluntatis & sententiæ di-vinæ. Volebat autem & decreuerat De-us resipiscentibus parcere. Itaque nō ma-iorem veracitatis fideiq; suæ, quàm diui-næ voluntatis & gloriæ rationem Ionas habere debuit. Ac poterat Ionas condi-tionem de venia resipiscentibus danda, Niniuitis, si quid obiecissent, exponere.
units.tr: 2. Our truthfulness and sincerity are not to be held in greater account by the opinion of others than the will and pronouncement of God. But God willed and had decreed to spare those who repented. Therefore Jonah ought not to have had regard for his own truthfulness and faithfulness more than for the divine will and glory. And Jonah could have set out to the Ninevites the condition on which pardon was to be given to those who repented, if they had objected anything.

units.la: 3. Qui vel plantæ sibi utili & accomo-dæ interitum dolenter fert, multò magis dolore quidem ob interitum hominum multorum, gaudio autem ob eorundem coservationem, affici debebat. Maiorem enim hominum rationem nobis habendam esse, quàm vel plantarum, quis homo sanus addubitet? Atqui Ionæ dole-bat, bat, quòd cucurbita exaruisset, quæ fue-rat umbraculi uice. Itaque gaudere potius ob Niniuitarum conseruatione, quàm trifticia eum affici,oportebat.
units.tr: 3. One who grieves over the destruction of a plant useful and suitable to himself ought much more to be affected by grief over the destruction of many men, and by joy over their preservation. For who that is sane doubts that we must have more regard for men than for plants? But Jonah grieved that the gourd had withered, which had been a shade for him. Therefore he ought rather to have rejoiced at the preservation of the Ninevites than been saddened.

units.la: 4. Partitio. Totum autem hoc caput διχοτομεῖν poterimus. Primum enim Ionæ indignationem, μεταμελεια, & istorū caussas & circumstantias: deinde,defen-sionem iudicij diuini,à Spiritu sancto pro positam esse,res ipsa testatur.
units.tr: 4. Division. This whole chapter we can divide [διχοτομεῖν] into two parts. For first, the matter itself shows that Jonah's indignation, his change of mind [μεταμέλεια], and their causes and circumstances are set forth; then, that the defence of the divine judgement has been put forward by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 5. Supersunt theses singulorum uersu-um,quas ideo subiungam, ut studiosi iu-uenes uideant, quibus de rebus διεξοδος enarrationis nobis sit instituenda,& quid ipsis expectandum sit.
units.tr: 5. There remain the theses of the individual verses, which I shall therefore append, so that the diligent young may see on what matters the exposition is to be undertaken by us, and what they may expect.

units.la: VERSVS I. THESIS.
units.tr: VERSE I. THESIS.

units.la: Etiam atq; etiam nobis perpendendū est,quid tandem in operibus iudicijsque Dei,& quare nobis uel placeat,uel displiceat.
units.tr: We must consider again and again what in the works and judgments of God is truly to be found there, and why they either please or displease us.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Neque enim raro fit, ut carnis tum in-telligentia, tum affectus,sic nos cæcutire faciant,ut iudicium nostrum diuino præ-ferentes, quid precemur, ut oportet, ne-sciamus:Rom.8.26.nostriq; ipsorum ma-iorem quàm Dei rationem habeamus.
units.tr: For it often happens that the understanding and the affections of the flesh so blind us that, preferring our own judgment to the divine, we do not know what we ought to pray for, and we value our own reason more than God's. Rom. 8.26.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Et cùm Dei caussa conditi simus & ui- uamus,nō est seruiorum sic frangi aduer- sis,ut prius quàm Domino uniuersorum sit uisum,mori uelimus.
units.tr: Since we have been created for God's sake and live for him, it is not fitting for servants to be so broken by adversity that they wish to die before it has seemed good to the Lord of all.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Deus etiam meritò uidet acres illos motus cordium nostrorum, quos impa- tientia & tristicia pariunt.
units.tr: God also rightly sees those violent movements of our hearts which impatience and sadness produce.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Nec sic dolori indulgendum est,ut ho- minum uestigia & contubernium decli- nantes,nō tam quid ipsi agamus,quídue præstare debeamus, quàm quid alijs sit euenturum,μετεωρίζόμενοι obseruemus.
units.tr: Nor should we so indulge our grief that, shunning the footsteps and company of men, we look not so much at what we ourselves are doing or ought to accomplish, as at what is going to happen to others, contemplating things from on high.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Cum nihil eorum quæ homini contin- gunt fortuitum,sed omnia θεόπεμπτα habe ri debeant, non tam corporalium bono- rum & cõmodorum usumfructū, quàm etiam aliorum Dei operum contempla- tione,nobis exhilarádis seruire oportuit.
units.tr: Since nothing that befalls a man is accidental, but everything ought to be held to be sent from God, we ought to serve not only the enjoyment and use of corporeal goods and conveniences, but also, for our own delight, the contemplation of the other works of God.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Corporalia enim bona, cum ei uisum est,mediatè uel immediatè Deus adimit ut perse caduca esse καὶ πρόσκαιρα depre- hendantur.
units.tr: For corporeal goods, when it has seemed good to God, he takes away, mediately or immediately, so that they may be perceived to be perishable and temporary.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Nec uel corporis dolores, uel animi ægritudo eò nos adducere debent, ut decurtari uelimus fatalem uitæ periodum, ut ne quid nobis diutius molestum esse queat.
units.tr: Neither the pains of the body nor the sickness of the mind ought to lead us to wish to cut short the appointed span of life, so that nothing may be able to trouble us any longer.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Merito nos irridet Dominus, cū quasi nostra, non autem illius caussa simus cō diti, morte ideo uitę præferre uidet, quòd non pro nostro arbitrio & libitu suauiter uiuere & agere licet.
units.tr: The Lord rightly mocks us, since, as if we were created for our own sake and not for his, he sees us preferring death to life, because it is not permitted us to live and act pleasantly according to our own will and pleasure.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Errant, qui sui commodi gratia perpetuum aut certè diuturnum vsum earum rerum maximi faciunt, quæ Dei dono, non ipsorum merito parta fuerunt:
units.tr: They are mistaken who, for the sake of their own convenience, set great store by the perpetual or at least long-lasting use of those things which were obtained by God's gift and not by their own merit.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Nec uident hominum omnium ætatū & ordinum salutem, rerum illarum cadu carum participationi, æquissimo Dei iudicio, infinitis modis præferri. Hæc pau cis præfari uisum est. Deum oro, ut nobis adsit suo Spiritu, & det ut omnia piè expendamus, & ad usum nostrum transferamus.
units.tr: Nor do they see that the salvation of all men, of every age and rank, is, by the most just judgment of God, preferred in countless ways to the enjoyment of those perishable things. These few things it has seemed good to say beforehand. I pray God that he be present with us by his Spirit, and grant that we weigh all things piously and turn them to our use.

units.la: VERSVS PRIMVS capitis IIII,
units.tr: VERSE 1 of chapter 4,

units.la: Displicuit autem Iona displicentia magna, ma-gna, & iratus est.
units.tr: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry.

units.la: Cum & in hoc primo uersu, & sequentibus, propositum nobis sit exemplum luti cum figulo, id est, creaturę cum Creatore suo cotendentis:operæpretium fuerit, primum ὑπόθεσιν[?] rem tractare: deinde, ean-dem ad θέσιν[?] suam reuocare: ut discamus Dei iudicia adorare, & in eius beneplaci-to suauiter acquiescere.
units.tr: Since both in this first verse and in those that follow we have set before us the example of the clay and the potter, that is, of a creature contending with its Creator, it will be worthwhile first to treat the hypothesis [ὑπόθεσιν], and then to bring the same back to its thesis [θέσιν], so that we may learn to adore God's judgments and to acquiesce sweetly in his good pleasure.

units.la: Diuus Hieronymus caussas displicen-tię Ionæ hisce uerbis exposuit: Vides sub-intrare Gentium plenitudinem, & illud impleri quod in Deut.31.dicitur: Ipsi me irritauerunt in iis qui non sunt Dij: & e-go eos irritabo super gentę quæ non est; super natione stulta eos ad iracundiam concitabo. desperat de salute Israelis: & magno dolore concutitur, qui erumpit in uocem: & caussas mœroris exponit, & quodammodo loquitur: Ego solus electus sum de tanto numero prophetarum, qui per aliorum salutem ruinam meo populo nunciarem.Non igitur contristatur, ut quidam putant, quòd gentium multitudo saluetur,sed quòd pereat Israel.
units.tr: Saint Jerome set out the causes of Jonah's displeasure in these words: "You see the fullness of the Gentiles creeping in, and that which is said in Deuteronomy 31 being fulfilled: 'They have provoked me with those who are not gods; and I will provoke them with a people that is not; I will stir them to anger with a foolish nation.' He despairs of the salvation of Israel and is shaken by great grief, which breaks out into speech. He sets out the causes of his sorrow and in a way speaks thus: 'I alone have been chosen out of so great a number of prophets to announce to my people their ruin through the salvation of others.' He is not saddened, therefore, as some think, because the multitude of the Gentiles is being saved, but because Israel is perishing."

units.la: Ex hisce uerbis liquet, Hieronymum & alios præsuppofuiffe, hoc loco oraculum de Gentium fidelium assumptione, & de Iudæorum incredulorum reiectione,traditum esse. Vnde colligi potest,doloris Ionæ treis fuisse causas præcipuas.
units.tr: From these words it is clear that Jerome and others presupposed that this passage hands down an oracle concerning the taking up of the faithful Gentiles and the rejection of the unbelieving Jews. From this it can be gathered that Jonah's grief had three principal causes.

units.la: 1. Quòd Israelitas circumcisos, & de lege gloriantes,prætudicio laudatissimi exempli Niniuitarum laborare uideret.
units.tr: 1. That he saw the circumcised Israelites, who boasted of the law, suffering prejudice from the most praiseworthy example of the Ninevites.

units.la: 2. Quòd incircumcisis, & ritus legales non obseruantibus, donum pœnitentiæ & salutis per gratiam collatum animadverteret.
units.tr: 2. That he noticed the gift of repentance and salvation bestowed through grace upon the uncircumcised, who did not observe the legal rites.

units.la: 3. Quòd sese uanitatis & mendacij insimulari posse iudicaret: ut qui ea euentura denunciasset,& quidem publicius, quibus non responderet euentus: imò qui sacrosancto Dei nomine esset abusus, denunciata eius ira & impendente Niniuitis ϖαvoλιθ, quæ tamen non effet secuta. Hanc postremam causam tristitiæ & indignationis præcipuam fuisse,& maxime ad institutum pertinere,mihi persuadeo.
units.tr: 3. That he judged he could be charged with vanity and falsehood, as one who had announced those things as coming to pass, and indeed rather publicly, while the outcome did not correspond; indeed, as one who had abused the most sacred name of God, since the threatened wrath and the impending doom upon the Ninevites had been announced [ϖαvoλιθ], which nevertheless did not follow. I am persuaded that this last cause was the chief source of his sadness and indignation, and that it pertains most to the purpose.
