units.la: Græci cæcam speculationem eorum qui in tenebris impingunt, ἀλλοοπνοπίαν[?] uocât. Eius exempla quædam, aphorismis distincta, ideo proponam, ut tantò magis in nobis accendatur desiderium diuinæ gubernationis, qua nobis nunquam non summè opus est.
units.tr: The Greeks call the blind speculation of those who stumble in darkness allooposia [ἀλλοοπνοπίαν]. I will therefore set out some examples of it, distinguished in aphorisms, so that the desire for divine government, which we always greatly need, may be kindled all the more in us.

units.la: Aphorismus i.
units.tr: Aphorism 1.

units.la: Homo non renatus Dei opera & iudicia tantisper, donec carnalis est, nunquam probabit. Id sic probo.
units.tr: A man not reborn will never approve God's works and judgments so long as he is carnal. I prove it thus.

units.la: Nemo id uerè probare potest, quod non intelligentia sua assequitur. Sed animalis homo non est capax eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, sunt enim ei stultitia, nec potest ea cognoscere, quia spiritualiter dijudicatur: 1.Cor.2.14. Itaq; animalis homo ea quæ Deus dicit & facit, probare non potest.
units.tr: No one can truly approve what he does not grasp by his understanding. But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned (1 Cor. 2.14). Therefore the natural man cannot approve what God says and does.

units.la: Inimici non solent hostis facta proba-re, quæ ex eius uoluntate fiunt. Non re-nati, sunt inimici Dei: Roman.5.10.
units.tr: Enemies do not usually approve the deeds of an enemy that are done by his will. The unregenerate are enemies of God (Rom. 5.10).

units.la: Itaq; uoluntatis illius effecta non probant.
units.tr: Therefore they do not approve the effects of that will.

units.la: Aphorismus 2.
units.tr: Aphorism 2.

units.la: Etiam renati, interdum mentis errore & affectus intemperie fascinati, aliquan-diu uoluntati diuinae refragantur: sed de errore à Spiritu sancto admoniti, locum dant posterioribus curis, quae sunt meliores. Exemplo sunt summi uiri, Ionas, Petrus, Paulus.
units.tr: Even the regenerate, sometimes bewitched by an error of mind and an intemperance of feeling, for a time resist the divine will; but when the Holy Spirit admonishes them about their error, they give place to later concerns, which are better. Examples are the great men Jonah, Peter and Paul.

units.la: Ionas, dum uanus & impostor uideri recusat, irascitur, & cum Deo contendit, quòd eum Niniuitis parcere animaduerteret.
units.tr: Jonah, while refusing to appear vain and an impostor, grows angry and contends with God, because he noticed that God was sparing the Ninevites.

units.la: Petrus ea quae hominum, hac quidem in parte, non autem quae sunt Dei, sapiés, dehortatur Christum ne adeat crucis supplicium & mortem, qua redimendi eramus: Matt.16.
units.tr: Peter, wise in the things of men in this respect but not in the things of God, dissuades Christ from undergoing the punishment of the cross and death, by which we were to be redeemed (Matt. 16).

units.la: Paulus, Satanae colaphis uexatus, tet[?] Dominum rogauit, ut eo malo liberare-tur. Sed responsum illi fuit: Sufficit tibi gratia mea: nam potentia mea per infirmitatem perficitur: 2.Cor.12.9.
units.tr: Paul, troubled by the blows of Satan, asked the Lord that he might be freed from that evil. But the answer given him was: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor. 12.9).

units.la: Aphorismus 3.
units.tr: Aphorism 3.

units.la: Ne ergo exitio nobis sit illa ἀλλοφυλία[?], plus deferamus luci fidei, quàm naturae nostrae, & modeste obediamus Deo, eiq; uni demus gloriam, iuxta dictum: Cap.iuam ducimus omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo: 2.Cor.10,5. Vt de uita ciuili & omnis generis occupationi-bus dicitur: Eftuia quæ uidetur homini bona : sed exitus eius ducūt ad mortem. ita de dogmatis dici potest, multa,quòd specie fucosam ueri habeant,arridere im-peritis: sed ea tamen exitiosa esse ijs, qui illa non abijciunt,nec ueriora discunt.
units.tr: Therefore, lest that alienation of mind [ἀλλοφυλία] be our ruin, let us give more weight to the light of faith than to our nature, and let us obey God humbly and give glory to him alone, according to the saying: "We take captive every thought to obey Christ" (2 Cor. 10.5). As is said of civil life and of every kind of occupation: "There is a way which seems right to a man, but its end leads to death." So of doctrines it may be said that many things, because they have a deceptive appearance of truth, please the unskilled; yet these are destructive to those who do not cast them aside and learn what is truer.

units.la: Aphorismus 4,
units.tr: Aphorism 4.

units.la: Gradus autē peccatorum sunt,ἁμαρτωλία[?] cū iudicio Dei,ira seu affectus uehemens, & seu oratio seu facinus indignum homi-ne pio. Treis priores gradus Ionæ tribu-untur, qui argumeto sunt, etiam Sanctos interdum grauiter & multis modis pec-care. Fontem autem istorum malorū ex-posuit Iacobus Apostolus cap.1.13.14.15. Nemo,cum tentatur,dicat fe à Deo tenta-ri: nam Deus tentari malis nō potest, nec quenquam tentat. Sed unufquifq; tenta-tur, dum à propria cupiditate abstrahitur & inescatur.Deinde cupiditas,postquam concepit,parit peccatum:peccatum uerò peractum gignit mortem.
units.tr: The degrees of sin are: sinfulness [ἁμαρτωλία] together with the judgment of God; anger, or a vehement emotion; and either a speech or a deed unworthy of a pious man. The first three degrees are attributed to Jonah, which is an argument that even saints sometimes sin grievously and in many ways. The source of these evils, however, James the Apostle set out in chapter 1, verses 13 to 15: "Let no one who is tempted say that he is tempted by God; for God cannot be tempted by evils, nor does he tempt anyone. But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, after it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full grown, brings forth death."

units.la: Ex ijs quæ iam diximus,colligimus,e-tiam atq; etiā nobis perpendendū, quid tandem & quamobre in Dei operibus & iudicijs nobis seu placeat,seu etiā displiceat.nō enim ita nobis indulgere fas est, ut etiam praeiudicium nostrum diuino iudicio praeferre, & petere ut Deus nostris desiderijs seruiat,audeamus. Sed de his omnibus in ἀδιαφορίᾳ[?] sequetium uersuum agemus.
units.tr: From what we have already said we gather that we must weigh again and again, and why and for what cause, in God's works and judgments, we are either pleased or even displeased. For it is not right for us to indulge ourselves so far that we dare to set our own prejudice above the divine judgment and ask that God serve our desires. But we shall deal with all these matters under the adiaphora [ἀδιαφορίᾳ] of the following verses.

units.la: VERSVS II.
units.tr: VERSE 2.

units.la: Orauit itaq; ad Iehouam,& dixit: Obsecro Iehouah, nónne hoc est uerbum meum, cū adhuc essem in terra mea? Ideo praeoccupaui fugere in Tharsis: sciebam enim, quod tu es Deus clemens & misericors, longanimis & multa misericordia, & poenitens super malo. 3. Nunc ergo, ô Iehouah, tolle quaeso animam meam a me: quoniam melior est mihi mors, quam uita.
units.tr: So he prayed to the LORD and said: "Please, LORD, was this not my word while I was still in my own country? That is why I hurried to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that you are a gracious and merciful God, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from punishing. 3. Now therefore, O LORD, take my life from me, I beg you, for it is better for me to die than to live."

units.la: DE PRAEPOSTERA DEI invocatione.
units.tr: ON THE PERVERSE INVOCATION OF GOD.

units.la: Propositum nobis est demonstrare, etiā Sanctos subito quodā tum metis errore, tum cordis affectu commotos, sic preces concipere, ut cum nimium sibi indulgeat, plurimum ipsorum interfit, nō id quod ipsi inconsulte petunt, sed quod Deus summè bonus καὶ φιλανθρωπος[?] optimo consilio de creuit, fieri. iuxta hæc dicta: Matth.20.22. Nescitis quid petatis. Rom.8.26. Quid enim precemur ut oportet, nō nouimus. sed ipse Spiritus interpellat pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus. Iacobi 4.3. Petitis, & nō accipitis, eo quòd male petatis, ut in uoluptates uestras insumatis. Sedenim thesi κεφαλαιωδῶς[?] præmissa, hypothefin de Iona propheta postea tractabimus.
units.tr: It is our purpose to show that even holy men, moved at times by a sudden error of mind and an emotion of heart, so frame their prayers that, while they indulge themselves too much, what matters most to them is that not what they ask rashly but what God, supremely good and loving to mankind, has decided by his best counsel, should come to pass. In accordance with these words: Matthew 20:22, "You do not know what you are asking." Romans 8:26, "For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered." James 4:3, "You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your pleasures." But having laid down this thesis in summary, we shall afterwards treat the hypothesis concerning the prophet Jonah.

units.la: 1. Est è re hominis pij, trifticiq; spiritu laborantis, fi ad Deum Patrem clementiffimum conuersus, preces fundat. Vt maximè enim is filios suos, ferulæ paternæ subiectos, acerbissimo doloris alicuius sensu adfici & tentari patiatur:tamē nunquam paternæ φιλοστοργίας[?] obliuiscitur, ac proinde gratiam illius implorantes benignissimè exaudit.
units.tr: 1. It befits a godly man, who labours in sorrow and sadness of spirit, to turn to God the most merciful Father and pour out his prayers. For although he allows his sons, subject to the rod of a father, to be affected and tried by some most bitter sense of grief, yet he never forgets his fatherly love, and therefore he most kindly hears those who implore his grace.

units.la: 2. Sed tamē à precibus longè abesse debet, expostulatio cum Deo, defensio antegressæ offensæ, sinistra de nimia indulgentia Dei opinio, & petitio pugnans cum uoluntate diuina. Etenim in uera Dei inuocatione sic Deo gloria dáda[?] est, ut Dei iudicium nostro præferamus, offensas nostras ingenuè fateamur, Dei clementiam nobis ipsis & alijs toto pectore gratulemur, & ea tantùm petamus, quae & Deo nobis dare placet.
units.tr: 2. Yet at the same time prayer must be far removed from: remonstrance with God, defence of a previous offence, a sinister opinion about God's excessive indulgence, and a petition at odds with the divine will. For in true invocation of God, glory is so given to God that we set God's judgment before our own, freely confess our offences, rejoice with our whole heart in God's mercy toward ourselves and others, and ask only for those things which it also pleases God to give us.

units.la: 3. Quód autem hæ querelæ auctoribus noxiæ non sunt, ei uni acceptum ferre decet, de quo diuinus ille noster Apostolus: Non enim, ait, habemus Pontificem, qui non possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, sed tetatum in omnibus similiter, excepto peccato. Heb. 4. 15.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, that these complaints are not harmful to their authors is owed to him alone, of whom our divine Apostle said: "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin." Hebrews 4:15.

units.la: HYPOTHESIS.
units.tr: HYPOTHESIS.

units.la: 1. Propositio est, Ionam, ut infamiæ no tam effugere possit, ex huius ærumnosæ uitæ statione ab imperatore Deo euocā-dum esse.
units.tr: 1. The proposition is that Jonah, so that he might escape disgrace, must be called away by God, the commanding Lord, from the station of this wretched life.

units.la: 2. Ratio: Quia fi ferui fui honori & existimationi consulere nolit Dominus, saltem ut pudoris eiusdem habeatur ratio, è cōnspectu & cōtubernio hominum, quibus Dei uoluntatem & decretum exposuerit, subducendum esse.
units.tr: 2. The reason: because if the Lord is unwilling to care for the honour and reputation of his servant, then at least, for the sake of his shame being taken into account, he must be withdrawn from the sight and company of the men to whom he has declared the will and decree of God.

units.la: 3. Partes orationis duæ sunt, Expostulatio & Petitio.
units.tr: 3. The parts of the prayer are two: expostulation and petition.

units.la: DE EXPOSTVLATIONE.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE EXPOSTULATION.

units.la: Qui Deo ex aduerso respondent, ut maxime studeant τὰ ἁπλῶς μαλθακῶς λέγειν[?]; tamen, quia non secundum Deum loquuntur, modestiæ & humilitatis fines transiliunt. Loquor iam etiam de renatis, cum tetationis παροξυσμῷ cofliftantibus, quos Deus sibijpsis aliquantisper relinquit, ut tandem Deo tenebras diuidente, cū Dauide exclament: Quousque Iehoua oblituisceris mei penitus? Quousque abscondes faciem tuam à me? Quandiu dispones consilia in anima mea?anxietatem in corde meo quotidie? Psal.13.1.2. Eius rei exemplum hoc loco occurrit. Ionas enim, initio Deum memorem sane monens, sibi inter Israelitas suos uersanti istud in mentem uenisse, propemodum gloriatur: uidelicet futurum, ut Deus Niniuitis resipiscentibus parceret, nulla admodū existimationis ferui sui ratione habita. Hic primus offensæ uiri, alioquin sancti, gradus fuit. Quasi uero præscientiam Dei quicquam fugiat, ut ab homine aliquid suggeri Deo possit: aut etiam illa προγνώ-σις non sit definitum & optimum Dei de rebus omnibus consiliū. Addit deinde nō tam confessionem de sua fuga, quàm eius excusatione: plane in illo tetationis τῇ παροξυσμῷ suijpsius & antegressæ castigationis oblitus. Hic secudus gradus offensæ sensæ fuit. Graue autem est,fuijpsius,& reuerentiæ conditori Deo debitæ,in ten-tationis paroxysmo non admodum memorem esse:sed grauius est,errorum suorum & subsecutæ castigationis sic obliui-sci, ut nec offensam,nec eius austorame-tum (etsi huius sensus non multo ante a-cerbissimus fuit) agnoscas: ut grande παρα-[?] [?]παράπτωμα tuum opineris esse præclarum [?]κατόρθωμα[?]. Tertio loco subiungit eiusmodi misericordiæ & clementiæ diuinæ elogium, ut tamen specie quadam reprehensionis non careat. Enimuero stolidus & [illegible, ~9 letters] homuncio, Deo, quid eo dignum sit, indicare,& modum aliqueipsius clementiæ præscribere poterit,cum sibi præter meritum habito,uitilitigationis ansam exhibitam putabit. Tertius hic offensæ gradus fuit. Postremo,quasi homo sibi viuat & moriatur, & optimeno-ritu uitæ & mortis optima momenta, non autem ei uni à quo conditus est,mortem uitæ præfert, & à Deo se auocari ex hac vita cupide precatur. Fuit hic gradus quartus,de quo suo tempore,si volet Deo minus,dicam.Nunc enim illud fatis fue-rit ostedisse, etiam Sanctos interdum nō ex fide precari, sed ea quae caro dictat, proloqui.
units.tr: Those who answer back to God, however much they strive to speak mildly and simply, nevertheless, because they do not speak according to God, overstep the bounds of modesty and humility. I am speaking now also of the regenerate, who struggle in the paroxysm of temptation, whom God for a while leaves to themselves, so that at last, when God divides the darkness, they cry out with David: "How long, O LORD, will you forget me utterly? How long will you hide your face from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart day after day?" Psalm 13:1-2. An example of this thing occurs in this passage. For Jonah, at first rightly mindful of God, and reflecting that this had come into his mind while he was living among his own Israelites, almost boasts of it: namely, that God would spare the Ninevites when they repented, with no regard at all for the reputation of his servant. This was the first step of the offence of this man, otherwise holy. As if God's foreknowledge escaped anything, so that anything could be suggested to God by a man; or as if that foreknowledge were not the defined and best counsel of God concerning all things. He then adds not so much a confession of his flight as an excuse for it, plainly forgetting, in the paroxysm of his temptation, both himself and the chastisement that had gone before. This was the second step of the offence. It is a serious matter to be not very mindful of oneself and of the reverence owed to the Creator God in the paroxysm of temptation; but it is more serious to forget one's errors and the chastisement that followed so completely that you acknowledge neither the offence nor its severity (although the feeling of this had not been very long before most bitter), so that you suppose your great transgression to be a notable achievement. In the third place he adds an encomium of divine mercy and clemency of such a kind that it nevertheless does not lack a certain appearance of reproof. For indeed a foolish little man, who has been given a reason beyond his merit, will be able to declare to God what is worthy of him and to prescribe some measure of his own clemency, since he will think that an occasion for complaint has been offered to him. This was the third step of the offence. Finally, as if a man lived and died for himself, and as if he preferred death to life, and so judged the best moments of life and death in the best order, and not him alone by whom he was created, he eagerly prays that he be called away from this life by God. This was the fourth step, of which, at its proper time, I shall speak more fully, if God wills. For now it will be enough to have shown that even holy men sometimes pray not out of faith, but utter what the flesh dictates.

units.la: DE ATTRIBVTIS QVIBVSDAM Dei, quorum hoc loco mentio fit.
units.tr: ON CERTAIN ATTRIBUTES OF GOD, WHICH ARE MENTIONED IN THIS PLACE.

units.la: Tria hac praelectione paucis tractabimus. Primo, An ne & qua lege Deo tribuantur. Secundo, quae nam inter alia de eo praedicentur. Postremo, qua religione de eo praedicanda sint.
units.tr: In this lecture we shall deal briefly with three things. First, whether and by what right these are ascribed to God. Second, what things are predicated of him among the others. Last, with what reverence those things should be said of him.

units.la: Obiectio: Non cadunt in Deum accidentia. Misericordia, Clementia, Longanimitas, Poenitentia, sunt accidentia: quia sunt πάθη[?]. Non igitur recte Deo attribuuntur, qui est essentia simplicissima, immutabilis, expers passionum.
units.tr: Objection: accidents do not fall upon God. Mercy, clemency, longsuffering and repentance are accidents, since they are πάθη[?] (passions). Therefore they are not rightly ascribed to God, who is the most simple essence, unchangeable and free from passions.

units.la: Respondeo, Longe alia ratione ista attributa de Deo, alia autem de angelis & hominibus praedicari. In Deo enim sic insunt, ut non sint accidentia, & ut ab essentia non τῷ εἶναι, sed τῷ λόγῳ differant. In hominibus autem insunt, ut qualitates, quae non idem sunt cum essentia. Tribuuntur autem Deo, ut eius naturam melius cognoscamus, & qualis sit, ac quo ergo nos animo fit, intelli-gamus.
units.tr: I answer: these attributes are said of God in a quite different way from how they are said of angels and men. In God they inhere so that they are not accidents, and they differ from the essence not τῷ εἶναι (in being) but τῷ λόγῳ (in definition). In men, however, they inhere as qualities, which are not the same as the essence. They are ascribed to God so that we may know his nature better, and what he is like, and with what disposition toward us he acts.

units.la: Quotuplicia autem sunt Dei attributa?
units.tr: But how many kinds of divine attributes are there?

units.la: Duplicia. Quædam enim meram Dei naturam prædicant, ac proinde creaturis nullo modo communicari possunt, nec ad eas respectum habent: ut æternitas, immēsitas, simplicitas summa. Quædam verò, etsi quatenus in Deo summa sunt, communicari nequeunt, ut summè bonum, summè iustum, summè misericordem esse: tamen ex parte creaturis rationalibus, & similitudinis respectu, rectè tribuuntur: ut aliquo modo iustum, bonum, misericordem esse, de homine prædicatur.
units.tr: Two kinds. For some declare the pure nature of God and therefore cannot in any way be communicated to creatures, nor do they have any relation to them: such as eternity, immensity, and supreme simplicity. Others, although in God they are supreme, cannot be communicated in that supreme sense, as being supremely good, supremely just, or supremely merciful; yet, on the side of rational creatures and by way of likeness, they are rightly ascribed, just as it is said of man that he is in some measure just, good and merciful.

units.la: De nomine אֵל[?] El.
units.tr: On the name אֵל[?] El.

units.la: Deus à fortitudine גבור[?] fortis appellatur. Hier.32.18. Ipse El magnus & fortis, gibbor. Num.16.22. El Elohe, Fortis fortium spirituum universæ carnis, num si vir unus peccaverit, contra totum cœtum irasceris?
units.tr: God is called גבור[?] (strong, mighty) from strength. Jer. 32:18: "The great and mighty God, El, gibbor." Num. 16:22: "O God, God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and wilt thou be angry with the whole congregation?"

units.la: Sic autem fortis est Deus, ut sit omnipotens. Omnipotens autè est, quia apud Deum nõ est impossibile ullum verbum: Luc.1.37. Nihil enim non potest Deus, nisi quod pugnat cum eius natura. ut metiri, seipsum abnegare, non potest. 2.Tim.2. Tit.1.
units.tr: God is so strong that he is almighty. He is almighty because with God no word is impossible: Luke 1:37. For God can do all things, except what contradicts his nature, as to deny himself, which he cannot do. 2 Tim. 2; Titus 1.

units.la: {y} Ex consideratione autem diuinæ fortitudinis, eximiq; consolationis fructus redit ad nos, qui infirmitatis sensu nunquam non afficimur. Discimus enim, Deum esse fortitudinem nostram: Psal. 18.2. ac spe rantes in Iehouam mutare robur, nō lassfari, si quando currunt: & cum ambulant, non defatigari: Isa. 40.31. Itaq; unusquisque nostrum precari potest & debet:
units.tr: {y} From the consideration of divine strength there comes back to us a remarkable fruit of consolation, since we are never free from a sense of weakness. For we learn that God is our strength (Ps. 18:2), and that those who hope in Jehovah renew their strength; they do not faint when they run, and when they walk they are not weary (Isa. 40:31). Therefore each of us can and ought to pray:

units.la: Non ego dura pati discrimina mille recuso, Dum tua constanti tueor mandata labore. Sed ne deficiam, ne sæuo uincar ab hoste, Tu mihi præsto ueni, tu suffice robora fesso.
units.tr: I do not refuse to endure a thousand dangers, while with steadfast labour I keep your commands. But lest I fail, lest I be overcome by the savage enemy, come to me at once, and give strength to me who am weary.

units.la: חַנּוּן[?], ἐλεήμων[?], Misericors.
units.tr: חַנּוּן[?], ἐλεήμων[?]: merciful.

units.la: Malim illud חַנּוּן[?], uertere gratiosum & ipsam gratiam, cum de Deo prædicetur. Gratiam autē uoco fauorem gratuitum, seu beneuolentiam, qua nos Deus pro infinita sua benignitate prosequi dignatur. Gratiosum esse Deum ideo dico, quòd cum summa sit ipsius uirtus, summè quoque est amabilis ijs, qui per fide eum ex parte nunc intuiti, olim facie ad faciem uidere cupiunt. Vt autem hæc doctrina illustretur, addam aliquot aphorismos.
units.tr: I would rather render חַנּוּן[?] as gracious, and grace itself, since it is predicated of God. I call grace the free favour, or goodwill, by which God, in his infinite kindness, deigns to bless us. I say that God is gracious because, since his power is supreme, he is also supremely lovable to those who now behold him in part through faith and long one day to see him face to face. To illustrate this teaching, I shall add some aphorisms.

units.la: 1. Gratia hæc Deo tribuitur, iuxta dictum: Illuxit enim gratia illa Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus. Tit.2.11.
units.tr: 1. This grace is ascribed to God, according to the saying: "For the saving grace of God has appeared to all men." Titus 2:11.

units.la: 2. Ac significat favorem, quo ille suos gratis prosequitur. Eph.1.6. Ad laudem gloriosæ suæ gratiæ, qua nos gratis effecit sibi gratos in illo suo dilecto.
units.tr: 2. It signifies the favour by which he freely blesses his own people. Eph. 1:6: "To the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he freely made us acceptable to himself in his beloved Son."

units.la: 3. Dei autem gratia opponitur hominū operibus seu meritis. Rom.11.6. Quod si per gratiam, non iam ex operibus: alioquin gratia iam nō est gratia. Sin ex operibus, iam non ex gratia: alioquin opus iam non est opus. Eph.2.8. Gratia enim estis seruati per fidem: idq; non ex vobis. Dei donum est.
units.tr: 3. The grace of God is set against the works or merits of men. Rom. 11:6: "But if it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is by works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work." Eph. 2:8: "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God."

units.la: οἰκτίρμων, Misericors.
units.tr: οἰκτίρμων[?]: merciful.

units.la: Apostolus Paulus Deum non solum misericordem, sed etiam Patrem misericordiarum, & omnis consolationis auctore esse, docet, 2.Cor.1.3. Dauid autem canit: Qui redimit ab interitu vitam tuam, & cingit te pietate & miserationibus: Psal. 103.4. Ex hoc dicto & illo priore liquet, cur Deus misericors & miserator dicatur. Etenim citra omnem ægritudinem, serio sensu nostrarum miseriarū afficitur, & gratuitæ suæ misericordiæ tempore nos liberat. Definitio misericordiæ ab Aristotele Rhet.2. tradita, etsi hominibus potis-simum simum conuenit, non tamen nihil ad nostrum institutum facit: ἔλεος ἐγὶ λύπης τὴς ἐπὶ φοινομένῳ λαχνῷ φθαρτῷ καὶ λυπηρῷ τῆς αὐτα-ξίας. Et illa Phauorini: ἔλεος ἐγὶ ϖαῦθος ἐπὶ τὴς ϖαρ' αξίαν τεταγμένον. Difficile sane est homini, sapere pariter & miserere: Deus autem noster, cum miseretur, sapit ac cō-sultissimū nobis est, ab irato Deo ad placatum confugere: ut monet Augustinus super Psal.74. Digna autem sunt memoria hæc dicta eiusdem Augustini, quæ, ut piarum cogitationum materiam suggeram, recitabo.
units.tr: The apostle Paul teaches that God is not only merciful but also the Father of mercies and the author of all comfort (2 Cor. 1:3). David sings: "Who redeems your life from destruction, and crowns you with kindness and compassion" (Ps. 103:4). From this saying and the former it is clear why God is called merciful and compassionate. For, free from all sickness, he is truly affected by a sense of our miseries, and in the time of his free mercy he delivers us. The definition of mercy handed down by Aristotle in the Rhetoric, book 2, although it applies chiefly to men, is nonetheless not irrelevant to our purpose: ἔλεος ἐγὶ λύπης τὴς ἐπὶ φοινομένῳ λαχνῷ φθαρτῷ καὶ λυπηρῷ τῆς αὐτα-ξίας (mercy is a kind of pain at the sight of an undeserved evil that destroys and grieves). And that of Phavorinus: ἔλεος ἐγὶ παθος ἐπὶ τὴς παρ' αξίαν τεταγμένον (mercy is a passion concerning one who is undeservedly placed in misfortune). Indeed it is hard for a man to be wise and merciful at the same time; but our God, when he shows mercy, is also wise, and it is most advantageous for us to flee from an angry God to a God who has been reconciled, as Augustine warns on Psalm 74. These sayings of the same Augustine are worth remembering, and I shall recite them to supply matter for pious thoughts.

units.la: 1. In misericordia Deus iudicium non præterminittit. Super Psal.32.
units.tr: 1. In mercy God does not set aside judgement. On Psalm 32.

units.la: 2. Misericorditer multos occidit Deus. Contra literas Petiliani lib.3.
units.tr: 2. God kills many out of mercy. Against the letters of Petilianus, book 3.

units.la: 3. Misericordia Domini desperationi opponenda. De Temp.Ser.122.
units.tr: 3. The mercy of the Lord is to be set against despair. On the Temporal Sermons, 122.

units.la: אֵל רַחוּם וְחַנּוּן μακροθύμος.
units.tr: אֵל רַחוּם וְחַנּוּן μακροθύμος.

units.la: Psal.103.8. Misericors & clemens Iehouah, אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, longus ira, & multus misericordia. Num.14.18. Iehouah tardus ad iram, & multus misericordia, remittens iniquitatem. Est enim Deus alienus ab omni ὀξυθυμία, ut qui nec commouea-tur ita ut nos commoueri solemus, nec pœnas ante tempus infligat.
units.tr: Ps. 103:8: "Jehovah is merciful and gracious, אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, slow to anger, and abounding in mercy." Num. 14:18: "Jehovah is slow to anger and abounding in mercy, forgiving iniquity." For God is far from all ὀξυθυμία (quickness of temper): he is neither moved as we are accustomed to be moved, nor does he inflict punishments before the time.

units.la: Ei qui est אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם opponitur קָצַר אַפַּיִם. Prouerb.14.17. Qui est breuis irarum, seu pronus ad iram: seu,qui facilè irascitur,facit stulticiam.
units.tr: The opposite of אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם is קָצַר אַפַּיִם. Prov. 14:17: "He who is short of anger, or prone to wrath, or who is quick to be angry, commits folly."

units.la: Cur autem Deus longanimis erga nos sit,& quæ sint μακροθυμίας seu longanimitatis illius cognata, docuit Apostolus hisce uerbis: An copiam benignitatis illius, & tolerantiæ ac lenitatis cótemnis,ignorans te benignitate Dei ad refipiscetiam deduci? Rom.2.4. Interpres μακροθυμίαν, lenitatem uertit.
units.tr: Why God is long-suffering toward us, and what things are akin to that long-suffering (μακροθυμία), the apostle taught in these words: "Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?" Rom. 2:4. The interpreter renders μακροθυμίαν as gentleness.

units.la: רַב חֶסֶד πολυέλεως.
units.tr: רַב חֶסֶד πολυέλεως.

units.la: Multus pietate,seu φιλοστοργία, qualis est in parentibus erga suos liberos. Pfal.103. 13. Sicut misericors est Pater erga filios, misericors est Iehouah erga timentes se. 14. Quia ipse cognoscit figmentum nostrum, recordatur quòd puluis sumus. Isa.49.14. Dixit autem Sion, Dereliquit me Iehouah,& Dominus oblitus est mei. 15. Nunquid obliuiscetur mulier infantis sui, ita ut non misereatur filij uteri sui? etiam istæ obliuiscantur,sed ego non obliuiscar tui.
units.tr: Abounding in kindness, or φιλοστοργία (tender affection), such as parents have toward their children. Ps. 103:13: "As a father has compassion on his children, so Jehovah has compassion on those who fear him. 14. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust." Isa. 49:14: "But Zion said, 'Jehovah has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me.' 15. Can a woman forget her nursing child, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you."

units.la: נחם על הרעה[?] Pœnitens super malo.
units.tr: Pœnitens super malo [נחם על הרעה]

units.la: De malo pœnæ intelligatur. Verè miseret Deum calamitosorum: ac cum illi resipiscũt, vel mitigat afflictiones, vel tollit. Immò, ne quidem cæterorum interi-tu delectatur, sicut est videre in historia diluvij. Etsi autem non est Deus volens iniquitatem,Psal.5. & irascitur omni die impio: tamen propter paucos bonos parcit multis malis,Gen.18.
units.tr: This should be understood of punishment. God truly pities the afflicted, and when they repent, he either softens their afflictions or takes them away. Indeed, he does not even take delight in the destruction of others, as can be seen in the story of the flood. Yet although God is not a God who wills iniquity (Psal. 5), and is angry with the wicked every day, he nevertheless spares many wicked for the sake of a few good (Gen. 18).

units.la: Dicitur etiam pœnitere super malo, cū eos in gratiam recipit, quibus nisi resipiscerent, atrocissimas pœnas denunciaverat: ut Ninivitarum exemplum ostendit. Pepercit enim illis Dominus,cum ad meliorem frugem essent conversi.
units.tr: It is also said that he repents concerning evil when he receives into favour those for whom he had announced the most terrible punishments unless they repented, as the example of the Ninevites shows. For the Lord spared them when they had turned to better conduct.

units.la: Ex ijs quę iam dicta sunt, discimus, Nō esse cur nostri iudicij maiorem, quàm divinæ bonitatis rationem habeamus: ac non indulgentiæ nimiæ Deum nobis insimulandum, sed eius erga nos bonitate & φιλανθρωπίαν[?] religiosè celebradam,nobisq; & alijs congratulatione summa excipiendam.
units.tr: From what has already been said we learn that we have no reason to value our own judgment above the reasoning of divine goodness, nor to accuse God of excessive indulgence towards us; rather we should devoutly celebrate his goodness toward us, which is love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία], and receive it with the greatest thanksgiving, both for ourselves and for others.

units.la: VERSVS III.
units.tr: VERSE III.

units.la: Nunc ergo, ô Iehovah, tolle quæso anima[?] meam à me: quoniam melior est mors mihi, quàm uita mea.
units.tr: Now therefore, O Jehovah, take, I pray, my soul from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.

units.la: Quemadmodum incontinés, τὸ ἄλογον[?], uidelicet, frenandas esse homini cupiditates, nec eis indulgendum, non nescit, sed κατὰ πάθος[?] labitur: ita ij qui tristicia immodica & impatientia laborant, uniuersale (res uidelicet aduersas infracto ani-mo, decenter & eleganter esse ferendas) non ignorant, sed de particulari, de suis miserijs, non recte pronunciant.
units.tr: As the incontinent man knows, indeed, that the reason (τὸ ἄλογον) ought to be the bridle of human desires and that one must not yield to them, yet slips through passion (κατὰ πάθος), so those who suffer from immoderate sadness and impatience do not ignore the general principle (namely, that adversities are to be borne with an unbroken spirit, becomingly and gracefully), but they do not rightly pronounce on the particular case, that is, on their own miseries.

units.la: Ionas τὸ ἄλογον recte agnoscit, uideli-cet, penes unum Deum esse uitae & mortis nostrae arbitrium: sed particulare, περὶ τῆς πράγματος[?] ignorat. Itaque quo tempo-re ipsi, non autem quo Deo uidebatur, sibi moriendum esse, perperam opinatus est.
units.tr: Jonah rightly recognises the general principle, namely, that the power over our life and death lies with God alone; but he does not know the particular case concerning the matter (περὶ τῆς πράγματος). Therefore he wrongly supposed that he had to die at the time when it seemed so to himself, and not at the time when it seemed so to God.

units.la: DE VITA ET MORTE hominis, Aphorismi.
units.tr: On the Life and Death of man, Aphorisms.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Vitæ naturalis donum θεόδοτον, nemini pio aspernandum aut abijciedum est.
units.tr: The gift of natural life is a gift of God [θεόδοτον], and no pious person should spurn or cast it away.

units.la: Vitam naturalem uoco ἔμψυχωσιν[?], quæ animæ in suo corpore permansione & σύστασις[?] constat. Eam quidam esse dicunt nutriri: cum omne quod nutritur uiuat, & quod uiuit plerumque nutriatur: exceptis ijs quae aliquandiu uiuunt, nec tamen nutriuntur: ut oua, femina nondum terrae mandata. Nihil autem attinet, de prodigiosa quorundam inedia, qualis fuit Nicolai eremitae Heluetij, qui multis annis à cibo citra simulatione abstinuit, hoc loco intempestiuè uerba facere.
units.tr: I call natural life the animation [ἔμψυχωσις], which consists in the soul's remaining in its body and in the body's constitution [σύστασις]. Some say it is sustained by nourishment, since everything that is nourished lives, and what lives is generally nourished. The exceptions are things that live for a while without being nourished, such as eggs, or seeds not yet committed to the earth. Nor is it relevant here to speak out of place about the prodigious fasting of certain people, such as the Swiss hermit Nicholas, who for many years abstained from food without any pretence.

units.la: Existimo Ariftotelem ideo dixisse, Vitam esse conseruationem caloris natiui. Vt enim in lychno flamma alitur oleo aut cera iusta quantitate: ita uitalis spiritus rapit alimetum ex humido radicali, quod utcunque fouetur ab alimentari: quod cum impurius fit, senium accersit, illo paulatim deficiente.
units.tr: I think Aristotle called life the conservation of natural heat for this reason: just as a flame in a lamp is fed by oil or wax in due quantity, so the vital spirit draws nourishment from the radical moisture, which is in some way cherished by the nutritive faculty. When this moisture becomes more impure, it brings on old age, as the radical moisture gradually fails.

units.la: Anima autem est id quo uiuimus, sentimus, mouemur & intelligimus: utin 2 de Anima docuit Ariftoteles.
units.tr: The soul is that by which we live, feel, move and understand, as Aristotle taught in the second book On the Soul.

units.la: Iam uero, cum quid vitae naturalis sit, breuiter dixerimus: cur ea homini pio & prudenti no sit aspernanda, nedum abijcienda, uideamus.
units.tr: Now that we have briefly said what natural life is, let us see why it should not be spurned by a pious and prudent man, much less cast away.

units.la: 1. Ab efficiente principe. Nullum Dei donum, seu eximiu, seu mediocre homini religioso contemnendum est. Summa enim cum gratitudine ea dona amplecti, &ijs frui oportet,quæ à perenni & inex-hausto fonte omnis boni promanant, & proinde modis omnibus salutaria sunt. Atqui uita naturalis Dei donû est. Gen. 2.7. Formauerat ergo Iehouah Deus hominem è puluere terræ,insp irauerat[?] in faciem eius spiraculum uitæ, & fuit homo in animam uiuētem. Act.17.25. Ipse dat omnibus uitam, halitum & omnia. 28. Peripsum uiuimus, monemur & sumus. Quare uita naturalis nemini religioso est aspernanda. de qua scitè Augustinus: Vita uitæ mortalis, spes est uitæ immortalis.
units.tr: 1. From the efficient cause. No gift of God, whether excellent or ordinary, is to be despised by a religious man. For such gifts ought to be embraced with the greatest gratitude and enjoyed, since they flow from the perennial and inexhaustible fountain of all good, and are therefore wholesome in every way. But natural life is a gift of God. Gen. 2.7: the LORD God had formed man from the dust of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul. Acts 17.25: he himself gives to all life, breath and all things. v. 28: in him we live, move and have our being. Therefore natural life is not to be despised by any religious person. On this Augustine says well: the life of mortal life is the hope of immortal life.

units.la: 2. A' priuantibus. Eccl.9.4. Conso-ciato cum omnibus uiuentibus est spes: quia canis uiuus est melior leone mortuo. Vita igitur morti logisimè est ante-ponéda. Ac eo nomine nō cupimus exui, sed superindui, ut absorbeatur mortalitas à uita. 2.Cor.5.4.
units.tr: 2. From the privations. Eccl. 9.4: for to him who is joined with all the living there is hope, since a living dog is better than a dead lion. Life, therefore, is rightly to be preferred to death. And for this reason we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed upon, so that mortality may be swallowed up by life. 2 Cor. 5.4.

units.la: 3. A' fine.Psal.115.17. Mortui non laudabunt te Deus: neque ullus eorum qui descendunt in sepulcrum. 18. Sed nos benedicemus Deum. Ideo cõditi sunt homines, & ideo redemti, ut non solum domi suæ priuatim, sed etiam in cœtibus benedicat Iehouae, ad multorum aliorum in-staurationem. Sed uita hac functi, & è su-perstitum contubernio semoti, id prǣsta-re nequeunt. Quare uita haec ἀθεολογίας[?] Dei cum seruire possit, non est uilipendenda.
units.tr: 3. From the end. Ps. 115.17: the dead do not praise you, O God, nor does anyone who goes down into silence. v. 18: but we will bless God. Men were therefore created, and therefore redeemed, so that they may bless the LORD not only privately in their own homes but also in assemblies, for the edification of many others. But those who have departed this life and are removed from the company of the living cannot do this. Therefore, since this life can serve the praise of God, it is not to be held cheap.

units.la: II. Mors prima hominis pio ante tempus nec uotis, nec manu accersenda.
units.tr: II. A pious man should not seek the first death before its time, either by prayer or by his own hand.

units.la: Primam mortem uoco, animae à cor-pore migrationem, quae peccati auctora-mentum est. Rom.6.23. Notum est Si-monidis monostichon:
units.tr: I call the first death the migration of the soul from the body, which is the wage of sin. Rom. 6.23. The well-known line of Simonides is this:

units.la: ἀναλύεται τὸ σῶμα πνεύματος φυγόντος[?].
units.tr: The body is dissolved when the spirit has fled. [ἀναλύεται τὸ σῶμα πνεύματος φυγόντος]

units.la: Non autem optandum diem summum, sic probo. Non decet pium hominem do-lore[?] aut tædio fractum, secus quàm sit Deo uisum, de migratione sua è uiuis sta-tuere. At qui mortem sibijpsis imprecantur, aut quod grauius est, consciscunt, de ea secus statuunt quàm uelit Deus, qui cuiusque uitae certum terminum praestituit. Anteuertere enim conantur momen-tum temporis à Deo definitum. Itaq; ni-hil dubium est, eos grauiter peccare.
units.tr: That one should not wish for the last day, I prove as follows. It does not befit a pious man, broken by pain or weariness, to decide about his departure from the living otherwise than God has determined. Yet those who call death down upon themselves, or, what is more grievous, bring it about with their own hands, judge concerning it otherwise than God wills, who has fixed a certain limit for each one's life. For they try to anticipate the moment of time defined by God. Therefore there is no doubt that they sin grievously.

units.la: Obiectio: Quid ergo de Iobo & Hiere-mia propheta & Iona nostro nobis statu-endum erit, qui omnes mortem sibi im-precati precati sunt, etiam uitae initio & progres-sione mirum in modu deplorata? An'ne hi culpandi sunt?
units.tr: Objection: What then are we to hold concerning Job, the prophet Jeremiah and our Jonah, who all called death down upon themselves, their life's beginning and course having been deplored in a remarkable manner? Are these men to be blamed?

units.la: Respodeo: Non exemplis, sed legibus iudicandum. Neque uero quae recitatiue de istorum hominum μεμψιμοιρίας Spiritus sanctus memorię prodidit, ea ἐγκωμιαστικῶς nobis accipienda sunt. Peccauerunt sane & isti & eorum similes, quorum offensae tanto conspectiores fuerunt, quo maius fuit uniuscuiusq; illorum ἀξίωμα.
units.tr: I answer: we must judge by laws, not by examples. Nor are the things the Holy Spirit has recorded as the complaints of these men to be taken by us as praise [ἐγκωμιαστικῶς]. Certainly they, and others like them, sinned, and their offences were the more conspicuous the greater the dignity of each of them.

units.la: Etsi autem non opus est nobis in hoc argumenti Theologici genere, Ethnicorum suffragatione: tamen nihil uetat, quo minus Ciceronis uerba è Scipionis Somnio uel eā ob causam repetamus, quòd religio nobis esse debet, minus recte pieq; de re tanta statuere, quàm uisum est igna ro uerae religionis homini. Et tibi Publi, inquit Africanus, & pijs omnibus retinédus est animus in custodia corporis: nec iniussu eius, à quo ille est uobis datus, ex hominum uita migrandum est, ne mu-nus humanum assignatum à Deo desu-gisse uideamini.
units.tr: Although there is no need for us, in this kind of theological argument, to rely on the support of the heathen, nevertheless nothing prevents us from repeating Cicero's words from the Dream of Scipio, for this reason: it ought to be a matter of religion for us not to judge so great a matter less rightly and piously than it seemed to a man ignorant of true religion. "And you, Publius," says Africanus, "and all the pious, must keep your spirit under guard in the body; nor should you depart from human life without the command of him who gave you that life, lest you seem to have shirked the human duty assigned you by God."

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Sed tamen donū uitae spiritualis, mo-dis dis omnibus anteponendum est uitæ naturali.
units.tr: Yet the gift of spiritual life must in every way be preferred to natural life.

units.la: Quæ uita à Christo capite uiuis solùm membris datur, & est cum salute æterna coniuncta, ea hauddubiè anteponeda est ei uitæ,quàm omnibus in uniuersum hominibus Christus conditor dat,& quęca duca & euanida est.
units.tr: The life which is given by Christ the Head only to the living members, and which is joined with eternal salvation, is without doubt to be preferred to that life which Christ the Creator gives in general to all men, and which is fleeting and vanishing.

units.la: Spiritualis autem uita non nisi ijs qui Christo sunt concorpores conceditur, & quidem ea lege,ut sit æterna & beatisima.iuxta dictum:Viuo autem non ampli us ego,sed uiuit in me Christus:& uitam quam nunc uiuo in carne, uiuo per fidem filij Dei,qui dilexit me,& tradidit semetipsum pro me.Gal.2.20.
units.tr: Spiritual life is granted only to those who are fellow-bodies with Christ, and indeed on this condition, that it be eternal and most blessed, according to the saying: "I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." Gal. 2.20.

units.la: Sicut autem anima substantia & forma est,per quam uiuit homo: uita autem est τὸ ζῆν, secundum quod ad actiones non solùm animalis, sed creaturæ rationalis sese mouere potest,ut uiuat,sentiat, locum mutet, intelligat, aliud ex alio ratiocinando colligat: deniq; actiones istæ sunt effecta uitæ. ita Spiritus Christi in nobis habitans,is est,cuius in nobis habitantis beneficio uiuimus spiritualiter. Vita porrò spiritualis, est ipsum esse spirituale nouum, quod à Christo habemus. Fru-ctus autè Spiritus, charitas, pax, gaudiū, lenitas, benignitas, bonitas, fides, masue-tudo, temperantia, Gal.5.22. sunt uitæ illius spiritualis effectus.
units.tr: Just as the soul is the substance and form through which a man lives, while life is the being alive, by which we are able to move ourselves to the actions not only of an animal but of a rational creature, so that we live, feel, change place, understand, and by reasoning draw one thing from another; and finally those actions are the effects of life, so the Spirit of Christ dwelling in us is the one by whose benefit, dwelling in us, we live spiritually. Moreover, spiritual life is that new spiritual being itself which we have from Christ. The fruits of the Spirit, love, peace, joy, gentleness, kindness, goodness, faith, meekness, self-control (Gal. 5.22), are the effects of that spiritual life.

units.la: Demostratiuè ergo cocludimus, quòd naturali uitæ, spiritualis longè præstet, eoq; maioris à nobis sit facienda quàm il-la, de qua dicitur: Quæ'nam est enim uita uestra? Vapor enim est, qui ad exiguum (tempus) apparet, & deinde euane-scit.Iac.4.14.
units.tr: Therefore we conclude by demonstration that spiritual life far surpasses natural life, and so it is to be valued by us far more than that life of which it is said: "For what is your life? It is a vapour which appears for a little while and then vanishes away." James 4.14.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IIII.

units.la: Mortem uerò secundam nemo sine scelere sibi imprecari, ne dicam accersere potest.
units.tr: But no one can call down the second death upon himself, let alone bring it on, without sin.

units.la: Secundam mortem, non exstinctione & internecione animæ & corporis, sed utriusque τῇ ἀπωλείᾳ[?], & gehenæ doloribus, definire solet Spiritus sanctus. Apoc.21. 8. Timidis autem, & incredulis, & exsecrabilibus, et homicidis, & scortatoribus, & ueneficis, & idololatris, & omnibus medacibus pars (assignata) est in stagno ardente igni & sulphure, quod est mors secunda.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit usually defines the second death not as the extinction and destruction of soul and body, but as the destruction of both [τῇ ἀπωλείᾳ] together with the pains of Gehenna. Rev. 21.8: but for the fearful, the unbelieving, the abominable, murderers, whoremongers, sorcerers, idolaters and all liars, their portion is in the burning lake of fire and sulphur, which is the second death.

units.la: Contrà: Quod præcipuè laudi datum est Mosi & Paulo, id alijs vitio dari non debet. Sed ille quidem expungi voluit e libro vitae, Exod.32.32. hic autem ἀνά-θεμα ἀπὸ τῆς χριστῆς[?] fieri, Roman.9.3. Quare nec alij incusandi sunt, qui exitio sese devouent.
units.tr: On the contrary: what has been especially praised in Moses and Paul ought not to be a fault in others. But the former wished to be blotted out of the book of life (Exod. 32.32), and the latter wished to be made anathema from Christ (Rom. 9.3). Therefore neither should others be blamed who devote themselves to destruction.

units.la: Respondeo, primum ad Maiore: Regu-lariter à summis viris facta, si ipsi quoque eorum vestigijs insistentes faciamus, reprehendi non posse, cum eadem lex o-mnibus sit praescripta à Deo. Sed tamen ex eo nō recte colligas, recte omnia summorum hominum facta nos quoq; imi-tari. Sunt enim quaedam extraordinaria κατορθώματα[?], ab heroico & ardente Spiritu profecta: ut Phinees factum, Psal.106. In Minore est paralogismus à dicto secundum quid ad simpliciter dictum. Non enim ἁπλῶς Moses & Paulus exitium sibi-ipsis imprecati sunt, sed secundum quid, si videlicet aliorum incolumitati & eme-dationi ea res seruire posset, secundum Dei consilium. Parati erant, modò ita placeret Deo, sempiterno suo exitio, multo-rum aliorum instaurationem redimere: non autem vel vilipendebant vitae aeter-nae gratiam, vel exitium perpetuum temere merè sibijpsis imprecabantur.
units.tr: I answer first to the major premise: things done by the greatest men cannot be found fault with if we, following in their footsteps, do them as well, since the same law is prescribed to all by God. Yet from this you do not rightly infer that we may imitate all the deeds of the greatest men. For there are certain extraordinary achievements [κατορθώματα] proceeding from a heroic and burning spirit, such as the deed of Phinehas (Ps. 106). In the minor premise there is a paralogism, moving from a statement made in a certain respect to one made absolutely. For Moses and Paul did not call destruction upon themselves absolutely, but in a certain respect, namely if that might serve the safety and recovery of others, according to God's counsel. They were ready, provided it pleased God, to redeem the restoration of many others with their own eternal destruction. But they neither held the grace of eternal life cheap, nor rashly invoked perpetual destruction upon themselves.

units.la: Ex ijs quae jam nobis dicta sunt, the-sim colligimus: Cum Domini Dei nostri causa conditi simus & uiuamus,non esse cur serui taedio aut dolore fracti,uitae donum sibi aspernandum putent. Semper itaq; in conspectu nobis sit dictum Pauli: Nullus enim nostrûm sibijpsi uiuit,& nullus sibijpsi moritur. Nam siue uiuimus, Domino uiuimus: siue morimur, Domino morimur. Siue igitur uiuamus, siue moriamur, Domini sumus. Rom. 14. 7. 8.
units.tr: From what has already been said we draw this thesis: since we were created and live for the sake of the Lord our God, there is no reason for servants, broken by weariness or grief, to think they should spurn the gift of life. Let the saying of Paul therefore always be before our eyes: "For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord; and if we die, we die to the Lord. Whether we live therefore or die, we are the Lord's." Rom. 14.7, 8.

units.la: VERSVS IIII.
units.tr: VERSE 4.

units.la: Dixit autem Jehouah: Nonne uehemes ira est tibi? Aut, Nunquid benefacit tibi ira?
units.tr: And Jehovah said: Is it right for you to be angry? Or, does anger do you good?

units.la: Hieronymus, Verbũ, ait, הֵיטֵב חָרָה לָךְ[?], & Iratus es tu, & Contristatus es tu, transferri potest, quod utrum q; & Prophetae & Domini personae conuenit: quòd uel iratus sit, ne uideretur apud Niniuitas esse men titus: uel contristatus, intelliges Israelem esse periturum.
units.tr: Jerome says that the Hebrew words הֵיטֵב חָרָה לָךְ can be rendered "Are you angry, and are you grieved?", and that this fits both the prophet and the person of the Lord. He is angry, lest he seem to be a liar among the Ninevites; or he is grieved, and you will understand that Israel is about to perish.

units.la: Thesis: Deus merito irridet acres illos motus cordium nostrorum, quos impatientia & tristicia pariunt.
units.tr: Thesis: God rightly mocks those fierce movements of our hearts which impatience and sadness produce.

units.la: Etsi enim nemo fere est, qui non ταῖς[?] προπαθείαις[?] saepius & uehementius quàm expediat & deceat, commoueatur: uult tamen Deus, nos nequaquam indulgere affectibus istis, & non erumpere in facta quae pugnant cum diuina uoluntate. iuxta illud: Irascimini, & ne peccate. Psal.4. 4. Eph.4.26.
units.tr: For although there is hardly anyone who is not moved more often and more violently than is useful and fitting by the first emotions [ταῖς προπαθείαις], God nevertheless wills that we by no means indulge these affections or break out into deeds that conflict with the divine will, according to that saying: "Be angry, and do not sin." Ps. 4.4; Eph. 4.26.

units.la: Ideo precatur Dauid: Etiam à superbijs (sic uocat effrenes affectus) contine Seruū tuū,ne dominetur mihi. Psal.19.13.
units.tr: Therefore David prays: "Keep your servant also from presumptuous sins (so he calls unbridled affections), that they may not have dominion over me." Ps. 19.13.

units.la: Sed cur irridere Deus dicitur istos motus cordis humani?
units.tr: But why is God said to mock these movements of the human heart?

units.la: Quia ut maximè in cæteris rebus sapi-ant, qui istis motibus indulgent: ridiculi tamen sunt, cum & denunciationes diuinas, & earum euetus, suo potius arbitrio, quàm Dei consilio æstimant. Quasi uerò miseri & stolidi homunculi Deo à consilijs esse possimus? Rom.11.34. Si sus Miner-uam doceat, & homo suijpsius oblitus memoriam moneat, sibiq; in eo placeat & adplaudat, an non ridiculus ceseri[?] debet?
units.tr: Because, however wise those who indulge these motions may be in other matters, they are ridiculous when they judge God's threats and their outcomes by their own opinion rather than by God's counsel. As if we miserable little men could be counsellors to God! Rom. 11.34. If a pig were to teach Minerva, and a man forgetful of himself were to admonish memory, and be pleased with himself and applaud himself, would he not rightly be thought ridiculous?

units.la: Quinam uerò hoc pacto præ cæte-ris peccant?
units.tr: But who sin in this way beyond others?

units.la: Qui nondum plenè didicerunt, in sua statione τῷ ταξιάρχῳ[?] Deo obedire, nec suâ fortem boni consulunt:sed taedio & fastidio laborantes,ut Graeci loquuntur,τὰ ϖαϱ̓ⅰ- ϙόντα μὴ φρόνδι, & inani spe prosequuntur etiam illicita,aut uiribus suis maiora.
units.tr: Those who have not yet fully learned to obey God in their own station [τῷ ταξιάρχῳ], nor are content with their own lot, but, labouring under weariness and disgust, as the Greeks say, [τὰ παρόντα μὴ φρονεῖν] (not to value what is at hand), and pursue with empty hope even unlawful things, or things greater than their strength.

units.la: De taedio eorum quae haec sunt & fiunt.
units.tr: On the weariness of those things which are and which happen.

units.la: Inter ceteras uanitatis,cui obnoxia est uita hominum, formas, neutiquam potiore tremum locum fastidio rerum praesentiu tribuere conuenit. An non enim miranda est uanitas,ex ijs quibus uti et frui licebat, fructum nullu percipere, & inani spe rerum abfentiu & futurarum sese lactare? Notum est exotericu illud:τὰ ϖαϱ̓ονϊα μὴ φέ- ϱεων ... τὰ μεγάλα ἀιῶπαι, μαινομένων οἱ δὲ τρό- ποι. Et illud Herodoti: ἐχθέϱα δ' οὐδὲν τ' εν ἀνθρώποισι ϖολλὰ φρονέοντα μηδὲν ἑπιν̓χείϱ.
units.tr: Among the other vanities to which the life of men is subject, it is by no means fitting to give the last place to disgust with present things. Is not their vanity remarkable, that from things they were allowed to use and enjoy they gain no fruit, and boast of the empty hope of things absent and future? The well-known saying runs: [τὰ παρόντα μὴ φέρειν ... τὰ μεγάλα ἰᾶσθαι, μαινομένων οἱ δὲ τρόποι], "not to bear what is present ... great things are healed; these are the ways of madmen." And that saying of Herodotus: "Nothing is more hateful among men than to think many things and attempt nothing." [ἐχθέρα δ' οὐδὲν τ' ἐν ἀνθρώποισι πολλὰ φρονέοντα μηδὲν ἐπιχειρεῖν].

units.la: Propositum autem est ostendere, meritò Deum taedium & faftidiū istud praesentium rerum irridere:ut agnito mentis nostrae errore, erubescamus,& Deo gloriam in omnibus demus. Vt autem uia quadam & ordine utamur, cauflas quasdam eius fastidij, & eiusdem destinatum persequemur.
units.tr: The purpose, however, is to show that God rightly mocks this weariness and disgust with present things, so that, once the error of our mind is acknowledged, we may blush and give glory to God in all things. In order to proceed by a certain method and order, we shall pursue some causes of this disgust, and its intended destination.

units.la: 1. προηγούμενον est,satietas rerū etiam adamatarum, Graecè ἀψινοθία. Nihil fano & bono homini adamatum esse debet, nisi quod
units.tr: 1. The primary cause is satiety even of things that are loved, in Greek [ἀψινοθία]. Nothing should be loved by a sound and good man except what is

units.la: quod honestum bonum q; est. Iam uero, secundum prouerbium Platonicum, Honesti nulla facietas est, λόγος ἰδέας ἀλλὰ καλῶν [?]. Quae igitur haec uanitas est, fastidio pro-sequi honesta & bona?
units.tr: also honourable and good. Indeed, according to the Platonic proverb, there is no satiety of the honourable [λόγος ἰδέας ἀλλὰ καλῶν]. What vanity, then, is it to pursue honourable and good things with disgust?

units.la: Sedenim inde fastidiū istud, iusto Dei iudicio, in hominū animis nascitur, quòd donorum Dei usumfructū suis delitijs & uoluptatibus, suae quinetiam gloriae serui-re uolunt: cum tamen is ad Dei filius [?] gloriam referri debeat, iuxta oraculum: Siue igitur editis, siue bibitis, siue quid facitis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite. 1.Co-rinth.10.31.
units.tr: But this disgust arises in men's minds by the just judgment of God, because they wish to serve the use and enjoyment of God's gifts for their own delights and pleasures, indeed for their own glory, whereas these ought to be referred to the glory of God, according to the oracle: "Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God." 1 Cor. 10.31.

units.la: 2. προκαταληπτικόν [?] est, genus omne obie-ctorum, quibus irritantur et veluti exacu-untur vehementiores motus seu affectus humani cordis, ut veluti caliginem offun-dant menti, secundum illud: Impedit ira animum, ne possit cernere verum. Saul iniusta æmulatione erga Dauidem ardes, beneficiorum eius & rerum bello & pa-ce feliciter gestarum obliuiscitur, & eum implacabili odio prosequitur, quem diligere debebat ob virtutem & merita. Ab-solon φιλαρχίας seu regnadi cupiditate ac-census, nulla reuerētiae & obedientiae pa-tri tri debitæ, nulla præsentis fortunæ, quæ contetus esse poterat, ratione habita, bellum ei facit, & hostiliter eū persequitur.
units.tr: 2. The προκαταληπτικόν is every kind of object by which the more violent motions or affections of the human heart are provoked and, as it were, sharpened, so that they cast a mist over the mind, according to that saying: "Anger hinders the soul, so that it cannot see the truth." Saul, burning with unjust rivalry toward David, forgets his benefits and the things successfully done by him in war and peace, and pursues with implacable hatred the one he ought to have loved for his virtue and merits. Absalom, inflamed by love of rule [φιλαρχία], or the desire to reign, has no regard for the reverence and obedience owed to his father, nor for the present fortune with which he could have been content; he wages war on his father and pursues him as an enemy.

units.la: Sancti quinetiam uiri, interdum carnis intemperie perculsi, non satis memores sunt[?] fortis suæ, & acceptorum a Deo beneficiorum, cum acerbus repentini alicuius doloris sensus eos fere totos occupat, sibiq; uendicat:ut est uidere in exemplis Ieremiæ, Ionæ & similium.
units.tr: Holy men too, sometimes struck by the intemperance of the flesh, are not sufficiently mindful of their own strength and of the benefits received from God, when the bitter sense of some sudden pain almost wholly occupies them and claims them for itself, as may be seen in the examples of Jeremiah, Jonah and the like.

units.la: §. Iam, si docedi causa (quasi formam tanti mali indicaturi) quibus uitijs illud constet, perpenderimus, animaduertemus non solum risum, sed etiam iustam indignationem illud mereri. Primum enim habet τὴν ἀγνωσίαν[?]. Non enim satis norunt, quo loco Dei dona habenda sint, qui fastidio ea prosequuntur. Exemplo sunt Israelitæ, dicentes: Anima nostra arida est, nec quicquam præter Man oculi nostri uident: Num.11.6. Deinde ἀχαρι-στίαν[?] ingratitudinem comite secum ducit. Ac tantum abest, ut pro malis gratias agat, ut ne quidem pro bonis in se collatis Deo uti celebrent. Tertio accedit hyperbolica μεμψιμοιρία[?] seu querela de magnitudine malorum ingruentium, & de acerbis-simo simo eorum sensu: eo faciens, ut praeter meritum male tractari homo videatur.
units.tr: §. Now, if we weigh, for the sake of teaching (as if about to describe the form of so great an evil), of what vices it consists, we shall notice that it deserves not only laughter but also just indignation. For first it has ignorance [τὴν ἀγνωσίαν]. Those who pursue God's gifts with disgust do not sufficiently know in what place those gifts are to be held. The Israelites are an example, saying: "Our soul is dry, and our eyes see nothing but the manna." Num. 11.6. Then ingratitude [ἀχαριστία] brings itself along as a companion. And so far is it from giving thanks for evils that they do not even praise God for the goods conferred on them. Thirdly, there is added hyperbolic complaining [μεμψιμοιρία], or querulousness about the magnitude of the evils that press upon us and the most bitter sense of them, so that a man seems to be treated badly beyond his deserts.

units.la: 4. Porrò si materiam, circa quam taedium istud versatur, spectes, an non indigna res est, eas res, quarum usus multis nominibus homini iucundissimus & saluberrimus esse & poterat & debebat, stolido fastidio odiosas & infrugiferas fieri?
units.tr: 4. Moreover, if you look at the matter with which this weariness is concerned, is it not an unworthy thing that things whose use could and should have been most pleasant and wholesome to man in many respects are made odious and unfruitful by foolish disgust?

units.la: Inductionis instrumento logico adhibito, docebimus, Nihil fere esse posse tam sanctum, tam utile, tam honestum, cuius satietas oboriri non possit in animo hominis, qui carnis intelligentiae nimium quandoq; tribues, perturbationibus frenum laxat.
units.tr: With the logical instrument of induction applied, we shall teach that there can be nothing so holy, so useful, so honourable, that satiety of it cannot arise in the mind of a man who sometimes gives too much weight to carnal understanding and loosens the reins for his passions.

units.la: 1. Quàm sit homini vita suavis & pretiosa, vel ex unico dicto hostis generis humani liquet: Cuncta quae sunt viro, dabit pro anima sua: Iob.2.4. Sed quoties eius satietas etiam sanctis oboritur?
units.tr: 1. How sweet and precious life is to a man is clear from the single saying of the enemy of the human race: "All that a man has he will give for his life." Job 2.4. But how often does satiety of it arise even in the saints?

units.la: 2. Dona Dei, quae sunt praeclara tũ prę-sidia, tum ornamenta, quoties & quàm turpiter defodiunt homines? Matt.25.
units.tr: 2. How often, and how shamefully, do men bury the gifts of God, which are both splendid protections and ornaments? Matt. 25.

units.la: 3. Vocatio autem ad muneris alicuius functione, quoties uilescit in animis nostris? quoties alias functiones appetimus?
units.tr: 3. And how often does the calling to the performance of some office become cheap in our minds? How often do we desire other functions?

units.la: 4. Κατορθώματα[?], nisi seruiant nomini nostro illustrando, ut quæ propemodum à nobis tantum profecta uideri uelimus, quoties paruifacimus?
units.tr: 4. Good deeds [κατορθώματα], unless they serve to illustrate our name, as things we almost wish to appear to have come from us alone: how often do we undervalue them?

units.la: 5. παραπτώματα[?] autem nostra uel nulla, uel exigua esse, falsò opinamur: & sic nobis blandimur, ut non satis nos submittamus sub potenti manu Dei.
units.tr: 5. Our transgressions [παραπτώματα], however, we falsely think to be none or slight, and so we flatter ourselves that we do not sufficiently humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God.

units.la: 6. Rerum euentus, etsi Dei consilium nunquam fallant, tamen eo nomine improbamus, quòd nostro iudicio & expectationi non satisfaciunt.
units.tr: 6. The outcomes of things, although they never frustrate God's counsel, we nevertheless disapprove of on this account, that they do not satisfy our judgment and expectation.

units.la: 7. Aduersa, cum neutiquam sine ἀναγκ-ία[?] sint, nos tamen nunquam non incusamus, & dolenter ferimus.
units.tr: 7. Adversities, since they are by no means without necessity [ἀνάγκη], we nevertheless never cease to blame, and bear them with grief.

units.la: 8. Res secundas, etsi eò faciunt, ut animi luxurient, nunquam tamè non requirimus, quasi qui digni simus, ut omnia ex sententia succedant.
units.tr: 8. Prosperous things, although they make our minds grow wanton, we nevertheless never cease to seek, as if we were worthy that everything should turn out according to our wish.

units.la: 9. Dei opera intermedia contraria fie-ri, ac tenebras nostras diuidere, humiliando nos exaltare, in media rerum humanarum ἀταξίᾳ[?] Dei ordinem lucere, nō ita ut par erat cogitamus.
units.tr: 9. God's intermediate works become contrary to us, dividing our darkness, humbling us in order to exalt us, and shining God's order in the midst of the disorder [ἀταξία] of human affairs; we do not think about this as we ought.

units.la: Idem autem iudicium est de omni-bus uitæ humanæ occupationibus & ad-iunctis. Vnde liquet, satietatem in re-bus omnibus tandem suboriri. 5. Destinatum. Omnes hominum (tantisper donec sunt ψυχικοί) cogitationes, consilia omnia eo tendunt, ut homo sibi ipsi uiuat, sibi consulat & blandiatur. At qui hoc pugnat cum fine, cuius gratia cō diti sunt homines. Conditi enim & redemti sunt, ut Deum agnoscant, inuocet & celebrent, ut ei uni uiuant, moriantur, resurgant, & in aeternum beatam agant uitam.
units.tr: Moreover, the same judgment applies to all the occupations and circumstances of human life. From this it is clear that satiety eventually arises in all things. 5. Purpose. All the thoughts and plans of men (for as long as they are ψυχικοί, that is, natural) tend to this end: that a man should live for himself, look after himself and flatter himself. But this fights against the purpose for which men were created. For they were created and redeemed so that they might acknowledge God, call upon him and celebrate him, so that they might live, die and rise for him alone, and lead a blessed life for eternity.

units.la: Ex ijs omnibus quae [illegible, ~8 letters] licuit, colligimus, Deum merito irridere nostra carnalia consilia, ματαιότητα[?] & conatus inanes & ridiculos: ac nobis eo nomine nefuspecta esse debere omnia carnis nostrae consilia: & orandum, ut non nostra, sed Dei uoluntas fiat. Haec de θεῖα[?] uersus 4.
units.tr: From all those things which [illegible] has been permitted, we gather that God rightly mocks our carnal plans and our vain and ridiculous attempts (ματαιότητα), and that on this account all the designs of our flesh ought to be regarded with suspicion by us; and that we ought to pray that not our will but God's will be done. These things concerning the divine [θεῖα] from verse 4.

units.la: VERSVS V.
units.tr: VERSE 5.

units.la: Egressus est itaq; Ionah ex urbe ipsa, & sedit ad Orientem eius, fecitq; sibi illic tabernaculum, & mansit subter illud in umbra ipsa, donec uideret quid futurum esset urbi ipsi.
units.tr: So Jonah went out of the city and sat down to the east of it, and made himself a booth there, and sat under it in the shade, until he might see what would become of the city.

units.la: Transitio est ad historiam de ijs Ionae dictis & factis, quę extra urbem Niniuen euenerunt. Etsi autem quidam allegoriam diam diligenter concinnare studuerunt: tamen chreiam & grammaticum sensum nos quidem, quantum dabit Deus, persequemur.
units.tr: This is a transition to the story of the words and deeds of Jonah that took place outside the city of Nineveh. Although some have diligently worked to fashion an allegory, we, as far as God gives us grace, will pursue the plain sense and the grammatical sense.

units.la: Videtur Propheta noster persuasum habuisse, futurum ut tota ciuitas uel terra dehiscente absorberetur: uel (ut olim accidit Pentapoli) igne & sulphure cœlitus depluente, incendio absumeretur: uel alia ratione deleta, fieret miserabile πολυ-ἀνθρώπων[?] incolarum. Fuit autem hæc persuasio minus digna tanto uiro, quem nō fugiebat, Deum in resipiscentes non ita, ut in eos qui sunt ἀμετανόητοι, animaduertere: sed poenas uel mitigare, uel etiam prorsus relaxare: ac piorum esse, gratulari aliis resipiscentiæ donum, & liberationem à malo.
units.tr: Our Prophet evidently was persuaded that the whole city was going to be swallowed up by the opening of the earth, or, as once happened to the Pentapolis, consumed by fire and brimstone raining from heaven, or destroyed in some other way, so that the populous inhabitants would be left in a miserable state. But this persuasion was less worthy of so great a man, who did not fail to know that God deals with those who repent not as he deals with those who are impenitent, but mitigates their punishments or even altogether remits them; and that it is the mark of the godly to rejoice that others have been given the gift of repentance and deliverance from evil.

units.la: THESIS DE SOLITARIA VITA.
units.tr: THESIS ON THE SOLITARY LIFE.

units.la: Nequaquā eum ad modum dolori indulgendum nobis est, ut hominum contubernium & uestigia derelinquetes, nō tam quid ipsi agamus, quidue præstare debeamus, quàm quid aliis sit euenturū, μετεωριζόμενοι exspectemus.
units.tr: By no means are we to indulge grief to such an extent that, abandoning the fellowship and footsteps of men, we wait in suspense not so much for what we ourselves ought to do or provide, but for what is going to happen to others.

units.la: Non enim hoc etiam ingens dolor no bis persuadere debet, ut societatis legitimæ & officij nostri obliti, & ea tantum quæ molesta nobis, non autem quæ iu- cūda & utilia sunt tum nobis, tum etiam alijs,spectantes, illud ethnicū, λάθε βιώσας [?], sectemur. Neq; enim nobis nati sumus, aut etiam uiuimus, ut integrum nobis sit de nobis ipsis id quod seu dolor, seu fasti- dium rerum præsentium dictat, statuere.
units.tr: For this great grief ought not to persuade us either, forgetful of lawful society and of our duty, to follow that pagan maxim, "live hidden," looking only at what is troublesome to us and not at what is pleasant and useful both to ourselves and to others. For we were not born for ourselves, nor do we live so that it is up to us to decide, as sorrow or weariness with present things dictates.

units.la: Sint itaque nobis in conspectu hæ gra- uissimæ rationes, quæ monent, quenq; suo loco in honesta societate hominum viuere, & ad extremum usque vitæ spiri- tum perseuerare debere.
units.tr: Let these very weighty reasons therefore be before our eyes, which warn that each of us should live in his own place in honest human fellowship, and persevere in it to the last breath of life.

units.la: 1. Quia homo est animal λογικόν [?], ac natura & lege tenetur diligere proximū tanquam seipsum. Dilectionem autem hanc factis, & quidem tota sua vita testa- ri debet: id quod ab eo præstari nequit, si sese subducat è contubernio aliorum hominum. Etsi autem hominum usibus, & mutuis uerę beneficentiæ officijs, contu- bernium eorum seruire debet: principa- lis tamen eius finis est, uerę de Deo doctrinæ studiosa propagatio. Placent sane mihi plurimū hi dulces uersus Stigelij:
units.tr: 1. Because man is a rational animal, and by nature and by law is bound to love his neighbour as himself. This love, however, he ought to attest by deeds, and indeed throughout his whole life; this cannot be done if he withdraws himself from the company of other men. Although that company ought to serve the uses of men and the mutual offices of true beneficence, its principal end is the fruitful spreading of true doctrine concerning God. Indeed I am very pleased with those sweet verses of Stigel:

units.la: Postquam ubi senserunt se femina ducere cœlo, Atq; aliquem, mundum qui regat, esse Deum;
units.tr: After women perceived that they were led by heaven, and that there is some God who rules the world,

units.la: Tunc primum amplexi iuncti consortia coetus, Tegmina vicinis composuere casis: Vtq; alij alios de religione docerent, Contiguas pietas iussit habere domos. Hinc urbes struct, quarum est ante omnia munus, Asseruisse Deo, quam iubet esse fidem.
units.tr: Then for the first time they embraced the fellowship of joined assembly, and built roofs for their neighbouring huts. And so that they might teach one another about religion, piety bade them have adjoining homes. Hence they built cities, whose chief duty above all is to assert God, whom faith bids us acknowledge.

units.la: Dignum autem est memoria Aristotelis dictum in 1.lib.Politicorum: Ἀνθρωπός ἐστι φύσει πολιτικὸν ζῷον· ὁ δ᾽ ἄπολις διὰ φύσιν ἢ διὰ τύχην, ἤτοι φαῦλός ἐστιν ἢ ἀνθρωπος, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐν τῷ Ὁμήρου λοιδορηθείς, ἀφρήτωρ, ἀθέμιστος, ἀνέστιος, ἅμα γὰρ φύσει τοιοῦτος καὶ πολέμου ἐπιθυμητής, &c. Paulo post: ὁ μὲν ἀναγκαῖος κοινωνεῖν, ἢ μηδὲν ἀπόμενος διὰ αὐτάρκειαν, ἀλλὰ πόλεως μέρος ἢ θηρίον ἢ θεός.
units.tr: Worthy of remembrance is the saying of Aristotle in the first book of the Politics: Man is by nature a political animal; and he who is without a city, by nature and not by chance, is either base or more than human, as the one reviled in Homer, "without clan, without law, without hearth," for such a one is by nature both lover of war, etc. Shortly after: He who is unable to share in community, or has no need because of self-sufficiency, is either a part of a city or a beast or a god [ὁ μὲν ἀναγκαῖος κοινωνεῖν, ἢ μηδὲν ἀπόμενος διὰ αὐτάρκειαν, ἀλλὰ πόλεως μέρος ἢ θηρίον ἢ θεός].

units.la: 2. Quia non sine graui periculo uiuitur in solitudine extra aliorum hominū consortium, iuxta haec dicta: Gen.2.18.Di-xerat autem Iehouah Deus: Non est bonum hominem esse solum, propterea fa-ciam ei adiutorium, quod sit coram eo. Ecclesiast.4.9. Meliores sunt duo quàm unicus, quia est eis merces melior ex la-bore suo. 10. Quia si ceciderint, unus eri-get socium suum, uae ergo uni: quia cum ceciderit, non erit secundus ad subleuandum eum. Ac de ecclesiastica societate dicitur: ἐγκαταλείποντες τὴν ἐπισυναγωγὴν ἑαυτῶν, καθὼς ἔθος τισίν, ἀλλὰ παρακαλοῦντες. Heb.10.25.
units.tr: 2. Because it is not without grave danger that one lives in solitude, outside the fellowship of other men, according to these words: Gen. 2.18. The LORD God said: It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him. Eccles. 4.9. Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labour. 10. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him that is alone when he falleth, for he hath not another to help him up. And concerning ecclesiastical fellowship it is said: not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is, but exhorting one another [ἐγκαταλείποντες τὴν ἐπισυναγωγὴν ἑαυτῶν, καθὼς ἔθος τισίν, ἀλλὰ παρακαλοῦντες]. Heb. 10.25.

units.la: 3. Quia sua cuiq; uocatio magnificienda est, & sparta diuinitus delegata exornanda, nec de [illegible, ~12 letters] ferio cogitandum. 1.Cor.7.20. Unusquisque in qua uocatione uocatus fuit, maneat. Luc.19.13. Negociamini, inquit homo nobilis, donec veniam. At qui eremos petunt, & in ijs delitescunt, negociando lucrifacere eos non possunt, è quorum cospectu sese subducunt.
units.tr: 3. Because each person's calling is to be esteemed highly, and the place assigned to him by God is to be adorned, nor should one think of deserting it. 1 Cor. 7.20: Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called. Luke 19.13: "Trade," said the nobleman, "until I come." But those who seek deserts and hide themselves there cannot make gain by trading, since they withdraw from the sight of those for whose sake they would trade.

units.la: 4. Quia ut maxime demus, multa è libro naturæ in secessu disci posse: tamen cum exhortationibus crebris, seria increpatione, institutione familiari & fideli, nobis sit opus, horum omnium causa nō sunt nobis fugiendi cōgressus hominum piorum & in doctrina Ecclesiæ exercitatorum. Recte Plato: Inter homines, inquit, non inter arbores uiuendum est. Quod si Socrates, philosophiæ discendæ gratia, negabat sibi integrum concedere in loca amœna, in quę inuitabatur, dicés, Arbores non docere, sed homines: multò minus nobis piorum hominum contubernium bernium fugiendum est, cum in cœtibus pia ueraq; & discenda nobis & docenda sint, ad Dei gloriam, & nostram ac proximorum nostrorum instaurationem.
units.tr: 4. Because, however much we concede that many things can be learned in retirement from the book of nature, yet we need frequent exhortations, serious rebuke, and faithful and familiar instruction; for all these reasons we must not flee the gatherings of godly men who are trained in the teaching of the Church. Plato rightly says: "One must live among men, not among trees." And if Socrates, for the sake of learning philosophy, said that he did not allow himself to go into the pleasant places to which he was invited, saying that trees do not teach but men do, then much less must we flee the fellowship of godly men, since in their assemblies true and godly things are to be learned and taught by us, to the glory of God and the restoration of ourselves and our neighbours.

units.la: 5. Quia ut distractio membrorum in corpore humano, non solùm dedecori est toti corpori, sed etiam membrorum συμπα-θεῖ[?] tollit: ita cum distrahuntur Ecclesiæ ciues, qui sunt Christi capitis membra, solu-itur perfectionis uinculû, quod est charitas, & ansa charitatis officia præstandi sæpe tollitur. Econtrà, ut salutaris & honesta est partium corporis humani conspiratio, συμπνοΐα[?], κοινωνία[?]: ita Ecclesiæ summo ornamento est coniunctio ciuium, uno spiritu consentientium, nec se inuicem deserentium.
units.tr: 5. Because just as the dislocation of the members in the human body is not only a disgrace to the whole body but also takes away the sympathy of the members, so when the citizens of the Church, who are the members of Christ the head, are scattered, the bond of perfection, which is love, is loosed, and the occasion of performing the duties of love is often removed. Conversely, just as the harmonious agreement and fellowship of the parts of the human body is healthful and honourable, so for the Church the greatest ornament is the joining of citizens who agree in one spirit and do not desert one another.
