units.la: Quid igitur statuendum nobis est de Eremi-tis & Anachoretis, & in uniuer-sum de Monachis?
units.tr: What, then, are we to think of hermits and anchorites, and of monks in general?

units.la: Nequaquam eodem omnes loco habendi sunt: sed quid quenq; ad eiusmodi uitæ institutum perpulerit, & quomodo se in eo gesserit, considerandum est.
units.tr: They are by no means all to be held in the same regard. Rather, we must consider what drove each person to adopt this kind of life, and how he conducted himself in it.

units.la: Si qui, tyrannis θηριομάχοις[?] perfequutione aduersus fideles exercentibus, neglectis facultatibus, in solitudines uitæ tuendæ caufla sese receperunt,&in eis miferri- mam uitam egerunt: commiseratione, fi afflictiones: laude autem,fi uirtutem in fi de spe&es, digni sunt. Notum enim est illud Apostolicum di&um: Oberrauerut cum ouillis & caprinis pellibus,destituti, oppressi,male habiti,quibus indignus e- rat mundus,in defertis errantes,& montibus ac speluncis & cauernis terrę: Heb. 11.37.38. Nihil autem dubium est hosce, fi modo per sæuitiam tyrannorum licuif- set,ad sua redire paratos fuisse, ac oppor- tunitate oblata pie usos esse, ut uel unius Heliae exemplum monet.
units.tr: Those who, when tyrants waged war on the faithful, abandoned their property and withdrew into deserts to save their lives, and lived there in great misery, deserve pity if they were afflicted and praise if they kept faith and hope. The apostle's words are well known: "They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, of whom the world was not worthy, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and holes of the earth" (Heb. 11:37, 38). There is no doubt that these people, if the cruelty of the tyrants had allowed it, would have been ready to return to their homes, and would have taken the first opportunity to do so, as the example of Elijah alone shows.

units.la: Proxime ad illos accessisse uidentur, qui praepotentibus æmulis,& armatis au &oritate publica, [illegible, ~16 letters] bi pacis caussa cedendum iudicauerunt, ne praefentia sua Ecclesijs maiores motus & turbas etiam inuiti parerent: & ut liberius pijs studijs, ac suæ aliorumq; institutioni operam dare possent. In horũ numero fuerunt Hieronymus Stridonen fis, & Gregorius Naziazenus, & alij quidam: qui tamé non deerant suo muneri, cum & sacros libros uiua uoce in coetu piorum auditorum,& eruditis commentarijs, in illis suis cœnobijs exponeret, & nequaquam operâ suam Ecclesiæ, si quan do fideli illorum ministerio ei opus esset, denegarent.
units.tr: Those come closest to them who, when powerful enemies and armed public authority pressed hard upon them, judged that for the sake of peace they should yield, so that their presence would not, even against their will, stir up greater disturbances and tumults in the churches, and so that they could devote themselves more freely to pious studies and to the instruction of themselves and others. Among these were Jerome of Stridon, Gregory of Nazianzus, and some others. Yet they did not fail in their office: they expounded the sacred books by living voice to assemblies of pious hearers, and by learned commentaries, in those monasteries of theirs, and they never withheld their labour from the Church whenever it needed their faithful service.

units.la: Si qui autem uel tædio & fastidio com munium in uita humana & Repub. æ- rumnarum & difficultatum, uel uanisi- ma meritorum uitæ monachalis fiducia, uel deniq; uentris ocijq; studio moti,su- is desertis, nemorum latebras & cœno- biorum fecerunt captauerunt, eos Timo- nis μισανθρώπως, & agrestis cuiusdam Ono- phrij (quem fingunt totos 60 annos ho- minem alium non conspicatum fuisse) imitatores & uerè feruû pecus esse, quis dubitet? Vel enim ὑπερόπτης, uel uana super- stitio, eos ad istud nunquam à Deo præ- ceptum uitæ genus impellit: quibus de caussis digni sunt, qui uelut καθαρμάτα, & humani generis purgamenta, è societate hominum submoueantur, & reatus sui fi- gna, rasum uerticem, cucullam, restim, & alia desertionis suæ symbola portent.
units.tr: As for those who, moved either by weariness and disgust at the common troubles and difficulties of human life and of the commonwealth, or by the empty confidence in the merits of the monastic life, or finally by a love of belly and idleness, chose the hidden corners of woods and the cloisters of their own deserted places, who doubts that they are imitators of Timon, who was misanthropic, and of a certain rustic Onophrius (whom they imagine did not see another human being for sixty years), and truly a herd of slaves? For either arrogant contempt or vain superstition drives them to this way of life, which God never commanded. For these reasons they deserve to be removed from human society as the refuse and offscourings of the human race, and to bear as marks of their guilt a shaved crown, a cowl, a cord, and the other badges of their desertion.

units.la: VERSVS VI.
units.tr: Verse 6

units.la: Et præparauit Iehouah Deus cucurbi- tam, quæ ascendit super Ionam, ut esset um- bra bra capiti eius, ut erueret eum a malo eius. Latatus est itaq; Ionah ob cucurbitam laeticia magna.
units.tr: And Jehovah God prepared a gourd, which came up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head, to deliver him from his evil. So Jonah rejoiced over the gourd with great gladness.

units.la: De uoce Kikaion non existimo mihi uerbosè rhetoricâdum, cum ne quidem Hebraeis de ea coueniat. Malo autem diui Hieronymi uerba de illa dictione uobis recitare. Pro cucurbita siue hedera, in Hebraeo legimus קִיקָיוֹן[?] Kikaion: quae etiâ lingua Syra & Punica Elkeroa dicitur. Est autè genus uirgulti uel arbusculę, lata habes folia in modu pampini, & umbrâ denfisimam, suo trunco fe sustinens: quae in Palaestina creberrimè nascitur, & maximè in arenosis locis: mirûq; in modum, si sementem in terram ieceris, citò confota consurgit in arborè, & intra paucos dies, quam herbam uideras, arbuscu-lam conspicis. Paulo post: Cucurbita & hedera huius naturae sunt, ut per terram reptent: & abfq; furcis seu adminiculis, quibus innituntur, altiora non appetant. Quomodo igitur, ignorate Prophe ta, cucurbita in una noctè consurges umbracu-lü praebuit, quae natura nô habet sine per gulis & calamis uel hastilibus in sublime consurgere? Kikaion autem cum in ortu subito miraculum præbuerit,& potentiâ ostéderit Dei in protectione uirentis um braculi, & naturam suam sequuta est.
units.tr: I do not think I should spend many words on the word Kikaion, since even the Hebrews do not agree about it. I prefer to recite to you the words of the blessed Jerome about that term. For "gourd" or "ivy" we read in the Hebrew Kikaion [קִיקָיוֹן], which in Syriac and Punic is called Elkeroa. It is a kind of shrub or small tree, with broad leaves like a vine tendril and very dense shade, supporting itself on its own trunk. It grows most abundantly in Palestine, especially in sandy places, and remarkably, if you throw the seed into the ground, it quickly springs up into a tree, and within a few days the little plant you had seen has become a small tree. A little later: gourds and ivy are of such a nature that they creep over the ground and do not reach higher unless they have forks or supports to lean on. How then, ignorant prophet, could a gourd in one night rise up and provide a shade, when by nature it cannot rise on high without props and canes or stakes? But the Kikaion, though it presented a sudden miracle in its growth and showed God's power in protecting the green shade, nevertheless followed its own nature.

units.la: THESIS.
units.tr: Thesis

units.la: Cum nihil eorū quæ homini eueniût, fortuitū,sed omnia θεόπεμπτα haberi debe ant:non tam corporalia bona & commo- da,quàm etiam alia Dei opera, nobis erū diendis & exhilarandis plurimum serui- re,existimâdum est. Recte sane Iobus or- batus liberis,& fortunis exutus: Bonum, dicebat,accepimus à Deo, & malum nō suscipiemus?Iob.2.10.
units.tr: Since nothing that befalls a man is by chance, but all things must be regarded as sent by God, we must judge that not only bodily goods and advantages but also other works of God serve greatly to instruct and gladden us. Job rightly, bereft of his children and stripped of his fortune, said: "Shall we receive good from God and not receive evil?" (Job 2:10).

units.la: Cæterum in hac thesi hæc ἱερὰ λόγια no- bis annotanda sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, in this thesis the following sacred sayings are to be noted for us.

units.la: 1. Totum hoc mundi theatrum,& natu- ræ parientis fructus sic nobis spectandi sunt, ut interim Opifex & Dominus na- turæ agnoscatur & celebretur.iuxta hæc dicta: Psal.19.1. Cœli enarrât gloriam Dei, & opus manuum eius annunciat expan- sio,&c. Act.14.17. Deus non passus est se esse expertem testimonij, nobis benefa- ciendo,dans nobis cœlitus pluuias & tem- pora fructifera,imples cibo & lætitia cor- da nostra. Actor.17.27. Ζητεῖν τὸν θεὸν, εἰ ἄρα γε ψηλαφήσειαν αὐτὸν καὶ εὕροιεν, καίτοι γε οὐ μακρὰν ἀπὸ μακρὰν
units.tr: 1. This whole theatre of the world and the fruit of fertile nature are to be viewed in such a way that, meanwhile, the Maker and Lord of nature is acknowledged and celebrated, according to these sayings: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows forth the work of his hands" (Ps. 19:1). "God did not leave himself without witness, doing us good, giving us rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness" (Acts 14:17). "That they should seek God, if perhaps they might feel after him and find him, though indeed he is not far from each one of us" (Acts 17:27) [Ζητεῖν τὸν θεὸν, εἰ ἄρα γε ψηλαφήσειαν αὐτὸν καὶ εὕροιεν, καίτοι γε οὐ μακρὰν ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν ὑπάρχοντα].

units.la: ὁ μακάριος ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν ὑπαρχόντα, &c.
units.tr: [ὁ μακάριος ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν ὑπαρχόντα, &c.] ...&c.

units.la: 2. Vt nec solis naturę uiribus, nec etiam casu bona naturalia & alia commoda huius uitæ sparguntur, sed prouidentia diuina κατὰ μέτρον omnia dispensantur: sic ea miscentur & temperantur malis & incommodis quibusdam, quæ etiam nō sunt αὐτὸν τινὸς συγγνώμης.
units.tr: 2. Just as natural goods and the other conveniences of this life are dispensed not by the powers of nature alone, nor by chance, but are all distributed by divine providence in measure, so they are mingled and tempered with certain evils and inconveniences, which are also not deserving of any indulgence.

units.la: Humanarum rerum necessariū quod-dam temperamentum esse, consensus omnium intelligentium, & experientia uni-uersalis testantur. Est enim hominum generi luctandum & laborandum inter uitam & mortem, spem & metum, bona & mala, commoda & incommoda, uelut inter contrarios fluctus.Diuinitus autem ita comparatum esse, quis sanus, finem rerum istarum intuens, non uideat? Res secundæ animum addunt, spem fouent, mitigant sensum dolorum quem aduersa pariunt. Hæc autem modestos & cautos efficiunt. Dona Dei, quæ parturiente rerum natura nobis subministrantur, uelut large Dei manu percipere oportet cum gratiarum actione: non autem partim naturæ uiribus, partim nostris meritis accepta ferre.
units.tr: That a certain necessary mixture of human affairs exists is attested by the agreement of all thinking people and by universal experience. For the human race must struggle and labour between life and death, hope and fear, good and evil, advantage and disadvantage, as between opposing waves. That this has been ordained by God, who that is sane, looking to the end of these things, does not see? Prosperous circumstances encourage the mind, nurture hope, and soften the sense of pain that adversity brings. Adversity, however, makes us modest and cautious. The gifts of God, which are supplied to us while nature is in labour, we ought to receive as from the generous hand of God, with thanksgiving, and not to ascribe them partly to the powers of nature and partly to our own merits.

units.la: 3. Nec solùm ab iis rebus quae carni gratae sunt, sed etiam ab iis quae eidem insuaues[?] & molestae sunt, fructum nobis percipere convenit. Monent enim, Deum nequaquam esse ἐπιφθαλμον[?], sed alias quidem gratiam suam benedicendo, alias iustum iudicium maledicedo declarare: eoq; nobis & amandum & reverendum esse.
units.tr: 3. We should derive fruit not only from those things which are pleasing to the flesh, but also from those which are unpleasant and troublesome to it. For they remind us that God is by no means envious, but declares his grace by blessing in one way and his just judgment by cursing in another, and therefore he is to be both loved and revered by us.

units.la: Ac si in nosmetipsos descenderimus, facile deprehedemus, eam esse nostram φιλαυτίαν, tam etiam φιλοδοξίας[?] nos esse, ut nunquam non luxurient animi nostri in rebus secundis. Ideo Deus sensu rerum aduersarum, ad agnitionem nostrae infir-mitatis, & (ut συναλλάσσῃ[?] omnia comple-ctar) vanitatis nos adducit.
units.tr: And if we descend into ourselves, we shall readily perceive that we are so full of our self-love and love of glory that our minds never cease to run riot in prosperous circumstances. Therefore God, by the sense of adverse things, leads us to the recognition of our weakness and (to sum up everything in one word) of our vanity.

units.la: 4. Non tam autem nostro commodo, quàm alieno, nos delectari convenit. Vult enim Deus, nos non ea solùm quae nostra sunt, sed etiam ea quae sunt aliorum, studiosè quaerere, aliorum utilitati & aedificationi servire. Itaq; humanum quiddam Ionas passus est, cum ob cucurbitae umbraculum gauderet: non autè ob Ni-nivitarum incolumitatem, & poenitentiae donum eius concessum, laetaretur.
units.tr: 4. We ought to take delight not so much in our own advantage as in that of others. For God wills that we seek diligently not only what is ours but also what belongs to others, and serve the usefulness and edification of others. Thus Jonah suffered something human when he rejoiced over the shade of the gourd, but was not glad over the safety of the Ninevites and the grace of repentance granted to them.

units.la: 5. Affectus nobis sic moderandi sunt, ne subitò &leuibus de caussis nobis i-psis dissimiles efficiamur. Ionas dolet metu infamiæ motus, læticia perfundi-tur ob insperatum, opportunum tamen, umbraculum:inuocat Deum,litigat pro-pemodum cum eodem,&c.Hæc sanè in-digna sunt cordato Dei seruo.
units.tr: 5. Our affections are to be so moderated that we are not suddenly and for slight reasons made unlike ourselves. Jonah grieves, moved by fear of disgrace; he is overwhelmed with joy over an unexpected, though timely, shade; he calls upon God and almost quarrels with him, and so on. Surely these things are unworthy of a thoughtful servant of God.

units.la: VERSVS VII.
units.tr: VERSE 7.

units.la: Præparauit autem Deus ipse uermem, ascendente aurora postero die, & percussit cucurbitam,quæ aruit.
units.tr: And God prepared a worm when the dawn rose the next day, and it struck the gourd, so that it withered.

units.la: THESIS PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST THESIS.

units.la: Corporalia bona & commoda,quibus utuntur homines,Deus,qui ea dat,idque uel mediatè uel immediatè, eadem,cum ei uisum est,aufert:ut caduca & πρόσκαιρα [?] esse,reipsa intelligamus.
units.tr: The bodily goods and comforts which people enjoy are given by God, who also takes them away again, whenever it pleases him, whether through intermediaries or directly. We should thereby actually understand them to be perishable and transitory [πρόσκαιρα].

units.la: Iob: Nudus,inquit,egressus sum ex utero matris meæ, & nudus reuertar illuc: Iehouah dedit,& Iehouah abstulit.sit no-men Iehouæ benedictum.cap.1.21.
units.tr: Job: "Naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked I shall return there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Job 1:21.

units.la: Psal.107. inductione idem ostendit,& inter alia uersu 38. Et benedicit eis,& multiplicatur ualde,&iumenta ipsorum non minuit.
units.tr: Psalm 107 shows the same by induction, and among other things at verse 38: "And he blesses them, and they are greatly multiplied, and he does not diminish their cattle."

units.la: Idem docetur toto 28.cap.Deuteron.
units.tr: The same is taught throughout Deuteronomy chapter 28.

units.la: Hos.2.8. Etipsa nesciebat, quòd ego dedissem ei frumentum & vinum & oleum: immò argentum quod ei multiplicaueram, & aurum fecerunt in Baal. 9.Idcirco conuertar, & sumam frumenti meum tempore suo, & vinum meum temporefuo: auferamq; lanam meam & linū meum, quae dederam ad tegendam ignominiam eius.
units.tr: Hos. 2:8. "And she did not know that I had given her grain, wine and oil, indeed the silver which I had multiplied for her and the gold, which they made into Baal. 9. Therefore I will turn back and take my grain in its time and my wine in its time, and I will take away my wool and my linen, which I had given to cover her shame."

units.la: 1.Tim.6.7.Nihil in mudum intissimus[?], uidelicet nec efferre quicquam possumus.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 6:7. "For we brought nothing into this world, and certainly we can carry nothing out."

units.la: §. Sed habentes alimenta, & quibus tegamur, his contenti sumus.
units.tr: "But having food and clothing, with these we are content."

units.la: THESIS SECVNDA.
units.tr: SECOND THESIS.

units.la: Bruta animatia, plantae, & ea quae è terra nascuntur, Dei prouidentiae non funte-ximenda[?], & cum aliquid agunt, & cum patiuntur.
units.tr: Brute animals, plants, and the things that grow out of the earth are not to be excluded from God's providence, both when they act and when they suffer.

units.la: Ita rem habere, inductione adhibita ostendemus.
units.tr: That this is so we will show by induction.

units.la: 1. Ortus & conseruatio specierum statuum omnium non nisi Deo accepta ferri debent. Gen.1. Et Psal.36.7. Hominem & animal feruas Iehouah. Psal.104.14. Deus germinare facit fœnum pro iumentis, herbam ad usum hominum, ut educat panem e terra.
units.tr: 1. The origin and preservation of all kinds of species must be credited wholly to God. Gen. 1; and Psalm 36:7: "Man and beast you preserve, O LORD." Psalm 104:14: God causes grass to grow for the cattle and herbs for the use of man, that he may bring forth bread from the earth.

units.la: 2. Ornatus & usus plantarū & animalium, hominū generi à Deo concessus, idē te stātur: iuxta hęc dicta. Psal.8.7. Dominari fecisti ipsum (hominem) operibus manuum tuarū: omnia posuisti sub pedibus eius: 8. pecudes & boues, uniuersa ipsa, & etiam bestias agrestes: 9. uolucres cœli, & pisces maris, &c. Matt.6.28. Perdiscite quomodo lilia agri crescant: non faligantur, neque nent. 29. Sed dico uobis, quod ne Solomon quidem in uniuersa sua gloria sic amictus fuit, ut unū existis.
units.tr: 2. The adornment and use of plants and animals, granted by God to the human race, bear witness to the same, according to these sayings. Psalm 8:7: "You made him (man) to rule over the works of your hands; you put all things under his feet; 8. sheep and oxen, all of them, and also the wild beasts; 9. the birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea," etc. Matt. 6:28: "Learn how the lilies of the field grow; they neither toil nor spin. 29. But I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these."

units.la: 3. Interitus etiam abiectissimorum animalium & plantarum, non citra prouidentiam accidit. iuxta hæc dicta:
units.tr: 3. The death even of the most abject animals and plants does not happen apart from providence, according to these sayings:

units.la: Matt.10.29. Nónne duo passerculi assa rio ueneunt? & unus ex illis nō cadet hu mi sine patre uestro.
units.tr: Matt. 10:29. "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And one of them shall not fall to the ground without your Father."

units.la: Matt.6.30. Quod si herbam agri, quæ hodie exstat & cras in clibanū mittitur, Deus ita circumuestit, nónne uos multò magis, ô exigua fide præditi?
units.tr: Matt. 6:30. "But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?"

units.la: Mirificè sanè mihi arridēt elegantissimi uersus Stigelij: Obuia nam pićti lustrans miracula campi, Naturæ intueor dum parientis opes: Aut mihi planta suis nume demonstrat ab herbis,
units.tr: The most elegant verses of Stigelius delight me wonderfully: Roaming over the marvels of the flowering field, I behold the riches of Nature giving birth; or a plant among its herbs shows me God by its nod;

units.la: PræscnPræsentemq; refert una vel herba Deum: Aut operis series auctorem tota recensèt, Qui facit & læto cuncta vigore fovet. Emicat ex ipsis divina potentia terris, Et levis est cespes qui probat esse Deum.
units.tr: or a single herb presents God to us as present; or the whole series of works recounts its maker, who creates all things and cherishes them with joyful vigour. Divine power shines forth from the very lands, and the light turf proves that God exists.

units.la: Et hoc loco in Ionæ historia, dicitur divinitùs factum, ut erosa àverme cucurbita aresceret.
units.tr: And in this passage of Jonah's history it is said that the gourd, eaten away by the worm, withered by divine action.

units.la: 4. Bestiarum quinetiam & herbarum ministerio Deus quandoq; utitur ad exercenda iudicia sua mala.
units.tr: 4. God also sometimes uses the ministry of beasts and herbs to carry out his judgments.

units.la: Ezech.14.15. Si bestiam malam transire fecero per terram, & orbauerit eam,& fuerit desolata absq; transeunte propter bestiam.
units.tr: Ezek. 14:15. "If I cause an evil beast to pass through the land, and it bereaves it, and it is made desolate, so that no one passes through because of the beast."

units.la: Huc facit narratio de leone, qui occidit Prophetam missum in Bethel ad Regem Iarobeamum: 1.Reg.13.24. Et illa de ursis narratio, qui lacerauerunt quadraginta duos pueros, qui contumelia affecerant Elizæum prophetam: 2.Reg.2.24.
units.tr: To this belongs the account of the lion that killed the prophet sent to Bethel to King Jeroboam, 1 Kings 13:24; and that account of the bears that tore forty-two boys who had mocked the prophet Elisha, 2 Kings 2:24.

units.la: 5. Nec raró brutorum opera ad gloriam suam utitur Deus, ut suis servis benefaciat: vel illorum θηριότητα[?] & immanitatem sic coercet, ut eos lædere nō ausint. Exemplo sunt corui, panem & carnes Eliæ in deserto agenti adferentes, 1.Reg.17.6. & leones, qui non lacerauerunt Danielem in lacum leonum missum, etsi essent famelici,Dan.6.20.22. Saepe etiam Ethnicis θηριομάχοις[?] in fideles sæuientibus, bestiae alioquin immanes nō attigerunt sanctorum Martyrum corpora: ut est uidere in Historia Ecclesiastica Eusebij lib.8. cap. 7.cuius haec uerba sunt:
units.tr: 5. Not rarely, too, God uses the works of animals for his own glory, to benefit his servants, or so restrains their savagery and fierceness that they do not dare to harm them. Examples are the ravens bringing bread and meat to Elijah in the desert, 1 Kings 17:6; and the lions that did not tear Daniel, cast into the lions' den, although they were hungry, Dan. 6:20–22. Often too, when pagans who fought wild beasts raged against the faithful, beasts otherwise savage did not touch the bodies of the holy martyrs, as may be seen in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History, book 8, chapter 7, whose words are these:

units.la: [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~45 letters] τὸ φόβ[?]ος [?] αὖθις [?]
units.tr: [illegible in the scan]

units.la: 6. Medicamentis autem uim salutarem esse insitam, hoc Syracidæ testimonio probatur, cap.38.4. Dominus medicamenta procreauit de terra, & uir prudens nō abhorrebit abeis. 5.Nónne aqua à ligno accepit dulcedinem,ut potentia eius homini innotesceret? 6.Et ipse scientiam hominibus dedit,ut in mirabilibus suis gloriam consequatur. 7.Ipse fanat per hæc, atque hominis dolorem tollit. 8.Pharmacopola mixturas his suas temperat: neque ullum opera eius finem habent: 9.sed prosperitas ab eo demanat super universam terram.
units.tr: 6. That a healing power is implanted in medicines is proved by the testimony of Jesus the son of Sirach, chapter 38. 4. "The Lord created medicines from the earth, and a prudent man will not abhor them. 5. Did not water receive its sweetness from wood, so that its power might become known to men? 6. And he gave knowledge to men, that he might be glorified in his wonders. 7. By these he heals and takes away pain. 8. The apothecary makes his mixtures from these, and his works have no end; 9. and prosperity flows from him over the whole earth."

units.la: Idem iudicium est & de aliis omnibus, bus,quæ in historia animalium & plantarum [illegible, ~10 letters] tradi solent. Itaque etiam istorum ordinum creaturas,prouidentiæ uel eam ob caussam subijcimus, ut ipsi quoque discamus omnem curam nostrã conijcere in Dominum, cui nos & res nostræ præcipuè curæ sunt.
units.tr: The same judgment holds of all the others too, which are customarily set out in the natural history of animals and plants. Therefore we also subject the creatures of these kinds to providence, so that we ourselves may learn to cast all our care upon the Lord, to whom we and our affairs are especially dear.

units.la: VERSUS VIII.
units.tr: VERSE 8.

units.la: Fuit verò oriente Sole, præparavit Deus ventum orientalem vehementem, & per-cussit Sol caput Iona, qui astuabat, petivitq; animæ suæ ut moreretur, & dixit: Melior est mors mihi quàm vita mea.
units.tr: And when the sun had risen, God prepared a vehement east wind, and the sun beat upon the head of Jonah, so that he grew faint, and he asked that he might die, and said: It is better for me to die than to live.

units.la: THESIS.
units.tr: THESIS.

units.la: Neque verò vel corporis dolores & morbi, vel animi ægritudo, eò usque nos adducere debent, ut molestiæ omnis se-mel finiendæ gratia, fatalem vitæ nostræ periodum abbreviari velimus.
units.tr: Pains and diseases of the body, or sickness of the mind, ought not to drive us so far that, to be rid of our troubles all at once, we wish the appointed course of our life to be cut short.

units.la: Etenim, sententia Iacobi Apostoli, pro summo gaudio nobis ducendū est, quoties in tentationes varias inciderimus: probationem enim fidei nostræ parit pa-tientia, quę & perfectum opus habet: Iac. 1.2.3. Ac cum nostræ cum Christo συμμορφώσως [?] pars aliqua sit, mortificatio nostra per crucem & afflictiones, non est cur uel praepropera morte eam finiri uelimus. ἀ-πέρ [?] συμπάσχομεν [?], ἵνα καὶ συνδοξασθῶμεν [?]: Rom.
units.tr: For according to the saying of the Apostle James, we ought to count it pure joy whenever we fall into various temptations, since patience produces the proof of our faith, and patience has a perfect work (Jas. 1.2, 3). And since our conformity to Christ [συμμορφώσως] is partly our mortification through the cross and afflictions, there is no reason why we should wish it ended by an untimely death. "If we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified together" [συμπάσχομεν, ἵνα καὶ συνδοξασθῶμεν] (Rom. 8.17).

units.la: 8.17. Item: Fidus hic est sermo. nam si cum eo mortui sumus, cum eo etiam uiuemus: si toleramus, cum eo etiam regnabimus. 2. Tim. 2. 11. 12.
units.tr: "It is a faithful saying: for if we died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him" (2 Tim. 2.11, 12).

units.la: DE AEGRA VALETVDINE.
units.tr: ON ILL HEALTH.

units.la: Cum de ualetudine aduersa nobis propositum sit ἀμαθέστερον [?] καὶ σαφέστερον [?] agere, libet praemittere quaedam praeclara Scripturae diuinae dicta, sed tamen παρὰ [?] λόγια [?], ut pij adolescentes uidere possint, e quibus fontibus hausta sit tota haec doctrina, quam subijciemus. Psal. 41. 4. Ego dixi: Iehouah miserere mei: sana animam meam, quia peccaui tibi. Psal. 107. 17. Stulti alij propter uiam flagitiorum suorum, & propter iniquitates suas affligAuntur. 18. Omnem escam abominatur anima eorum: & appropinquant ad portam mortis, &c. Ioan. 5. 14. Ecce, sanus factus es: ne pecca amplius, ut ne quid deterius tibi contingat. 1. Cor. 11. 30. Propter rea inter uos multi sunt debiles & inuali di, & dormiunt multi. 21. Etenim si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non puniremur, &c. Et ecce, obtulerunt Christo paralyticum in lecto proiectum: quumq; uidisset Iesus fidem eorum, dixit paralytico: Confide fili, remissa sunt tibi peccata tua. Monent autem haec dicta, propter peccata Deum morbis & aliis afflictionibus nos castigare, ac resipiscentibus mederi peccatorum remissione, & ualetudinis pristinae dono: cum eiusdem sit percutere & sanare.
units.tr: Since we have set ourselves to treat of adverse health more clearly and more plainly [ἀμαθέστερον καὶ σαφέστερον], it is worth first setting out some outstanding sayings of divine Scripture, though placed beside the oracles [παρὰ λόγια], so that pious young people can see from which springs this whole teaching, which we shall set forth, has been drawn. Psalm 41.4: "I said, LORD, have mercy upon me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you." Psalm 107.17, 18: "Fools, because of the way of their transgressions, and because of their iniquities, are afflicted. Their soul abhors all food, and they draw near to the gates of death," etc. John 5.14: "Behold, you are made whole; sin no more, lest something worse befall you." 1 Cor. 11.30, 21: "For this reason many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep. For if we judged ourselves, we should not be judged," etc. And behold, they brought to Christ a paralytic lying on a bed; and when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: "Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven you" (Matt. 9.2). These sayings admonish that God chastises us with diseases and other afflictions on account of sins, and that, when we repent, he heals us by the remission of sins and by restoring our former health, since it is the same hand that strikes and heals.

units.la: Principiö illud obseruandum est, quot modis homo seu bene, seu male habere dicatur.
units.tr: First, it must be observed in how many ways a man is said to be well or ill.

units.la: 1. Optimè habet, qui mente sana in corpore sano praeditus est. Restè Menander, ὑγίεια [?] νῦς, ἀλλὰ [?] τῷ βίῳ ἄλυο, pronunciauit.
units.tr: 1. He is very well who has a sound mind in a sound body. Menander pronounced it thus: [ὑγίεια νῦς, ἀλλὰ τῷ βίῳ ἄλυο].

units.la: 2. Pesssimè autem habet, qui aegritudine animi & corporis morbis conficitur, id quod accidisse uidemus Ἀντιόχοις illis tyrannis, Antiocho Epiphani, Herodi magno, Galerio Imperatori, & multis aliis, quorū nonnulli σωληνοβρόγοι, & conscientiae doloribus excarnificati, miserè interiere.
units.tr: 2. He is worst off who is worn down by mental anguish and bodily disease, as happened to those tyrants like Antiochus, namely Antiochus Epiphanes, Herod the Great, the Emperor Galerius, and many others, some of whom, eaten by worms [σκωληκόβρωτοι] and tormented by the pangs of conscience, perished wretchedly.

units.la: 3. Malè habet, qui morbo corporis laborat. Ac uere dixit Hesiodus: Νόσοι δ' ἀνθρώποισιν ἐφ' ἡμέρῃ, αἱ δ' (αἱ δ')ἐπὶ νυκτὶ αὐτόματοι φοιτῶσι, λυγρὰ θνητοῖσι φέρουσαι.
units.tr: 3. He is ill who labours under a bodily disease. And Hesiod truly said: "Diseases come upon men by day, and others by night, wandering of their own accord, bringing woes to mortals" [Νοῦσοι δ' ἀνθρώποισιν ἐφ' ἡμέρῃ, αἱ δ' ἐπὶ νυκτὶ αὐτόματοι φοιτῶσι, λυγρὰ θνητοῖσι φέρουσαι].

units.la: 4. Peius autem habet, qui ægro est animo. Verè enim quidam apud Stobæum dixit: βέλτιόν ἐςι σῶμά γ' ἢ ψυχὴ νοσοῦσα.
units.tr: 4. Worse off is he who is sick in mind. For someone truly said in Stobaeus: "A sick soul is better than a sick body" [βέλτιόν ἐστι σῶμά γ' ἢ ψυχὴ νοσοῦσα].

units.la: Secundò, quæ sint caussæ efficientes tot tantorumq; malorum, quibus hominum natura est obnoxia, uideamus.
units.tr: Second, let us consider what are the efficient causes of so many and so great evils to which human nature is subject.

units.la: Si efficientem principem spectes, occurret Deus, quem penes est bonæ ualetudinis & inualetudinis, uitæ & mortis nostræ, arbitrium omne. Iuxta hæc dicta: Deut.28.27. Percutiet te Iehouah ulcere Ægypti, & morbis ani, & scabie, & pruritgine, quibus non possis curari. 28. Percutiet te Iehouah ametia, & cæcitate, & stupore mentis. Hac tristi comminatione animi & corporis morbos complexus est Deus. 1.Sam.2.6. Iehouah mortificat & uiuificat: deducit ad inferos, & reducit.
units.tr: If you look at the principal efficient cause, God presents himself, in whose power lies every decision about good and poor health, our life and death. In accordance with these words: "The LORD will smite you with the boil of Egypt, with the emerods, the scab and the itch, of which you cannot be cured" (Deut. 28.27). "The LORD will smite you with madness and blindness and confusion of mind" (28). With this grim threat God has embraced diseases of both body and mind. "The LORD kills and makes alive; he brings down to the grave and brings up" (1 Sam. 2.6).

units.la: Si efficientes famulantes caussas spectes, occurrent Satan, aeris intemperies, hominum intemperatia & peccata multiplicia, & aliæ quædam caussæ: quæ tamen seruiunt Dei consilio, si spectes huius destinatum.
units.tr: If you look at the secondary and serving causes, there will present themselves Satan, the intemperance of the air, human intemperance and manifold sins, and certain other causes; yet these serve God's counsel, if you consider its purpose.

units.la: Sæpe morbi Satanæ flagellum uocantur, & eius uincula. Marc.3.10. Multos enim sanauerat, adeo ut ruerent in eum, ut ipsum tangerent, quotquot tenebantur flagellis. Marc.5.29. Hæmorrhu-fa sensit corpore se sanatam esse ex eo flagello. Luc.13.16. Hanc aute filiam Abra-hæ, quam vinxerat Satan ecce decem & octo annos, non oportuit a vinculo isto solui die Sabbathi?
units.tr: Often diseases are called Satan's scourge and his chains. "For he had healed many, so that they pressed upon him to touch him, as many as were held by scourges" (Mark 3.10). "The woman with an issue of blood felt in her body that she was healed of that scourge" (Mark 5.29). "But this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound for eighteen years, ought she not to have been loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?" (Luke 13.16).

units.la: De æstu Solis lædente corpora nostra, exemplum habemus in hac ipsa historia de Ionah, qui arefacta hedera, propter Solis æstum doloribus capitis laborauit. Aliud exemplum de puerulo Sunamitidis filio, quę Elisæus resuscitauit, exstat 2.Reg.4.18.19.
units.tr: On the heat of the sun harming our bodies, we have an example in this very story of Jonah, who, when the ivy had withered, suffered pain in his head from the heat of the sun. Another example, of the little son of the Shunammite woman whom Elisha raised, is found in 2 Kings 4.18, 19.

units.la: De intemperantia, quæ multorum morborum causa est, obseruent Studiosi di-ftū[?] memorabile Prouerb.23.29. Cuinam uæ? cui (inquam) uæ? cui rixæ? cui murmur? cui vulnera absque causa? cui rubor oculorum erit? 30. His qui immorantur circa vinum, euntibus ad disquirendum miftū[?]. 31. Ne igitur intuearis vinū quod rubrum fit, quod det in calice colorem suum, agitet se probè. 32. In fine velut serpens mordebit, & velut regulus dolore afficiet.
units.tr: On intemperance, which is the cause of many diseases, let students note the memorable passage in Proverbs 23.29-32: "Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has contentions? Who has complaints? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Those who linger long over wine, who go to seek mixed wine. Do not look upon wine when it is red, when it gives its colour in the cup, when it goes down smoothly. In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder."

units.la: Etsi autem peccata sæpenumero cau-fæ[?] sunt fæ sunt inualetudinis & morborum, ut ex antea à me adductis Scripturæ sanctæ testimoniis liquet: tamen fatendum est, morbos interdum δοκιμασίας, non τιμωρίας esse: & etiam eximios Dei seruos graui-bus morbis explorari, uelut aurum igni examinari solet.
units.tr: Although sins are often the causes of ill health and diseases, as is clear from the testimonies of Holy Scripture I have already adduced, yet it must be admitted that diseases are sometimes for trial [δοκιμασίας], not for punishment [τιμωρίας], and that even outstanding servants of God are tested by grievous diseases, just as gold is commonly tested by fire.

units.la: De aeris intemperie, & uicisitudine tempestatum, recte monet hi ueteris poetæ uersus:
units.tr: Concerning the unsettled state of the air and the changes of the weather, the following verses of an ancient poet rightly warn:

units.la: Sæpe sub autumno, cum formosissimus annus, Plenaq; purpureo subrubet uua mero: Cum modo frigoribus premimur, modo soluimur æstu, Aere non certo corpora languor habet.
units.tr: Often in autumn, when the year is most lovely and the full grape blushes with purple wine, now we are pressed by cold, now loosened by heat; in uncertain air the body is held by languor.

units.la: Sed ut de efficientibus istis causis nihil amplius dicam, uice coronidis addam elegantes uersus Euripidis, qui apud Sto-bæum exstant:
units.tr: But so that I may say no more about these efficient causes, I will add, as a finishing touch, the elegant verses of Euripides which are found in Stobaeus:

units.la: Νῆσοι δὲ θνητῶν μὲν εἰσ' αὐθαίρετοι [?] ἀλλ' ἐν θεῖς πάσχουσιν ἀλλὰ τῷ νόμῳ [?] ἰώμεθ' αὐτάς. ἀλλά σοι λέξω θέλω, [?] εἰ θεοί τι ἀρῶσιν ἀχρόνῳ ἐστὶ θεοί. [?]
units.tr: [Νῆσοι δὲ θνητῶν μὲν εἰσ' αὐθαίρετοι, ἀλλ' ἐν θεῖς πάσχουσιν, ἀλλὰ τῷ νόμῳ ἰώμεθ' αὐτάς. ἀλλά σοι λέξω θέλω, εἰ θεοί τι ἀρῶσιν ἀχρόνῳ ἐστὶ θεοί.] The diseases of mortals are not self-caused; they come from the gods, yet we heal them by custom. But I will tell you what I wish, if the gods do anything, they are not without time.

units.la: Postremo & de remediis eorumq; auctore cogitandum est.
units.tr: Lastly, we must also consider the remedies and their author.

units.la: Deus remittit peccata nostra, & sanat omnes infirmitates nostras: redimit de foueæ fouea uita nostrâ, & coronat nos miseri-cordia & miserationibus. Pfal.103.3.&4. Sanat autem ad fe conuersos & obedientes legi, iuxta dictum: Si obediendo obedieris uoci Iehouae Dei tui,& rectum in oculis eius feceris, & aures praebueris praeceptis eius,custodierisq; omnia statu-ta eius: uniuersum morbum quem posui in Ægypto,non ponam super te:quia ego Iehouah sanans te.Exod.15.26.
units.tr: God forgives our sins and heals all our infirmities; he redeems our life from the pit and crowns us with mercy and compassion (Ps. 103.3, 4). He heals, moreover, those who turn to him and obey the law, according to the saying: "If you diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in his eyes, and give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put upon you none of the diseases which I put upon Egypt; for I am the LORD who heals you" (Exod. 15.26).

units.la: Idq; hac methodo praestat,ut primum quidem animae per remissionem peccatorum & consolationem Spiritus sancti, deinde etiam corporis morbis & dolori-bus medeatur. Hanc medendi rationem Siracides pulcre describit cap.38.γρωμολ[?] υἱας[?] uerf.9. Fili,ne praetermittas in mor-bo tuo, ut Deum ores, & ipse te sanabit. 10.Recede à delicto,& manum dirige:atque ab omni peccato cor emunda. 11.Suf-fimentu suauis odoris adole,monumen-tumq; similaginis: opimumq; munus offer, ut qui priores non feras. 12.Deinde medico locum des, ut cuius creator Deus est: non discedat abs te,quoniam ipsius indiges. 13.Euenit cum medicorum quoq; manus successum consequantur.
units.tr: In this way he provides for the healing of the soul first, through the forgiveness of sins and the consolation of the Holy Spirit, and then also for the diseases and pains of the body. Sirach describes this method of healing well in chapter 38, verse 9: "My son, do not neglect yourself in your sickness, but pray to the Lord, and he will heal you. (10) Turn away from wrongdoing, and direct your hands aright, and cleanse your heart from every sin. (11) Offer a pleasing fragrance and a memorial of fine flour, and a rich offering, as far as you are able. (12) Then give the physician his place, for the Lord created him, and let him not leave you, for you need him. (13) There are times when success comes from the hands of physicians too."

units.la: 14. Nam & ipsi Dominum orant, ut levamentum sibi fortunet, cauffaq; vitæ curationem. 15. Qui in creatorem suum peccauerit, in manus medici incidet.
units.tr: (14) "For they also pray to the Lord, that he may grant them relief and success in healing. (15) He who sins against his Maker will fall into the hands of the physician."

units.la: Hæc autem omnia alias mediate, adhibito ministerio feruorum suorum, alias immediate Dominus (pro immensa sua bonitate &φιλανθρωπία) efficit, ut hæc dicta & exempla ostendunt:
units.tr: Whether the Lord brings all these things about mediately, through the ministry of his servants, or immediately (by his immense goodness and philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία]), these sayings and examples show:

units.la: Jac.5.14. Infirmatur quis inter vos? accersat presbyteros Ecclesiæ, & orent pro eo, ungentes eum oleo in nomine Domini. 15. Et oratio fidei seruabit laborantem, erigetq; eum Dominus, &c.
units.tr: Jac.5.14. Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. 15. And the prayer of faith will save the one who labours, and the Lord will raise him up, etc.

units.la: Exemplum commemorabile de paralytico, cui primo peccata remissa sunt, ac deinde valetudo & sanitas restituta, occurrit Matt.9.2.
units.tr: A memorable example is the paralytic, whose sins were first forgiven and then his health and soundness restored, at Matt.9.2.

units.la: Sed illis omisisis, hoc etiam observemus, cuius Jonæ exemplum nos præcipue admonet, etiam atq; etiam nobis videndum, quid nobis & quid alijs eveniat secundum divinę voluntatis propositum. Intentos enim in Dei opera esse oportet. juxta illud: Vident hæc recti, & lætantur: & omnis iniquitas claudit os suum. Quis sapiens, & observabit hæc, & aduertet animum ad misericordias leho uæ?Psal.107.42.43.
units.tr: But setting those aside, let us also observe this, which the example of Jonah especially warns us about: we must again and again see what happens to us and to others according to the purpose of the divine will. For we ought to be attentive to the works of God, according to that saying: "The upright see these things and rejoice, and all iniquity shuts its mouth. Who is wise, and will observe these things and consider the mercies of the Lord?" Psal.107.42.43.

units.la: VERSVS IX.
units.tr: VERSE 9.

units.la: Dixit itaq; Deus ad Ionam: Nonne ue-hemens ira est tibi ob cucurbitam? Qui respondit: Melior est mors mihi, quàm uita mea.
units.tr: So God said to Jonah: Is your anger over the gourd so intense? He answered: It is better for me to die than to live.

units.la: Hactenus magna ex parte historia, de dictis,factis & affectibus Ionæ prophetæ, tradita fuit, ut ἀφορμὴ Chriæ,quæ nunc tra-ctanda erit,tantò effet illustrior. Nunc ipsa quoque Chria proponitur.
units.tr: Hitherto the history has been related, for the most part, of the sayings, deeds and feelings of the prophet Jonah, so that the occasion for the chreia, which is now to be treated, might be the more illustrious. Now the chreia itself is set forth.

units.la: Duo autem obseruabimus,Interroga-tionem & Refponsionem.
units.tr: We shall observe two things: the question and the answer.

units.la: Interrogatio : Itáne uehementer com-motus es,propterea quòd exaruit tua il-la cucurbita? Iram interdum pro tristicia fumi, liquet uel ex illo dicto: Caligauit præ ira oculus meus,inueterauit propter omnes inimicos meos:Psal.6.8.Nec sanè ἀπροσδιόνυσον[?] fuerit, de ira pariter & moe-rore ista interpretari. Doluit enim Ionæ, quòd mendax à nonnullis haberi posset: & quòd Niniuitæ resipiscentes, exemplo suo μετανοοῦντας[?] in populo Israel dánarent.
units.tr: Question: Are you so greatly moved because that gourd of yours has withered? That anger is sometimes taken for sadness is clear even from that saying: "My eye has wasted away with anger, grown old because of all my enemies" (Psal.6.8). Nor would it be out of place to interpret it as both anger and grief. For Jonah grieved that he might be thought a liar by some, and that the Ninevites, repenting, would by his example condemn the people of Israel.

units.la: In hac autem interrogatione latet syllogifmus ἐπιζημίωσις[?], quo graviter, & quidem optimo iure, perstringitur Ionas.
units.tr: In this question lies a hidden syllogism, by which Jonah is sharply and with the best right rebuked.

units.la: Non est viri tum pij, tum prudetis, re maxima non affici, minima & levicula maiorem in modum commoveri. Atqui tu incolumitate Ninivitarum, quibus resipi scentibus peperci, non sic afficeris, ut par erat. Rursum, illo incomodo, quod arescente cucurbita tua ad te redijt, sic commoveris, ut nihil non tibi displiceat, & ut non cogites[?] divinitus ista fieri, nec des gloriam Deo. Hac igitur in parte nec pie, nec prudenter agis: quod quàm nō te deceat, etiam atque etiam vide.
units.tr: It is not the mark of a man both pious and prudent to be affected by nothing great, yet to be moved beyond measure by the smallest and slightest matters. But you are not affected by the safety of the Ninevites, whom you spared when they repented, as you ought to have been. Again, by that inconvenience, that your gourd withered and came back upon you, you are so moved that nothing pleases you, and you do not reflect that these things happen by divine will, nor give glory to God. In this part, then, you act neither piously nor prudently. Consider well how little this becomes you.

units.la: Neque vero est, cur Ionæ magis quàm nobis, tale aliquid accidere potuisse opinemur. Dum enim nimium sane φιλαύτοι[?], nostrisq; commodis addicti, nobis cosul tum volumus: quid, te quaesso, saepius nobis, quàm hoc ipsum accidit, ut de nobis tantum foliciti aliena negligamus? Deploramus nostras miserias: aliorum instaurationem & emendationem, quasi ea nihil ad nos pertineat, sufq; deq; facimus. Quasi vero quid de eorum, qui in Christo nobis concorpores sunt, incolumitate, deq; Dei gloria, quae illis resipiscentibus illustratur, fiat, parum admodum nostra interfit expendere.
units.tr: Nor is there reason to think such a thing could happen to Jonah more than to us. For while we, too much given to self-regard and devoted to our own advantages, want to be consulted on our own behalf: what, I ask you, happens to us more often than this, that we, anxious only about ourselves, neglect the affairs of others? We lament our own miseries, but the restoration and amendment of others we treat as if it had nothing to do with us, and we make light of it. As if indeed it mattered little to us to weigh the safety of those who are our fellow members in Christ, and the glory of God which is displayed in their repentance.

units.la: Responsio Ionae: Melior est mors mihi, quàm uita mea.
units.tr: Jonah's answer: It is better for me to die than to live.

units.la: Non respondet ad rogatū, sed id quod de uita & morte carnis intelligentia suggerebat, μεμψίμοιρος repetit, eò uidelicet res suas adductas studio seruiendi Deo, ut mori eum expediat, quàm uiuere.
units.tr: He does not answer the question, but, complaining of his lot [μεμψίμοιρος], repeats what his fleshly understanding suggested about life and death: namely, that his affairs have been brought to such a pass by his zeal for serving God that it is better for him to die than to live.

units.la: Etsi autem dicta & facta Prophetarū, quoad eius fieri potest, ἐπιεικῶς [?] nobis interpretanda sunt: sicubi tamen grauius impegerunt, nō sunt, tanquam si fuissent ἀναμαρτήτοι [?], excusandi. Quis autem pius Ionam Deo respōsantem excusset, cū defensio eius fuerit cōtumeliosa in Deum? Nam si quis prefsius rem perpendat, animaduertet sic fuisse argumētatum: Quicunque fidelissimos suos seruos, dum illi officium faciunt, sic tractat, ut mors eis exoptata, uita uerò acerba sit, ei quis homo sanus libenter seruiat? Atqui tu Domine sic me nunc tractas. Hanc Minorē, in qua τὸ ὑπόλοιπον [?] latet, consultò praetermisit Ionas. Difficile itaq;, immò periculosum est tibi seruire: ac me quod attinet, praestat moriendo semel istis malis defungi, fungi, quàm diutius viuentem sæpius ad eundem lapidem impingere.
units.tr: Although the sayings and deeds of the prophets are, as far as possible, to be interpreted charitably for us, yet where they have stumbled more heavily they are not to be excused as if they had been free from sin. Yet what pious man would excuse Jonah for answering God, when his defence was insulting toward God? For if anyone weighs the matter more closely, he will see that Jonah argued thus: whoever treats his most faithful servants, while they perform their duty, so that death is desired by them and life is bitter, whom would a sane man willingly serve? But you, Lord, now treat me so. Jonah deliberately passed over this minor premise, in which the conclusion lies hidden. Hence it is difficult, indeed dangerous, to serve you; and as far as I am concerned, it is better to be done with these evils once by dying, than to live longer and strike again and again against the same stone.

units.la: QVOMODO AFFECTVM esse oportet Dei seruum?
units.tr: HOW THE SERVANT OF GOD OUGHT TO BE AFFECTED?

units.la: Primùm sic animatū esse decet, ut non solùm tum, cum [?]ἀνχμόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν pro q; voto, seu omnia, seu quaedam fiunt & succedunt: sed etiam, cum omnia ferè præposterè geri, bona impediri, mala magno impetu ferri, & iam pios obruitura uidentur, nequaquam sit deiecto animo. Sæpenumerò enim ex longa pace carnali maiora mala & incommoda redeunt ad Ecclesiam, quàm ex diuturna persecutione: quæ ut maximè horribilis sit, nunquam tamen præualebit aduersus inuictâ illam petram, Matt.16.18. Semper ergo in conspectu nobis sit illud præclarum dictum Dauidis: Deus est nobis tutamen & robur, in quo auxilium in afflictionibus inuenimus abunde. Propterea non timebimus, cum mouebitur terra, & concidét mõtes in medio mari, &c. Psal.46.v.1.2.3.
units.tr: First, he ought to be so disposed that not only when all things happen and succeed in good order and according to his wish, but also when almost everything is carried on topsy-turvy, good things are hindered, evils rush in with great force, and the pious seem about to be overwhelmed, he is in no way cast down in spirit. For often a long carnal peace brings greater evils and troubles back upon the Church than a long persecution does; and however dreadful that may be, it will never prevail against that invincible rock (Matt.16.18). Let that famous saying of David therefore always be before our eyes: "God is our refuge and strength, a help in afflictions that we find in abundance. Therefore we will not fear when the earth is moved and the mountains fall into the midst of the sea," etc. Psal.46.1.2.3.

units.la: Secundò, sollicitè sibi caueat ab impostura carnis, qua tanta caligo menti offunditur, ut tristi specie præsentium ærumnarum homo perculsus, non possit reminifci priorum operū Dei, & successuum ac donorum, quorum memoria ad nos exhilarandos plurimum conferre poterat. Qui enim recolunt apud semetipsos, quoties & quàm certis argumentis præsentiam & gratiam Dei sint experti, inde piè colligunt, futurum ut Deus opus suū, quod in ipsis orsus est, ad gloriā suam, & seruorum suorū salutè, randem[?] perficiat.
units.tr: Second, let him carefully guard against the deceit of the flesh, by which such thick darkness is poured over the mind that a man struck by the sad appearance of present troubles cannot recall the former works of God, his successes and gifts, the memory of which could greatly help to cheer us. For those who recall within themselves how often, and by how certain proofs, they have experienced God's presence and grace, rightly infer from this that God will at last complete the work he has begun in them, to his own glory and the salvation of his servants.

units.la: Tertiò, ne nimium hilares sint & securi, cum sibi Principes quosdam & Politarchas nutricios & patronos habere videntur: neve brachio carnis destituti nimium perturbentur, & de Ecclesia actum putent. Nam & illorum animi, nisi perpetuo regantur à Spiritu consilij & pietatis, mutabiles sunt: & Ecclesia sub umbra alarum omnipotentis Dei satis est tuta, etiamsi totus mundus contra eam insurgat. Regnat enim Christus in medio inimicorum suorum.
units.tr: Third, let him not be too cheerful and secure when certain princes and civic magistrates seem to be his nurturing fathers and patrons; nor, deprived of the arm of flesh, be too disturbed and think the Church is finished. For their minds too are changeable unless they are constantly ruled by the Spirit of counsel and piety; and the Church is safe enough under the shadow of the wings of almighty God, even if the whole world rises against her. For Christ reigns in the midst of his enemies.

units.la: Quartò, affectus suos sic iniecto freno in officio contineat, ut semper sibi similis sit, ne se à rapidissimis perturbationibus ἀθύμου[?] & varium effici patiatur. Τετράγωνος[?] enim Christi seruum esse convenit & immotum.
units.tr: Fourth, he should so hold his emotions in check, with the bridle put on, that he always remains like himself, and does not allow himself to be made dejected and unsettled by the most violent disturbances. For it is fitting for a servant of Christ to be square and unmoved.

units.la: Quintò, non tam suis commodis aut incommodis, quàm alienis serió eum afficí oportet. Ne maioris faciat existimationem, facultates, uitæ commoda, quàm Ecclesiæ ædificationem & honorem.
units.tr: Fifth, he ought to be seriously affected not so much by his own advantages or disadvantages as by those of others. Let him not set a higher value on his resources and the comforts of life than on the edification and honour of the Church.

units.la: Sextò, paratus sit Christo seruire per gloriam & ignominiam, per conuicia & laudes: ut seductor, & tamen uerax: ut ignotus, & tamen notus. 2.Cor.6.8.9.
units.tr: Sixth, let him be ready to serve Christ through glory and dishonour, through reproaches and praises: as a deceiver, and yet truthful; as unknown, and yet well known (2 Cor.6.8.9).

units.la: Septimò, si Deo uisum sit ad uindicanda hominum scelera, submotis Pastoribus, lupos aut mercenarios substituere: locomotus, cogitet obedientiam suam in hac conuersione rerum non minus Deo probari, quàm paulo ante fidem, uigilan-tiam & diligentiam in officio præstitam. Agat ergo Deo gratias, cuius gratia factū est, ut etiam breuis temporis ministerii fructuosum esset Ecclesiæ: & acquiescat in Dei, quem penes sunt rerum conuersi-ones & momenta, beneplacito: nec in homines potius & alias secundas causas respiciat, quàm in Deum, qui omnia facit optimè, etiamsi fines actionum nō statim à nobis deprehenduntur.
units.tr: Seventh, if it has seemed good to God, in order to punish the sins of men, to remove the pastors and put wolves or hirelings in their place, let him, if he is moved from his post, reflect that his obedience in this upheaval of affairs is no less approved by God than the faith, watchfulness and diligence he showed a little before in his office. Let him therefore give thanks to God, by whose grace it has come about that even a ministry of brief duration was fruitful for the Church; and let him acquiesce in the good pleasure of God, in whose hands lie the turns and changes of affairs; nor let him look to men and secondary causes rather than to God, who does all things most excellently, even when the ends of his actions are not at once perceived by us.

units.la: Octauò, ut non debet sibijpsi meliore uitæ & uocationis forte deposcere, quàm uidet[?] fuisse Prophetarum & Apostolorum, & aliorum Dei seruorum: ita, si se malis exosum, uenenatæ linguæ spiculis peti uideat, seipsum exhilarare debet. Turpe enim foret, istis placuisse: honorificum, di splicuisse. Præstat Therfitas habere hostes & accusatores, quàm defensores.
units.tr: Eighthly, he must not demand for himself a better life and calling than those of the prophets and apostles and other servants of God, whom he sees to have been what they were. So, if he sees himself hated by the wicked and attacked with the venomous darts of their tongues, he ought to cheer himself up. It would be shameful to please them; it is an honour to displease them. It is better to have enemies and accusers like Thersites than defenders.

units.la: Nonò, det operam, ut ex coniunctione dulcissima cum paucis, sed bonis, fructus consolationis, qui à συμφωνίᾳ fidei proficiscuntur, percipiat. Etsi autem illi plerumque sunt calamitosi & miserabiles: quia tamen in Christi nauicula sunt, cum iis periclitari, tutissimum & optimum fuerit. Noti sunt uersus Philippi Melanchthonis de Naui Christi, quæ est Ecclesia, digni quos ad unguem teneamus.
units.tr: Ninthly, he should take care to receive the fruit of comfort that comes from the sweetest fellowship with a few, but good, men, which arises from agreement in the faith [συμφωνία]. Although such men are for the most part afflicted and wretched, yet since they are in Christ's little ship, it is safest and best to share their dangers. The verses of Philip Melanchthon about the ship of Christ, which is the Church, are well known and worth holding to the letter:

units.la: Auricomum uellus postquam transfuexit Iason In patriam, sperans debita regna sibi, Oppressit dominum nauis de culmine lapsa.
units.tr: After Jason had carried the golden fleece into his homeland, hoping for the kingdom owed to him, a ship's beam fell from the top and crushed its lord.

units.la: Sed quia defessus iam cubat ipse domi: Non te Christe tamē tua, quà regis, opprimet Argo Quamuis & rimis est lacerata suis.
units.tr: But since he now lies weary at home, yet you, Christ, will not let Argo be crushed by you, though she is torn by her own cracks.

units.la: Tum quoq; cum fluctus ciet imo ex gurgite Orion, Et rapidi uenti prælia sæua cient, Quassatam medio in pelago tua dextera seruat, Et uere es Nautis anchora sacra tuis. O' uiua effigies æterni luxq; Parentis, Defendas cœtus optime Christe tuos: Qui tua non ficta discunt oracula mente, Aq; tuo poscunt Numine semper opem.
units.tr: Then also, when Orion stirs the waves from the deep abyss, and the swift winds stir up savage battles, your right hand keeps her shaken in the middle of the sea, and you truly are the sacred anchor of your sailors. O living image of the eternal Father, best of Christs, defend your assemblies, who learn your oracles with an unfeigned mind and always ask for help from your divine power.

units.la: Decimò, ne illud moleste ferat, quòd hypocritas & mercenarios breui tempore florere, & [illegible, ~12 letters] uidet.
units.tr: Tenthly, he should not take it ill that he sees hypocrites and hirelings flourish for a short time, and [...].

units.la: Quid enim? An non Iudex ille mundi suo tempore ad tribunal suum Harmo-stas istos uocabit, & [illegible, ~12 letters] subire coget? Cum Deus eos ad tempus breue Ecclesiam uastantes toleret, tu'ne eos ferre recusabis?
units.tr: For what then? Will not that Judge of the world, in his own time, call those Harmostae to his tribunal and compel them to undergo it? Since God for a short time tolerates them, as they lay waste the Church, will you refuse to bear them?

units.la: Vndecimò, det operam, ut in eos, qui malam caussam alias male & cyclopicè agunt (cum uidelicet [illegible, ~10 letters] & conuicijs & anathematismis superiores esse contendunt) alias bene seu potius sophistice agunt, intentus, Christi optimam caussam optimè agat, & quoscunque potest Christo lucrifaciat, uel priuata institutione, uel inculpatæ uitæ exemplo.
units.tr: Eleventhly, he should take care that, while those who defend a bad cause do so badly and in a Cyclopean manner (when they insist, that is, that they are superior by abuse, insults and anathemas), others act well, or rather sophistically, Christ's best cause be pursued in the best way, and that he win to Christ whomever he can, either by private instruction or by the example of a blameless life.

units.la: Postremò, non solum iudicium posteritatis cordatæ, quod melius erit, præferat stolido præiudicio æmulorum, qui bonos oppugnando inclarescere conantur: sed etiam spe aeternae uitae, & dulcissimę consuetudinis cum tota in cœlis olim triumphatura Ecclesia, leniat & mitiget dolores & angores, quibus in his terris piorum uita est obnoxia. Dominus det, ut ista & alia eis σύμφωνα perpendamus, & in fide uirtutem declaremus, in patientia uera animas nostras possidentes. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, he should not only prefer the judgement of sound-minded posterity, which will be better, to the foolish prejudice of rivals who try to gain fame by attacking good men; but also, by the hope of eternal life and of the sweetest fellowship with the whole Church, which will one day triumph in heaven, he should soothe and mitigate the sorrows and anguish to which the life of the godly is subject in this earth. May the Lord grant that we weigh these and other things in agreement [σύμφωνα], and show forth virtue in faith, possessing our souls in true patience. Amen.

units.la: POSTREMI DVO uersus.
units.tr: THE LAST TWO VERSES.

units.la: Cui dixit Iehouah: Tu pepercisti cucur-bitae ipsi, in qua non laborasti, nec fecisti crescere eam: quae una nocte nata est, & una nocte periit: Et ego non parcam Nini-veh urbi illi magnae, in qua sunt plures quàm duodecim myriades hominum, qui non nouerunt inter dexteram suam & si-nistram suam, & animalia multa.
units.tr: To him Jehovah said: You have spared the gourd, in which you did not labour, nor made it grow; it sprang up in one night and perished in one night. And should I not spare Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than twelve myriads of men who do not know their right hand from their left, and many animals?

units.la: 1. Nihil dubium est, Ionam prophetam, nimium indulgentem perturbationibus suis, ideo graviter à Domino reprehensum, ut disceret antefere dam sibi esse voluntatem diuinam perfuasioni priuatae, & ut se submitteret sub potenti manu Dei, ac daret Deo gloriam cum Dauide dicente: Tacui, quia tu fecisti: Psal.39.9. Est igitur hæc postrema oratio [illegible, ~9 letters].
units.tr: 1. There is no doubt that the prophet Jonah, who indulged his passions too much, was for this reason sharply rebuked by the Lord, so that he might learn that the divine will is to be preferred to his private persuasion, and that he should submit himself under the mighty hand of God and give glory to God, saying with David: "I was silent, because you did it" (Ps. 39:9). This last speech is therefore [...].

units.la: 2. Status iuredicialis est.Hoc enim quæritur,Iurène,an uerò iniuria Ionæ doleat, quòd cucurbita interijsset,quæ umbracu li uice (sancto prophetæ,Dei nomine in tantas angustias coniecto,ut mors etiam ei expetenda uideretur) fuerat: & quòd Niniuitis,quibus internecionem denun- ciari Dominus uoluerat,parceret?Negan tem sententiam Deus tuetur: aientem ue rò Ionas propheta.Occurrit autem,ut uidetis,hoc loco exemplum hominis alio- quin sancti & prudentis,qui tamen in te- tationis [illegible, ~12 letters] modestiæ nonihil ob- litus,Deo ex aduerso respondit. Vtinam uerò,infirmitatis & gradus nostri consci- entia, & summi istius uiri offensa com- monefacti,nunquam non Dei,cuius ma- gna & mirabilia opera sunt, iudicia ado- remus,ut maximè causæ & destinata nos longo tempore fugiant. Satis enim hoc nobis esse debet, quòd Deû omnia quæ uult,in cœlo & in terra facere scimus: Psal.115.3. Nam eius uoluntas iustissima, optima & sapientissima est.
units.tr: 2. The question is judicial. For what is asked is this: whether Jonah is right, or rather wrongly grieves, because the gourd, which had been a shade for the holy prophet, perished, and because God spared the Ninevites, whom the Lord had wished to be threatened with destruction. God upholds the sentence that denies this, while Jonah the prophet affirms it. Now, as you see, there occurs at this point the example of a man otherwise holy and wise, who nevertheless, forgetting somewhat his modesty under the stress of temptation, answered God back. Would that we, reminded by the consciousness of our weakness and our rank, and by the offence of that great man, would never cease to revere the judgements of God, whose works are great and marvellous, so that, above all, causes and set purposes may long escape us. For it ought to be enough for us that we know God does whatever he wills, in heaven and on earth (Ps. 115:3). For his will is most just, best and most wise.

units.la: 3. Argumetum quo Deus utitur ad co-vincendum Ionam, ducitur ab ἀντιθέσει præiudicij humani & iudicij diuini.
units.tr: 3. The argument by which God uses to convince Jonah is drawn from the antithesis between human prejudgement and divine judgement.

units.la: Non est anteponendum hominis (qui animi ægritudine laborans, rei leuiculæ iactura mirificè, multorum autem hominum incolumitate parum adficitur) præ-iudicium, diuino iudicio, quod neutiquam ille assequitur, de quo dicitur: Iusticia tua, Iehouah, est ut montes Dei: iudicia tua sunt abyssus magna: hominem & bestias seruas Iehouah: Psal.36.6. Et Isa.55.6: Non enim cogitationes meæ, cogitationes uestræ: nec uiæ uestræ uiæ meæ, dicit Iehouah. Rom.11.33: O profundas diuitias tū sapientiæ, tū cognitionis Dei: quàm inscrutabilia sunt eius iudicia, & imperuestiga-biles eius uiæ. 34. Quis enim cognouit mente Domini? aut quis ei fuit à cōsilio?
units.tr: The prejudgement of a man (who, labouring under a sickness of mind, is wonderfully affected by the loss of a trifling thing, but little moved by the safety of many men) must not be preferred to the divine judgement, which he by no means reaches, of which it is said: "Your righteousness, O Jehovah, is like the mountains of God; your judgements are a great deep; O Jehovah, you preserve man and beast" (Ps. 36:6). And Isa. 55:6: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways, says Jehovah." Rom. 11:33: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgements, and his ways past finding out! 34. For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?"

units.la: Tu uerò, ô Ionah, temerario præiudicio peccas: & ut ęger animus, donec æger est, nunquam nō erratis, grauiter hallucinaris, quòd nimium infamiæ metu torqueris: quòd cucurbitæ arefactionem dolenter fers: quòd non gratularis Niniuitis resipiscentiæ & conseruationis dona, ita ut hominem ἐπιχαρίτωσθαι[?] facere oportuit: quòd rebus paruis nimium, rebus maximis nō satis afficeris: deniq; quòd sic tibi places et blandiris, ut etiam non dubites opinionem tuam diuinae sententiae anteponere.
units.tr: But you, O Jonah, sin by rash prejudgement; and like a sick mind, which always errs as long as it is sick, you gravely go astray, in that you are tormented too much by fear of disgrace; in that you bear with grief the withering of the gourd; in that you do not rejoice at the gifts of repentance and preservation granted to the Ninevites, so that the man ought to have been made to rejoice [ἐπιχαρίτωσθαι]; in that you are too moved by small things and not enough by the greatest; and finally, in that you so please and flatter yourself that you do not hesitate to set your own opinion above the divine sentence.

units.la: Quamobrem cum te graviter peccavisse animadvertas, Dei tui iudicio acquiesce, et vitilitigatione istam servo Dei indignam, et in Deum contumeliosam, omitte. Respira, respira tandem ab illa affectuum, qui te transuersum egerunt, intemperie et uiolentia, et da locum τῇ [?] ἀν- θυμίᾳ.
units.tr: Wherefore, since you perceive that you have sinned grievously, submit to the judgement of your God, and lay aside this quarrelsome contention, unworthy of a servant of God and insulting to God. Take breath, take breath at last from that intemperance and violence of the passions which have driven you off course, and give room for good cheer [ἀνθυμία].

units.la: Ex iis quae paucis dicta sunt, liquet, quaenam huius loci grammatica sententia sit. Allegorias si quis desiderat, consulat Hieronymum et Lutherum. Mihi ab allegoriis abstinendum censeo, cum historia plena est salutaris doctrinae, nec opus habet speculationibus longiuscule petitis, nec semper certis.
units.tr: From what has been said briefly, it is clear what the plain sense of this passage is. If anyone wants allegories, let him consult Jerome and Luther. For my part I think one should abstain from allegories, since the history is full of saving doctrine, and needs no speculations sought from afar, nor always certain ones.

units.la: DE IMPARI LVCTA luti cum figulo.
units.tr: On the Unequal Struggle: clay with the potter.

units.la: Quid, quaeso te, aliud est, si homo cum Deo congressus, ei ex aduerso respon-deat, quam si lutum cum figulo contendat, nec sit memor dicti Pauli Apostoli: Im-mò uerò, ô homo, tu quis es, qui ex aduerso responsas Deo? num dicet figmen-tum tum fi[?]ctori, Cur me talem fecisti? An non habet potestatem figulus in lutum, ut ex eadem massa faciat aliud quidem uas ad decus, aliud uero ad dedecus? Roman.
units.tr: What else, I ask you, is it when a man, meeting God, answers back to him, than when a lump of clay contends with the potter? He forgets the saying of the Apostle Paul: "Nay but, O man, who are you that answer back against God? Will the thing formed say to him who formed it, 'Why have you made me thus?' Has not the potter power over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?" (Rom. 9.)

units.la: Et sane hoc certamen ftulticiae cum summa sapientia, ignorantiae cum omniscientia, infirmitatis cum omnipotentia, finiti cum infinito, creaturae cum Creatore, quam fit & impar & alienum a Chri-ftiana modestia, nemo intelligens non uidet. Nam (ut est Ifa.40.13.) Quis direxit Spiritum Iehouę, & quis uir consilij eius, indicauitq; illi? 14. A' quo petijt consilium, & instruxit eum, docuitq; eum semitam iudicij, atque erudiuit eum scientia, & uiam intelligentiarū oftedit ei? 15. En Gentes sicut stilla situlae, & puluis tenuis staterae reputantur: en infulas tanquam puluerem proijcit. 16. Nec Libanus sufficit ad accendendum, & ferę eius non sufficiunt ad holocaustum. 17. Omnes Gentes tanquam nihilum sunt coram eo, minus quàm nihilum & inane reputantur præ ipso.
units.tr: Indeed, anyone who understands can see how unequal and how foreign to Christian modesty this contest is: foolishness against the highest wisdom, ignorance against omniscience, weakness against omnipotence, the finite against the infinite, the creature against the Creator. As Isaiah 40:13 says: "Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or being his counsellor has taught him? 14. With whom did he take counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him in the path of judgment, and showed him the way of understanding? 15. Behold, the nations are as a drop from a bucket, and are counted as the dust on the scales; behold, he takes up the islands as a very little thing. 16. Lebanon is not enough to burn, nor its beasts enough for a burnt offering. 17. All nations are as nothing before him; they are counted as less than nothing and emptiness."

units.la: Aliter tamen cum Deo contendunt filij huius seculi, aliter filij lucis. Nam illi quidem, cum sint inimici Dei, & mentes caliginosas, uolutates distortas & a Deo auersas habeant, Cyclopum more per o-mnem uitam θεομαχεῖν[?] solent. Hi uero, carnis intelligentia fucum ipsis faciente, & perturbationibus desideriisq; carnalibus solicitati, interdum sui officij ad tempus non ita ut par erat memores, Dei iudicia per incogitantiam reprehendunt. Verum a Deo in uiam reuocati, errata sua agnoscunt, & Deo gloriam dant.
units.tr: Yet the children of this world contend with God in one way, and the children of light in another. The former, since they are enemies of God and have darkened minds, crooked wills and wills turned away from God, are accustomed to fight against God [θεομαχεῖν] all their lives, like the Cyclopes. The latter, when their fleshly understanding deceives them and they are stirred by passions and carnal desires, sometimes forget for a time the duty they should remember, and through thoughtlessness find fault with God's judgments. But once they are called back to the way by God, they acknowledge their errors and give glory to God.

units.la: Nos in praesentia illis omissis, de his a-gamus, productis in medium selectissimis aliquot exemplis, quae recte perpen-sa plurimum ad nos erudiendos & consolandos facere possunt. Quotusquisq; autem nostrum est, qui si anteactae suae uitae fata secum recolat, non deprehendat id sibi ob nescio quas causas displicuisse, quod tamen Deo placuit? Quoties & quàm leuiculas ob causas taedium earum rerum oboritur, pro quibus obtinendis non solùm ipsi olim uehementer laborauimus, sed etiam aliorum subsidiaria o-pera usi sumus, & quarum μετοχὴν[?] nobis postea tacitè gratulati sumus?
units.tr: Leaving those others aside for now, let us deal with these, setting before us some very select examples, which, if weighed rightly, can do much to teach and comfort us. But how few of us are there who, if we recall the course of our past lives, do not find that something displeased us for reasons we cannot name, though it pleased God? How often, and for how trivial reasons, does weariness arise with those things which we once laboured hard to obtain, and with the help of others, and whose share we later secretly rejoiced to have gained?

units.la: Abraham pio affectu commiserationis permotus,pro Sodomitis jamjam perituris ferió & suppliciter intercesit:Gen.18.
units.tr: Abraham, moved by a pious feeling of compassion, struck and pleaded earnestly for the Sodomites, who were about to perish. (Gen. 18.)

units.la: Atqui cum etiam Judex mundi Deus sit, & ruina interituq; impiorum hominum, gloriam justiciæ judicijq; divini illustra-ri & sanciri plurimū interfit, ne ἐπιφθό[?]-μον Deum, & misericordem solùm, non aute justum, agnoscere videretur, sic pro illis intercedendum erat viro sancto, ut tamen id demum fieri vellet, quod apud semetipsum jam constituisset Dominus, seruoq; suo familiariter aperverat. Videmus ut interdum in judicio de Deo deerret etiam religiosa mens, cum nonnihil subveretur, ne sic Deus justiciam suam declaret,ut interim misericordiæ obliui-scatur.
units.tr: Yet since God is also the judge of the world, and it matters greatly that the ruin and destruction of wicked men should display and vindicate the glory of divine justice and judgment, lest God seem to be known only as merciful and not also as just, the holy man had to intercede for them in such a way that he still wished only what the Lord had already decided within himself, and had made known to his servant in friendly fashion. We see that sometimes even a devout mind goes astray in its judgment of God, when it is a little afraid that God might declare his justice in such a way as to forget his mercy in the meantime.

units.la: Videamus autem,quomodo etiam pij homines in judicio de seipsis & alijs hallucinentur. Recusant, Moses gubernati-onem Jsraelitici populi: Jeremias munus propheticum: uterque infantiæ &infir-mitatis suæ conscientiam allegat. Samu-el,cum ex Jsai filijs Rex eligendus esset,à natu maximo initium fecit,minimū natu illis præferendum esse, minimè, ut appa-ret, suspicatus. Sed Deus,quid de unoquoq; statuendum, & quid cuiquę illorū faciendum esset, ostendit. Ac recte postea ab illis omnibus factum est, quòd nō suo, sed Dei iudicio sibi standum esse iudicauerunt.
units.tr: Let us see, moreover, how even godly men go wrong in judging themselves and others. Moses refused the leadership of the Israelite people; Jeremiah refused the prophetic office; each pleaded his awareness of his own youth and weakness. Samuel, when a king was to be chosen from the sons of Jesse, began with the eldest, not at all suspecting, as it appears, that the youngest should be preferred. But God showed what must be decided about each one and what must be done for each of them. And rightly afterwards they all did this, judging that they must abide by God's judgment and not their own.

units.la: Quoties autem fit, ut in æstimatione rerum earum, quæ uitæ huius adminicula sunt, & quarum miro quodam desiderio afficimur, cum Israelitis peccemus, de quibus dicitur: Festinauerunt, obliti sunt operum eius, non exspectauerunt consilium eius. Et concupierunt concupiscentiam in deserto, & tentauerunt Deum in solitudine. Et dedit eis petitionem eorū: ueruntamē immisit maciem in animam eorum: Psal. 106. 13. 14. 15. Et Psal. 78. 17. Et addiderunt adhuc peccare ei, ut prouocarent Excelsum in solitudine. 18. Et tentauerunt Deum in corde suo, petendo cibum animæ suæ, &c.
units.tr: But how often it happens that in estimating those things which are aids to this life, and for which we feel a strange longing, we sin as the Israelites did, of whom it is said: "They hastened, they forgot his works, they did not wait for his counsel. And they lusted exceedingly in the wilderness, and tempted God in the desert. And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul." (Ps. 106:13-15.) And Psalm 78:17: "And they added yet more to sin against him, provoking the Most High in the wilderness. 18. And they tempted God in their heart, asking food for their soul," etc.

units.la: Cum suppetit copia rerum necessariarum, tum ijs perinde ut nostra industria partis utimur: cum aliquid deficit, tum uè hominem uiuere nō ex solo pane, sed ex omni uerbo quod procedit ex ore Dei, non satis perpendimus: sed angimur animis, & cur hæc uitæ præsidia, quibus nobis bis opus esse Deus intelligit, subtrahat, nō satis mirari possumus: ægrè etiam ab odiosa & impia μεταμελείας[?] abstinemus.
units.tr: When there is an abundance of necessary things, we use them as if they were the product of our own industry; when something is lacking, we do not weigh enough that man does not live by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Rather, we are troubled in mind, and cannot sufficiently wonder why God takes away those supports of life which he knows we need. We scarcely refrain from that hateful and impious regret [μεταμελείας].

units.la: Moses, etsi edoctus erat de culpa, qua sibi ipsi aditum in terram Canaan præclu serat, ac poterat & debebat contentus esse gratia diuina, quam diu multisq; modis expertus fuerat: tamen, dum id unum spectat, quid sibi amabile esse posset, non autem quid hac in parte à Deo decretum, frustrà petijt, ut liceret Iordane transmisso, ingredi cum populo Israel in terram patribus promissam.
units.tr: Moses, although he had been taught about the fault which had shut him out from the land of Canaan, and although he could and should have been content with the divine grace which he had long and in many ways experienced, nevertheless, looking only at what seemed to him pleasant, and not at what God had decreed in this matter, vainly asked that, having crossed the Jordan, he might be allowed to enter with the people of Israel into the land promised to their fathers.

units.la: Petrus, quasi Christo Domino, qui Patris æterni sapientia est, à consilijs esse posset, dehortatur eum à profectione Ierosolymitana, & à supplicio crucis, quod tamen pro salute generis humani ei adeundum erat. - Sed acriter eo nomine à Christo reprehenditur, quòd ea solùm sapere quæ hominum sunt, non autem ea quæ sunt Dei.Matt.16.22.23.
