units.tr: Peter, as if Christ the Lord, who is the wisdom of the eternal Father, could be advised by him, dissuades him from his journey to Jerusalem and from the suffering of the cross, which nevertheless he had to undergo for the salvation of mankind. But for this he was sharply rebuked by Christ, because he savoured not the things that are of God, but the things that are of men. (Matt. 16:22-23.)

units.la: Maximè autem hæc concertatio luti cum figulo, in quæstionibus de religione & de militia Ecclesiæ, deprehendi potest. Quoties enim homo, quatenus est ψυχικὸς[?], offenditur ijs, quæ tamen ad consola-tionem tionem & institutionem nostram rectè perpensa plurimùm faciunt?
units.tr: But this struggle of clay with the potter can be seen most clearly in questions about religion and about the warfare of the Church. For whenever a man, insofar as he is psychical [ψυχικὸς], takes offence at those things which, if rightly weighed, do so much to console and instruct us?

units.la: Miratur,quare Deus eos,quos Filio donare dignatur,elegerit ab æterno,cæteris præteritis. Quasi uero figulus potestate luti non habeat. Miratur,cur alios nun-quam uocet, alios uel serius, uel citius quàm alios quosdam. Atqui nihil non in tempore is facit, qui rerum momenta in sua habet potestate. Miratur,quòd in par-[?]uulis dicitur esse peccatum originis,idq; natura propagatum,nō imitatione trans-latum. Atqui is optimè nouit hominem, cuius oculi etiam imperfectum eius uide-runt:Psal.139.16. Miratur,cur fide,gratis, absque operibus legis homo iustificari dicatur: cum admodum consentaneum ui-deatur,si homo in seipso iustificationis suæ principia quærat & constituat. De-nique,ut infinita omittam,miratur,cur Ecclesiam suam Deus cruci subiectam esse uelit,floretibus,ut apparet,infidelibus: cum æquissimum uideatur,ut illi bene sit,his autem male. Ac quasi in medijs olim delitijs & uoluptatibus omne æuum traduxerint Prophetæ, Christus Dominus, Apostoli, Martyres, Athanasius,Gregorius Nazianzenus, & infinitis alij, ualde commouetur, cùm egregia doctrina, uirtute & auctoritate uiros, ex Ecclesiarum & Academiarum alueolis, ab inglorijs su-cis hoc tempore pelli uider. Nec dubium est, hominem, qua parte adhuc animalis est, non posse non offendi tristissima specie Ecclesiae militantis, & sua uulnera deplorātis. Sed ut ἀθυμία [?] tandē, solis instar, in cordibus nostris exoriens, nebulas discutiat & tempestate sedet, recurrendum nobis est ad Deum, & firmiter statuendum, nihil temere fieri: Deum ex malis nostris bona facere: eundem efficere, ut omnia nobis adiumento sint in bonum: & mirando modo tenebras diuidere, sic ut in medijs malis ingentia bona, in summa (ut apparet) rerum confusione ἀντα-ξίαν [?] operum Dei, in oppresione & deformatione seruorum Dei liberatione, gloriam ueram & exaltationem, tandem aliquando animaduertamus.
units.tr: He wonders why God chose from eternity those whom he deigns to give to his Son, passing over the rest. As if the potter did not have power over the clay! He wonders why God calls some never, others sooner or later than others. Yet he who has the moments of all things in his own power does nothing out of time. He wonders that in infants there is said to be sin of origin, and that this is propagated by nature, not transmitted by imitation. Yet he knows man best, whose eyes saw his unformed substance (Ps. 139:16). He wonders why man is said to be justified by faith, freely, without the works of the law, since it seems quite reasonable that man should seek and establish the grounds of his justification in himself. Finally, to omit countless other things, he wonders why God wills his Church to be subject to the cross, while the unbelievers, as it appears, flourish; since it seems most just that it should go well with the one and badly with the others. And as if the Prophets, Christ the Lord, the Apostles, the Martyrs, Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen and countless others had spent their whole life in the midst of delights and pleasures, he is greatly disturbed when he sees men of outstanding learning, virtue and authority, from the nurseries of the Churches and the Academies, driven at this time from their inglorious sweets. And there is no doubt that man, in so far as he is still an animal, cannot help being offended by the very sad sight of the militant Church, and by her wounds, which she laments. But so that dejection [ἀθυμία] may at last, like the sun rising in our hearts, scatter the clouds and calm the storm, we must return to God, and firmly settle that nothing happens by chance: that God makes good out of our evils; that he himself brings it about that all things work together for good for us; and that in a wonderful manner he divides the darkness, so that in the midst of evils there are great goods, and that, in the apparent confusion of affairs, we may at last perceive the worth [ἀντάξιον] of God's works, the true glory and exaltation in the oppression and humbling of God's servants, and their deliverance.

units.la: Haec cum ita se habeant, ne intremus in iudicium cùm eo iudice, cui de mille interroganti ad unicum respondendo satisfacere non possumus. Adoremus eius iudicia & sanctam uoluntatem, & hanc nostræ semper & libenter anteferamus: Id donum ut nobis det, Dominũ Iesum toto pectore oro.
units.tr: Since these things stand as they do, let us not enter into judgment with that Judge, to whom, when he asks a thousand questions, we cannot make satisfactory answer even to one. Let us adore his judgments and his holy will, and always and willingly prefer it to our own. I pray with all my heart to the Lord Jesus that he may grant us this gift.

units.la: DE RECTA RERVM æstimatione.
units.tr: ON THE RIGHT ESTIMATION OF THINGS

units.la: Si quando instituenda nobis est censu-ra bonorum naturalium & moralium, stu-diosè recurrendum nobis fuerit ad æsti-mationem Opificis sapientissimi & opti-mi. Ut autem is homines ἰσῳ ζυγῷ[?] se inui-cem amare & complecti, non autem φιλαυ-τίᾳ[?] cum aliorum neglectione, nedum cū odio coniungere voluit: sic eas res, quae ut hominum usibus seruirent condidit, nequaquam maioris à nobis, quàm proximos, fieri vult. Peccavit igitur Ionas, cum ob arefactam cucurbitam plurimū indoluit: Ninivitis interim non gratula-tus est incolumitatem & veniam. Quasi verò ea potius nobis spectanda sint, quae usum habent momentaneum, parumq; ad Dei faciunt laudem, quàm quæ ad lau-dem gloriosæ Dei gratiæ, & ad multorum millium hominum instaurationem & sa-lutem plurimum faciunt. Sint igitur no-bis in conspectu hi canones, quos ut mul-ta pauta paucis perstringamus, ὡς ἐν τύπῳ oculis subijciemus.
units.tr: Whenever we are to undertake an assessment of natural and moral goods, we must diligently have recourse to the estimation of the most wise and best Maker. For he willed that men should love and embrace one another on equal terms [ἴσῳ ζυγῷ], and not join themselves together in self-love [φιλαυτίᾳ] at the neglect of others, much less in hatred. So too, he does not wish those things which he made to serve human uses to be valued by us more highly than our neighbours. Jonah therefore sinned when he grieved so greatly over the withered gourd, and meanwhile did not rejoice at the safety and pardon of the Ninevites. As if those things ought rather to be regarded by us which have only a momentary use and contribute little to God's praise, than those which contribute greatly to the praise of his glorious grace, and to the restoration and salvation of many thousands of men. Let these rules therefore be before our eyes, which we shall set out before our eyes as in a sketch [ὡς ἐν τύπῳ], so that we may touch briefly on many things in few words.

units.la: 1. Non quid de singulis rebus nobis, sed quid Deo uideatur, spectandum est.
units.tr: 1. We must consider not what seems good to us about individual things, but what seems good to God.

units.la: 2. Ea quae hominū causa condita sunt, ipsis hominibus potiora censeri non debent.
units.tr: 2. Things made for the sake of men ought not to be judged more valuable than men themselves.

units.la: 3. Priuatis commodis & reculis [?] publica utilitas semper est anteponenda.
units.tr: 3. Public usefulness must always be placed before private advantages and wishes.

units.la: 4. Prudentis est, iactura rerum caducarum non nimium affici.
units.tr: 4. It is the mark of a prudent person not to be too much affected by the loss of perishable things.

units.la: 5. Religiosi hominis est, praecipuam ex eo uoluptate percipere, si quibus ad meliorem frugem reuocatis, Deum reconciliatum esse compererit.
units.tr: 5. It is the mark of a religious person to take especial pleasure from this, if, when people have been called back to better conduct, he finds that God has been reconciled.

units.la: 6. Dei erga nos & alios ἐπιεικεία [?], summa cum gratitudine nos amplecti par est: indulgentiae autem nimiae Deum insimulare, piaculum.
units.tr: 6. We ought to embrace with the greatest gratitude God's kindness [ἐπιείκεια] towards us and others; but to accuse God of excessive indulgence is a sin.

units.la: Etsi autem, quanta sit discrepantia iudicij piorum & filiorum huius seculi, circa delectum & aestimationem bonorum terrenorum & spiritualium, non solum discrepantes eorum sermones, sed etiam experientia docet: nihil tamen uetat, hoc loco unico testimonio rem omnem, quasi uno fasce, complecti. De filijs huius mundi, qui negleƈtis cœlestibus donis, terrenis opibus auidissimè inhiant, dicitur: Multi dicunt, Quis ostendet nobis bonum? id est, qua tandem ratione ditescemus? Sed econtrà piorum hoc uotū est: Attolle super nos lumen uultus tui, Ieuhouah. Sciunt enim Deum, sereno uultu propter Christum, qui est placamentum nostrum, nos respicientem, genus omne bonorum spiritualium larga manu suis impertiri. Inter hęc autem bona, celebratur lætitia, de qua dicitur: Dedisti lætici-am in corde meo maiorem, quàm quę est tempore quo frumentum & uinum ipsorum multiplicantur. Item pia securitas ex fide oriens, quæ his uerbis celebratur: In pace simul cubabo & dormiam: quoniam tu Iehouah solus securè facis me habitare. Psal. 4. v. 6. 7. 8.
units.tr: Although the great difference between the judgment of the godly and the children of this age, in choosing and valuing earthly and spiritual goods, is shown not only by their differing words but also by experience, nothing prevents us from embracing the whole matter here, as if in a single bundle, with one testimony. Of the children of this world, who neglect heavenly gifts and greedily gape after earthly wealth, it is said: "Many say, Who will show us good?" that is, by what means will we at last grow rich? But on the contrary, this is the prayer of the godly: "Lift up the light of your face upon us, O LORD." For they know that God, looking upon us with a serene countenance for Christ, who is our propitiation, bestows with a generous hand every kind of spiritual good. Among these goods is celebrated the joy of which it is said: "You have put gladness in my heart, greater than that which is in the time when their grain and wine are multiplied." Likewise there is celebrated the godly security arising from faith, which is praised in these words: "In peace I will lie down and sleep together, for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety." Psalm 4:6, 7, 8.

units.la: Sollicitè autem nobis cauendum est, primùm ne bona physica tanti faciamus, ut præ illis fastidiamus cætera Dei θεωρ-[?] ἠματα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα[?]: deinde, ne natura-lia bona auidè captates, moralia interim negligamus, cum horum non minor nobis habenda sit ratio, quàm illorum: nisi forte pecuinam cū Epicuri de grege porcis, non autem verè humanam & religiosam vitam, nobis agendam putamus: postremò, ne chamæleonte mutabiliores vi deamur, diu multumq; quæsita & adamata sastidientes, & seu consilio seu affectu pride perosa venantes & laudantes.
units.tr: We must be careful, first, not to value physical goods so highly that we despise the other divine and human matters [θεωρήματα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα]; second, not to eagerly seize natural goods while neglecting moral goods in the meantime, since we must have no less regard for the latter than the former, unless perhaps we think we should live the life of Epicurus' herd of pigs, and not a truly human and religious life; and finally, lest we appear more changeable than the chameleon, despising things long sought and loved, and then, whether by reason or by passion, hunting after and praising other things.

units.la: Nunquam autem nobis excidat saluberrimum Christi præceptum, quo monemur, ut spiritualia corporalibus præferentes, quæramus primò regnum Dei, & iusticiam eius: nec dubitemus futurum, ut cætera omnia nobis adijciantur. Matthei 6.33.
units.tr: Let us never lose sight of Christ's most wholesome precept, by which we are warned, placing spiritual things before bodily ones, to seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and not to doubt that all other things will be added to us. Matthew 6:33. ## DE PROVIDENTIA DEI.

units.la: DE PROVIDENTIA DEI.
Quæ tibi videntur divinæ providentiæ documenta hoc loco exstare?
units.tr: What evidences of divine providence seem to you to appear in this passage?

units.la: Hæc duo, Distinctio specierum, & æstimatio earum.
units.tr: These two: the distinction of kinds, and the valuation of them.

units.la: Etsi autem nō meminit Dominus hoc loco omnium specierum, præcipuas tamē complectitur. Prima est earum, quæ sunt & viuunt: ut plantæ, arbores, &c. Harum κατὰ συνεπιλογὴν[?] mentio fit, allegata cucurbita. Secunda est animalium: tertia, hominum. Est autem humanum genus maximum ornamentum terris: ut alicubi dixit Augustinus. Nam, ut Oppianus cecinit,
units.tr: Although the Lord in this place does not mention all kinds, he nevertheless includes the principal ones. The first is of those that exist and live, such as plants, trees, etc. Of these there is a collective mention made, in the gourd that was alleged. The second is of animals; the third, of men. The human race is indeed the greatest ornament of the earth, as Augustine said somewhere. For, as Oppian sang,

units.la: —ἡ γὰρ τὶ πόλις ἀδυνατώτερον ἀλλ[?]ων [?]νόσφι ἰδίων μυρ[?]ίων ἀδαμαντίνοισιν.
units.tr: "For what city is weaker than the others, apart from its own things, with adamantine..." [ἡ γὰρ τὶ πόλις ἀδυνατώτερον ἀλλ[?]ων [?]νόσφι ἰδίων μυρ[?]ίων ἀδαμαντίνοισιν.]

units.la: Quo autem loco illas Dominus Deus noster haberi uelit, uel ex eo colligere licet, quòd uitio uertit Ionæ deploranti in teritum plantæ, non autem periculum, in quo tot hominum millia, & animantia plurima uersabantur. Cæterùm in oratione de hominibus ἀνθρώποις obseruanda est. Ducitur autem illa primùm à quantitate seu numero hominum: deinde à qualitate, seu simplicitate & ignorantia. Tu unicam cucurbitam arefactam doles, quòd ea desijt umbraculi uice esse, & æstus tibi molestus est. Atqui tot millium hominum, in urbe Niniueh uersantium, multò maiorem rationem habendam, quis homo sanus & pius non uideat? Videtur etiam appellatione conscientiæ tacitè uti in hunc modum. παροιμιολογία: Age, dabo tibi libenter, multos esse perditissimos homines apud Niniuitas, urbemq; promeritam hoc esse, ut Sodomorum instar [?] flagret, fiatq; ὠλυ[?]ιον ciuium. ἀντιρρη[?]σις: Sed tamen te nunc interrogo, an ne, cum in ea urbe multæ sint myriades hominum, qui partim per ætatem, partim ob ob simplicitatem nescíut quid interipsorum dextera & sinistra intersit, nullámne horum rationem habendam censeas? Si id hominum opinione erronea iustum uidetur, nullam uidelicet illorum rationem habendam: illud cogitare debebas, aliud esse Dei iudicium, & hoc solo uobis mortalibus esse standum.
units.tr: In what place our Lord God wishes these to be held can be gathered from this: he finds fault with Jonah for lamenting the perishing of a plant, but not the danger in which so many thousands of men and very many living creatures were. Moreover, in the matter of men, regard must be had to the discussion of their number and kind. This is taken first from the quantity or number of men, and then from their quality, or their simplicity and ignorance. You grieve over one withered gourd, because it has ceased to serve as a shade, and the heat is troublesome to you. Yet what sane and godly person does not see that much greater account must be taken of so many thousands of men living in the city of Nineveh? It seems that by an appeal to conscience one is tacitly used in this way. [Proverbial speech]: Come, I will readily grant you that there are many most wicked men among the Ninevites, and that the city has deserved to burn like Sodom and become a ruin of its citizens. [Objection]: But still I ask you now, do you think no account should be taken of them, since in that city there are many myriads of men who, partly through age and partly through simplicity, do not know what lies between their right hand and their left? If this seems just by an erroneous opinion of men, then clearly no account should be taken of them; but you ought to have considered that God's judgment is different, and that you mortals must abide by this alone.

units.la: Ex his quae [illegible, ~9 letters] licuit, colligere licet, quàm sit illud uerum, quod dixit Dauid Psal.51.6. Iustificaris cū loqueris, & es purus dum iudicas. Caeterum ad quas theses referri debeat postremi duo uersus, ex Prolegomenis in cap.4. colligere promptum est.
units.tr: From these things, which it has been possible to gather, it is easy to see how true is what David said in Psalm 51:6: "You are justified when you speak, and pure when you judge." Moreover, to which theses the last two verses ought to be referred, it is easy to gather from the Prolegomena on chapter 4. [illegible]

units.la: Quod superest, publico omnium nostrum nomine gratias ago Domino & Doctori nostro unico, Iesu Christo, quòd eius inestimabili beneficio nobis datum est, in celebri Academia Basiliensi formâ sanorum sermonū fidei & charitatis docere & discere: & quòd sic sapientissimū nostrum Magistratū flectit & regit, ut nu-tricium agat Ecclesiae & Academię, & pia docentes protegat. Eundem Dominum nostrum Iesum Christū toto pectore oro, ut nobis det uerae conuersionis donum, & efficiat, ut Ionæ exemplo admoniti, diligenter nostro munere fungamur, nec unquam de ἀποταξίᾳ[?] cogitemus, Deiq; consilio per omnem vitam seruiamus. Amen. Anno Domini 1581. mense Iulio, Sit nomè Domini benedictum in seculà.
units.tr: For the rest, I give thanks in the name of us all to the Lord and our only Teacher, Jesus Christ, because by his inestimable benefit it has been granted to us, in the famous Academy of Basel, to teach and learn in the form of sound words of faith and love; and because he so guides and rules our most wise magistracy that it acts as a nursing mother to the Church and the Academy, and protects those who teach godly things. I pray with my whole heart to the same Lord Jesus Christ that he would give us the gift of true conversion, and bring it about that, admonished by the example of Jonah, we diligently discharge our duty, never think of renunciation, and serve God's purpose all our life. Amen. In the year of the Lord 1581, in the month of July. May the name of the Lord be blessed for ever.

units.la: PSALMVS CIII, REDA-ctus in Carmen Heroicum.
units.tr: PSALM 103, rendered into heroic verse.

units.la: Mens mea, prompta Deum meritis, age, lau-dibus effer, (m imo[?] Sanctum eius celebret nomè, quæ pectore Sunt fibræ, & toto collectæ è corpore vires.
units.tr: My mind, ready to exalt God for his merits, come, extol him with praises; let all that is in my breast, the fibres and the strength gathered from my whole body, celebrate his holy name.

units.la: Mens mea, tolle Deum meritis, age, laudibus, atq; irrita ferre sinas huius benefacta cauęto, Et vacuum celeres dispergere in aera ventos,
units.tr: My mind, lift God up with merits, come, with praises; do not let his benefits be carried off in vain. Take care, and let the swift winds scatter empty things into the air.

units.la: Ille tibi scelera & delicta admissa remittit: Ille salutarem membris bonus admonet ægris Sponte manum, ignotaq; fouet mortalibus artę; Ille tuam seruat medio in discrimine vitam:
units.tr: He forgives you your wicked deeds and sins. He, being good, gladly stretches out his hand to the sick limbs and warms them with an art unknown to mortals. He preserves your life in the midst of danger.

units.la: Ille necem, quoties tibi adest infesta, suisq; Te iamiam telis est confixura, repellit: Ille tuis semper precibus respondet amicę, Teque beat donis variis, rebusque secundis:
units.tr: Whenever death is hostile to you and is about to pierce you with its weapons, he drives it back. He always answers your prayers as a friend, and blesses you with varied gifts and prosperous circumstances.

units.la: Ille tuo angores, & tristes pectore curas Eijcit, ac largum potumq; cibumq; ministrat;
units.tr: He drives out your anguish and the sad cares of your heart, and supplies you with ample food and drink.

units.la: Ille niues capitis cani, rugasq; seniles E fronte ingrata demit, lumenq; iuuenta Purpureum,& lætos oculis adspirat honores, Consuetum ut retinet uolucrum Regina uigorem. Subsidio oppressis Dominus uenit: efficit idem, Omnia subsidant meliori ut peruia causæ: Ille uoluntatem Mosi concredidit: ille Testibus Isacidis pollentis robore dextræ Maxima in Aegypto, atq; in rubræ fluctibus undæ, Et desolatis fecit miracula terris.
units.tr: He takes the white snows of your head and the wrinkles of old age from your ungrateful brow, and breathes back the purple light of youth and joyful honours into your eyes, so that, as the queen of birds, the eagle keeps its accustomed vigour. The Lord comes to the aid of the oppressed; he makes all things sink down, so that they yield to a better cause. He entrusted his will to Moses, and to the sons of Israel as witnesses of the mighty strength of his right hand, very great in Egypt and in the waves of the Red Sea, and he worked wonders in desolate lands.

units.la: Est DOMINVS clemens, hominum ærumnisq; mouetur; Est bonus, est patiens, & iustam tardus ad iram, Est piger ad poenas, & non examinat æqua, Quæ quasi certatim cumulamus crimina, lancem, Tanta eius bonitas, tanta est clementia, quanto Inter se spatio tellus & sidera distant.
units.tr: The Lord is merciful, and he is moved by the troubles of men. He is good, he is patient, and slow to anger that is just. He is slow to punish and does not weigh the scales of justice, though we heap up our crimes as if in rivalry. So great is his goodness, so great is his mercy, as much as the earth and the stars are distant from each other.

units.la: Quam procul Aurora succendit lumina Vesper, Tam procul a nobis facit ut peccata facessant.
units.tr: As far as the dawn is from the evening, when it kindles its light, so far does he cause our sins to vanish from us.

units.la: Vt tenerae prolis miserentur sæpe parentes, Si meruit forsan puerili verbera culpa, Condonantq; (uident quia corda infirma) reatum; Sic Deus his parcit, qui ipsum metuuntq; colunt. Nam nouit quales nos simus, debile quamq; Simus opus: nouit ferri nos pulueris instar.
units.tr: As parents often have pity on a tender child, if perhaps a childish fault has deserved a beating, and pardon the guilt, seeing that their hearts are weak, so God spares those who fear and worship him. For he knows what we are and how frail a work we are; he knows that we are like dust blown away.

units.la: Gramini homo est similis campi, floriq; caduco, Qui modò picta suo mirè ornat prata colore, Simile ignotus eapris[?], nec lasus aratro, Quem mulcet Zephyri, firmat Sol, excitat imber, Mox Austri tactus flatu, Boreæ ve nivalis, Arescit moriens, & prono pondere corpus Deflectens, post se vestigia nulla relinquit.
units.tr: Man is like grass and the fading flower of a field, which for a time adorns the painted meadows wonderfully with its colour; unknown to the plough, it is like a wild flower of the field. The Zephyr soothes it, the sun strengthens it, the rain makes it grow; but soon, struck by the blast of the south wind or the snowy north wind, it withers and dies, bending its body under its own weight, and leaves no trace behind it.

units.la: At Domini bonitas omnes perdurat in annos, Quæ sibi devotos complectitur. Eius in ævum Iustitia, & quotquot sunt sæcla futura, manebit Erga hos, qui priscum formidant rumpere fœdus, Et seruare studeant sancitas fulmine leges.
units.tr: But the goodness of the Lord endures for all years, and it embraces those who are devoted to him. His justice remains for ever, and for all the ages to come, towards those who fear to break the ancient covenant and strive to keep the laws sanctioned by thunder.

units.la: Sedes est Domini cælum, regumq; vocatur Rex merito, ut totum nutu qui temperet orbem.
units.tr: Heaven is the seat of the Lord, and he is rightly called King, who by a nod governs the whole world.

units.la: Aligeri, Dominum vestrum celebrate, ministri, Magnanimi heroes: Domini explorare quid optet, Est labor: at vobis mandata capessere fas est.
units.tr: Winged ministers, celebrate your Lord, you magnanimous heroes. To search out what the Lord wishes is labour; but it is right for you to take up his commands.

units.la: Vos etiam ætherea Dominum laudate cohortes, Vosq; omnes Domini servi, famuliq; fideles, Vosq; creaturæ Dominum celebrate potentem, Vosq; opera, in vasto struxit quæ plurima mundo, Mens mea, prōpta[?] Deū meritis, age, laudibus effer.
units.tr: You also, heavenly hosts, praise the Lord; you, all his servants and faithful attendants; you creatures, celebrate the mighty Lord; you works that he has built in the vast world in great numbers. My mind, ready to exalt God for his merits, come, extol him with praises.

units.la: V. à PL. Mechelburgensis.
units.tr: Verses by P. L. of Mecklenburg.

units.la: PSALMUS CXX.
units.tr: PSALM 120.

units.la: Quum me solliciti angerent dolores, Et rebus Dominum vocavi in arctis, Is meos gemitus, meas querelas,
units.tr: When painful sorrows troubled me, and in my distress I called upon the Lord, he heard my groans and complaints with a kindly and gentle ear.

units.la: Audiuit facili benignus aure. Me, quæso, asserito bilingui ab ore, Rerum summe Opifex: & à ueneno Linguæ, nil nisi uana, uirulenta Et confista meum in caput crepantis. Quid fructus tibi fraudulenta lingua, Aut quid adferet, o maligne, lucri? Quanquam hæc (confiteor) perinde lædit, Ac dtro [?] illita toxico sagitta, Quam Parthus resonante uibrat arcu, Flammarumq; refert edacium ignes Pingui in iunipero, aridáue sago. Eheu me miserum, inter efferorum Cogor degere quòd greges latronum, Quos cædes iuuat atq; parta præda. Eheu quàm graue, quàm mihi molestum est, In lustris Mezokiticis, apudq; Vagantes habitare Kedarenos. Vitæ me piget huius atq; tædet. Nam pacem tolerem libens: at illi, Cum de pace loquor, ruunt feroces In ferrum, & furor arma quæ ministrat.
units.tr: Deliver me, I beg you, O supreme Maker of all things, from a double-tongued mouth and from the poison of a tongue, which is nothing but empty, venomous words, fixed back upon the head of the one who chatters. What profit will a deceitful tongue bring you, or what gain, O wicked one? Yet these words (I admit) wound just as an arrow smeared with deadly poison, which the Parthian shoots from his twanging bow, and they bring back the fires of devouring flames in fat juniper and dry broom. Alas, wretched me, I am forced to dwell among the savage bands of robbers, whom slaughter delights and plunder won. Alas, how grievous and how troublesome it is for me to live among the Mesochite haunts, and among the Kedarenes who wander about. I am weary and sick of this life. For I would gladly bear peace; but they, when I speak of peace, rush fiercely to the sword, and fury supplies their arms.

units.la: V. à PL. Mech.
units.tr: V. à PL. Mech. (the version of P.L. of Mecklenburg)

units.la: PSALMUS LXXIII.
units.tr: PSALM LXXIII.

units.la: Quàm bonus Israeli Deus, &c.
units.tr: How good God is to Israel, etc.

units.la: Quicquid malorum concitet improbi[?] Turba insolentum, certa manet tamenProlis beatæ & innocentisSpes Deus, & solidum leuamen.
units.tr: Whatever evils the wicked crowd of the insolent may stir up, God remains the sure hope of a blessed and innocent offspring, and a solid support.

units.la: Meos at error pene fefelleratGressus, dolebam, quod male pertinaxSors cuncta misceret benignè,Quæ cuperent stolidè superbi.
units.tr: But error had almost led my steps astray. I grieved that fortune, stubborn and ill-disposed, mingled all things kindly, things which the proud fools desired foolishly.

units.la: Nam nulla fati dira necessitasHos tangit unquam: sed velut arduaFundata firmis arx columnis,Mole sua mala quæq; frangunt.
units.tr: For no dire necessity of fate ever touches these men. Like a citadel built high on firm columns, they break every evil by their own mass.

units.la: Et certa quæ nos perpetuò manetSors, qui gementes incolimus breuemVitam, ut malis exerceamur,Hos onerat quoq; sæua nunquam.
units.tr: And that sure lot which abides with us always, we who groan as we dwell in this brief life, so that we may be exercised by evils, never burdens these men with savage harm.

units.la: Hinc efferunt tantos quoq; spiritus,Quæcunq; mente inflatius asseruntVt summa iactent, cæterorumPræq; suis pia facta temnant.
units.tr: Hence they lift up their spirits so high, and with a mind more inflated than is right, they claim that they can utter the highest things, and they despise the pious deeds of others and of their own people.

units.la: Et impotenti sunt quoq; turgidiFastu, intumescunt præ nimio malo,Et perpetrant quodcunq; tandemMens agitat malesuada crimen.
units.tr: They are swollen with impotent pride and puffed up with excessive wickedness, and they perpetrate whatever crime their evil-counselling mind drives them to.

units.la: Carpunt superbè quælibet, intonantEx alto, & omnes despiciunt bonos:Sed quicquid illi dictitarint,Lege volunt stabili teneri.
units.tr: They carp proudly at whatever they please, thundering from on high, and they despise all good men. But whatever they have pronounced, they want it held fast as a settled law.

units.la: Sic ergo vulgus decipiunt rude, Plebemq; technis illaqueant suis, Vt qualis auctus fertur amnis, Affluat his[?] numerosa turba.
units.tr: Thus they deceive the uneducated crowd and ensnare the common people with their tricks, so that, like a river said to swell, a numerous throng flows toward them.

units.la: Dicunt: Inanes spes fouet indigus, Suæ salutis qui locat anchoram In Numen æternum, superbè Despicit & Deus hæc caduca.
units.tr: They say: the needy man nourishes empty hopes, he who fixes the anchor of his salvation in the eternal Godhead; and God proudly disregards these fleeting things.

units.la: Sic insolescunt perpetuò impij, Dumq; hæc loquuntur, largiter affluunt Rebus, beati, nec quietum Exigit his magis alter æuum.
units.tr: Thus the wicked grow insolent without end, and while they talk like this they abound richly in goods, happy, and another age does not demand a quieter life from them.

units.la: Sed, Rector orbis, num tua sedulò Mandata frustra iugiter exequor? Est nulla vel merces reposta Integritati animoq; puro?
units.tr: But, Ruler of the world, do I diligently and continually follow your commands in vain? Is there no reward laid up for integrity and a pure mind?

units.la: Indigna quæ non me miserum quatit Sors? plaga quando vel residet[?] mea? Nam manè lucem cum refundit Sol, mea pars oritur laboris.
units.tr: What unworthy fate does not shake me, wretched as I am? When does my affliction ever subside? For when the sun pours forth its light in the morning, my share of toil rises with it.

units.la: Erat malorum dicta ferocia Voto ut probarem penè meo: leuis Sed reprobassem quos amata Pignora tu tibi seuocasti.
units.tr: The fierce words of the wicked were spoken so that I almost approved them with my own wish. Yet I would have rejected, as inconstant, those beloved children whom you have set apart for yourself.

units.la: Tandem retrusum hoc consilium stupens, Id mente fixa inquirere perstiti: Frustra sed æternis minorem
units.tr: At last, astonished by this hidden counsel, I persisted in seeking its meaning with a fixed mind; but in vain, for my mind, too small for eternal things,

units.la: Consilijs animum occupauit.
units.tr: was occupied with the counsels.

units.la: Donec sacratum consulerem, Deus,Limen, benignus quo bona diuidis:Tibiq; me uellem doceri,Vltima respicerem & malorum.
units.tr: Until, O God, I should consult your sacred threshold, where you graciously distribute good things, and wished to be taught by you, and would consider the final end of the wicked.

units.la: Tunc euidenter protinus haec mihi,Abstrusa primò, res patuit: graduHos lubrico nam collocasti,Quos penitus tua dextra fundit.
units.tr: Then at once these things, hidden at first, were made plain to me. For you have placed these men on slippery ground; your right hand casts them down into the depths.

units.la: Cladi propinquum percipiunt bonum,Et plane eorum fit breue gaudium:Merguntur undis, nec regressusExitij trepidi patebit.
units.tr: They perceive good near their ruin, and their joy is plainly brief. They sink beneath the waves, and no way of return from trembling destruction will lie open to them.

units.la: Vt uana fuco ludificant leuiMentem inquietam somnia, soluiturSic omnis in fumum malorumPompa, refert nec imago statum.
units.tr: As vain dreams deceive a restless mind with false images, so all the pomp of evils dissolves into smoke, and the appearance does not restore its former state.

units.la: Sed interim ardor macerat anxiumLiuore pectus perpetuo mihi,Quòd censeor stultus, uelutq;Fermè carens ratione brutum.
units.tr: But meanwhile burning envy wears down my anxious breast, because I am judged a fool and am almost like a brute beast lacking reason.

units.la: Vtcunq; diris haec animum modisVexent, refractum non tamen auferent
units.tr: However these things may vex my soul with dreadful ways, they will not, however, take from me my broken spirit

units.la: Abs te, Deus, me quando dextraVsq; regas bonus atq; firmes.
units.tr: from you, O God, while your good right hand guides me on and keeps me firm.

units.la: Immensa ualde uis sapientiae,Et certa ducis qua fragilem uia: Vicunq;[?] tristibus fatigar, Fine bono mala fata claudis.
units.tr: Immense is the power of wisdom, and sure is the way by which you lead the frail. However much I am worn down by sad things, you bring evil fates to a good end.

units.la: Non templa Olympi,non ego possidet Quæcunq; mundus,pro solido tuo Mutem fauore.hæc cuncta sperno, Tu modo si mihi promptus adsis.
units.tr: Not the temples of Olympus, nor anything the world possesses, would I exchange for your favour, which is solid. I despise all these things, if only you are ready to be present to me.

units.la: In peius ergo cuncta ruant licet: Tabescat æstu cor trepidum mihi: In morte dira tu salutis Spes remanes mea,forsq; dulcis.
units.tr: Let all things therefore fall into worse ruin; let my trembling heart waste away in the heat. In dire death, you remain my hope of salvation, and a sweet one.

units.la: Nam iussa spernunt qui tua, duriter Punis:rebelles,ac alijs diis Qui fornicantur,sæuus ira, Perpetuis tenebris recondis.
units.tr: For those who scorn your commands you punish harshly: the rebels, and those who play the harlot after other gods, you, cruel in wrath, hide in perpetual darkness.

units.la: Sincera uitæ me iuuat unica Ergo hæc uoluptas,ut celebrem,Deus, Te iugiter,tum magna mundo Facta canam tua semper ore.
units.tr: A sincere life is my one delight, and this alone pleases me: therefore, O God, I shall continually praise you, and always sing your great deeds with my mouth.

units.la: AD. B. POM.
units.tr: To B. Pom.

units.la: E Y X H.
units.tr: Prayer [Εὐχή]

units.la: Nate Dei:cum Patre,sacro & Spiramine Numen Unum:qui motu cuncta quietus agis: Qui residens intra te,ambis uertigine cuncta, Illustrans uultu quæq; creata tuo:. Conspicuus,pariterq; inuisus:temporis author Absq; æuo:Modicus,fine modoq; carens:
units.tr: Son of God, one Godhead with the Father and the holy Spirit, you who by your motion drive all things in quiet; you who, dwelling within yourself, encompass all things in a whirling motion, illuminating all created things with your face; visible and yet unseen, author of time, without age, moderate, lacking end and measure:

units.la: Omnia complectens, nulli tamen ipse prehensus: Omnibus infusus, labis at omnis inops: Abripe me sursum, miro cum flamine mirus Allabens lutea pectora sece lava: Inque tuam rape naturam, correptaque flammis Attenua, & formans attenuata jove. Vnum sim tecum, maneam tibi semper adhærens, Numen idem veluti cum genitore manes. Plasma tuum instaura natiuo crimine fissum, Assere & amissum vindice iure tibi: Vt mea damna meo fatear tribuamque furori, Atque accepta tibi commoda cuncta feram: Qui mira bonitate malum convertere nostrum In tua lætaris, Christe benigne, bona. Pectoris ab hyemem, si non pietate calescat Tam mira, & vero flagret amore tui. Attonitum ab mentis somnum tristemque veternum, Ni vigilet tantis illa agitata bonis. Hoc opus haud nostræ: me Patris o alma voluptas Christe mihi occidas, sic tibi vivus agam: Meque mihi excidas, vti quo palmes adorner Florescamque tibi, marcidus ipse mihi. Incipiam nihil esse mihi: sic omnia abunde Adveniant gremio suppeditata tuo.
units.tr: embracing all things, yet grasped by none; poured into all, yet free of all stain. Snatch me upward, marvellously, with a wondrous flame, sweep my clay-stained breast clean and wash it; carry me into your own nature, and, seized by flames, make me thin, and when thinned, form me anew with joy. Let me be one with you, and remain always clinging to you, the same divine being as the Begetter. Restore your creature, split by its native guilt; reclaim for yourself by avenging right what was lost. So that I may confess my losses, ascribe them to my own madness, and bear all received blessings back to you: you who, with wondrous goodness, turn our evil into your good, and rejoice in your good things, gentle Christ. Unless the heart's winter warms with such wonderful piety, and burns with true love for you, let the mind not be roused from its astonished, dreary sleep, unless it wakes, stirred by such great goods. This work is not of our own doing: O kindly delight of the Father, Christ, may you slay me to myself, so that I may live for you; and may you cut me off from myself, so that I may be adorned as a branch for you, and flourish for you, though withered to myself. I shall begin to be nothing to myself; so may all things come to me in abundance, supplied in your bosom.

units.la: A. T. H.
units.tr: To A. T. H.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

Seize my nature into yours, and, seized by flames, make me thin, and cherish me as one made thin. May I be one with you, and remain ever clinging to you; as the same divinity, may I abide with the Father. Restore your creature, split by native sin, and claim for yourself by avenging right what was lost: that I may confess my losses and ascribe them to my own madness, and bear all the benefits received from you. You who with wondrous goodness turn our evil into good, and rejoice, gracious Christ, in your own good gifts. Unless the breast's winter is warmed by such wondrous piety and burns with true love of you... Unless that mind, stirred by such great goods, keeps watch, it is stunned by sleep and sad lethargy. This work is not ours: O nourishing delight of the Father, Christ, let me die to myself so that I may live for you. Cut me off from myself, that I may be adorned as a vine-branch and flourish for you, withering to myself. I shall begin to be nothing to myself; so all things will come abundantly, supplied from your bosom.
